note: Original short lives written for this app from published sources (see each entry); no source text copied. Keyed by the saint's identifier in data/kalendar/synaxarium/decisions.json.

UO-SIN-000790.name: Basil the Great and Gregory of Nazianzus
UO-SIN-000790.life: Basil and Gregory were friends from their student days in Athens, and both were born in Cappadocia in what is now Turkey. Basil became bishop of Caesarea in 370, where he defended the Nicene faith, wrote on the Holy Spirit, drew up rules for community monastic life, and built a great hospital for the poor. Gregory, a gifted preacher and poet, was drawn from quiet retirement to lead the small orthodox flock in Constantinople, where his five theological orations on the Trinity earned him the title "the Theologian." He later returned home to his family estate and wrote there until his death.
UO-SIN-000790.place: Caesarea and Nazianzus in Cappadocia; Constantinople

UO-SIN-000793.name: William Passavant
UO-SIN-000793.life: William Alfred Passavant was a Lutheran pastor born in 1821 in Zelienople, Pennsylvania. Ordained in 1842, he served congregations in Baltimore and Pittsburgh. In 1849 he brought German deaconesses from Kaiserswerth to nurse in the Pittsburgh Infirmary, which began the Lutheran deaconess movement in America. Over the following decades he raised money for hospitals, orphanages, homes for the sick and disabled, and schools, among them Thiel College, serving many German and Scandinavian immigrants. He also helped to found Lutheran synods and a seminary in Chicago. His works of mercy grew into a large network of Lutheran social ministry. He died in Pittsburgh in 1894.

UO-SIN-000620.name: Elizabeth Ann Seton
UO-SIN-000620.life: Elizabeth Bayley was born in New York in 1774 into an Episcopalian family and married William Seton, with whom she had five children. After his death from tuberculosis in Italy in 1803, she was drawn to the Catholic faith and was received into the Catholic Church in 1805, losing the support of many friends and relatives. Seeking a way to support her children, she founded a school and in 1809 gathered a small community of sisters at Emmitsburg, Maryland, later the Sisters of Charity of St Joseph. They gave free schooling to poor girls and pioneered Catholic parish education. She died there in 1821.

UO-SIN-000621.name: Sarah, Theodora, and Syncletica of Egypt
UO-SIN-000621.life: These three women are among the Desert Mothers, the "ammas" whom seekers visited in the Egyptian wilderness for a word of guidance. Sarah lived as a hermit for about sixty years beside the Nile and was admired for her fierce discipline and her sharp, humble replies. Syncletica, from a wealthy family, gave away her inheritance and lived in a tomb outside Alexandria, where women gathered to learn from her; she taught moderation and steady thanksgiving. Theodora, according to tradition, left a troubled marriage, lived disguised as a monk in the Thebaid, and bore false accusation in silence. Their sayings still guide those who pray.
UO-SIN-000621.place: Egypt: the Nile, Scetis, Alexandria, the Thebaid

UO-SIN-000623.name: Lucian of Antioch
UO-SIN-000623.life: Lucian was born around 240 at Samosata in Syria and became a priest at Antioch, where he led a school of Christian learning. He is remembered for careful work on the Greek text of the Bible, favouring the plain, literal meaning of scripture. Some of his pupils later sided with Arius, so his own teaching was long debated, though church authorities came to accept his statements of faith. During the persecution under Emperor Maximinus he was arrested and held at Nicomedia, where he suffered torture and died in January 312, refusing to deny Christ. Tradition remembers him as a martyr who stayed steadfast to the end.

UO-SIN-000624.name: Harriet Bedell
UO-SIN-000624.life: Harriet Bedell was born in Buffalo, New York, in 1875 and trained as a teacher before becoming a missionary. From 1907 she taught and gave simple medical care among the Cheyenne at Whirlwind Mission in Oklahoma, then served in Alaska, where she was set apart as a deaconess in 1922. In 1932 she began work among the Miccosukee and Seminole people in the Florida Everglades, where she helped families earn a living by selling their traditional crafts. They called her "Woman Who Prays." She worked in the Everglades until Hurricane Donna and her age ended her mission in 1960, and she died in 1969.
UO-SIN-000624.place: Oklahoma, Alaska and the Florida Everglades

UO-SIN-000625.name: Julia Chester Emery
UO-SIN-000625.life: Julia Emery was born in 1852 at Dorchester, Massachusetts, one of eleven children of a devout sea captain. In 1876 she succeeded her sister Mary as national secretary of the Women's Auxiliary to the Episcopal Church's mission board, a post she held for forty years. She travelled to dioceses across the United States and visited mission stations in Europe and Asia, encouraging women to pray and give for the Church's work. She helped to start the United Offering, now the United Thank Offering, in which women set aside a small gift in thanksgiving. It still supports mission work. She died in New York in 1922.

UO-SIN-000626.name: William Laud
UO-SIN-000626.life: William Laud was born in Reading in 1573 and became a fellow, then president, of St John's College, Oxford. He rose to be bishop of St Davids, Bath and Wells, and London, and in 1633 Archbishop of Canterbury under Charles I. He worked for order and reverence in worship, the repair of churches, and strict use of the Book of Common Prayer, which brought him into conflict with Puritans. His attempt to impose English worship on Scotland helped spark the Bishops' Wars. Parliament imprisoned him in the Tower in 1640, and after a long trial passed a bill of attainder. He was beheaded on Tower Hill on 10 January 1645.

UO-SIN-000627.name: Theodosius the Cenobiarch
UO-SIN-000627.life: Theodosius was born about 423 in Cappadocia and, as a young man, went to the Holy Land. He lived for many years in a cave near Bethlehem in prayer and severe self-denial. As disciples gathered, he founded a large monastery in the Judean wilderness, which cared for the poor, the elderly, and the sick, and welcomed monks of several languages. When his friend Sabbas was set over the hermits of Palestine, Theodosius was given charge of the monks living in community, hence his title "Cenobiarch." Together they defended the Council of Chalcedon against Emperor Anastasius, who briefly removed him. He died in 529, aged about one hundred and five.

UO-SIN-000628.name: Aelred of Rievaulx
UO-SIN-000628.life: Aelred was born around 1110 at Hexham in Northumbria and was raised at the court of King David of Scotland, where he became royal steward. About 1134 he left court to enter the Cistercian abbey of Rievaulx in Yorkshire. He served as abbot of Revesby and, from 1147, of Rievaulx, which grew greatly under his care. Though often ill, he travelled to visit other houses and counselled bishops and kings. His writings, especially The Mirror of Charity and On Spiritual Friendship, praise friendship as a path to God. He died at Rievaulx on 12 January 1167 and has been called the "Bernard of the North."
UO-SIN-000628.place: Hexham, Scotland, and Rievaulx Abbey, Yorkshire

UO-SIN-000629.name: Hilary of Poitiers
UO-SIN-000629.life: Hilary was born in Gaul to a pagan family, studied widely, and came to Christian faith through reading scripture. He was baptised with his wife and daughter and about 353 was chosen bishop of Poitiers. When he refused to condemn Athanasius and join the Arian cause, Emperor Constantius exiled him to Phrygia in 356. In exile he wrote On the Trinity, the first great Latin work on the subject, and explained the Eastern debates to western bishops. Returning about 361, he pressed Gaul to hold to the Nicene faith and encouraged Martin of Tours. He died in 367 and is honoured as the "Athanasius of the West."

UO-SIN-000810.name: Macrina the Elder
UO-SIN-000810.life: Macrina the Elder lived in Neocaesarea in Pontus, in what is now Turkey, in the late third and early fourth centuries. She learned the faith from the followers of Gregory Thaumaturgus, the great bishop of her region. When Galerius and Diocletian persecuted Christians, she and her husband fled to the forests and hills of Pontus, where they endured hunger and hardship for years, and later lost their property. She became the grandmother of Basil the Great, Gregory of Nyssa, Peter of Sebaste, and Macrina the Younger, and taught Basil his first lessons in the faith. She is remembered for handing on the teaching she had received.

UO-SIN-000631.name: Ita of Killeedy
UO-SIN-000631.life: According to tradition, Ita was born in County Waterford around the late fifth century, of a noble family, and chose a life of prayer. She settled at Killeedy near Newcastle West in County Limerick, where she founded a community of women and a school. She became known as the "foster mother of the saints of Ireland" because she cared for and taught many children, among them, as tradition holds, the young Brendan the Voyager, who sought her counsel throughout his life. Stories praise her wisdom, simplicity, and generosity. She is said to have died about 570, and Killeedy still bears her name.

UO-SIN-000630.name: Richard Meux Benson and Charles Gore
UO-SIN-000630.life: Richard Benson, born in London in 1824, was vicar of Cowley near Oxford. In 1866, with two companions, he founded the Society of St John the Evangelist, the "Cowley Fathers," the first religious community for men in the Anglican Church since the Reformation; it later spread to America, India, and South Africa. He died in 1915. Charles Gore, born in 1853, edited the essays of Lux Mundi, which sought to join Catholic faith with modern learning. He founded the Community of the Resurrection in 1892 and became bishop of Worcester, Birmingham, and Oxford, caring deeply about social justice. He died in 1932.

UO-SIN-000633.name: Antony of Egypt
UO-SIN-000633.life: Antony was born about 251 in Egypt to a Christian family. Around the age of twenty he withdrew to the desert, first near his village, then in an abandoned fort, and later at a mountain near the Red Sea. He lived on bread, salt, and water, and fought against temptation by prayer and fasting. Disciples gathered around him, and many came for advice, so that he became known as the father of monks. Athanasius's account of his life spread the monastic ideal throughout the Church. He died, according to tradition, in 356, aged one hundred and five.
UO-SIN-000633.place: Egyptian desert, near the Red Sea

UO-SIN-000792.name: Macarius the Great
UO-SIN-000792.life: Macarius was born in the Egyptian Delta about the year 300. He worked as a cattle-herder before turning to the ascetic life, and he was a follower of Antony the Great. He settled in the desert of Scetis, was ordained priest, and drew many monks to live near him, so that the monasteries of Wadi Natrun grew from his community. During the reign of Valens he was briefly exiled to an island in the Nile because of the controversy over the Nicene faith. Fifty Spiritual Homilies, long attributed to him, speak of the Spirit's work in the heart. He died about 390, and his monastery is still inhabited.

UO-SIN-000636.name: Fabian
UO-SIN-000636.life: Fabian was a layman from Rome who, according to the historian Eusebius, was chosen bishop of Rome in 236 after a dove settled on his head as the clergy and people gathered to elect a leader. During his fourteen years in office he made peace with the imperial authorities, divided the city into districts under deacons, appointed notaries to record the acts of the martyrs, and sent missionary bishops to Gaul. When Emperor Decius began a persecution in 250, Fabian was among the first victims and died, probably in prison, on 20 January. He was buried in the Catacomb of Callixtus.

UO-SIN-000637.name: Agnes and Cecilia of Rome
UO-SIN-000637.life: Agnes and Cecilia are two of the most beloved virgin martyrs of Rome. According to tradition, Agnes was a girl of twelve or thirteen who refused marriage because she belonged to Christ, and was put to death in the persecution of Diocletian about 304; she was buried on the Via Nomentana. Cecilia, a noblewoman of the third century, is said to have converted her husband Valerian and his brother, given her wealth to the poor, and been beheaded after surviving attempts to kill her. Because she is said to have sung to God at her wedding, she is honoured as patron of musicians. Details of both lives are legendary.
UO-SIN-000637.period: Agnes died about 304; Cecilia died in the 3rd century

UO-SIN-000638.name: Vincent of Saragossa
UO-SIN-000638.life: Vincent was a deacon of the church at Saragossa in Spain, who preached on behalf of his bishop, Valerius, who had difficulty speaking. In the persecution under Diocletian, around 304, both were arrested and taken in chains to Valencia before the governor Dacian. Valerius was exiled, but Vincent was put to the torture, on the rack and the burning gridiron, yet would not yield. According to tradition he died in prison, remaining at peace. The poet Prudentius celebrated his courage, and his shrine drew pilgrims across Spain and Portugal. Many details are legendary.

UO-SIN-000639.name: Phillips Brooks
UO-SIN-000639.life: Phillips Brooks was born in Boston in 1835 and educated at Harvard before being ordained in the Episcopal Church in 1859. He served as rector in Philadelphia and then, from 1869, at Trinity Church, Boston, where he became one of the most admired preachers in America, known for his height and warm, direct manner. He taught that preaching was "truth through personality." He wrote the Christmas hymn "O Little Town of Bethlehem." Elected bishop of Massachusetts in 1891, he served only about fifteen months and died in Boston in January 1893.

UO-SIN-000640.name: Florence Li Tim-Oi
UO-SIN-000640.life: Florence Li was born in Hong Kong in 1907 and was baptised as a schoolgirl, taking the name Florence. She became a deaconess and, during the Second World War, ministered to refugees in Macau, where no priest could reach the people. In 1944 Bishop Ronald Hall ordained her priest, the first woman ordained in the Anglican Communion. The decision caused controversy, and after the war she resigned her licence to protect the Church's unity, though she remained a priest. She endured hardship and forced labour in China during the Cultural Revolution. She later served the Chinese community in Toronto, where she died in 1992.

UO-SIN-000642.name: Timothy and Titus
UO-SIN-000642.life: Timothy and Titus were younger companions and trusted helpers of the apostle Paul. Timothy, from Lystra, had a Jewish mother, Eunice, and grandmother, Lois, who taught him the scriptures; Paul called him his "beloved child." He travelled with Paul, was sent on delicate missions, and, by tradition, led the church at Ephesus. Titus, a Gentile convert, was Paul's troubleshooter, who carried letters to Corinth and helped to heal the church there. Tradition holds that Paul left him to organise the church on Crete. Letters addressed to each of them guide pastors still.

UO-SIN-000348.name: John Chrysostom
UO-SIN-000348.life: John was born at Antioch about 347, and was raised by his widowed mother. After training in rhetoric and a time among hermits, he became a priest and, for years, preached at Antioch, earning the name Chrysostom, "golden mouth." In 397 he was made archbishop of Constantinople. He reformed the clergy, founded hospitals, and spoke fearlessly for the poor, which angered the wealthy. Conflict with the empress Eudoxia and Bishop Theophilus of Alexandria led to his exile. He was sent to the Black Sea region and died in 407 on the journey, at Comana in Pontus. His sermons and commentaries remain widely read.

UO-SIN-000643.name: Thomas Aquinas
UO-SIN-000643.life: Thomas was born about 1225 at Roccasecca in Italy and was educated at Monte Cassino and Naples. Against his family's wishes he joined the Dominican friars, and studied in Paris under Albert the Great. He became a master of theology and taught in Paris and Italy. His great works, the Summa contra Gentiles and the unfinished Summa Theologiae, joined Christian faith with the philosophy of Aristotle. He died on 7 March 1274 at Fossanova Abbey on his way to the Council of Lyon, and was canonised in 1323.

UO-SIN-000644.name: Liliʻuokalani of Hawaiʻi
UO-SIN-000644.life: Liliʻuokalani was born in Honolulu in 1838 and educated in a mission school. She married John Owen Dominis and in 1891 succeeded her brother Kalākaua as queen, the first woman to rule Hawaiʻi alone. In 1893 a group of American and European businessmen, backed by US Marines, overthrew her after she tried to give the kingdom a new constitution. She yielded peacefully to avoid bloodshed and appealed for justice. Imprisoned in 1895 after a failed uprising, she later wrote Hawaii's Story by Hawaii's Queen and composed songs, including "Aloha ʻOe." A devout Christian, she died in Honolulu in 1917.

UO-SIN-000645.name: Charles I
UO-SIN-000645.life: Charles I became king of England, Scotland, and Ireland in 1625. He held a strong belief in the divine right of kings, and quarrelled with Parliament over taxation and royal power; his support for ceremonial worship in the Church of England alarmed many Protestants. These disputes led to civil war from 1642, and after defeat he was handed over to Parliament. He was tried for treason in January 1649 and denied the court's authority. He was beheaded at Whitehall on 30 January 1649. Many Anglicans honour him for his steadfast loyalty to the Church and the dignity of his death.

UO-SIN-000646.name: Marcella of Rome
UO-SIN-000646.life: Marcella was born into a noble Roman family around 325. Widowed early in her marriage, she turned her palace on the Aventine Hill into a house of prayer, charity, and study of scripture, gathering women around her. She lived this life for decades before Jerome arrived in Rome, and he wrote to her more than to any other woman, praising her knowledge of the Bible and asking for her judgment. When the Goths sacked Rome in 410, soldiers beat her, seeking treasure; she pleaded for her young companion Principia and died soon after.

UO-SIN-000647.name: Brigid of Kildare
UO-SIN-000647.life: Brigid is one of Ireland's three national patron saints, though her story is wrapped in legend. According to tradition she was born around 450 near Faughart in County Louth, the daughter of a chieftain and an enslaved mother. She refused marriage, took the veil, and founded a monastery at Kildare, the first nunnery in Ireland, which grew into a double house of monks and nuns with a famous school. Stories tell of her generosity to the poor and of a cloak that stretched to cover the Curragh plain. She died around 525, and pilgrims still weave rush crosses in her memory.

UO-SIN-000649.name: Anskar
UO-SIN-000649.life: Born around 801 near Amiens and schooled by the Benedictines at Corbie, Anskar became known as the Apostle of the North. From about 826 he carried the gospel to Denmark and to Sweden, where he built a small congregation at Birka. Around 831 he was appointed bishop of Hamburg, with a mandate for missions across northern Europe, and later also governed Bremen. Viking raids destroyed Hamburg and much of his work, yet he persevered, living simply, fasting, and caring for the poor. He died at Bremen on 3 February 865. His disciple Rimbert wrote his life, and he is honoured as patron of Scandinavia.

UO-SIN-000650.name: Manche Masemola
UO-SIN-000650.life: Manche Masemola was a young Pedi woman born around 1913 at Marishane in Sekhukhuneland, South Africa. When an Anglican mission opened there in 1919, she began attending its classes in preparation for baptism, though her parents strongly opposed it. She was beaten for her persistence and, it is said, told others she would die at her parents' hands. About 4 February 1928, when she was around fifteen, she was taken to a lonely hillside and killed. Her story spread across the Anglican Communion, and her statue stands above the west door of Westminster Abbey among the twentieth-century martyrs.

UO-SIN-000651.name: Agatha of Sicily
UO-SIN-000651.life: Agatha was a young Christian woman of Catania in Sicily, martyred around 251 during the persecution under Emperor Decius. Her surviving story is mostly legend. It says she came from a wealthy family and rejected the advances of the Roman governor Quintianus, who in revenge had her imprisoned and cruelly tortured. According to tradition she was comforted by a vision of Saint Peter in prison, and an earthquake interrupted her sentence of burning before she died in her cell. She was honoured early across the Church. Catania has long invoked her in times of fire and the eruptions of Mount Etna.

UO-SIN-000652.name: The Martyrs of Japan / Paul Miki and Companions
UO-SIN-000652.life: On 5 February 1597 twenty-six Christians were crucified on a hill outside Nagasaki, victims of the suspicion of the ruler Toyotomi Hideyoshi toward foreign missionaries. They included Franciscan friars, three Japanese Jesuits, and lay catechists and converts, some of them boys. Forced to march some six hundred miles from Kyoto in winter, they reportedly sang the Te Deum along the way. Paul Miki, a Japanese Jesuit preacher, preached from his cross and forgave his executioners. With Joan Soan and Santiago Kisai he is the best known of the group. Their courage became the seed of a hidden Christian community that survived generations of persecution.

UO-SIN-000848.name: Richard of Wessex
UO-SIN-000848.life: Richard was an Anglo-Saxon nobleman of Wessex, remembered as the father of three saints: Willibald, bishop of Eichstatt, Winnibald, abbot of Heidenheim, and Walburga, abbess of Heidenheim. Around 720 he gave up his lands and set out on pilgrimage with his two sons, sailing from the south coast of England and travelling through Francia toward Rome and the Holy Land. He fell ill with a fever at Lucca in Italy and died there, and he was buried in the church of San Frediano. Miracles were reported at his tomb. Later legend styled him a king of the English, but nothing reliable supports that.

UO-SIN-000653.name: Bakhita (Josephine Margaret Bakhita)
UO-SIN-000653.life: Born around 1869 in Darfur, in present-day Sudan, Bakhita was kidnapped by slave traders as a small child and spent years being sold from owner to owner, enduring cruel beatings. The name Bakhita, meaning fortunate, was given to her by her captors, and she forgot her birth name. In 1883 an Italian consul bought her and later took her to Italy. There the Canossian Sisters of Venice taught her the faith, and an Italian court declared her free. Baptised in 1890, she became a Canossian sister and spent decades at Schio as cook, sacristan and doorkeeper, loved for her gentleness. She died on 8 February 1947.
UO-SIN-000653.place: Darfur, Sudan; Venice and Schio, Italy

UO-SIN-000654.name: Apollonia of Alexandria
UO-SIN-000654.life: Apollonia was an elderly Christian woman of Alexandria, Egypt, honoured as a deaconess or devout virgin. Our chief account comes from Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria, who describes a mob uprising against Christians around 249, shortly before the official persecution under Decius. The crowd seized her and struck her face until her teeth were broken. They then built a fire outside the city gate and threatened to burn her unless she spoke blasphemous words. She asked for a moment, and then of her own will stepped into the flames. Because of her sufferings she has long been invoked against toothache and is the patron of dentists.

UO-SIN-000655.name: Scholastica
UO-SIN-000655.life: Scholastica was the sister of Benedict of Nursia, and later tradition made her his twin. According to Pope Gregory the Great, she was dedicated to God from childhood and lived as a consecrated woman near Monte Cassino, where Benedict founded his monastery. They met once a year for prayer and conversation. On their last visit Benedict refused to stay past nightfall, but Scholastica prayed and a violent storm kept him there, so they talked through the night about the things of God. She died three days later, around 543, and Benedict is said to have seen her soul rise as a dove. They share a tomb.

UO-SIN-000855.name: Fanny J. Crosby
UO-SIN-000855.life: Frances Jane Crosby was born in 1820 in southeastern New York and lost her sight as a baby, after an illness at six weeks old. She studied and later taught at the New York Institution for the Blind. Beginning around 1864 she wrote thousands of hymns, among them Blessed Assurance, Pass Me Not, O Gentle Saviour, and Rescue the Perishing, often under pen names. She also gave much of her life to the poor, working at rescue missions in New York's tenements. She died in Bridgeport, Connecticut, in 1915, aged ninety-four.

UO-SIN-000858.name: Charles Freer Andrews
UO-SIN-000858.life: Born in northern England in 1871 and educated at Cambridge, Charles Andrews was ordained in the Church of England and went to India in 1904 to teach at St Stephen's College, Delhi. Troubled by British racism, he made deep friendships with Indians and threw himself into their cause. He befriended Rabindranath Tagore at Santiniketan and became Mahatma Gandhi's closest friend, meeting him in South Africa in 1914 and helping bring about his return to India. He investigated the harsh conditions of indentured labourers in Fiji and elsewhere, and supported striking workers. Indians called him Deenabandhu, friend of the poor. He died in Calcutta on 5 April 1940.

UO-SIN-000658.name: Absalom Jones
UO-SIN-000658.life: Born into slavery in Delaware in 1746, Absalom Jones taught himself to read, was taken to Philadelphia, and eventually bought his freedom. With Richard Allen he founded the Free African Society in 1787 after Black worshippers were pulled from their knees in a white church. During the yellow fever epidemic of 1793 the two led Black volunteers in nursing the sick and burying the dead. Jones founded the African Church, later St Thomas African Episcopal Church, in Philadelphia, and was ordained the first Black priest in the Episcopal Church, in 1802. He also petitioned Congress against the slave trade. He served his congregation until his death on 13 February 1818.

UO-SIN-000659.name: Cyril and Methodius
UO-SIN-000659.life: The brothers Cyril and Methodius were born in Thessalonica, sons of a Byzantine official. In 863 Prince Rastislav of Moravia asked Constantinople for teachers, and they were sent. Cyril devised the Glagolitic alphabet so that the Slavs could have Scripture and worship in their own language, and the brothers translated the Bible and liturgical texts into what became Old Church Slavonic. Rivals among the German clergy opposed them, and in Rome Pope Adrian II approved their work. Cyril died there as a monk on 14 February 869. Methodius carried on as archbishop until he died in 885. Their disciples spread the Slavic Christian tradition across eastern Europe.

UO-SIN-000660.name: Thomas Bray
UO-SIN-000660.life: Thomas Bray was an English priest, born in Shropshire in 1656. Chosen in 1696 as the Bishop of London's commissary for Maryland, he recruited clergy for the colonies and travelled there briefly in 1699 and 1700. He believed that ministers needed books, and he set up parish libraries in America and in England. He helped found the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge in 1698 and the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in 1701. Late in life he formed a group, known as Dr Bray's Associates, to support the education of enslaved and Black people in the colonies. He died in London on 15 February 1730.

UO-SIN-000661.name: Charles Todd Quintard
UO-SIN-000661.life: Born in Connecticut in 1824, Charles Quintard trained as a physician and practised in Georgia and Tennessee before turning to the ministry, being ordained in 1855 and 1856. In the Civil War he served the First Tennessee Regiment as chaplain and surgeon, tending the wounded and handing out devotional books. In 1865 he became Bishop of Tennessee, and he worked to rebuild churches broken by the war and to minister to freed African Americans. As first vice-chancellor of the University of the South at Sewanee, he helped revive the school after it was destroyed, raising funds in America and England. He died in 1898.

UO-SIN-000662.name: Janani Luwum
UO-SIN-000662.life: Born around 1922 among the Acholi of northern Uganda, Janani Luwum was converted in the East African revival in 1948, and was ordained in the 1950s. He became Bishop of Northern Uganda in 1969 and in 1974 Archbishop of Uganda. As Idi Amin's regime turned to murder and disappearances, Luwum spoke out and in February 1977 joined the other bishops in a letter of protest. On 16 February he was arrested with two cabinet ministers and accused of treason. The government said all three died in a car accident, but his body bore bullet wounds. He is honoured as a martyr of the Anglican Communion.

UO-SIN-000663.name: Colman of Lindisfarne
UO-SIN-000663.life: Colman was an Irish monk trained at Iona who in 661 became bishop of Lindisfarne, the Northumbrian see founded by Aidan. At the Synod of Whitby in 664 he defended the Irish way of reckoning Easter, but the king ruled for the Roman method. Colman refused to give way, resigned his see, and left with the Irish monks and about thirty English brothers. After a time in Scotland he settled on Inishbofin off the Irish coast and then founded a house at Mayo for his English monks. Bede, who differed with him over Easter, still spoke of him with respect. He died in the 670s, around 674 to 676.

UO-SIN-000664.name: Agnes Tsao Kou Ying, Agatha Lin Zhao, and Lucy Yi Zhenmei
UO-SIN-000664.life: These three Chinese Catholic women taught the faith to others and died for it in the nineteenth century. Agnes Tsao Kou Ying, a widow from Guizhou, taught girls in Guangxi and died in a prison cage in 1856 after refusing to deny Christ. Agatha Lin Zhao, a catechist at Maokou in Guizhou, was beheaded in 1858 with two companions. Lucy Yi Zhenmei, from Sichuan, taught women in her parish, then moved to Guizhou and was beheaded in 1862 for refusing to renounce her faith. All three remained steadfast under pressure from officials. They were canonized in 2000 among the Martyrs of China.

UO-SIN-000665.name: Frederick Douglass
UO-SIN-000665.life: Born into slavery in Talbot County, Maryland, about 1818, Frederick Bailey taught himself to read despite the efforts to prevent him. In 1838 he escaped to New York, took the name Douglass, and settled in Massachusetts, where he became a licensed preacher and a commanding speaker for the abolitionist cause. His 1845 Narrative made him famous, and he edited the newspaper The North Star. During the Civil War he urged Abraham Lincoln to enlist Black soldiers and to end slavery. Later he served as a marshal of the District of Columbia and as minister to Haiti,. He died in Washington in 1895.

UO-SIN-000261.name: John Henry Newman
UO-SIN-000261.life: Born in London in 1801, John Henry Newman became a fellow of Oriel College, Oxford, and vicar of the University Church. He was the leading figure of the Oxford Movement, writing many of the Tracts for the Times and calling the Church of England to recover its Catholic heritage. His studies of Christian history led him in 1845 to be received into the Roman Catholic Church. He later founded the Oratory in Birmingham, directed a Catholic university in Dublin, and wrote the Apologia pro Vita Sua. Made a cardinal in 1879, he died in Birmingham on 11 August 1890.

UO-SIN-000666.name: Margaret of Cortona
UO-SIN-000666.life: Born in 1247 at Laviano in Tuscany, Margaret lost her mother young. At seventeen she left home with a young nobleman and lived with him for nine years as his partner and the mother of his son. When he was murdered, she was overcome with grief and repentance. Turned away by her family, she took refuge with the Franciscans of Cortona, and in about 1277 was admitted to the Third Order. She lived in strict poverty, nursing the sick, and persuaded the city to found a hospital. She also began a community of sisters, the Poverelle. She died on 22 February 1297 and was canonized in 1728.

UO-SIN-000667.name: Polycarp of Smyrna
UO-SIN-000667.life: Polycarp was bishop of Smyrna in Asia Minor and a bridge between the apostles and the later Church. Tradition names him a disciple of John; Ignatius of Antioch wrote to him. In old age Polycarp went to Rome to talk with Bishop Anicetus about differences over the date of Easter, and the two parted in peace. Back in Smyrna he was arrested and brought before the proconsul, who urged him to curse Christ. He answered that he had served Christ eighty-six years and been done no wrong. He was burned, or according to the account killed by the sword, around 155 or 156; some date it later.

UO-SIN-000668.name: Matthias the Apostle
UO-SIN-000668.life: Matthias is known from the first chapter of Acts. After Judas Iscariot's death, the disciples sought a replacement among those who had followed Jesus from his baptism until the ascension, and they put forward Joseph Barsabbas and Matthias. They prayed and cast lots, and the lot fell on Matthias, who was counted with the eleven apostles. The New Testament says no more about him. Later traditions are uncertain and conflicting, sending him to preach in Judaea, then to Cappadocia or around the Black Sea, and variously reporting that he was stoned, beheaded, crucified or died in old age.

UO-SIN-000669.name: Emily Malbone Morgan
UO-SIN-000669.life: Emily Malbone Morgan was born in Hartford, Connecticut, in 1862 into a well-established family and never married. In 1884, with her friend Adelyn Howard, who was an invalid, and Harriet Hastings, she founded the Society of the Companions of the Holy Cross, a fellowship of Episcopal women bound by intercessory prayer, thanksgiving, simplicity of life and concern for justice. She also opened summer holiday houses for working women and their children, funding them by writing. Under her leadership the Companions built Adelynrood, a retreat house at Byfield, Massachusetts. She guided the society for over fifty years and died in 1937.

UO-SIN-000670.name: Photini, the Samaritan Woman
UO-SIN-000670.life: Photini is the name given by the Church to the woman who met Jesus at Jacob's well near Sychar, in the Gospel of John. He asked her for a drink, spoke of living water, and told her what she had done. She hurried back to her town to say, Come and see, and many Samaritans believed through her word. Later Orthodox tradition says she was baptized as Photini, meaning the enlightened one, and preached in Carthage and Rome. According to that tradition she was tortured under Emperor Nero around 66 and thrown into a well. These details come from late legend, not from Scripture.

UO-SIN-000671.name: George Herbert
UO-SIN-000671.life: Born in Wales in 1593 into a distinguished family, George Herbert studied at Trinity College, Cambridge, and became its Public Orator and briefly a member of Parliament, with hopes of advancement at court. After the death of his patrons he turned to the Church, was ordained, and in 1630 became rector of Bemerton near Salisbury. There he restored the church, held daily prayers, visited and fed the poor, and wrote A Priest to the Temple on pastoral care. Dying of consumption in 1633, he sent his poems to his friend Nicholas Ferrar, and they were published as The Temple, one of the great collections of English devotional verse.

UO-SIN-000672.name: Anna Julia Haywood Cooper
UO-SIN-000672.life: Born enslaved in Raleigh, North Carolina, in 1858, Anna Julia Cooper entered St Augustine's school as a girl, later graduated from Oberlin College, and taught mathematics, science and Latin in Washington, D.C. Her 1892 book A Voice from the South argued that the progress of Black women was central to the progress of her people. She served as principal of the M Street High School, which prepared its pupils for top universities, and later led Frelinghuysen University for working adults. At sixty-six she earned a doctorate from the Sorbonne in Paris. She remained active until she died in Washington in 1964, aged 105.
UO-SIN-000672.place: Raleigh, North Carolina; Washington D.C., USA

UO-SIN-000887.name: Oswald of Worcester
UO-SIN-000887.life: Born around 925 of Danish descent, Oswald was raised by his uncle, Archbishop Odo of Canterbury, and studied at the reformed abbey of Fleury in France. Returning to England, he became Bishop of Worcester in 961 and, in 972, Archbishop of York, keeping Worcester as well. With Dunstan and Aethelwold he was a leader of the great tenth-century renewal of English monasticism. He founded Ramsey Abbey, helped reform houses at Winchcombe, Pershore and Evesham, and replaced the clergy of Worcester cathedral with monks. He died at Worcester on 29 February 992, according to tradition while washing the feet of the poor.

UO-SIN-000673.name: David of Wales
UO-SIN-000673.life: David was a sixth-century monk and bishop who became the patron saint of Wales. He is associated with Mynyw, now St Davids, in Pembrokeshire, where he is said to have founded a monastery of severe simplicity, its monks working the land by hand and living on bread, herbs and water. Tradition holds that at the Synod of Brefi his preaching was so persuasive that a dove settled on his shoulder and the ground rose beneath him. His reported last words urged his followers to keep to the little things. Much of his story comes from a late eleventh-century Life, so details are uncertain.

UO-SIN-000674.name: Chad of Lichfield
UO-SIN-000674.life: Chad was a Northumbrian monk, trained at Lindisfarne under Aidan and later in Ireland, who followed his brother Cedd as abbot of Lastingham. In 664 he was made bishop of the Northumbrians at York, holding that post until 669, and was known for his humility. In 669 he became bishop of the Mercians and Lindsey, settling at Lichfield, where he built a church and monastery. He travelled the countryside on foot to preach, and is remembered as the apostle of Mercia. He died of plague on 2 March 672, and miracles were reported at his tomb.

UO-SIN-000675.name: John and Charles Wesley
UO-SIN-000675.life: John and Charles Wesley were brothers, born at Epworth in Lincolnshire, the sons of an Anglican rector, and both ordained priests of the Church of England. At Oxford they gathered the disciplined little group nicknamed the Holy Club, and after spiritual awakenings in 1738 they became leaders of the Methodist revival. John travelled and preached tirelessly, organised societies and trained lay preachers. Charles, an eloquent preacher, wrote thousands of hymns, among them Love Divine, All Loves Excelling and Hark! The Herald Angels Sing. Charles died in London in 1788 and John in 1791, both still Anglican clergymen.
UO-SIN-000675.place: Epworth, Oxford, Bristol and London, England

UO-SIN-000676.name: Adrian of May Island and Companions
UO-SIN-000676.life: According to tradition, Adrian was a bishop or abbot who laboured on the Isle of May in the Firth of Forth, building hermitages and a monastery there. About 875, Viking raiders are said to have landed and slaughtered the whole community, traditionally numbered in the thousands, making them martyrs. The island later became a great pilgrimage place, visited by Scottish kings and queens and by people seeking healing and blessing. Scholars think the story may be a memory of the seventh-century saint Ethernan, killed among the Picts in 669, whose cult was later joined to Adrian's. The details remain uncertain.
UO-SIN-000676.place: Isle of May, Firth of Forth, Scotland

UO-SIN-000896.name: Non of Wales
UO-SIN-000896.life: Non, also called Nonna or Nonnita, is remembered as the mother of Saint David. Little is known with certainty, and her story comes largely from the late eleventh-century Life of David. According to that tradition she was a nun near Whitesands Bay in Pembrokeshire, and David was born after she was assaulted by a local chieftain, though she lived chastely and austerely thereafter. Legend says a storm raged at his birth, the place was filled with light, and she gripped a stone so hard it split. A chapel and holy well near St Davids bear her name, and she is also honoured in Brittany.

UO-SIN-000678.name: Baldred
UO-SIN-000678.life: Baldred was a Northumbrian monk and hermit, probably trained at Lindisfarne, who became known as the apostle of the Lothians in south-east Scotland. He is said to have founded a monastery at Tyninghame in East Lothian and to have withdrawn for prayer to a hermitage on the Bass Rock, a great crag in the sea, where tradition says he died. According to a later legend, when three parishes quarrelled over his burial, three identical bodies were found after a night of prayer, so that each could have one. His well at Whitekirk drew large crowds of pilgrims in the later Middle Ages.
UO-SIN-000678.period: died c. 757 (some sources give the early 7th century)
UO-SIN-000678.place: Tyninghame and Bass Rock, East Lothian, Scotland

UO-SIN-000679.name: Perpetua and Felicity
UO-SIN-000679.life: Perpetua, a well-born young mother of about twenty-two, and Felicity, an enslaved woman expecting a child, were Christian catechumens arrested at Carthage in North Africa about 203, with Revocatus, Saturninus, Secundulus and their teacher Saturus. While in prison Perpetua kept a diary of her trial, her visions and her anguish at parting from her infant son, which is the earliest surviving writing by a Christian woman. Refusing to renounce their faith, they were condemned to the arena, attacked by wild animals, and finally killed by the sword. Their courage was long remembered by the African Church.

UO-SIN-000680.name: Edward King
UO-SIN-000680.life: Edward King was born in Kent in 1829 and ordained in 1854. He was a pastor first, then principal of Cuddesdon theological college and professor of pastoral theology at Oxford, shaping hundreds of future clergy and helping to found St Stephen's House. In 1885 he became Bishop of Lincoln. He was loved for his gentleness, simple preaching and care for people of every rank, rich and poor, and he travelled widely about his diocese. He was prosecuted in 1888 over ritual practices, and the archbishop's judgment largely upheld him. He died in 1910, and was long described as a most saintly bishop.

UO-SIN-000681.name: Gregory of Nyssa
UO-SIN-000681.life: Gregory was born in Cappadocia about 335, the younger brother of Basil the Great, who made him bishop of Nyssa around 372. Deposed in 376 during an Arian campaign, he returned in 378 and became one of the leading defenders of the Nicene faith, working alongside Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus. His writings, including the Life of Moses, the Great Catechism and works against Eunomius, describe the soul's endless journey toward the infinite God. He also spoke boldly against the buying and selling of human beings, since all are made in God's image. He died about 394.

UO-SIN-000682.name: Harriet Ross Tubman
UO-SIN-000682.life: Born into slavery in Maryland about 1822 and named Araminta Ross, Harriet Tubman was badly beaten as a child and suffered a head injury that left her with lasting seizures and vivid dreams, which she took to be messages from God. In 1849 she escaped to Philadelphia, then returned about thirteen times to lead some seventy people to freedom, earning the name Moses. During the Civil War she served the Union as nurse, scout and spy, and guided the Combahee River raid. She later settled in Auburn, New York, cared for the elderly and poor, supported women's suffrage, and died in 1913.
UO-SIN-000682.place: Maryland, Philadelphia and Auburn, New York

UO-SIN-000683.name: Sophronius of Jerusalem
UO-SIN-000683.life: Born in Damascus about 560, Sophronius was a scholar and monk who travelled to the monasteries of Palestine, Egypt and Rome, and became a close friend of John Moschus. He was a fierce defender of the teaching that Christ has both a divine and a human will, against the Monothelite compromise favoured in Constantinople. Chosen patriarch of Jerusalem in 634, he led his people through a long siege by the Arab armies, and agreed to surrender the city to Caliph Umar on terms protecting Christians and their holy places. He also wrote sermons, hymns and saints' lives, and died around 638.

UO-SIN-000318.name: Gregory the Great
UO-SIN-000318.life: Gregory was born into a wealthy Roman family about 540 and became prefect of Rome before turning his family home into a monastery. As pope from 590 until his death in 604, he faced plague, famine and Lombard invasion, organising relief for the poor and negotiating for the city's safety. He wrote the Pastoral Rule, the Moralia on Job and many letters, and called himself servant of the servants of God. Moved, according to tradition, by the sight of English slaves in Rome, he sent Augustine and his companions to bring the gospel to the English.

UO-SIN-000502.name: James Theodore Holly
UO-SIN-000502.life: James Theodore Holly was born free in Washington, D.C., in 1829, the son of formerly enslaved parents, and trained as a shoemaker. Raised Roman Catholic, he joined the Episcopal Church in 1851 after Catholics refused to ordain Black priests. Ordained deacon in 1855 and priest in 1856, he served in New Haven and urged Black Americans to settle in Haiti. In 1861 he led about 110 emigrants there; his mother, wife, two children and many settlers died of disease. He stayed on, built churches and schools, and in 1874 was consecrated the Episcopal Church's first Black bishop. He died in Port-au-Prince in 1911.

UO-SIN-000684.name: Matilda of Ringelheim
UO-SIN-000684.life: Matilda was born about 895 into a Saxon noble family and educated at a convent, though she did not become a nun. In 909 she married Henry the Fowler, who later became king of Germany, and she bore him several children, among them Otto the Great, Henry of Bavaria and Bruno, archbishop of Cologne. Known as humble, pious and generous, she gave freely to the poor and the church. After Henry's death in 936 she founded Quedlinburg and supported other convents at Nordhausen and Enger. Her sons once accused her of wasting resources before they were reconciled to her. She died in 968.

UO-SIN-000685.name: Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac
UO-SIN-000685.life: Vincent de Paul, born in Gascony in 1581, was ordained young, spent two years enslaved in Tunis after pirates captured him, and later gave his life to serving the poor of France. He founded the Congregation of the Mission to preach to country people and train priests. Louise de Marillac, born in 1591 and widowed in 1625, became his partner in charity. Together in 1633 they began the Daughters of Charity, the first women's community of active service, not enclosed, who nursed the sick and taught in homes and hospitals. Louise died in March 1660 and Vincent in September of that year, both in Paris.

UO-SIN-000686.name: Boniface of Ross
UO-SIN-000686.life: Boniface, more often known by his Gaelic name Curetan, was a Pictish bishop who served at Rosemarkie on the Black Isle in northern Scotland around the turn of the eighth century. He is thought to have taken the name Boniface as a sign of loyalty to Rome. At the time, the Pictish king Nechtan ordered his churches to follow Roman custom in matters such as the date of Easter, and Boniface is remembered as helping bring this about. Churches and wells in Ross and beyond carry his name, including a healing well near Munlochy. Dates are uncertain, and the later legends about him are late and unreliable.

UO-SIN-000687.name: Patrick of Ireland
UO-SIN-000687.life: Patrick was a Romano-British Christian who, at sixteen, was seized by Irish raiders and kept as a shepherd slave for six years. He escaped, returned home, and later felt called in a vision to bring the gospel back to Ireland. He travelled the island baptising, confirming and ordaining, often in danger, and once imprisoned. Two of his own writings survive, the Confession and a letter condemning the raider Coroticus, and they show a humble, devout man. Later stories of the shamrock and of banishing snakes are legend. His dates are uncertain, with death placed in the later fifth century or earlier.

UO-SIN-000688.name: Cyril of Jerusalem
UO-SIN-000688.life: Cyril, born about 313, became bishop of Jerusalem around 350. His long ministry was troubled: disputes with Acacius of Caesarea and with Arian emperors saw him exiled three times before he returned for good in 378. He accepted the Nicene faith and took part in the Council of Constantinople in 381. He is best remembered for his Catecheses, lectures given to candidates for baptism explaining the creed, baptism and the Eucharist in clear and loving language. He helped make Jerusalem a place of pilgrimage, and died in 386.

UO-SIN-000689.name: Saint Joseph
UO-SIN-000689.life: Joseph was the husband of Mary and the earthly guardian of Jesus. The Gospels of Matthew and Luke tell us that he was of David's line and lived at Nazareth, and was called a carpenter. When he learned Mary was with child he meant to part from her quietly, but obeyed an angel's message in a dream and took her as his wife. He led the family to Bethlehem, fled with them to Egypt to escape Herod, and brought them home to Nazareth. He last appears when Jesus is twelve, in the Temple. He never speaks in the Gospels. Later writings that fill in his life are legend.

UO-SIN-000690.name: Cuthbert of Lindisfarne
UO-SIN-000690.life: Cuthbert was born in Northumbria about 634 and, as a young shepherd, felt called to the monastic life. He entered Melrose, later became prior there and then at Lindisfarne, where he supported the Roman customs adopted after the Synod of Whitby. He longed for solitude, and in 676 withdrew to a hermit's cell on Inner Farne. Reluctantly made bishop of Lindisfarne in 684, he served for two years before returning to his island, where he died in 687. He is remembered as a protector of birds and wild creatures. His body, found uncorrupted, is enshrined at Durham.
UO-SIN-000690.place: Melrose, Lindisfarne and Farne Islands, Northumbria

UO-SIN-000691.name: Thomas Ken
UO-SIN-000691.life: Thomas Ken was born in 1637 and became a fellow of New College, Oxford, then chaplain to Charles II. He famously refused to give up his Winchester house for the king's mistress, Nell Gwyn. As Bishop of Bath and Wells from 1685, he in 1688 he was one of the Seven Bishops who refused to publish James II's Declaration of Indulgence; all were tried and acquitted. After the revolution he could not in conscience swear allegiance to William and Mary and lost his see in 1691. His hymns, ending in the doxology Praise God from whom all blessings flow, are still sung. He died in 1711.

UO-SIN-000692.name: James De Koven
UO-SIN-000692.life: James De Koven was born in Middletown, Connecticut, in 1831 and educated at Columbia College and the General Theological Seminary. After ordination he taught at Nashotah House in Wisconsin and in 1859 became warden of Racine College, where he spent the rest of his life. A gifted preacher and a beloved teacher, he defended Anglo-Catholic ritual and teaching at General Conventions in 1871 and 1874. He was elected bishop of Wisconsin by the clergy and then of Illinois, but suspicion of his eucharistic teaching meant his election was never confirmed. He declined posts in great city parishes. He died at Racine in 1879.

UO-SIN-000393.name: Gregory the Illuminator
UO-SIN-000393.life: According to tradition, Gregory was born into a noble Parthian family and raised as a Christian in Cappadocia. Returning to Armenia, he refused to take part in pagan sacrifice, and King Tiridates III had him tortured and thrown into a deep pit, where he is said to have lived for about thirteen years. He was freed to heal the king, who then accepted baptism, and Armenia became the first nation to adopt Christianity, traditionally in 301. Gregory became the first head of the Armenian church, raised up churches, and saw his sons become bishops. He is said to have ended his life in a mountain cave around 330.

UO-SIN-000693.name: Óscar Romero and the Martyrs of El Salvador
UO-SIN-000693.life: Óscar Romero, born in 1917 and ordained in 1942, was made archbishop of San Salvador in 1977, expected to be a cautious churchman. Weeks later his friend, the Jesuit Rutilio Grande, was murdered for defending the poor, and Romero changed. In weekly sermons broadcast across the country he named the killings, tortures and disappearances of a brutal civil conflict and pleaded for justice and peace. On 24 March 1980 he was shot dead while celebrating Mass in a hospital chapel. With him are remembered the many Salvadoran priests, religious and lay people who were killed for standing with the poor.

UO-SIN-000695.name: Harriet Monsell
UO-SIN-000695.life: Harriet O'Brien was born in 1811 at Dromoland in County Clare, the daughter of an Irish baronet. In 1839 she married the Rev. Charles Monsell, who died in 1851, and she then turned her life to service. She joined Thomas Carter at Clewer near Windsor, where a small mission cared for women trying to leave the streets, and in 1852 helped found the Community of St John Baptist. She became its first Mother Superior, forming the sisters in prayer and work. The community grew to run orphanages, schools and hospitals, with houses in England, India and America. She retired to Folkestone and died on Easter Day, 1883.

UO-SIN-000696.name: Charles Henry Brent
UO-SIN-000696.life: Charles Henry Brent was born in Ontario in 1862 and became an Episcopal priest, serving in Boston among the poor. In 1901 he was made the first missionary bishop of the Philippines, where he founded schools and hospitals and reached out to Igorots, Muslims and Chinese rather than only to Americans. He pressed for international action against the opium trade, helping bring about the Shanghai commission of 1909 and later the first international drug treaty. After the Edinburgh missionary conference of 1910 he championed Christian unity and presided at the first World Conference on Faith and Order at Lausanne in 1927. He died there in 1929.

UO-SIN-000697.name: James Solomon Russell
UO-SIN-000697.life: James Solomon Russell was born into slavery in Virginia in 1857. After the Civil War he studied at Hampton Institute and the Bishop Payne Divinity School, and was ordained deacon in 1882 and priest in 1887. Sent to Lawrenceville, Virginia, he began a small school in 1888 that grew into Saint Paul's Normal and Industrial School, later Saint Paul's College, training Black teachers. He served as its principal until 1929. As archdeacon from 1893 he helped raise the number of Black Episcopal congregations in southern Virginia from none to thirty-seven. He twice declined election as bishop to stay with his school, and died in 1935.

UO-SIN-000698.name: John Keble
UO-SIN-000698.life: John Keble was born at Fairford in Gloucestershire in 1792 and later became Oxford's Professor of Poetry. His devotional poems, The Christian Year (1827), were hugely popular. In 1833 his Assize Sermon on national apostasy, protesting government interference in the Church, is generally seen as the start of the Oxford Movement, and he wrote several of the Tracts for the Times. After 1835 he lived quietly as vicar of Hursley in Hampshire, caring for his parishioners. He remained loyal to the Church of England when Newman left it. He died at Bournemouth in 1866, and Keble College was founded in his memory.

UO-SIN-000937.name: John Climacus
UO-SIN-000937.life: John was born about 579, probably in Syria, and entered the monastery at Mount Sinai as a young man. He lived as a hermit for about twenty years, then in old age became abbot of the Sinai community. He wrote the Ladder of Divine Ascent, a guide in thirty chapters, one for each step of Jacob's ladder, describing the struggle against sin and the climb toward love and peace in God. It became one of the best-loved books of the Eastern church, and is still read in monasteries during Lent. He died about 649, and his name Climacus means of the ladder.

UO-SIN-000700.name: John Donne
UO-SIN-000700.life: John Donne was born in London in 1571 or 1572 into a Catholic family at a time when their faith was illegal. He studied at Oxford and later law, and his secret marriage to Anne More in 1601 ruined his career and brought years of poverty. Known for brilliant love poems and later searching religious verse, he was urged by King James to take holy orders, and was ordained in 1615. As Dean of St Paul's from 1621 he became the most famous preacher of his day. He wrote his Holy Sonnets and meditations on suffering and death, and died in 1631.

UO-SIN-000701.name: Frederick Denison Maurice
UO-SIN-000701.life: Born in Suffolk in 1805, Frederick Denison Maurice became one of the most original English theologians of the Victorian age. Ordained in 1834, he served as chaplain of Guy's Hospital and taught at King's College, London, until 1853, when he was dismissed after his Theological Essays questioned the popular teaching on eternal punishment. Undaunted, he helped launch the Christian Socialist movement in 1848, founded Queen's College for women, and in 1854 opened the Working Men's College. He taught that Christ's kingdom embraces all humanity and that the church should work for justice. He ended his career as a professor at Cambridge and died in 1872.

UO-SIN-000702.name: James Lloyd Breck
UO-SIN-000702.life: James Lloyd Breck, born in Pennsylvania in 1818, was an Episcopal priest who carried the church onto the American frontier. In 1842, with two companions from General Seminary, he founded Nashotah House in the Wisconsin wilderness, a community of prayer and study that still trains clergy. In 1850s Minnesota he started a mission among the Ojibway and a school at Faribault that grew into a seminary. Later he went west again and founded schools and a church in California. Often called the Apostle of the Wilderness, he lived simply, built patiently, and died at Benicia, California, in 1876.

UO-SIN-000703.name: Richard of Chichester
UO-SIN-000703.life: Born around 1197 at Droitwich, Richard studied at Oxford, Paris and Bologna and became chancellor of Oxford and then right-hand man to Archbishop Edmund of Abingdon. In 1244 he was chosen bishop of Chichester, but King Henry III, who favoured another man, seized the diocese's revenues and for two years left Richard without a home or income. Only after the pope intervened did Richard take up his see. He was a conscientious pastor, generous to the poor and tireless in visiting his parishes. He died at Dover in 1253 and was canonized in 1262. His prayer, to know, love and follow Christ more nearly, is still widely used.

UO-SIN-000704.name: Isidore of Seville
UO-SIN-000704.life: Isidore was born about 560 into a distinguished Spanish family and educated in Seville, where he succeeded his brother Leander as bishop around 600. Under Gothic rule he helped complete the Visigothic kingdom's move from Arianism to the Catholic faith and presided over the Fourth Council of Toledo in 633, which urged every cathedral city to found a school. His great work, the Etymologies, gathered the knowledge of the ancient world into twenty books and shaped medieval learning. Often called the last scholar of the ancient West, he died in Seville in 636. Later ages named him a Doctor of the Church.

UO-SIN-000705.name: Harriet Starr Cannon
UO-SIN-000705.life: Born in Charleston, South Carolina, in 1823 and raised in Connecticut, Harriet Starr Cannon was drawn to the religious life after losing her family. She joined an Episcopal sisterhood in New York but left it in 1863 after disagreements, and in 1865, with Bishop Horatio Potter's blessing, she and four companions founded the Community of St. Mary. As mother superior she guided the sisters in running schools, hospitals and orphanages. In 1878 four of her sisters died nursing victims of yellow fever in Memphis, and their sacrifice won the young community lasting respect. Mother Harriet died in 1896, having helped restore women's religious life to American Anglicanism.
UO-SIN-000705.place: New York, Peekskill and Memphis, USA

UO-SIN-000949.name: Celestine I
UO-SIN-000949.life: Celestine was a Roman who became bishop of Rome in 422 and led the church for ten years in a time of sharp doctrinal dispute. When Cyril of Alexandria appealed to him about the teaching of Nestorius, who resisted calling Mary the Mother of God, Celestine held a synod in Rome in 430 and backed Cyril, and he sent legates to the Council of Ephesus in 431. He also opposed Pelagian ideas about grace, supporting a mission by Germanus of Auxerre to Britain. In 431 he sent Palladius as bishop to Christians in Ireland. Celestine died in Rome in 432.

UO-SIN-000707.name: Tikhon of Moscow
UO-SIN-000707.life: Born Vasily Belavin in 1865, the son of a village priest in Russia, Tikhon became a monk in 1891 and a bishop six years later. From 1898 to 1907 he led the Russian Orthodox mission in North America, reorganizing the diocese, encouraging new parishes and building bridges to other churches; the Orthodox of America remember him as their enlightener. Back in Russia, he was chosen patriarch of Moscow in November 1917, as revolution broke out, restoring an office vacant for two centuries. He protested the Bolsheviks' violence against the church, was held under house arrest in 1922 and 1923, and died in 1925, widely trusted by his people.

UO-SIN-000952.name: William Augustus Muhlenberg and Anne Ayres
UO-SIN-000952.life: William Augustus Muhlenberg, born in Philadelphia in 1796, was an Episcopal priest who founded a boys' school at Flushing, New York, and later pastored the Church of the Holy Communion in Manhattan. He was a pioneer of church schools, parish charity and fuller worship. Anne Ayres, born in London in 1816, came to New York and in 1845 took vows before him, becoming the first Episcopal sister. Together they formed the Sisterhood of the Holy Communion. Muhlenberg founded St. Luke's Hospital in 1850, where Anne directed the nursing, and he started the Christian community of St. Johnland on Long Island. He died in 1877 and she in 1896.

UO-SIN-000709.name: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
UO-SIN-000709.life: Born in Breslau in 1906, Dietrich Bonhoeffer became a Lutheran pastor and a gifted theologian. When the Nazis took power he spoke out against their persecution of Jews and helped found the Confessing Church, and from 1935 he led an underground seminary at Finkenwalde. His book The Cost of Discipleship warned against cheap grace that asks nothing of the believer. He joined the resistance through German military intelligence and helped Jews escape to Switzerland. Arrested in April 1943, he spent two years in prison, where he wrote the letters later published as Letters and Papers from Prison. He was hanged at Flossenbürg on 9 April 1945.

UO-SIN-000710.name: William Law
UO-SIN-000710.life: William Law was born in 1686 at King's Cliffe in Northamptonshire and became a fellow of Emmanuel College, Cambridge, and a priest. When George I came to the throne in 1714, his conscience would not let him swear the new oath of allegiance, so he lost his fellowship and spent his life as a nonjuror. His Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life (1729) urged ordinary Christians to give every part of daily life to God, and it deeply moved people such as the Wesleys. Later he turned toward the mystical writings of Jacob Boehme. He spent his last years at King's Cliffe and died in 1761.

UO-SIN-000711.name: George Augustus Selwyn
UO-SIN-000711.life: Born in 1809, George Augustus Selwyn was consecrated the first Anglican bishop of New Zealand in 1841. Arriving in Auckland in 1842, he learned Maori, travelled the country on foot and by boat, and founded St. John's College. He shaped a church governed by clergy and laity together, and in 1859 the first General Synod met under his leadership as metropolitan. His concern for the islands of the Pacific led to the Melanesian Mission, and he consecrated John Coleridge Patteson its first bishop. His backing of the Waikato war strained relations with many Maori. In 1868 he returned to England as bishop of Lichfield, where he died in 1878.

UO-SIN-000712.name: Zeno of Verona
UO-SIN-000712.life: Zeno was a native of North Africa who became bishop of Verona in northern Italy around 362 and held the see for roughly a decade or more. He was known as a vigorous preacher who won converts from paganism, defended the church against Arian teaching, and baptized many. Some ninety sermons attributed to him survive, dealing with Scripture, baptism, the Virgin Mary and Christian living. Verona's great basilica of San Zeno honours him, and local tradition links him with fishing on the River Adige, so he is often shown with a fish. He died in the 370s.

UO-SIN-000713.name: Martin I
UO-SIN-000713.life: Born at Todi in Umbria, Martin was elected bishop of Rome in 649, without waiting for the emperor's approval. That October he called the Lateran Council, which rejected Monothelitism, the teaching that Christ had no human will, and condemned imperial decrees that tried to silence the debate. Emperor Constans II ordered his arrest. Martin was taken to Constantinople in 654, tried for treason, humiliated and imprisoned, and in 655 banished to Cherson on the Crimean coast. Weakened by hardship and hunger, he died there in September 655. He is remembered as the last pope honoured as a martyr, East and West alike.

UO-SIN-000714.name: Zenaida, Philonella, and Hermione
UO-SIN-000714.life: According to tradition, Zenaida and Philonella were sisters from a wealthy Jewish family of Tarsus who became Christians and trained in medicine. They settled in Thessaly, in Greece, where they treated the poor without payment and are counted among the first Christian physicians after Luke. Tradition says Zenaida specialized in children's illnesses, and Philonella worked to free medicine from superstition. Hermione, said to be a daughter of Philip the Evangelist, healed the sick at Ephesus and was martyred under the Emperor Hadrian, according to tradition. Little can be checked historically, but the three are honoured as caring women who healed freely in Christ's name.

UO-SIN-000715.name: Damien of Molokai and Marianne Cope of Hawaii
UO-SIN-000715.life: Father Damien, a Belgian priest born Joseph de Veuster in 1840, volunteered in 1873 to serve the leprosy settlement at Kalaupapa on Molokai. He nursed the sick, built homes and churches, and in 1884 contracted the disease himself. He died in 1889. Marianne Cope, born in Germany in 1838 and raised in New York, became a Franciscan sister and hospital founder in Syracuse. In 1883 she led sisters to Hawaii, ran hospitals for people with leprosy, and in 1888 went to Kalaupapa, where she cared for the dying Damien and then for the settlement's girls and women. She died in 1918.

UO-SIN-000716.name: Peter Williams Cassey and Anna Besant Cassey
UO-SIN-000716.life: Peter Williams Cassey was born in Philadelphia in 1831 into a prominent free Black family active in abolition. He went to California in the Gold Rush, worked as a barber in San Francisco, and with his wife Anna moved to San Jose. There they founded the Phoenixonian Institute, the first secondary school in California for African American students. Peter was ordained a deacon in the 1860s, among the first clergy of color ordained on the West Coast, and helped begin churches in San Francisco and San Jose. Anna, a teacher and community leader, died in 1875. Peter later served in North Carolina and Florida and died in 1917.
UO-SIN-000716.place: San Francisco and San Jose, California

UO-SIN-000208.name: Kateri Tekakwitha
UO-SIN-000208.life: Kateri Tekakwitha was born in 1656 in a Mohawk village in what is now New York. When she was about four, smallpox killed her parents and brother and left her scarred and with poor eyesight. She met Jesuit missionaries and was baptized at nineteen, taking the name Catherine. Her conversion brought hostility from her community, so in 1677 she travelled some two hundred miles to the mission village of Kahnawake near Montreal. There she lived in prayer and quiet service. She died there in 1680, aged about twenty-four. In 2012 she became the first Native American woman canonized in the Catholic Church.

UO-SIN-000717.name: Juana Ines de la Cruz
UO-SIN-000717.life: Born around 1648 near Mexico City, Juana Inés was a brilliant child who taught herself to read and hungered for learning. She entered the Hieronymite convent of Santa Paula in Mexico City in 1669, partly for the freedom it gave her to study. There she wrote poetry, plays and carols, and the philosophical poem First Dream, and built a library of thousands of volumes. In her Reply to Sister Philothea (1691) she defended women's right to education. Church authorities pressured her to give up her studies, and she sold her books. In 1695 she died of plague after nursing her sisters.

UO-SIN-000718.name: Alphege of Canterbury
UO-SIN-000718.life: Born around 954, Alphege (Ælfheah) became a monk at Deerhurst and then a hermit at Bath, where he was later made abbot. He became bishop of Winchester in 984 and archbishop of Canterbury in 1006. In 1011 Danish raiders sacked Canterbury and took him prisoner. Held for months, he forbade his poor people to be taxed to pay the ransom. On 19 April 1012 at Greenwich, drunken Danes pelted him with bones and one struck him down with an axe. His body was later moved to Canterbury.

UO-SIN-000719.name: Maelrubha of Applecross
UO-SIN-000719.life: Maelrubha was born in Ireland in 642 and trained at the great monastery of Bangor. At about thirty he sailed to Scotland with a band of monks and, after two years among the western Highlands, founded a monastery at Applecross in 673, in Pictish country. From there he and his monks brought the faith to the surrounding country, travelling as far as Skye, Lewis and the northern coast. He died in 722. Later tradition says he was killed by Vikings in Strathnaver, but this is uncertain. More than twenty churches in Scotland bear his name, a sign of how deeply he was loved.

UO-SIN-000720.name: Anselm of Canterbury
UO-SIN-000720.life: Born around 1033 at Aosta in the Alps, Anselm became a monk at Bec in Normandy, where he was prior and then abbot, known for his teaching and gentle rule. In 1093 King William Rufus pressed him to become archbishop of Canterbury. He soon quarrelled with the king, and later with Henry I, over the church's independence and the crown's right to appoint bishops, and was twice sent into exile. A compromise agreed in 1107 ended the struggle. Anselm's writings, including the Proslogion and Cur Deus Homo, explored how faith seeks understanding and earned him the name father of scholasticism. He died at Canterbury in 1109.

UO-SIN-000721.name: Hadewijch of Brabant
UO-SIN-000721.life: Hadewijch was a poet and mystic of the thirteenth century who lived in the Low Countries, probably in Brabant. Almost nothing is known of her life beyond what she reveals in her own writings. She was well educated, perhaps from a wealthy family, and seems to have belonged to the beguines, devout lay women who lived in communities without formal vows. Her letters suggest she led a household of women and met with opposition. Writing in Middle Dutch, she left poems, letters and visions, describing the soul's journey toward God as a passionate quest for love. Her work deeply influenced the later mystic Jan van Ruusbroec.

UO-SIN-000734.name: George of Lydda
UO-SIN-000734.life: George is remembered as a Christian soldier who was put to death at Lydda in Palestine, probably around 303, during the persecution under the Emperor Diocletian. Beyond that, very little is reliably known. Later legends describe his torture, his courage and his steadfast faith, and the tale of his killing a dragon to save a princess appeared centuries afterward, so it should be taken as story, not history. His cult spread widely in East and West by the fifth century, and Crusaders brought devotion to him to England. He is the patron saint of England, and a symbol of courage under persecution.

UO-SIN-000723.name: Mellitus of Canterbury
UO-SIN-000723.life: Mellitus, probably an abbot in Rome, was sent by Pope Gregory the Great in 601 to join Augustine's mission to the English. In 604 he became the first bishop of the East Saxons in London, where King Saberht built a church of St. Paul. After Saberht's death, his sons restored pagan worship and drove Mellitus out around 616, and he spent a time in Gaul. He returned to Kent and in 619 succeeded Laurence as archbishop of Canterbury, despite poor health. Bede reports that he once prayed and a fire threatening Canterbury was stopped. He died on 24 April 624 and was buried at Canterbury.

UO-SIN-000724.name: Mark the Evangelist
UO-SIN-000724.life: Mark, also called John Mark, appears in the New Testament as a young companion of Paul and Barnabas who set out with them on a missionary journey, left them at Perga, and later became useful to Paul again. Peter calls him his son, and early tradition says Mark wrote down Peter's preaching in the Gospel that bears his name. According to later tradition he carried the gospel to Alexandria in Egypt, founded the church there, and was martyred in about the year 68. Venice claims his relics and has taken him as its patron. Scholars debate the details, but Mark's short, vivid Gospel remains foundational for the church.

UO-SIN-000986.name: Albert Ernest Laurie
UO-SIN-000986.life: Born in Edinburgh in 1866, Albert Laurie studied divinity at the University of Edinburgh and in 1891 became curate of Old St Paul's, an Episcopal church in the city's poorest streets. He became its rector in 1897 and stayed for forty years. He helped create a Child Garden in the nearby courtyard for local children. In the First World War he served as an army chaplain in France and twice won the Military Cross for tending the wounded under fire. Afterward he built the Warriors' Chapel at Old St Paul's as a memorial to the fallen. A devoted Anglo-Catholic pastor, he died in Edinburgh in 1937.

UO-SIN-000726.name: Zita of Tuscany
UO-SIN-000726.life: Zita was born in the early thirteenth century to a poor family in a village near Lucca in Tuscany. At twelve she became a servant in the household of the Fatinelli, a wealthy family of Lucca, and she remained in their service for the rest of her life. She worked faithfully and quietly, treating her duties as service to God, and bore mistreatment from other servants with patience. In time she won the family's trust and was given charge of the household. She gave generously to the poor and visited the sick and prisoners. She died in 1272, or perhaps 1271, and is honoured as the patron of domestic workers.

UO-SIN-000727.name: Peter Chanel
UO-SIN-000727.life: Born in 1802 in eastern France, Peter Chanel was ordained a priest in 1827 and served as a parish priest before joining the Society of Mary, the Marists, in 1831. In 1837 he landed on the Pacific island of Futuna, the first missionary there. He learned the language and tended the sick. Although at first welcomed, he fell foul of King Niuliki, who feared for his own authority when his son asked for baptism. On 28 April 1841 Chanel was struck down with clubs and axes and died. After his death most of the islanders became Christians, and he is honoured as the first martyr of Oceania.

UO-SIN-000728.name: Catherine of Siena
UO-SIN-000728.life: Born in 1347 in Siena, Catherine felt called to God as a child and became a lay Dominican sister who lived at home. She tended the sick, including plague victims, and drew a circle of followers. Though she could not at first write, she dictated hundreds of letters to popes, rulers and ordinary people, urging peace and reform, and she helped persuade Pope Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome in 1376. Her book, the Dialogue, records her teaching. Worn out by severe fasting, she died in Rome in 1380, aged 33. She was named a Doctor of the Church in 1970.

UO-SIN-000729.name: Marie de l'Incarnation
UO-SIN-000729.life: Born Marie Guyart in 1599 at Tours, France, she married young and was widowed at nineteen, left with an infant son. She worked in business while giving herself to prayer, and in 1631 entered the Ursuline convent at Tours. Convinced she was called to Canada, she sailed in 1639 with the benefactor Madame de la Peltrie and founded the Ursuline monastery at Quebec, where she taught French and Indigenous girls. She learned several native languages and wrote catechisms and dictionaries, and rebuilt the convent after a fire in 1650. Her letters give a vivid picture of early New France. She died at Quebec in 1672 and was canonized in 2014.

UO-SIN-000730.name: Saint Philip and Saint James
UO-SIN-000730.life: Philip and James were two of the Twelve whom Jesus called in the first century. Philip came from Bethsaida in Galilee, answered the call to follow, and brought Nathanael to Jesus; in John's Gospel he is the one who speaks up at the feeding of the crowd. James, son of Alphaeus, appears only in the lists of the Twelve, and little else is certain about him; he should not be confused with James the Great or with James the Lord's brother. Later tradition says Philip preached in Asia Minor and died at Hierapolis, while James is said to have been put to death after preaching in Jerusalem.

UO-SIN-000731.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
UO-SIN-000731.life: Athanasius was born in Alexandria around 296 and, as a young deacon, accompanied Bishop Alexander to the Council of Nicaea in 325, where the Church affirmed that the Son is of one being with the Father. He became bishop of Alexandria in 328 and spent the next forty-five years defending that faith against the Arians. His stand cost him dearly: five times he was driven into exile by emperors, spending some seventeen years away from his flock. He wrote On the Incarnation and a life of the hermit Antony, which helped spread monastic ideals. He died in Alexandria in 373.

UO-SIN-000732.name: Elisabeth Cruciger
UO-SIN-000732.life: Elisabeth von Meseritz was born about 1500 into a noble family of Pomerania and, as a girl, entered a convent. Drawn to the teaching of the Reformation through the preacher Johannes Bugenhagen, she followed him to Wittenberg around 1522. There she married Caspar Cruciger, a student and colleague of Martin Luther, in 1524. That same year her hymn "Herr Christ, der einig Gotts Sohn", a song of praise to Christ, was printed in the Erfurt Enchiridion, making her the first woman hymn writer of the Protestant Reformation. She died in Wittenberg in 1535.

UO-SIN-000301.name: Monica
UO-SIN-000301.life: Monica was born around 332 in Thagaste in North Africa and was married to Patricius, a pagan of hot temper whose faithfulness she endured with patience. Of her children, it was Augustine who caused her most anguish, for he drifted into Manichaeism and a restless life. She wept and prayed for him for years and followed him to Rome and then Milan, where the preaching of Bishop Ambrose helped lead him to baptism in 387. Soon afterward, on the journey home to Africa, she fell ill at Ostia and died. Augustine's Confessions preserves her memory as a woman of steadfast prayer.

UO-SIN-001003.name: Jutta of Kulmsee
