He saw George Herbert's poems through the press as The Temple in 1633. Ferrar died at Little Gidding in 1637. T. S. Eliot later gave the place its place in modern poetry.

UO-SIN-000162.name: Juan Diego
UO-SIN-000162.life: Juan Diego, born in 1474 near what is now Mexico City, was an Indigenous man of Cuauhtitlán, baptized as an adult around fifty. According to tradition, in December 1531 the Virgin Mary appeared to him four times on Tepeyac hill and asked that a church be built there. When the bishop demanded a sign, Juan Diego carried roses in his cloak, and on its unfolding an image of Mary was found imprinted on the cloth. He spent his remaining years caring for the shrine and its pilgrims, and died in 1548. Some historians question the evidence for him, but he is loved as a bridge between peoples.
UO-SIN-000162.place: Cuauhtitlán and Tepeyac, near Mexico City

UO-SIN-000163.name: Thomas Merton
UO-SIN-000163.life: Born in France in 1915, Thomas Merton came to the Catholic faith while a student at Columbia University. In 1941 he entered the Trappist abbey of Gethsemani in Kentucky and was ordained priest in 1949. His autobiography The Seven Storey Mountain became a bestseller in 1948, and he went on to write on contemplation, then on race, nuclear weapons and peace, and he opened conversation with Buddhists and other faiths. He died in Thailand on 10 December 1968, during a monastic conference, by accidental electrocution or heart failure.

UO-SIN-000164.name: Frederick Howden Jr.
UO-SIN-000164.life: Frederick Bingham "Ted" Howden was born in 1902 in Cumberland, Maryland, the son of the Episcopal bishop of New Mexico and Southwest Texas. Ordained priest in 1929, he served small congregations across New Mexico and was chaplain of the state's 200th Coast Artillery, which was sent to the Philippines in 1941. After the fall of Bataan in April 1942 he endured the Death March and several prison camps. His fellow prisoners remembered him for holding services, giving comfort and handing his own scanty food to men he thought needed it more. He died of dysentery and starvation-related illness on 11 December 1942.
UO-SIN-000164.place: New Mexico; Bataan and prison camps, Philippines

UO-SIN-000165.name: Francis de Sales and Jane de Chantal
UO-SIN-000165.life: Francis de Sales, born in Savoy in 1567, became bishop of Geneva in 1602, though he lived at Annecy because Calvinists held Geneva. A gentle preacher and writer, he taught in his Introduction to the Devout Life that holiness belongs to ordinary people. Jane Frances de Chantal, born in Dijon in 1572, was widowed at twenty-eight and raised her children before turning to religious life under his guidance. Together in 1610 they founded the Order of the Visitation at Annecy, which welcomed women others turned away for age or poor health. Francis died at Lyon in 1622; Jane died at Moulins in 1641.

UO-SIN-000166.name: Lucy of Syracuse
UO-SIN-000166.life: Lucy was a young woman of Syracuse in Sicily who, according to tradition, vowed her life to Christ and wished to give her wealth to the poor. When her mother arranged a marriage, the rejected suitor denounced her as a Christian to the governor during the persecution under Diocletian. The old accounts say that she stood firm under every torment and was finally killed by the sword in about 304. Later stories add that her eyes were put out, which is why artists show her holding them on a dish and why she is invoked for sight. Her name suggests light, and she is honoured across Christendom.

UO-SIN-000167.name: John of the Cross
UO-SIN-000167.life: Born in 1542 at Fontiveros in Spain, John entered the Carmelites in 1563 and was ordained in 1567. Meeting Teresa of Ávila, he joined her reform and took the name John of the Cross, helping to found the Discalced, or barefoot, Carmelites. Opponents within his own order seized him in 1577 and held him for about eight months in a cell in Toledo, where he was beaten and where he composed some of his best poems. After escaping he continued to guide the reform. His Dark Night, Spiritual Canticle and Ascent of Mount Carmel describe the soul's journey to God. He died at Úbeda in 1591.

UO-SIN-000168.name: Nino of Georgia
UO-SIN-000168.life: Nino, according to tradition, was a young woman from Cappadocia who came to the kingdom of Iberia, in present-day Georgia, early in the fourth century. She is said to have carried a cross made of vine branches, bound with her own hair, and to have healed the sick, among them the queen. The story goes that King Mirian, lost and blinded while hunting, called on Nino's God and recovered his sight, after which he accepted baptism and made Christianity the faith of the kingdom, about 326. Nino is said to have ended her days preaching in eastern Georgia, and she is remembered as Georgia's enlightener.

UO-SIN-000169.name: Ralph Adams Cram, Richard Upjohn and John La Farge
UO-SIN-000169.life: These three Americans gave the Episcopal Church some of its most beautiful buildings. Richard Upjohn (1802-1878), born in England, designed Trinity Church in New York and many Gothic Revival parish churches, and helped found the American Institute of Architects. John La Farge (1835-1910), a painter from New York, made murals and invented a rich opalescent glass that revived American stained glass; his Ascension mural hangs in New York's Church of the Ascension. Ralph Adams Cram (1863-1942) championed Gothic design, reshaping the Cathedral of St. John the Divine and building the Princeton chapel and St. Thomas Church in Manhattan.

UO-SIN-000170.name: Dorothy L. Sayers
UO-SIN-000170.life: Born in Oxford in 1893, Dorothy L. Sayers was among the first women to take an Oxford degree, and she worked as an advertising copywriter before turning to fiction. Her detective novels, beginning with Whose Body? in 1923, introduced Lord Peter Wimsey and later Harriet Vane. Turning from crime to faith, she wrote The Man Born to Be King, a cycle of radio plays on the life of Christ broadcast by the BBC in 1941 and 1942, and essays such as Creed or Chaos? defending Christian doctrine with wit. She also translated Dante's Divine Comedy. She died suddenly at her home in Witham, Essex, on 17 December 1957.

UO-SIN-000594.name: Charles Wesley
UO-SIN-000594.life: Born at Epworth, Lincolnshire, in 1707, Charles Wesley was the younger brother of John. At Oxford he led the small group of students nicknamed the Holy Club, and in 1735 he sailed with John to Georgia, returning disappointed within a year. On 21 May 1738 he felt his faith made real, and he joined the Methodist revival as preacher and, above all, hymn writer. He wrote thousands of hymns, among them Hark! the Herald Angels Sing, Love Divine, All Loves Excelling, and Christ the Lord Is Risen Today. He died in London in 1788.

UO-SIN-000172.name: Lillian Trasher
UO-SIN-000172.life: Born in Jacksonville, Florida, in 1887 and raised in Georgia, Lillian Trasher trained at Bible schools and in 1910 left for Egypt as an independent missionary. A few months later she was called to the bed of a dying woman whose baby had no one to care for it. She took the infant in, and in 1911 began an orphanage at Assiut that grew over fifty years into a home for about twelve hundred children. Egyptians called her the Nile Mother. She worked without a long furlough. She died on 17 December 1961 and was buried in the grounds.

UO-SIN-000598.name: Ammon and Companions
UO-SIN-000598.life: Ammon, Zeno, Ptolemy, Ingenuus and Theophilus were soldiers in Alexandria during the persecution under the emperor Decius, around 250. As told by Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria, they were standing near the court when a Christian on trial seemed ready to deny his faith. They signalled their encouragement with gestures and looks, and when the crowd noticed, they stepped forward and declared themselves Christians. The governor and his officials were alarmed. The soldiers were condemned and led away in triumph, rejoicing in their witness. They are remembered together as the Alexandrian soldier martyrs of the Decian persecution.

UO-SIN-000003.name: Thomas the Apostle
UO-SIN-000003.life: Thomas, called the Twin, was one of the Twelve. The Gospel of John shows him honest, refusing to believe in the resurrection until he could touch the wounds. When the risen Lord appeared to him, he answered, "My Lord and my God." According to tradition he later carried the gospel eastward to India, where the Christians of the Malabar coast trace their origin to him, and he was killed there by a spear. Scholars disagree about how far the stories can be trusted, but his confession of faith remains one of the Gospel's high points.

UO-SIN-000601.name: Chaeremon of Nilopolis and Companions
UO-SIN-000601.life: Chaeremon was a very old bishop of Nilopolis in Egypt when the persecution under the emperor Decius broke out in 250. Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria tells that Chaeremon fled with a companion into the Arabian mountains and was never seen again; the brethren searched but found no trace of them. Dionysius also names Ischyrion, a steward who refused his master's order to sacrifice to idols and was cruelly killed for it. Many other Christians of that time died of hunger, cold, wild beasts or violence in the desert, or were carried off as slaves. They are remembered as witnesses of Egypt's Decian persecution.
UO-SIN-000601.place: Nilopolis and the Arabian desert, Egypt

UO-SIN-000603.name: Thorlak of Iceland
UO-SIN-000603.life: Born in 1133 in southern Iceland, Thorlak Thorhallsson was ordained young and studied abroad in France and England, becoming a canon regular of St. Augustine. Returning to Iceland, he founded a house of Augustinian canons and served as its abbot. In 1178 he became bishop of Skálholt and spent fifteen years pressing a lax church to keep clerical discipline and celibacy, resisting powerful chieftains who meddled in church property. He died on 23 December 1193. The Icelandic assembly honoured him as a saint in 1198, and in 1984 he was named patron of Iceland. His day, Þorláksmessa, is part of Icelandic Christmas.

UO-SIN-000178.name: Stephen
UO-SIN-000178.life: Stephen was a deacon of the early church in Jerusalem, a Greek-speaking Jew whom the Acts of the Apostles describes as full of faith and power. Disputes with members of several synagogues led to his arrest and trial before the council. He recounted Israel's history and said he saw Jesus standing at God's right hand, and an angry crowd dragged him out of the city and stoned him. As he died he prayed that God not hold the sin against them. A young man named Saul, later the apostle Paul, watched over the cloaks. He is honoured as the first Christian martyr.

UO-SIN-000179.name: John the Apostle and Evangelist
UO-SIN-000179.life: John, son of Zebedee, was a Galilean fisherman who with his brother James was among the first disciples of Jesus. With Peter and James he stood closest to the Lord at the Transfiguration, and tradition names him the disciple whom Jesus loved, who stood by the cross. After the resurrection he worked with Peter in Jerusalem and Samaria. Church tradition makes him the author of the fourth Gospel, three letters and Revelation, though scholars debate this, and holds that he lived to old age at Ephesus, the only apostle not martyred. His tomb is traditionally located at Ephesus.

UO-SIN-000175.name: Thomas Becket
UO-SIN-000175.life: Born in London around 1118, Thomas Becket was educated at Merton Priory and in Paris, and became archdeacon of Canterbury. Henry II made him chancellor in 1155, and he served the king brilliantly. Made archbishop in 1162, he changed, defending the rights of the church against royal claims, and he refused the Constitutions of Clarendon. He fled to France for six years. After returning to England, he was murdered in Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170 by four knights who believed they were carrying out the king's wish. He was canonized in 1173, and his shrine drew pilgrims until 1538.

UO-SIN-000612.name: Egwin of Worcester
UO-SIN-000612.life: Egwin, said to be of Mercian royal blood, became the third bishop of Worcester after 693, chosen, his biographers say, by popular demand. He enforced moral and clerical discipline so strictly that he met resentment at home and went to Rome to be vindicated. According to a famous legend, he locked fetters on his feet and threw the key in the River Avon, and at Rome a servant found the key in a fish caught in the Tiber. After a vision of Our Lady, he founded Evesham Abbey around 701, and its Benedictine monks kept his memory. Sources give his death as 717, though one older reckoning says 720.

UO-SIN-000181.name: Frances Joseph-Gaudet
UO-SIN-000181.life: Born in 1861 at Holmesville, Mississippi, to a formerly enslaved father, Frances Joseph went as a teenager to New Orleans and studied at Straight College. Married young and divorced after her husband's drinking, she raised three children as a seamstress. In 1894 she began holding prayer meetings for prisoners, bringing them letters, clothes and care, and she became a respected prison reformer who helped win a juvenile court for New Orleans. In 1902 she founded the Colored Normal and Industrial School, an orphanage and school on 105 acres, and in 1919 gave it to the Episcopal Diocese of Louisiana. She died in Chicago in 1934.

UO-SIN-000063.name: David Pendleton Oakerhater
UO-SIN-000063.life: Born around 1847 on the southern plains, Oakerhater, whose name meant Making Medicine, grew up a Cheyenne warrior and fought in the Red River War. After surrendering in 1875 he was held with other prisoners at Fort Marion, Florida, where he drew vividly, became a sergeant of the guard and began to learn about Christianity. Baptized in 1878 and taking the name David Pendleton, he studied in New York and was ordained deacon in 1881. He then returned to Oklahoma and spent decades among the Cheyenne and Arapaho, founding the Whirlwind Mission and urging his people to follow what he called a new road. He died in 1931.

UO-SIN-000064.name: The Martyrs of New Guinea
UO-SIN-000064.life: When Japanese forces invaded Papua and New Guinea in 1942, the Anglican mission there chose to stay with its people rather than flee. Priests such as Vivian Redlich and Henry Holland, nurses and teachers such as May Hayman, Margery Brenchley, Lilla Lashmar and Mavis Parkinson, and the builder John Duffill were captured around Buna and Gona and killed, several of them beheaded. Lucian Tapiedi, a young Papuan evangelist and teacher, was killed after protesting their capture. Others, including Henry Matthews and Leslie Gariadi, died at sea or elsewhere. They are remembered for faithfulness to the people they served, whatever the cost.

UO-SIN-000065.name: Phoebe
UO-SIN-000065.life: Phoebe appears in the closing verses of Paul's letter to the Romans, where he commends her to the Christians of Rome. She belonged to the church at Cenchreae, the eastern port of Corinth, and Paul calls her a servant or deacon of that church and a benefactor of many, himself included. Most scholars think she carried his letter to Rome and was probably a woman of means who gave hospitality and support to the early Christian community. Nothing more is known of her life, but she stands as the first woman in the New Testament named as holding a ministry in the church.

UO-SIN-000066.name: Paul Jones
UO-SIN-000066.life: Born in 1880 in Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, Paul Jones was a clergyman's son who studied at Yale and in Cambridge, Massachusetts. He was consecrated Bishop of Utah in 1914 and travelled widely among miners, railroad workers and Native Americans. In 1917, as the United States entered the First World War, he said publicly that war is unchristian. The press attacked him and a commission of bishops urged his resignation, which he gave in 1918. He then worked for the Fellowship of Reconciliation, served as a college chaplain at Antioch College, and helped found the Episcopal Pacifist Fellowship. He died in 1941.

UO-SIN-000326.name: Bertin
UO-SIN-000326.life: Bertin was born near Lake Constance around 615 and entered the monastery of Luxeuil, where he was trained in the strict rule of Columbanus. About 638 he set out with two companions for the marshy north of France to help his kinsman Bishop Omer teach the Christian faith to the Morini. They were given land at Sithiu, near the present Saint-Omer, and built a monastery there. Bertin later became its abbot, and his reputation for learning and holiness drew more than a hundred monks, including Winnoc and companions from Brittany. He lived to great age, chose Rigobert to succeed him, and died around 709.

UO-SIN-000068.name: Hannah More
UO-SIN-000068.life: Hannah More was born in 1745 near Bristol and taught in her family's school before going to London, where her plays and poems won her friends such as Samuel Johnson, Joshua Reynolds and David Garrick. Her faith deepened, she gave up the theatre, and she joined William Wilberforce and the Clapham circle, speaking against the slave trade. With her sister Martha she opened schools for poor children in the Mendip villages in the face of local opposition. Her penny Cheap Repository Tracts, written to counter revolutionary ideas, sold in the millions. She died in 1833 at Clifton and left much of her fortune to charity.

UO-SIN-000069.name: Kassiani
UO-SIN-000069.life: Kassiani, also called Kassia, was born in Constantinople about 810 to a wealthy family. A well-known story says that at the emperor Theophilos's bride show she answered his remark about women with a quick reply about the salvation that came through a woman, and he passed her over; chroniclers tell it, though how far it is true is uncertain. By 843 she had founded a convent and become its first abbess. Said to have suffered for defending holy images, she wrote around fifty hymns and many short verses. Her hymn on the woman who anointed Christ is still sung in Holy Week. She died around 865, perhaps on Kasos.

UO-SIN-000071.name: Constance, Thecla, Ruth, Frances, Charles Parsons, and Louis Schuyler
UO-SIN-000071.life: In the summer of 1878 yellow fever swept Memphis, Tennessee, killing more than five thousand people while most residents fled. Sisters of the Community of Saint Mary, an Episcopal order, stayed to nurse the sick and shelter orphans. Sister Constance, their superior, died on September 9, followed by Sisters Thecla, Ruth and Frances. Two priests stayed with them: Charles Parsons, rector of Grace Church and a former army officer, and Louis Schuyler, who had travelled from New Jersey to help and died within about a week of arriving. All were struck down by the fever, and their care for the dying is remembered as a witness of love.

UO-SIN-000072.name: Alexander Crummell
UO-SIN-000072.life: Alexander Crummell was born in New York City in 1819 to free Black parents active in the antislavery cause. Refused entry to the General Theological Seminary because of his race, he studied privately and was ordained, then raised funds in England and went on to Queens' College, Cambridge, becoming its first recorded Black graduate. From 1853 he spent about twenty years in Liberia as missionary and teacher. Back in the United States he founded St. Luke's Church in Washington, the first independent Black Episcopal parish there, and in 1897 helped found the American Negro Academy. He died in 1898, and his ideas of African solidarity influenced later leaders.

UO-SIN-000073.name: Deiniol
UO-SIN-000073.life: Deiniol is remembered as the founder of the monastery of Bangor in Gwynedd and, according to tradition, the first bishop of Bangor, in the sixth century. Welsh tradition holds that the local ruler Maelgwn Gwynedd gave him land and privileges, and that he may have studied under Cadoc at Llancarfan. Some accounts credit him with a second Bangor on the River Dee, though this is disputed. He is said to have died around 572 or 584 and to have been buried on Bardsey Island. Churches in north Wales, including Hawarden, bear his name, and Bangor Cathedral stands where his community is said to have lived.

UO-SIN-000074.name: John Henry Hobart
UO-SIN-000074.life: Born in Philadelphia in 1775, John Henry Hobart studied at Princeton, was ordained in 1798 and served parishes before becoming assistant minister at Trinity Church, New York. He became assistant bishop of New York in 1811 and bishop in 1816. A forceful High Churchman, he stressed apostolic order and the sacraments alongside evangelical preaching, and he travelled constantly to visit his parishes and encourage missions, including work among the Oneida. He helped found the General Theological Seminary and Geneva College, now Hobart and William Smith Colleges. Worn out by his labours, he died in Auburn, New York, in 1830.

UO-SIN-000075.name: Cyprian of Carthage
UO-SIN-000075.life: Cyprian was a wealthy teacher of rhetoric in Carthage who became a Christian about 246, gave much of his property to the poor, and within a few years was chosen bishop. When Decius's persecution broke out in 250 he withdrew from the city, a choice some criticized, and guided his flock by letter. Afterward he insisted that Christians who had lapsed do penance before returning, and he wrote On the Unity of the Church. He cared for the sick during a great plague. Under Valerian he was exiled, then tried, refused to sacrifice, and was beheaded near Carthage on September 14, 258.

UO-SIN-000350.name: Albert of Jerusalem
UO-SIN-000350.life: Born around 1149 in northern Italy, Albert became a canon regular, then bishop of Bobbio and bishop of Vercelli, and served the papacy as a trusted peacemaker. In 1205 Pope Innocent III made him Patriarch of Jerusalem. Because Jerusalem was held by Muslim rulers, he lived at Acre. There he mediated between Christian rulers, and hermits living on Mount Carmel asked him for a way of life. The short rule he gave them became the foundation of the Carmelite order. On September 14, 1214, while taking part in a procession at Acre, he was stabbed to death by a man he had earlier removed from office.

UO-SIN-000077.name: Catherine of Genoa
UO-SIN-000077.life: Born in 1447 to the noble Fieschi family of Genoa, Catherine wished to enter a convent but at sixteen was married to Giuliano Adorno, whose unfaithfulness and extravagance made her years unhappy. In 1473, while making her confession, she was overwhelmed by a vivid sense of God's love and of her own sinfulness, and her life changed. She and her husband, who later returned to the faith, gave themselves to the care of the poor sick at Genoa's Pammatone hospital, where she became its manager, nursing through the plagues. Her teaching on purification after death was gathered into writings published later. She died in 1510.

UO-SIN-000078.name: Ninian
UO-SIN-000078.life: Very little is certain about Ninian. The Venerable Bede, writing around 731, says he was a Briton instructed at Rome who built a stone church called Candida Casa, the White House, at Whithorn in Galloway and brought the faith to the southern Picts. Later tradition, especially a twelfth-century Life by Aelred of Rievaulx, adds that he met Martin of Tours and dedicated his church to him. Dates around 400 to 432 are traditional, and some scholars doubt how much of the story is secure. Whithorn became a monastic centre and a medieval place of pilgrimage, and many churches in Scotland carry his name.

UO-SIN-000079.name: Hildegard of Bingen
UO-SIN-000079.life: Born around 1098 into a noble family in the Rhineland, Hildegard was given as a child to the care of the anchoress Jutta at Disibodenberg and later became head of the nuns there. She had experienced visions from childhood, and in her forties she was encouraged to write them down; the result was Scivias. About 1150 she moved her community to Rupertsberg near Bingen. She composed sacred songs and a morality play, wrote on medicine and the natural world, and travelled to preach, speaking boldly to clergy and rulers. She died on September 17, 1179, and was named a Doctor of the Church in 2012.

UO-SIN-000080.name: Edward Bouverie Pusey
UO-SIN-000080.life: Born in Berkshire in 1800, Edward Pusey became a fellow of Oriel College, studied in Germany, and in 1828 was appointed Regius Professor of Hebrew at Oxford, a post he held for over fifty years. From 1833 he joined John Keble and John Henry Newman in the Oxford Movement, writing tracts on fasting and baptism, and after Newman left for Rome he became the movement's leading voice, so that its followers were called Puseyites. A sermon on the Eucharist led to his suspension from preaching in 1843. He promoted confession and the first Anglican sisterhoods, and cared for cholera victims. He died in 1882.

UO-SIN-000081.name: Theodore of Tarsus
UO-SIN-000081.life: Born in Tarsus around 602, Theodore was a learned Greek monk living in Rome when Pope Vitalian chose him in 668 to be Archbishop of Canterbury, after other candidates had failed. He reached England in 669 at about the age of sixty-seven. Travelling throughout the land, he appointed bishops, divided large dioceses, and called the Synod of Hertford in 673, the first gathering of the whole English church. With his companion Hadrian he set up a school at Canterbury teaching Greek, Latin and Scripture. His division of Northumbria led to a dispute with Wilfrid, later settled. He died in 690, and the diocesan pattern he began endured.

UO-SIN-000082.name: John Coleridge Patteson and his Companions
UO-SIN-000082.life: Born in London in 1827 and educated at Eton and Oxford, John Patteson answered Bishop Selwyn's call in 1854 and sailed for the South Pacific. He learned many Melanesian languages, helped found a mission school on Norfolk Island, and in 1861 became first Bishop of Melanesia. He opposed the kidnapping of islanders for labour. On September 20, 1871, he went ashore alone at Nukapu in the Santa Cruz islands and was killed, probably in revenge for abductions by labour recruiters. His companions Joseph Atkin, a New Zealand priest, and Stephen Taroaniara, a Solomon Islander, were struck by arrows and died of tetanus within a week.

UO-SIN-000083.name: Saint Matthew
UO-SIN-000083.life: Matthew was a tax collector at Capernaum, a man many of his neighbours despised, when Jesus called him to follow. The other Gospels name him Levi, and he gave a dinner for Jesus at which tax collectors and sinners sat at table. He was one of the twelve apostles. Early church writers credit him with the first Gospel, though many modern scholars think its author is unknown. Of his later life little is certain; tradition says he preached in Judea and then in lands to the east, and some traditions say he died a martyr. He is remembered for leaving his counting table to answer Christ's call.

UO-SIN-000084.name: Philander Chase
UO-SIN-000084.life: Born in New Hampshire in 1775, Philander Chase found the Book of Common Prayer as a student at Dartmouth and became an Episcopal priest, serving in New York, New Orleans and Hartford. In 1817 he moved to Ohio and in 1819 became its first bishop. Convinced the frontier needed its own clergy, he travelled to England, raised money, and founded Kenyon College in 1824. After disputes he resigned in 1831, then became first Bishop of Illinois in 1835 and founded Jubilee College near Peoria. A tireless rider among scattered settlements, he served as Presiding Bishop from 1843 and died in 1852.

UO-SIN-000085.name: Thecla of Iconium
UO-SIN-000085.life: Everything we have about Thecla comes from the Acts of Paul and Thecla, a story written about 180 that is largely legendary, though it may preserve memory of a real woman. According to that account, Thecla of Iconium heard Paul preach, broke her engagement and chose a life of devotion. She was sentenced to burning and to wild beasts and was saved each time, then taught the gospel and finally settled at Seleucia. Eastern Christians honoured her greatly as an apostle and the first woman martyr, and shrines grew up at Seleucia and elsewhere, so that her story helped shape the memory of early women disciples.

UO-SIN-000086.name: Anna Ellison Butler Alexander
UO-SIN-000086.life: Born about 1865 on the Georgia coast to parents who had been enslaved on the Butler plantation, Anna Alexander became a teacher in rural Glynn County. In 1894 she helped found the mission of the Good Shepherd at Pennick, which grew into a church and a school where Black children learned to read. In 1907 Bishop Cleland Nelson made her a deaconess, the only African-American woman to hold that office in the Episcopal Church. Through poverty and little support she served her community for forty years, once sending her church's building fund to relief work after the 1923 Japanese earthquake. She died on September 24, 1947.

UO-SIN-000087.name: Sergius of Radonezh
UO-SIN-000087.life: Born in 1314 near Rostov and baptised Bartholomew, Sergius came from a boyar family ruined by civil strife. With his brother Stefan he withdrew to the forests of Radonezh north of Moscow and built a small chapel to the Trinity, where a community gathered around him. As abbot he insisted that monks live by their own labour and shared their simple life. His disciples founded dozens of monasteries across northern Russia. Respected as a peacemaker, he urged Russian princes to unite and is said to have blessed Dmitry Donskoy before the 1380 victory over the Tatars at Kulikovo. He died on September 25, 1392.

UO-SIN-000088.name: Lancelot Andrewes
UO-SIN-000088.life: Born in London in 1555, Lancelot Andrewes studied at Cambridge, was ordained in 1580 and became known as a brilliant linguist and preacher. As Dean of Westminster from 1601 he cared for the school there. He became bishop of Chichester in 1605, Ely in 1609 and Winchester in 1619, and served as a court preacher under James I. He led the Westminster group of translators for the King James Bible, published in 1611. His sermons, especially those preached at Christmas and Easter, are admired for their depth, and his private devotions, the Preces Privatae, have nourished generations. He died in 1626 and was buried at Southwark.

UO-SIN-000089.name: Euphrosyne/Smaragdus of Alexandria
UO-SIN-000089.life: According to a well-loved legend, Euphrosyne was the daughter of a wealthy man named Paphnutius in Alexandria in the fifth century. Facing marriage at eighteen, she is said to have disguised herself as a man, taken the name Smaragdus and entered a monastery, where she lived in prayer for thirty-eight years. When her grieving father came seeking comfort, the abbot placed him under the guidance of this monk, and he never recognised his daughter. Only on her deathbed did she reveal herself, and Paphnutius then became a monk and lived in her cell. Scholars regard the story as legend rather than history.

UO-SIN-000090.name: Paula and Eustochium of Rome
UO-SIN-000090.life: Paula, born in Rome in 347 into a noble family, was widowed at thirty-two and gave herself to a life of prayer and charity. In 382 she met Jerome, and soon she and her daughter Eustochium followed him to the East. They visited the desert hermits of Egypt, then settled in Bethlehem, where Paula's wealth paid for a monastery for men, convents for women and a guest house for pilgrims. Both women learned Hebrew and studied Scripture with Jerome, who dedicated commentaries to them. Paula died in 404, and Eustochium led the community until her own death in 419 or 420.

UO-SIN-000092.name: Jerome
UO-SIN-000092.life: Born around 342 at Stridon on the border of Dalmatia, Jerome studied in Rome and was baptized there. He lived for years as a hermit in the Syrian desert, where he began learning Hebrew, then was ordained at Antioch. In Rome, Pope Damasus encouraged his work on the Latin Bible, and he guided devout women such as Paula. After Damasus died in 384 he left, and in 386 settled in Bethlehem near a convent founded by Paula and Eustochium. There he translated the Old Testament from Hebrew, wrote commentaries and letters, and argued fiercely with opponents. His Latin Bible became the Vulgate. He died in 420.

UO-SIN-000126.name: Richard Hooker
UO-SIN-000126.life: Richard Hooker was born near Exeter in 1554 and studied at Corpus Christi College, Oxford, where he became a fellow and was ordained priest in 1579. As Master of the Temple in London he found himself in public disagreement with Walter Travers, a Puritan lecturer at the same church, and the dispute led him to write Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity, a long and carefully argued defence of the Church of England. He taught that Scripture, tradition and reason belong together, and he wrote in graceful English prose. He spent his last years as a country parson in Kent and died at Bishopsbourne in 1600.

UO-SIN-000127.name: Adeline Blanchard Tyler and her Companions
UO-SIN-000127.life: Adeline Blanchard Tyler was born in Massachusetts in 1805 and lived in Boston as a devout Episcopalian. Widowed in 1853, she trained in nursing among the deaconesses of Kaiserswerth in Germany. In 1856 she and three other women, Caroline Guild, Evaline Black and Catherine Minard, were set apart as deaconesses, among the first in the Episcopal Church in America. Tyler ran a church-funded infirmary in Baltimore, and during the Civil War she nursed wounded Union soldiers and later led hospitals in Maryland and Pennsylvania. She finished her working life at the Midnight Mission in New York, helping women in need, and died in January 1875.

UO-SIN-000128.name: Zechariah and Elizabeth
UO-SIN-000128.life: According to the Gospel of Luke, Zechariah was a priest of the order of Abijah and Elizabeth, his wife, was a descendant of Aaron. Both were righteous and elderly, and they had no children. While Zechariah was serving at the altar of incense in the Jerusalem temple, the angel Gabriel promised that Elizabeth would bear a son, John. Zechariah doubted and lost his speech until the child was born; then he wrote, His name is John, and broke into the song of praise we call the Benedictus. Elizabeth welcomed her kinswoman Mary with joy. Their son became the forerunner of Christ, John the Baptist.

UO-SIN-000129.name: William Temple
UO-SIN-000129.life: William Temple was born in 1881, the son of an earlier Archbishop of Canterbury, and studied at Balliol College, Oxford. He was a leading figure in the Workers' Educational Association, then Bishop of Manchester from 1921, Archbishop of York from 1929 and Archbishop of Canterbury from 1942. Temple believed the Church must speak about society and the economy, and his book Christianity and Social Order, published in 1942, shaped the postwar hope for fairer common life. He also championed cooperation between the churches, helping prepare the way for the World Council of Churches. He died in October 1944, worn out by wartime labour.

UO-SIN-000130.name: Willibrord
UO-SIN-000130.life: Willibrord was born about 658 in Northumbria and spent years of study in Ireland before crossing the sea to preach to the pagan Frisians. Sponsored by the Frankish leader Pepin of Herstal, he travelled to Rome, where Pope Sergius consecrated him bishop of the Frisians in 695, and he made Utrecht his base. In 698 he founded the abbey of Echternach. Persecution under the Frisian king Radbod drove him back for a time, but he returned with the support of Charles Martel and worked for a while alongside Boniface. He died at Echternach in 739 and is honoured as the apostle of the Netherlands.

UO-SIN-000131.name: Ammonius
UO-SIN-000131.life: Ammonius was a hermit among the monks of the Egyptian desert at Nitria in the later fourth century, and tradition counts him among the four Tall Brothers, with Dioscorus, Eusebius and Euthymius, who were known for fasting and learning. A well-known story says that when people tried to make him a bishop, he cut off one of his own ears to show he was unfit, and threatened to cut out his tongue if they tried again. Opposed by Theophilus of Alexandria, the brothers fled to Constantinople, where John Chrysostom welcomed them. The exact dates of his life, and his identity with the earless hermit, are not certain.

UO-SIN-000132.name: Richard Rolle, Walter Hilton, and Margery Kempe
UO-SIN-000132.life: Three English mystics of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. Richard Rolle, born in Yorkshire about 1300, left Oxford to live as a hermit, wrote The Fire of Love, and guided nuns at Hampole, where he died in the plague of 1349. Walter Hilton studied at Cambridge and became an Augustinian canon at Thurgarton in Nottinghamshire; his Scale of Perfection is a wise guide to the contemplative life, and he died in 1396. Margery Kempe, a merchant's daughter from Lynn in Norfolk and mother of fourteen children, wept and saw visions, made pilgrimages to Jerusalem, Rome and Santiago, and dictated her Book, often called the first English autobiography.

UO-SIN-000133.name: Leo the Great
UO-SIN-000133.life: Leo became bishop of Rome in 440 and held the office until his death in 461, at a time when the western empire was crumbling. His letter known as the Tome, sent against the teaching of Eutyches, set out that Christ is one person in two natures, divine and human, and the Council of Chalcedon in 451 received it with acclaim. In 452 he led an embassy that met Attila the Hun and helped turn him from Italy, and in 455 he persuaded the Vandals to spare Rome from burning. His letters and sermons made him a great teacher, and he became a Doctor of the Church in 1754.

UO-SIN-000134.name: Martin of Tours
UO-SIN-000134.life: Martin was born about 316 in Pannonia, the son of a soldier, and was conscripted into the Roman cavalry in Gaul. Sulpicius Severus tells how at Amiens he cut his cloak in two to clothe a freezing beggar and then dreamed of Christ wearing it. He was baptised, and around 361 he left the army, saying he was a soldier of Christ. He founded a hermitage at Ligugé, the first monastery in Gaul, and in 371 was made bishop of Tours, where he also established Marmoutier. He travelled through the countryside bringing the gospel and died at Candes in 397, honoured as a saint though not a martyr.

UO-SIN-000135.name: Charles Simeon
UO-SIN-000135.life: Charles Simeon was born at Reading in 1759 and studied at King's College, Cambridge. From the early 1780s until his death in 1836 he was minister of Holy Trinity Church in Cambridge, a post he held for more than fifty years. His faithful preaching and his care for undergraduates made him a leader of the evangelical movement in the Church of England. He helped found the Church Missionary Society, supported the Bible Society, wrote Horae Homileticae, a vast set of sermon outlines on the whole Bible, and set up a trust to place evangelical clergy in parishes. He died in Cambridge in November 1836.

UO-SIN-000136.name: Frances Xavier Cabrini
UO-SIN-000136.life: Frances Cabrini was born in 1850 at Sant'Angelo Lodigiano in northern Italy and in 1880 founded the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart of Jesus. In 1889 she arrived in New York with six sisters. Despite opposition from church leaders and prejudice against Italians, she set up schools, orphanages and hospitals for immigrants who had few friends in a strange country. In all she founded 67 institutions in Italy, the United States, Latin America and Europe, and she became an American citizen in 1909. She died in Chicago in December 1917 and was canonised in 1946, the first United States citizen to be named a saint of the Catholic Church.

UO-SIN-000138.name: Herman of Alaska
UO-SIN-000138.life: Herman was born in Russia around 1756 and became a monk, first near Saint Petersburg and then at Valaam Monastery on Lake Ladoga. In 1793 he joined a mission of monks sent to bring the gospel to the native peoples of Alaska, arriving at Kodiak in 1794. He outlived all his companions. He retired to nearby Spruce Island, which he called New Valaam, where he lived very simply, kept a garden and taught orphaned children their prayers and church music. He defended the native people against mistreatment and tended them in epidemics. He died in 1837 and was canonised in 1970, the first Orthodox saint of North America.
UO-SIN-000138.place: Valaam, Kodiak and Spruce Island, Alaska

UO-SIN-000139.name: Margaret of Scotland
UO-SIN-000139.life: Margaret was born about 1045 in Hungary, where her father Edward the Exile lived in exile from England. The family returned to England in 1057, and after the Norman Conquest she fled north and in 1070 married King Malcolm III of Scotland. A devout queen, she worked to bring Scottish church practice into line with the wider church, welcomed Benedictine monks to Dunfermline, provided ferries for pilgrims crossing the Forth, and cared for the poor. She bore eight children, among them three kings of Scotland. She died on 16 November 1093, days after hearing that her husband and eldest son had been killed near Alnwick, and was canonised in 1250.

UO-SIN-000140.name: Hugh of Lincoln
UO-SIN-000140.life: Hugh was born about 1140 at Avalon, in Burgundy, and became a Carthusian monk at the Grande Chartreuse. In 1179 King Henry II called him to England to lead the first Carthusian house, at Witham. Chosen bishop of Lincoln in 1186, he governed the largest diocese in England and began rebuilding his cathedral in the Gothic style after an earthquake. He was known for standing up to kings: he resisted demands for money and service in royal wars, and he protected Jewish people from persecution in the reign of Richard I. He died in London on 16 November 1200 and was canonised in 1220.

UO-SIN-000141.name: Hilda of Whitby
UO-SIN-000141.life: Hilda was born about 614 into the Northumbrian royal family and was baptised around 627 with her great-uncle, King Edwin. After serving as abbess at Hartlepool she founded the double monastery of Whitby about 657, ruling both monks and nuns. Bede praises her wisdom and energy, and says that all who knew her called her mother. Her abbey hosted the Synod of Whitby in 664, which settled the date of Easter for Northumbria. She encouraged the cowherd Caedmon to become a poet, and five men trained under her became bishops. She died at Whitby in 680.

UO-SIN-000142.name: Elizabeth of Hungary
UO-SIN-000142.life: Elizabeth was born in 1207, a daughter of King Andrew II of Hungary, and was brought up at the Thuringian court at the Wartburg. She married Louis IV of Thuringia when she was still very young, and their marriage was happy. After he died on his way to the Crusade in 1227, she left the court, joined a Franciscan lay community, and used her dowry to build a hospital at Marburg, where she nursed the poor and sick herself. Worn down by this work and by severe spiritual discipline, she died in 1231 at the age of twenty-four and was canonised four years later.

UO-SIN-000143.name: Edmund of East Anglia
UO-SIN-000143.life: Edmund became king of East Anglia in 855, still a young man. When the Danish Great Army invaded his kingdom, he was defeated and killed, in 869 according to the usual reckoning, though some give 870. According to later tradition, he was put to death because he refused to renounce Christ or to accept Danish overlordship, though it is uncertain whether he fell in battle or afterwards. Memorial coins bearing his name were being minted within a generation, and his body was later taken to Bury St Edmunds, where a great abbey grew up around his shrine. For centuries he was counted among the patron saints of England.

UO-SIN-000144.name: Mechthilde of Hackeborn and Gertrude the Great
UO-SIN-000144.life: Mechthilde and Gertrude were Benedictine nuns at the convent of Helfta in Saxony in the thirteenth century. Mechthilde of Hackeborn, who died in 1298, directed the choir, was called the Nightingale of Helfta for her singing, and was known for her visions of Christ's love, gathered in the Book of Special Grace. Gertrude, who lived from 1256 to 1302, entered the convent school at five. In 1281 she had visions that turned her from secular learning to prayer and theology, and she wrote the Herald of Divine Love, a work centred on the heart of Christ. She is the only woman saint to be called the Great.

UO-SIN-000145.name: Clive Staples Lewis
UO-SIN-000145.life: C. S. Lewis was born in Belfast in 1898 and became a fellow of Magdalen College, Oxford, in 1925, and later Professor of Medieval and Renaissance Literature at Cambridge. Raised in the Church of Ireland, he turned atheist as a teenager, but in 1931, after long conversations with friends including J. R. R. Tolkien, he returned to the Christian faith. His wartime radio talks became Mere Christianity, and he wrote The Screwtape Letters, the Narnia stories and many other books. In 1956 he married Joy Davidman, whose death in 1960 he described in A Grief Observed. He died at Oxford on 22 November 1963.

UO-SIN-000146.name: Clement of Rome
UO-SIN-000146.life: Clement was a leader of the church at Rome at the end of the first century, remembered as one of its early bishops. He is known above all for a letter sent to the church at Corinth about the year 96, when some of its leaders had been removed from office. He urged peace and good order. This letter is one of the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament and was once read in some churches. Later tradition says that he was banished to the Crimea under Trajan and drowned with an anchor tied to him, but this is legend and little else is certain.

UO-SIN-000147.name: Catherine of Alexandria, Barbara of Nicomedia, and Margaret of Antioch
UO-SIN-000147.life: These three young women are honoured as virgin martyrs of the early fourth century, though scholars doubt that much of their stories is historical. According to tradition, Catherine of Alexandria out-argued fifty pagan philosophers, survived a spiked wheel that shattered, and was beheaded. Barbara was shut up in a tower by her father, became a secret Christian, and was killed by him, after which he was struck by lightning. Margaret of Antioch refused to marry a pagan official, was tortured, and in legend overcame a dragon. Their stories were loved throughout medieval Europe, where they stood for courage and faithfulness under persecution.

UO-SIN-000148.name: James Otis Sargent Huntington
UO-SIN-000148.life: James Huntington was born in 1854, the son of the bishop of Central New York, and studied at Harvard. Ordained priest in 1880, he served working families in Syracuse and then the poor of New York's Lower East Side. In 1881 he and two other priests began a common life that became the Order of the Holy Cross, the first Anglican monastic community for men in the United States, and he made his life profession on 25 November 1884. He supported labour causes and Henry George's single tax. He was several times superior of the order, whose monastery stands at West Park, New York, and he died in 1935.
UO-SIN-000148.place: New York (Lower East Side, West Park)

UO-SIN-000546.name: Sojourner Truth
UO-SIN-000546.life: Sojourner Truth was born Isabella about 1797 in Ulster County, New York, into slavery, and grew up speaking Dutch. In 1826 she escaped with her infant daughter, and two years later she went to court and won back her small son Peter, who had been sold illegally. In 1843 she took the name Sojourner Truth, believing God called her to travel and preach. She spoke for the abolition of slavery and for women's rights, and her speech at the Ohio convention of 1851 became famous. During the Civil War she helped recruit Black soldiers and met President Lincoln in 1864. She died at Battle Creek, Michigan, in 1883.

UO-SIN-000150.name: Virgil of Salzburg
UO-SIN-000150.life: Virgil was an Irish monk, born about 700, who became abbot of Aghaboe. Around 745 he set out for the Holy Land but stayed in Frankish lands, where King Pepin welcomed him, and then went to Bavaria at the invitation of Duke Odilo. He became abbot of St Peter's at Salzburg and, about 767, bishop of the city. He built up his diocese and sent missionaries to the Slavs of Carinthia, earning the name Apostle of Carinthia.  Boniface accused him of teaching that there were lands on the opposite side of the earth, but Pope Zachary sided with Virgil. He died in 784, though some sources say 789.

UO-SIN-000151.name: Kamehameha and Emma of Hawai‘i
UO-SIN-000151.life: Kamehameha IV became king of Hawai‘i in 1855 and in 1856 married Emma Rooke. Together they asked the Church of England to send clergy to Hawai‘i, and both were baptised in 1862; the king translated the Book of Common Prayer into Hawaiian. They worked to found the Queen's Hospital for the care of the sick. Their young son died in 1862, and the king died the next year at the age of twenty-nine. Emma lived on until 1885, visiting patients, raising money for St Andrew's Cathedral, founding a school for girls, and travelling to Europe and America to seek support for her church and people.

UO-SIN-000152.name: Dorothy Day
UO-SIN-000152.life: Dorothy Day was born in 1897 and worked as a radical journalist in New York before her life changed. After her daughter's birth she became a Catholic in 1927. With Peter Maurin she founded the Catholic Worker newspaper and movement in 1933. It opened houses of hospitality where the poor were fed and housed, and farms where people could live and work together. Day was a committed pacifist; she supported conscientious objectors, protested nuclear weapons and civil defence drills, and was jailed several times. Her autobiography, The Long Loneliness, tells her story. She died on 29 November 1980, and the Catholic Church has opened her cause for sainthood.

UO-SIN-000153.name: Saint Andrew the Apostle
UO-SIN-000153.life: Andrew came from Bethsaida in Galilee and worked as a fisherman with his brother Simon Peter. According to John's Gospel, he first followed John the Baptist and then, after hearing the Baptist point to Jesus, followed Jesus and brought Peter to him. He was one of the first four apostles called, and the Gospel shows him pointing out the boy with loaves and fishes and bringing Greek visitors to Jesus. Tradition says that he preached around the Black Sea and in Greece and was crucified at Patras, on a cross shaped like an X, around the year 60. He is patron of Scotland and Russia.

UO-SIN-000032.name: Joseph of Arimathea
UO-SIN-000032.life: Joseph of Arimathea was a wealthy man from a town called Arimathea and, the Gospels say, a respected member of the Jewish council who was quietly waiting for the kingdom of God. After Jesus died on the cross, he went boldly to Pilate and asked for the body. With Nicodemus he wrapped it in linen with spices and laid it in a new rock-cut tomb, apparently his own, in a garden nearby, just before the Sabbath began. The Gospels tell us little more. Later medieval legends carried him to Britain and linked him with the Holy Grail, but these stories have no firm historical footing.

UO-SIN-000033.name: Samuel Ferguson
UO-SIN-000033.life: Samuel David Ferguson was born in Charleston, South Carolina, in 1842 and was taken to Liberia by his family at the age of six. He was ordained deacon in 1865 and priest in 1868, and in 1885 was consecrated a bishop at Grace Church, New York, the first man of African descent to sit in the American House of Bishops. As Missionary Bishop of Liberia he spent three decades building up the church there. He founded the school that grew into Cuttington University and established the Bromley Mission School. He remained in Liberia until he died in Monrovia in 1916.

UO-SIN-000034.name: Joanna, Mary, and Salome
UO-SIN-000034.life: These women were among the Galilean followers who travelled with Jesus and supported his ministry from their own means. Joanna was the wife of Chuza, a steward in Herod's household. Mary, mother of James and Joses, and Salome, often identified as the mother of the apostles James and John, stood near the cross while many fled. When the Sabbath had passed, they went at dawn with spices to anoint his body and found the tomb empty. The angels' message was entrusted to them, and they carried the news of the resurrection to the apostles, which is why the church remembers them as myrrh-bearers.

UO-SIN-000035.name: Anthony of Sourozh
UO-SIN-000035.life: Born Andrei Bloom in Lausanne in 1914 to Russian parents, he grew up in exile and settled in Paris, where he trained as a doctor. As a teenager he met Christ, as he later put it, when he was not looking for him. He secretly took monastic vows in 1939, served as a surgeon in the French army and worked in the Resistance. Sent to Britain in 1948, he became the founding bishop of the Russian Orthodox diocese of Sourozh and later a metropolitan. His broadcasts and books on prayer reached many Christians beyond his own church. He died in London in 2003.

UO-SIN-000251.name: Addai and Mari
UO-SIN-000251.life: Addai and Mari are honoured as the first teachers of the faith in Mesopotamia and Persia. According to tradition, Addai was one of the seventy disciples sent out by Jesus, who came to Edessa, healed King Abgar and preached the gospel there. Mari, said to be his disciple, carried the work further east. Little certain history survives, and the stories date from later centuries. Their names remain attached to the ancient Eucharistic prayer used in the Church of the East, which many scholars place in the early centuries of Syriac Christianity, so that their memory lives on in the worship of those churches.

UO-SIN-000038.name: John Mason Neale
UO-SIN-000038.life: John Mason Neale was born in London in 1818 and educated at Cambridge. Drawn into the Oxford Movement, he helped found the Cambridge Camden Society and was ordained in 1842, but chronic lung disease ended his parish work. From 1846 until his death he was warden of Sackville College, an almshouse in East Grinstead. There he co-founded the Society of St Margaret, a nursing sisterhood, and endured hostility, even mob violence, for his high-church views. He is best remembered for translating Latin and Greek hymns, among them O come, O come, Emmanuel and All glory, laud and honour, and for writing Good King Wenceslas. He died in 1866.

UO-SIN-000039.name: Dominic
UO-SIN-000039.life: Dominic was born around 1170 at Caleruega in Castile and became a canon at Osma. Travelling through southern France, he saw how little the people of Languedoc knew of the faith and how easily heresy took hold there. He chose to answer with careful preaching and a poor, simple way of life. He gathered companions at Toulouse, and in 1216 the pope approved them as the Order of Preachers, later called the Dominicans, who joined study and prayer to travelling ministry. He sent friars to the new universities and across Europe. Dominic died in Bologna in 1221, worn out by his labours.

UO-SIN-000040.name: Edith Stein (Teresa Benedicta of the Cross)
UO-SIN-000040.life: Edith Stein was born in 1891 into an observant Jewish family in Breslau and became an agnostic as a teenager. A brilliant philosopher, she studied under Edmund Husserl. Reading the autobiography of Teresa of Avila drew her to the Christian faith, and she was baptized in 1922. After the Nazis forced her out of her teaching post, she entered the Carmelite convent in Cologne in 1933 and later moved to Echt in the Netherlands for safety. In 1942 she and her sister Rosa were arrested and taken to Auschwitz, where she was killed in the gas chamber on 9 August. She is honoured as a martyr.

UO-SIN-000041.name: Laurence of Rome
UO-SIN-000041.life: Laurence was one of the seven deacons of Rome under Pope Sixtus II, and as archdeacon he looked after the church's funds and its distribution of alms to the poor. In August 258 the emperor Valerian ordered that bishops, priests and deacons be put to death. Sixtus was seized and executed, and the prefect of Rome then demanded the church's treasure from Laurence. He is said to have gathered the city's poor and sick and presented them as the church's true riches. He was put to death within days. Later tradition says he was roasted on a gridiron, though the earliest accounts speak only of his execution.

UO-SIN-000042.name: Clare of Assisi
UO-SIN-000042.life: Clare was born in 1194 to a noble family of Assisi. Hearing Francis preach, she was moved to give up her family's comfort, and on Palm Sunday night in 1212 she left home to join him. She settled with her followers at San Damiano, where they lived in strict poverty, prayer and enclosure, as the Poor Ladies. She wrote a rule for them, the first known to have been composed by a woman, and fought the papacy for the right to live without endowments. She outlived Francis by twenty-seven years, often ill and bedridden, and died in 1253. Her order is now known as the Poor Clares.

UO-SIN-000043.name: Florence Nightingale
UO-SIN-000043.life: Florence Nightingale was born in 1820 to a wealthy English family and felt called to serve God through nursing, though her family opposed it. In 1854, during the Crimean War, she took a party of nurses to the military hospital at Scutari. By insisting on cleanliness and care she helped cut the soldiers' death rate, and she became known as the Lady with the Lamp. Back in England she opened a training school for nurses at St Thomas' Hospital in 1860 and wrote Notes on Nursing. She also pressed for hospital and public health reform, and used statistics to make her case. She died in London in 1910.

UO-SIN-000265.name: Maximus the Confessor
UO-SIN-000265.life: Maximus was born around 580 and served as a senior secretary at the court of the emperor Heraclius before becoming a monk. Driven west by Persian invasions, he studied in North Africa under Sophronius. There he became the leading opponent of Monothelitism, the teaching that Christ had only one will, arguing that he had both a divine and a human will. For this he was arrested, tried in Constantinople, and had his tongue and right hand cut off. He was exiled to the Caucasus and died there in 662. His theology was vindicated at the Third Council of Constantinople. Orthodox and Western Christians alike honour his writings.

UO-SIN-000268.name: Maximilian Kolbe
UO-SIN-000268.life: Raymund Kolbe was born in 1894 in Zduńska Wola, Poland, and joined the Conventual Franciscans as a boy, taking the name Maximilian. A priest devoted to Mary, he founded the friary of Niepokalanów near Warsaw, published widely read magazines and even ran a radio station. He also served as a missionary in Japan. After the German invasion he was arrested and sent to Auschwitz in 1941. When a prisoner was chosen to die in reprisal for an escape, Kolbe offered to take his place, and was put in a starvation cell. After two weeks he was killed by injection on 14 August 1941.

UO-SIN-000273.name: Charles Inglis
UO-SIN-000273.life: Charles Inglis was born in 1734 in County Donegal, Ireland, and emigrated to America as a young man. He taught school, was ordained in England in 1758, and served as a missionary in Delaware before becoming a curate and later rector of Trinity Church, New York. A convinced loyalist, he answered Thomas Paine's Common Sense in print and prayed publicly for the king during the Revolution. He left New York in 1783 and in 1787 was consecrated the first Anglican bishop of Nova Scotia, a diocese covering much of British North America. He supported the founding of King's College at Windsor. He died in 1816.

UO-SIN-000048.name: Samuel Johnson, Timothy Cutler, and Thomas Bradbury Chandler
UO-SIN-000048.life: These three priests helped establish the Church of England in colonial America. Samuel Johnson and Timothy Cutler, both Congregational ministers, startled Connecticut in 1722 by declaring for episcopal ordination. Johnson was ordained in England, served the mission at Stratford for decades and became first president of King's College, now Columbia University. Cutler, rector of Yale, became the first rector of Christ Church, Boston, and served there until 1765. Chandler, Johnson's protege, was rector at Elizabeth, New Jersey, and argued publicly for an American bishop. Their efforts helped lay the ground for the Episcopal Church after independence.

UO-SIN-000049.name: William Porcher DuBose
UO-SIN-000049.life: William Porcher DuBose was born in 1836 in South Carolina and educated at the Citadel and the University of Virginia. In the Civil War he served in a Confederate legion, was wounded and briefly held prisoner, and later became a chaplain. Ordained priest in 1866, he served parishes in South Carolina before joining the University of the South at Sewanee, Tennessee, where he was professor, chaplain and dean of theology. There he wrote on the New Testament and the councils of the early church, including The Soteriology of the New Testament and The Gospel in the Gospels. He died in 1918.

UO-SIN-000282.name: John Eudes
UO-SIN-000282.life: Jean Eudes was born in 1601 on a farm in Normandy and educated by the Jesuits at Caen. He joined the Oratory, was ordained in 1625 and became a tireless preacher of parish missions across France. He was moved by the plight of women who had fallen into hardship, and in 1641 founded the Order of Our Lady of Charity to care for them. In 1643 he left the Oratory and founded the Congregation of Jesus and Mary, the Eudists, to train priests. He wrote the first Mass and Office for the Sacred Heart of Jesus and promoted devotion to it, despite Jansenist opposition. He died in 1680.

UO-SIN-000051.name: Bernard of Clairvaux
UO-SIN-000051.life: Bernard was born around 1090 near Dijon to a noble family. About 1112 he entered the strict new monastery of Cîteaux, bringing relatives with him, and in 1115 he was sent to found Clairvaux. There he became the most influential churchman in Europe, advising popes, mediating disputes and opposing theologians such as Peter Abelard. He preached the Second Crusade in 1146, which ended in failure and troubled him greatly. His sermons on the Song of Songs and his writings on love for God are classics of Christian spirituality. He remained abbot until his death at Clairvaux in 1153.

UO-SIN-000052.name: Tan Sri John Savarimuthu
UO-SIN-000052.life: John Gurubatham Savarimuthu was born in 1925 in South India and studied theology at Tirumaraiyur. Ordained in 1952 for the Diocese of Singapore and Malaya, he served as a curate and parish priest in Seremban and Johor. In 1972 he became the second bishop of West Malaysia and was consecrated in 1973. He championed theological education, helping to found the Malaysia Theological Seminary and urging that the church be led by Malaysians. He served as president of the Council of Churches of Malaysia and led delegations to government on matters such as the Malay Bible. Honoured with the title Tan Sri in 1980, he served until his death in 1994.

UO-SIN-000054.name: Martin de Porres, Rosa de Lima, and Toribio de Mogrovejo
UO-SIN-000054.life: Three saints of colonial Lima shaped the early faith of South America. Toribio de Mogrovejo, a Spanish lawyer, became archbishop of Lima in 1579, travelled widely over his huge diocese, defended the indigenous people and confirmed Rose and Martin. Rose Flores, born in Lima in 1586, became a Dominican tertiary known for severe penance and for caring for the poor. Martin de Porres, son of a Spanish nobleman and a freed woman of African descent, served the Dominicans as a lay brother, tending the sick and the poor. Toribio died in 1606, Rose in 1617 and Martin in 1639.

UO-SIN-000055.name: Bartholomew the Apostle
UO-SIN-000055.life: Bartholomew is named among the Twelve in the first three Gospels. Most scholars identify him with Nathanael, whom Philip brought to Jesus and whom Jesus called an Israelite without deceit. The New Testament says nothing more about him, but later traditions carry him far afield. Some say he preached in India, leaving a copy of Matthew's Gospel, and others say Mesopotamia, Ethiopia or Armenia, where tradition holds he was martyred, flayed and beheaded or crucified. None of this can be verified. What is certain is that he was one of the first to follow Jesus and to be sent out in his name.
UO-SIN-000055.place: Palestine, and tradition says India and Armenia

UO-SIN-000056.name: Louis IX of France
UO-SIN-000056.life: Louis IX was born in 1214 and became king at twelve, ruling first under his mother Blanche of Castile. As an adult he governed with unusual concern for justice, hearing complaints himself and sending inspectors to check royal officials. He lived simply, fasted, founded hospitals and gave generously to the poor, and he built the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris to house the relic of the crown of thorns. He led the Seventh Crusade and was captured in Egypt in 1250 and ransomed. In 1270 he set out on another crusade to Tunis, where he died of illness on 25 August. He was canonized in 1297.

UO-SIN-000057.name: Simeon Bachos the Ethiopian Eunuch
UO-SIN-000057.life: The Acts of the Apostles describes him as a high official, treasurer to the Candace, queen of the Ethiopians. He had travelled to Jerusalem to worship and was heading home in his chariot, reading the prophet Isaiah, when the evangelist Philip joined him on the road to Gaza. Philip explained that the passage pointed to Jesus, and the man asked to be baptized at the next water they reached. Philip was then taken away, and the official went on his way rejoicing. Early tradition, citing Irenaeus, says he carried the gospel home, and he is honoured as a founding figure of Ethiopian Christianity.

UO-SIN-000058.name: Thomas Gallaudet and Henry Winter Syle
UO-SIN-000058.life: Thomas Gallaudet, born in Hartford in 1822, was the son of a pioneer of deaf education and his deaf wife. After teaching at the New York Institution for the Deaf, he founded St Ann's Church for Deaf Mutes in New York City in 1852, and established a home for aged and infirm deaf people. His student Henry Winter Syle, born in Shanghai in 1846 and deaf from an early age, studied at Trinity College, Hartford, Cambridge and Yale. In 1883 Syle became the first deaf person ordained priest in the Episcopal Church, and founded a congregation for the deaf in Philadelphia. Syle died in 1890 and Gallaudet in 1902.

UO-SIN-000059.name: Augustine of Hippo
UO-SIN-000059.life: Augustine was born in 354 at Thagaste in North Africa. Brilliant but restless, he taught rhetoric, lived with a partner and had a son, and followed the Manichaean sect for some years, all while his Christian mother Monica prayed for him. In Milan, under the preaching of Ambrose, he turned to the faith and was baptized in 387. He returned to Africa, became a priest, and in about 396 bishop of Hippo. He wrote the Confessions, The City of God and many works against the Donatists and Pelagians, shaping Western theology for centuries. He died in 430 while the Vandals besieged Hippo.

UO-SIN-000061.name: Margaret Ward, Margaret Clitherow, and Anne Line
UO-SIN-000061.life: These three women died for helping Catholic priests in Elizabethan England, when such help was a capital crime. Margaret Clitherow, a York butcher's wife and convert, hid priests in her home and was pressed to death in 1586 after refusing to plead. Margaret Ward, a gentlewoman, smuggled a rope to a priest imprisoned in Bridewell so that he could escape, and was hanged at Tyburn in 1588 after refusing to ask pardon. Anne Line, a widow, ran a refuge for hunted priests in London and was hanged at Tyburn in 1601. All three were canonized in 1970 among the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales.

UO-SIN-000062.name: Aidan of Lindisfarne
UO-SIN-000062.life: Aidan was an Irish monk of Iona. In 635 King Oswald of Northumbria, who had spent his exile at Iona, asked for a missionary, and Aidan was sent as bishop. He chose the island of Lindisfarne as his base, near the king's fortress at Bamburgh, and founded a monastery there. Bede describes him as gentle, humble and tireless, travelling on foot to speak with ordinary people and teaching those around him. He gave to the poor and ransomed slaves. He also trained young Englishmen for the priesthood. Aidan died in 651, and he is known as the apostle of Northumbria.

UO-SIN-000290.name: Philip Benizi
UO-SIN-000290.life: Philip Benizi was born into a respected family in Florence in 1233 and trained as a physician before joining the Servite friars in 1254. Ordained priest, he became the order's superior general in 1267 and guided it through uncertain years, helping it grow across Europe. In a land torn by feuding Guelph and Ghibelline factions, he travelled as a gentle peacemaker, notably to the divided town of Forlì in 1283. According to tradition, he hid rather than accept election as pope. He died at Todi in 1285, remembered for humility, patience and the reconciling of enemies.

UO-SIN-000053.name: Alicia “Cristina” Rivera, OSH
UO-SIN-000053.life: Sister Cristina Rivera belonged to the Order of Saint Helena, a community of Episcopal Church women founded in 1945 at Versailles, Kentucky. Sisters of the order live under a rule of prayer, common life and service, praying the daily offices together and carrying their work into parishes, schools and mission fields. Sister Cristina gave her life to that calling, and she died in 1996. Little detail of her work has been recorded in the sources available, but the church remembers her as a faithful monastic, one whose days were shaped by the hours of prayer and by service to the people around her.
UO-SIN-000053.place: Order of Saint Helena, United States

UO-SIN-000787.name: Fulgentius of Ruspe
UO-SIN-000787.life: Fulgentius was born in the North African town of Thelepte into a once-wealthy family ruined by the Vandal conquest. After a spell as a tax official he turned to the monastic life, inspired by the writings of Augustine. Reluctantly made bishop of Ruspe about 508, he kept to monastic simplicity. The Arian Vandal king Thrasamund banished him to Sardinia with dozens of other Catholic bishops, where he became their leader and wrote in defence of Catholic faith and Augustine's teaching on grace. Allowed home after Thrasamund's death in 523, he spent his last years caring for his diocese and died in the early 530s.

UO-SIN-000788.name: William of Volpiano
UO-SIN-000788.life: William was born in 962 on the island of San Giulio in northern Italy and became a monk, joining the great reforming abbey of Cluny. In 990 he was made abbot of Saint-Bénigne at Dijon, which he turned into a centre of prayer and learning. Duke Richard II of Normandy then invited him to Fécamp, and from there he renewed monastic life across Normandy, at Jumièges, Mont-Saint-Michel and elsewhere. He is said to have helped reform some forty houses, and he cared deeply for good liturgy and building. He died on 1 January 1031.

UO-SIN-000789.name: Zdislava of Lemberk
UO-SIN-000789.life: Zdislava was born about 1220 into a Bohemian noble family and, while still young, was married to Havel, lord of Lemberk. He wished her to share the fashions and feasting of his rank, while she gave herself to the poor, nursing the sick and sheltering the homeless. Her patience and gentleness gradually won him over, and together they founded Dominican priories. She became one of the earliest lay members of the Dominican family and received communion unusually often for her time. Tradition tells of visions and miracles. She died at Lemberk in 1252 and was canonized in 1995.

UO-SIN-000618.name: Vedanayagam Samuel Azariah
UO-SIN-000618.life: Born in 1874 in southern India, Azariah was the son of an Indian clergyman. He worked for the YMCA, then helped found the Indian Missionary Society in 1903 and the National Missionary Society two years later, so that Indian Christians could evangelize their own land. Ordained in 1909, he was consecrated in 1912 as bishop of Dornakal, the first Indian bishop in the Anglican Communion. Under him the diocese grew to over two hundred thousand members, many from poor village communities, and he encouraged Indian forms of worship. He worked tirelessly for Christian unity and died on 1 January 1945, two years before the Church of South India was born.

UO-SIN-000791.name: Seraphim of Sarov
UO-SIN-000791.life: Born Prokhor Moshnin to a merchant family in Kursk in the mid-eighteenth century, Seraphim entered the monastery of Sarov as a young man and was later ordained. He spent years as a hermit in the forest, fasting and praying, and was said to feed the wild animals from his hand. After a long seclusion he began to receive visitors, greeting everyone with the words 'Christ is risen, my joy!' Thousands came for counsel and healing, and he cared for the sisters of nearby Diveyevo. He taught that the aim of Christian life is to receive the Holy Spirit. He died at prayer on 2 January 1833.

UO-SIN-000619.name: Geneviève of Paris
UO-SIN-000619.life: Geneviève was born at Nanterre, near Paris, in the early fifth century. Tradition says Bishop Germanus of Auxerre, passing through, saw her promise and encouraged her to give her life to God. Settling in Paris, she lived a strict life of prayer. When Attila and the Huns threatened the region in 451, she urged the frightened citizens to trust in God rather than flee, and the city was spared. She also brought food to the hungry during sieges and pleaded with the Frankish rulers for mercy toward prisoners. She helped begin a church for Saints Peter and Paul, and is honoured as patroness of Paris.

UO-SIN-000794.name: Morris Williams
UO-SIN-000794.life: Morris Williams, known by his bardic name Nicander, was born in Caernarfon in 1809 and educated at Chester and Jesus College, Oxford. Ordained in 1836, he served as curate in Holywell, Bangor, Pentir and Amlwch before becoming rector of Llanrhuddlad on Anglesey in 1859. He was a gifted Welsh poet, winning the chair at the Aberffraw eisteddfod in 1849, and he helped prepare the Welsh Prayer Book of 1841. He also produced a metrical version of the Psalms for singing, and shared the ideals of the Oxford Movement. He died at Llanrhuddlad on 3 January 1874.

UO-SIN-000795.name: Angela of Foligno
UO-SIN-000795.life: Angela was born in 1248 at Foligno in Umbria, married young and, by her own account, lived for a time in worldly pleasure. A deep sorrow for her sins led her to conversion, and around 1291 she joined the Third Order of Saint Francis. Her Franciscan confessor, Brother Arnold, wrote down her accounts of mystical visions and her teaching, gathered in the Book of Visions and Instructions. She gathered a community of women who shared her life of prayer and charity without enclosure. Admired as a teacher of theologians, she died on 4 January 1309 and was buried at the Franciscan church in Foligno.

UO-SIN-000796.name: John Neumann
UO-SIN-000796.life: John Neumann was born in 1811 at Prachatice in Bohemia and studied at Prague. Unable to be ordained at home, he sailed to America and was ordained in New York in 1836. He served German-speaking settlers in rural western New York, travelling long distances, then joined the Redemptorists in 1840. In 1852 he became bishop of Philadelphia. There he organized the first diocesan school system in the United States, built dozens of churches and schools for the swelling immigrant population, and promoted devotion to the Forty Hours. He died on 5 January 1860, and was canonized in 1977.

UO-SIN-000798.name: Raymond of Peñafort
UO-SIN-000798.life: Born near Barcelona about 1175, Raymond studied and taught law at Bologna, then joined the Dominicans in Barcelona. Pope Gregory IX called him to Rome and asked him to gather the scattered decrees of the Church into one orderly collection, which served as Church law for centuries. He wrote a handbook for confessors, declined the archbishopric of Tarragona, and for a time served as master of the Dominican Order. He encouraged the study of Arabic and Hebrew to speak with Muslims and Jews, and advised King James I of Aragon. He lived to about a hundred, dying in 1275.

UO-SIN-000799.name: Apollinaris of Hierapolis
UO-SIN-000799.life: Apollinaris was bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia, in what is now Turkey, during the second century. He was among the early Christian writers who defended the faith in print. He wrote against pagan teaching and against the Jews, and attacked heretical groups, showing that their errors were borrowed from pagan thought. About 177 he addressed an appeal for the Christians to the emperor Marcus Aurelius, recalling the story that the prayers of Christian soldiers had won him rain and victory in battle. Almost none of his writings survive, but later authors kept his name alive. He probably died during Marcus Aurelius's reign.

UO-SIN-000800.name: Lawrence Giustiniani
UO-SIN-000800.life: Lawrence was born in Venice in 1381 to the noble Giustiniani family. As a young man he entered the community of canons on the island of San Giorgio in Alga, later becoming its prior, and shaped its rule of simple living. In 1433 he was named bishop of Castello, and in 1451 became the first patriarch of Venice. He lived plainly and gave generously to the poor, restored churches and encouraged parish life, while winning the respect of both Church and Republic. He also wrote devout treatises on the spiritual life. He died on 8 January 1456 and was canonized in 1690.

UO-SIN-000801.name: Richard Watson
UO-SIN-000801.life: Richard Watson was born in 1781 at Barton-upon-Humber in Lincolnshire and became a Methodist preacher while still young. He rose to leadership of the Wesleyan movement, serving as secretary of its Missionary Society and as president of the Conference in 1826. His great work, the Theological Institutes, published from 1823, was the first full systematic presentation of Methodist teaching and served as a standard textbook for generations in Britain and America. He also wrote a Life of John Wesley and a Biblical and Theological Dictionary. Though he valued the Church of England, he defended Methodist doctrine firmly. He died in London on 8 January 1833.

UO-SIN-000802.name: Adrian of Canterbury
UO-SIN-000802.life: Adrian was a North African, probably from Cyrenaica, who became a monk near Naples and gained a reputation for learning in Greek and Latin. Pope Vitalian offered him the archbishopric of Canterbury, but he declined and proposed his friend Theodore instead, agreeing to accompany him to England in 668. Theodore made him abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter and Saint Paul at Canterbury. There he and Theodore built a famous school, teaching scripture, Latin and Greek, poetry, astronomy and church music to many students. Some of them still spoke Greek and Latin fluently decades later. Adrian died in 709 or 710.

UO-SIN-000803.name: Agatho
UO-SIN-000803.life: Agatho was born in Sicily, probably of Greek descent, and may have been a monk at Palermo before moving to Rome. He became bishop of Rome in 678, reportedly at a very great age. Early in his time he heard the appeal of Wilfrid of York against his removal from his see, and supported him. His chief achievement was to send legates to the Sixth Ecumenical Council at Constantinople, which met in 680 and 681. The council rejected Monothelitism, the teaching that Christ had only one will, and restored unity between Rome and the East. Agatho died in January 681, before the council ended.

UO-SIN-000804.name: David I of Scotland
UO-SIN-000804.life: David was the youngest son of Malcolm III and Saint Margaret, and spent much of his youth at the English court. He became king of Scots in 1124 and ruled until his death in 1153. He brought new towns, castles and royal officers, and issued the first Scottish coinage.
