Deeply pious like his mother, he reorganized the Scottish church into dioceses and founded many monasteries, notably Cistercian houses and Augustinian priories. He also took part in the English civil war on behalf of his niece Matilda. He died at Carlisle on 24 May 1153, remembered as a builder of the medieval kingdom.

UO-SIN-000805.name: Paulinus of Aquileia
UO-SIN-000805.life: Paulinus was born about 730 near Cividale in northeastern Italy and became a teacher in the church school there. After Charlemagne conquered the Lombards, he called Paulinus to his court as a master of grammar, among the scholars of the Carolingian revival. In 787 Charlemagne made him patriarch of Aquileia. He took part in the councils of Regensburg and Frankfurt against Adoptionism, a Spanish teaching about Christ, and wrote against it. He also encouraged the peaceful conversion of the Avars and the Slavs to the north and east. Paulinus wrote hymns and poems as well as treatises. He died in 802.

UO-SIN-000806.name: Benedict Biscop
UO-SIN-000806.life: Born about 628 into a noble Northumbrian family, Benedict served at the court of King Oswiu until, at about twenty-five, he travelled to Rome. He journeyed there several times, and took monastic vows at Lérins. He returned to help the new archbishop, Theodore, and then founded the monastery of Saint Peter at Wearmouth in 674 and its sister house of Saint Paul at Jarrow in 682. He brought masons and glassmakers from Gaul to build in stone, and gathered a fine library from his travels. The young Bede grew up in these monasteries. Benedict died on 12 January 689 or 690.

UO-SIN-000807.name: Marguerite Bourgeoys
UO-SIN-000807.life: Born in Troyes, France, in 1620, Marguerite sailed to the young colony of Montreal in 1653 at the invitation of its governor. In 1658 she opened the town's first school in a converted stable. She taught the children of settlers and Indigenous families, and welcomed the young women who came from France to marry. Believing that teaching sisters should be free to go among the people, she founded the Congregation of Notre Dame, a community of women who took vows but were not enclosed. Its rule was approved in 1698. She died in Montreal on 12 January 1700 and was canonized in 1982, Canada's first woman saint.

UO-SIN-000584.name: John Horden
UO-SIN-000584.life: John Horden was born in Exeter in 1828 and in 1851 went to Moose Factory on Hudson Bay as a teacher for the Hudson's Bay Company. He quickly learned Cree and was ordained priest in 1852. He travelled widely among the Cree, Ojibwa and Inuit, translating prayers, hymns and Scripture into their languages, many printed in syllabic script, and published a Cree grammar in 1881. He was consecrated first bishop of Moosonee in 1872 and served for over forty years, building churches and schools across a vast northern diocese. He died at Moose Factory on 12 January 1893 and is buried there.

UO-SIN-000808.name: Kentigern / Mungo
UO-SIN-000808.life: According to tradition, Kentigern was born near Culross in Fife, the son of a British princess, and was raised by Saint Serf. He became a missionary on the River Clyde, where a Christian community gathered around his cell and grew into the city of Glasgow. Tradition says hostility forced him into exile in Wales, where he founded a monastery at what became Saint Asaph, before he returned to Strathclyde. Known affectionately as Mungo, 'dear one,' he is remembered in stories of a robin, a tree, a bell and a fish, still shown in Glasgow's arms. He is Glasgow's patron, and his tomb lies in the cathedral.

UO-SIN-000809.name: Sava of Serbia
UO-SIN-000809.life: Born Rastko, youngest son of the Serbian ruler Stefan Nemanja, Sava ran away as a young man to Mount Athos and became a monk. With his father, who also became a monk, he founded Hilandar monastery, which became a Serbian spiritual centre. Returning home, he reconciled his quarrelling brothers and worked to strengthen the Church. In 1219 he was consecrated the first archbishop of an independent Serbian Church, and he translated Byzantine church law for his people. He twice went on pilgrimage to the Holy Land. He died at Tarnovo in Bulgaria on 14 January 1235, and is honoured as the patron of Serbia.

UO-SIN-000811.name: Felix of Nola
UO-SIN-000811.life: Felix lived in the third century at Nola near Naples, the son of a Syrian-born soldier. After his father's death he gave most of his goods to the poor and was ordained priest by Bishop Maximus. During the persecution under the emperor Decius he was seized, imprisoned and beaten. Stories tell that an angel freed him, and that a spider spun a web across the entrance to his hiding place so that his pursuers passed by. After Maximus died, Felix refused to be made bishop, and lived on a few acres he farmed himself, sharing the produce with the needy. His tomb at Nola drew pilgrims for centuries.

UO-SIN-000812.name: Paul the Hermit
UO-SIN-000812.life: Paul, from the Egyptian Thebaid, is remembered as the first Christian hermit. According to the account written by Jerome, he fled into the desert during a persecution in the third century and found a cave beside a spring and a palm tree. There, tradition says, he lived for decades in prayer, a raven bringing him half a loaf of bread each day. In his old age Antony the Great, led by God, visited him, and the two shared a loaf and spoke together. Paul soon died, and Antony buried him, helped by two lions that dug the grave. Paul is said to have lived to about 113.

UO-SIN-000813.name: Habakkuk and Micah
UO-SIN-000813.life: Habakkuk and Micah are two of the twelve Minor Prophets of the Old Testament. Micah came from the village of Moresheth in Judah and spoke in the eighth century before Christ, a contemporary of Isaiah. He denounced rulers who crushed the poor, and foretold a ruler from Bethlehem; his best known words ask what the Lord requires but to do justice, love kindness and walk humbly with God. Habakkuk prophesied near the end of the seventh century, as Babylon rose. He boldly asked God why evil seemed to prosper, and was answered that the righteous live by faith. His book ends with a hymn of trust.

UO-SIN-000632.name: Honoratus of Arles
UO-SIN-000632.life: Honoratus was born about 350 in northern Gaul into a distinguished pagan family, and he and his brother Venantius became Christians as young men. They set out for the East to visit holy places, but Venantius died on the way. Returning, Honoratus settled on the island of Lérins off the southern French coast, where disciples gathered and a monastery grew that sent out many bishops and writers. In 426 he was called to be archbishop of Arles, where he restored order while still guiding Lérins from afar. He died in Arles in about 429, and the island now bears his name.

UO-SIN-000814.name: Priscilla of Rome
UO-SIN-000814.life: Priscilla is remembered as a wealthy Roman Christian woman of the first century. According to tradition, Saint Peter converted her family, and she offered her villa on the Via Salaria as a base for his work. Her husband, the consul Manius Acilius Glabrio, and her son Pudens are said to have died for the faith, and tradition says Priscilla herself suffered martyrdom. The great Roman burial ground that bears her name, the catacomb of Priscilla, grew up on her land and holds early Christian paintings, among them an early picture of Mary with the child Jesus. Much about her remains uncertain, and the accounts rest on later tradition.

UO-SIN-000815.name: Sulpicius of Bourges
UO-SIN-000815.life: Sulpicius, called the Pious, was born at Vatan in central France to a noble family, and from youth gave himself to good works and the study of Scripture. Bishop Austregisilus of Bourges ordained him and put him in charge of the cathedral school. King Clotaire II made him chaplain to his armies, and around 624 he succeeded Austregisilus as bishop of Bourges. He worked to restore discipline among the clergy, to help the poor, and to speak up for his people over taxes. Near the end of his life he appointed a coadjutor and retired to a monastery he had founded, dying in 646 or 647.

UO-SIN-000635.name: Wulfstan of Worcester
UO-SIN-000635.life: Wulfstan was born about 1008 near Warwick, educated by monks, and became a monk and prior at Worcester. In 1062 he was made bishop of Worcester, and he remained bishop for over thirty years. After the Norman Conquest he submitted to William the Conqueror and kept his see, becoming the last of the English-born bishops of the old order. He was a devoted pastor who rebuilt his cathedral, founded Great Malvern Priory, and with Archbishop Lanfranc preached against the slave trade out of Bristol. He died in January 1095 and was canonized in 1203.

UO-SIN-000817.name: Commemoration of Scottish Saints and Martyrs of the Reformation Period
UO-SIN-000817.life: During the Reformation in Scotland, a number of people were put to death for their faith. Patrick Hamilton, a young scholar who had studied Lutheran teaching on the Continent, was burned at St Andrews in 1528 and became the first martyr of the Scottish Reformation. George Wishart, a gifted teacher and preacher who travelled the country, was hanged and burned there in 1546. Walter Myln, an elderly former priest, was burned in 1558, declaring that he was corn, not chaff, and would not be blown away by the wind. Their deaths strengthened the reforming cause and helped change Scotland's church.

UO-SIN-000819.name: Sebastian
UO-SIN-000819.life: Sebastian was a Roman martyr of the Diocletian persecution, honoured at Rome from at least the fourth century, and Ambrose of Milan tells us he came from Milan. According to tradition he was an officer of the imperial guard who quietly served persecuted Christians. Condemned, he was tied to a post and shot with arrows, but a Christian widow named Irene found him alive and nursed him back to health. He then confronted the emperor Diocletian about his cruelty and was clubbed to death, around the year 288. Sebastian has long been invoked in times of plague and is the patron of archers and athletes.

UO-SIN-000391.name: Richard Rolle
UO-SIN-000391.life: Richard Rolle was born around 1300 into a farming family at Thornton-le-Dale in Yorkshire and studied at Oxford, but left without a degree, about the age of nineteen, to become a hermit. He lived near Pickering on the estate of a former fellow student, John Dalton, and later in other solitary places in the north of England. He described a burning sense of divine love and wrote about it in Latin and English, in works such as The Form of Perfect Living, for ordinary readers and for nuns. He died at Hampole in 1349, probably of the plague, and many pilgrims visited his grave.

UO-SIN-000820.name: Agnes of Rome
UO-SIN-000820.life: Agnes was a young girl of Rome, perhaps twelve or thirteen, who died for her faith in the early fourth century, during the persecution under Diocletian. Tradition says she refused marriage because she had given herself to Christ, and that she was denounced as a Christian by disappointed suitors. She would not offer sacrifice, and she was beheaded. Her courage so moved the Roman people that, within a few decades, a church was raised over her grave on the Via Nomentana. Ambrose praised her in his preaching. Agnes is shown holding a lamb, a play on her name, which resembles the Latin word for lamb.

UO-SIN-000822.name: Anastasius the Persian
UO-SIN-000822.life: Anastasius was born in Persia, the son of a Zoroastrian priest, and was named Magundat. He served as a soldier in the army of King Khosrow II, which in 614 seized the True Cross at Jerusalem and carried it to Persia. Curious about the faith that the cross represented, he was baptised in Palestine, took the name Anastasius, and became a monk near Jerusalem. After seven years he went to Caesarea, openly challenged the Persian priests there, and was arrested. He refused every bribe and threat, was tortured, and was strangled and beheaded in 628, along with seventy others.

UO-SIN-000823.name: Ildephonsus of Toledo
UO-SIN-000823.life: Ildephonsus was born into a noble Visigothic family at Toledo around 607. Against his family's wishes he became a monk at the monastery of Agali near the city, where he was later elected abbot. In 657 King Recceswinth pressed him to become Archbishop of Toledo, and he held the office for about ten years. He was a learned writer, best known for a treatise defending the perpetual virginity of Mary, and he wrote a short book on illustrious men of the Spanish church. According to tradition, Mary appeared to him in the cathedral and gave him a vestment. He died in 667.

UO-SIN-000824.name: Mary Ward
UO-SIN-000824.life: Mary Ward was born in 1585 in Yorkshire, in an England where Catholics were fined, hunted and imprisoned. She crossed to the Continent and, in 1609, began a community of women at Saint-Omer. She wanted them to live as active teachers and carers in the world, free of the cloister, following a rule modelled on that of the Jesuits. Many opposed so new an idea. In 1631 the Pope suppressed her institute, and she was briefly imprisoned as a heretic. She kept faith and returned to England, and died near York in 1645. Her sisters, now known as the Sisters of Loreto and the Congregation of Jesus, run schools worldwide.

UO-SIN-000825.name: Francis de Sales
UO-SIN-000825.life: Francis de Sales was born in 1567 into a noble family of Savoy and trained as a lawyer before choosing the priesthood. He worked among Calvinists around Geneva, winning people by patient, gentle persuasion rather than argument. In 1602 he became Bishop of Geneva, though he lived at Annecy. He is best known for the Introduction to the Devout Life, which teaches that holiness is open to ordinary people in every walk of life, and for his Treatise on the Love of God. With Jane Frances de Chantal he founded the Sisters of the Visitation. He died in 1622, and his kindly spirit is still remembered.

UO-SIN-000368.name: Cadoc
UO-SIN-000368.life: Cadoc, also called Cadog, was a Welsh abbot of the late fifth and sixth centuries and founded the great monastery of Llancarfan in Glamorgan. By tradition he was the son of Gwynllyw, a petty king of Gwynllwg, and his wife Gwladys. Llancarfan became a famous centre of learning, and Illtud and Gildas are said to have studied or taught there. Cadoc is credited with founding churches in Wales, Cornwall and Brittany, and the Welsh remembered him as Cadoc the Wise for his many sayings. The old stories about him are legendary in detail, so his exact dates and travels are uncertain.

UO-SIN-000826.name: Poppo of Stavelot
UO-SIN-000826.life: Poppo was born around 977 in Flanders, a knight from a noble family. After a pilgrimage to Jerusalem and a visit to Rome, he was moved by a spiritual conversion, and around 1005 he entered the monastery of Saint-Thierry at Reims. He became a trusted helper of the reforming abbot Richard of Saint-Vanne. In 1020 the emperor Henry II made him abbot of Stavelot and Malmedy, and later emperors placed many other abbeys under his care. He spread stricter monastic observance across Lorraine and Germany and lived with severe self-denial. Poppo died at Marchiennes in 1048.

UO-SIN-000827.name: Timothy, Titus, and Silas
UO-SIN-000827.life: Timothy, Titus and Silas were fellow workers of the apostle Paul. Silas, a respected leader of the Jerusalem church, travelled with Paul on his second journey and shared his imprisonment at Philippi. Timothy, from Lystra, had a Jewish mother and a Greek father. He became Paul's close companion, and two New Testament letters are addressed to him as leader of the church at Ephesus. Titus, a Gentile convert, carried Paul's letters to Corinth and was later left in charge of the churches on Crete. Together they show how the gospel spread through trusted partners who shared the apostle's labours and dangers.

UO-SIN-000828.name: Paula of Rome
UO-SIN-000828.life: Paula was born in 347 into a noble Roman family, married young and was widowed with several children. Moved by the example of ascetic teaching in Rome, she embraced a life of prayer and charity. In 385 she travelled with her daughter Eustochium to the Holy Land and settled at Bethlehem near Jerome, whom she had met in Rome. There she gave away her wealth to found a monastery for men, a convent for women and a hostel for pilgrims. She studied Hebrew and Scripture with Jerome and supported his translating work. Paula died at Bethlehem in 404, and Jerome wrote a moving account of her life.

UO-SIN-000829.name: Lydia, Dorcas, and Phoebe
UO-SIN-000829.life: Lydia, Dorcas and Phoebe are women of the New Testament known for faith and service. Lydia was a merchant in purple cloth from Thyatira who met Paul at Philippi. She and her household were baptised, and she welcomed the missionaries into her home. Dorcas, also called Tabitha, lived at Joppa and was known for her good works and for making clothes for the poor widows. Acts tells how Peter raised her to life. Phoebe served the church at Cenchreae near Corinth, and Paul commended her as a deacon and benefactor and probably trusted her to carry his letter to Rome.

UO-SIN-000830.name: George Matulaitis
UO-SIN-000830.life: George Matulaitis was born in 1871 in Lithuania, into a peasant family, and became a priest after studies at Kielce, Warsaw and Fribourg. In 1911 he secretly joined the Marian Fathers, then nearly extinct, and as their superior general revived the congregation. In 1918 Pope Benedict XV made him Bishop of Vilnius, a city torn by Polish and Lithuanian rivalry. Caught between the two sides, he faced great pressure and resigned in 1925. He founded two communities of sisters, and later served as a papal envoy to Lithuania. He died at Kaunas in 1927 and was beatified in 1987.

UO-SIN-000831.name: Agnes Tsao Kou Ying
UO-SIN-000831.life: Agnes Tsao Kou Ying was born in 1821 in Guizhou, China, into a Catholic family. Orphaned young, she was taught the faith by missionaries and a devout widow, and later married, but her husband died after two years and she was driven out of his family's home. A French priest, Auguste Chapdelaine, recognised her knowledge of the faith and sent her to Guangxi province, where she taught Catholic families and children. In 1856 she was arrested with Chapdelaine. Refusing to renounce Christ, she was shut in a cage so small she could only stand, and died there after three days. She was canonised in 2000.

UO-SIN-000832.name: Andrei Rublev
UO-SIN-000832.life: Andrei Rublev, born around 1360, was Russia's greatest medieval icon painter. Little is known of his life. He probably lived as a monk at the Trinity Lavra of St Sergius, and in 1405 he worked in the Kremlin's Annunciation Cathedral beside Theophanes the Greek. He painted at Vladimir and at the Trinity Lavra, and later at the Andronikov Monastery in Moscow, where he died around 1430. His Old Testament Trinity, showing three angels seated around a chalice, is his one surviving work known to be entirely his own. It is admired for its calm, gentle harmony and became a model of Orthodox iconography.

UO-SIN-000833.name: Gildas
UO-SIN-000833.life: Gildas was a British monk of the sixth century, remembered as the Wise. He was educated in the monastic school of Illtud in Wales and became a renowned teacher. He is best known for his Latin work on the ruin of Britain, which scolds the kings and clergy of his day for their sins and tells how the island fell to the Saxons. It is one of the few written accounts of Britain in that age. Later tradition says he made a pilgrimage to Rome and settled in Brittany, where he lived as a hermit and then founded a monastery at Rhuys. He died around 570.

UO-SIN-000834.name: Bathild
UO-SIN-000834.life: Bathild was born around 626, probably in England, and was sold as a slave into the household of Erchinoald, a high official of the Frankish kingdom of Neustria. The king, Clovis II, noticed her and married her. As queen she was humble and generous, and she helped found the abbeys of Corbie and Chelles. After Clovis died, she ruled as regent for her young son Chlothar III. She worked to end the sale of Christian slaves and to free children who had been sold. When her political position weakened she withdrew to her abbey at Chelles, where she lived as a nun and died in 680.

UO-SIN-000835.name: Adelelmus of Burgos
UO-SIN-000835.life: Adelelmus was born at Loudun in Poitou and served as a soldier when young. On a pilgrimage to Rome he met Robert of Turlande, founder of La Chaise-Dieu, and left arms to become a Benedictine monk there. He became known for his holiness. About 1079 Queen Constance and King Alfonso VI of Castile invited him to Burgos and founded a monastery there with him as abbot. He added a hospital and a church to the foundation. He is said to have helped the king against the Moors, using his soldier's skills. Adelelmus died around 1097 and is still honoured as a patron of the city.

UO-SIN-000836.name: John Bosco
UO-SIN-000836.life: John Bosco was born in 1815 to a poor farming family near Turin. Ordained in 1841, he began gathering the street boys and young workers of the city, teaching them the faith and a trade, and giving them play and fellowship. His Oratory grew to hundreds of boys. He founded schools, workshops and hostels, and in 1859 started the Society of St Francis de Sales, the Salesians, to carry on the work, with later sisters to help girls. He relied on kindness, reason and cheerful affection rather than punishment. He died at Turin in 1888, and Salesians now serve young people around the world.

UO-SIN-000837.name: Samuel Shoemaker
UO-SIN-000837.life: Samuel Shoemaker, born in 1893, was an Episcopal priest and one of the most admired preachers of his time. As rector of Calvary Church in New York from 1925 to 1952, he made it a centre of lively evangelism, where people were encouraged to share their faith and to change. He founded the magazine Faith at Work. He worked closely with the Oxford Group, and its ideas of honesty and surrender influenced Bill Wilson, a founder of Alcoholics Anonymous. Shoemaker later served Calvary Church in Pittsburgh, retired in 1962 and died in 1963. He is remembered as a spiritual guide to many people in need.

UO-SIN-000838.name: Charles Mackenzie of Central Africa
UO-SIN-000838.life: Charles Mackenzie was born in Scotland in 1825 and studied at Cambridge, where he was a brilliant mathematician. Ordained in the Church of England, he went to Natal as an archdeacon. In 1860 he was chosen to lead the Universities' Mission to Central Africa, and he was consecrated bishop in Cape Town in 1861. He sailed up the Zambezi and Shire rivers with David Livingstone and settled at Magomero in the Shire highlands, where he opposed the slave trade. Short of medicine, he fell ill with fever and died on 31 January 1862 on an island in the Shire River, only a year after his consecration.

UO-SIN-000839.name: Laurence of Canterbury
UO-SIN-000839.life: Laurence was a Roman monk who came to England with Augustine's mission to convert the Anglo-Saxons. Augustine sent him back to Rome to report to Pope Gregory the Great, and he returned with the pope's replies to the mission's questions. About 604 he succeeded Augustine as Archbishop of Canterbury. He tried, without success, to reconcile the native British bishops with the Roman mission. When King Eadbald succeeded his father in 616 and turned back to paganism, Laurence nearly left the country. According to tradition, a vision of Saint Peter stopped him, and the king was won back to the faith. Laurence died on 2 February 619.

UO-SIN-000840.name: The Dorchester Chaplains
UO-SIN-000840.life: On 3 February 1943 the troopship Dorchester, carrying about nine hundred men to Greenland, was torpedoed by a German submarine in the freezing North Atlantic. Four army chaplains aboard calmed the frightened men and handed out lifejackets. They were George Fox, a Methodist minister, Alexander Goode, a Jewish rabbi, Clark Poling, a Dutch Reformed minister, and John Washington, a Catholic priest. When the lifejackets ran out they gave up their own. Survivors saw them last on the deck, arms linked, praying together as the ship went down. Only about 230 men survived. Their shared sacrifice across lines of faith has become a lasting witness.

UO-SIN-000841.name: Blaise of Sebaste
UO-SIN-000841.life: Blaise was bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, now Sivas in Turkey, and was martyred early in the fourth century, most likely under the emperor Licinius. Accounts of his life are late, and tradition holds that he may have been a physician before becoming bishop. It is said that he withdrew to a cave during persecution, where wild animals came to him and he healed them. Arrested, he cured a boy who was choking on a fishbone. He was tortured with iron combs and beheaded. In the Middle Ages he became one of the best loved saints in the West, and he is invoked against throat ailments.

UO-SIN-000842.name: Seiriol
UO-SIN-000842.life: Seiriol was a Welsh saint of the sixth century. According to tradition he was a son of Owain Danwyn, a prince of Rhos in north Wales, and a brother of two kings. He founded a small monastic community at Penmon on the eastern tip of Anglesey, beside a spring still known as his well. In old age he retreated to a nearby island, now called Puffin Island, and lived there as a hermit. Legend tells of his weekly meetings with his friend Cybi, who walked from Holyhead to meet him halfway across Anglesey. Seiriol was called the Fair and Cybi the Tanned.

UO-SIN-000843.name: Gilbert of Sempringham
UO-SIN-000843.life: Gilbert was born around 1085 at Sempringham in Lincolnshire, the son of a Norman lord. After studying in France he returned to teach and was ordained priest. Around 1131 he arranged a rule of life for a group of local women who wished to live as nuns. Helpers and lay brothers joined them, and canons were added to serve the nuns spiritually, so that he founded a new religious order, the Gilbertines, the only one of English origin in the Middle Ages. Pope Eugenius III approved it in 1148. Gilbert lived to a great age, and died at Sempringham in 1189. The order's houses cared for the poor and sick.

UO-SIN-000844.name: The Martyrs of Japan
UO-SIN-000844.life: In 1597, during the persecution of Christians ordered by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, twenty-six Christians were arrested in Kyoto and Osaka and made to walk some six hundred miles to Nagasaki. Among them were six European and Mexican Franciscan missionaries led by Peter Baptist, three Japanese Jesuits including Paul Miki, and seventeen Japanese laypeople, three of them boys serving at Mass. On 5 February 1597 they were crucified on a hill above the city. The dying men sang hymns and encouraged one another, and Paul Miki preached from his cross. Their deaths strengthened Japan's small Christian community, which survived underground for over two centuries.

UO-SIN-000845.name: Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson
UO-SIN-000845.life: Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson were two seventeenth-century colonists who challenged the Puritan leaders of Massachusetts over matters of conscience. Williams, a minister, argued that the state had no power over faith and that settlers should buy land fairly from the native peoples. Banished in 1635, he founded Providence in 1636 as a refuge for liberty of conscience. Hutchinson, a midwife in Boston, led gatherings that taught salvation by grace and criticised the colony's clergy. She was banished in 1638, helped found Portsmouth in Rhode Island, and was killed in 1643 in an attack on her new home near New York. Williams died in 1683.

UO-SIN-000846.name: Adelaide of Vilich
UO-SIN-000846.life: Adelaide was born around 970, a daughter of the Count of Geldern and a descendant of King Henry the Fowler. As a child she was placed in the convent of Saint Ursula in Cologne. Her parents founded a convent at Vilich, near Bonn, in memory of her brother Godfrey, who was killed in battle, and Adelaide became its first abbess. She led the community to follow the Rule of Saint Benedict. Around the year 1000 she was also made abbess of Saint Mary in the Capitol at Cologne, where she fed the poor in times of famine. She died around 1015.

UO-SIN-000847.name: Vedast of Arras
UO-SIN-000847.life: Vedast was a hermit near Toul in eastern Gaul who was chosen to instruct the Frankish king Clovis in the Christian faith as the king travelled toward baptism at Reims. Tradition says he restored the sight of a blind man on the road, and after Clovis was baptised by Remigius, Vedast was consecrated bishop of Arras, a region where the faith had faded. He later also oversaw Cambrai. He died about 540. His relics rest in the great abbey of Saint-Vaast, and in England his name became Foster, honoured in several old churches.

UO-SIN-000849.name: Pius IX
UO-SIN-000849.life: Giovanni Maria Mastai-Ferretti, born in Senigallia in 1792, was elected pope in 1846 and held the office for nearly thirty-two years, the longest papal reign in history. He began with an amnesty and modest reforms, but the revolutions of 1848 drove him from Rome and turned him firmly against liberalism. In 1854 he defined the Immaculate Conception as dogma, and the First Vatican Council, which he called, defined papal infallibility in 1870. That year Italian troops took Rome, and he lived on as a self-styled prisoner in the Vatican until his death in 1878.

UO-SIN-000850.name: Jerome Emiliani
UO-SIN-000850.life: Born in Venice about 1486 to a patrician family, Jerome Emiliani was a soldier who was captured while defending a fortress in 1508. According to tradition he was freed after praying to Our Lady, and he turned to a life of service. During the famine and plague of the 1520s he cared for abandoned and orphaned children, renting a house for them and helping them learn a trade and the faith. He founded orphanages and hospitals across northern Italy and, in 1532, a community of clergy and laymen at Somasca. He died there in 1537 of illness caught while nursing the sick.

UO-SIN-000851.name: Ælfflæd of Whitby
UO-SIN-000851.life: Ælfflæd was the daughter of King Oswiu of Northumbria, who dedicated her to God as an infant in thanksgiving for a victory in battle. She was raised at Whitby under the great abbess Hilda, and when Hilda died in 680 she became abbess there, ruling alongside her widowed mother Eanflæd. Respected as a counsellor across the kingdom, she helped reconcile Bishop Wilfrid with Archbishop Theodore, and she supported Cuthbert. She helped secure the throne for her young nephew Osred in 705. She died in 714, long remembered for her holiness and her care of the sick.

UO-SIN-000852.name: Teilo
UO-SIN-000852.life: Teilo was a Welsh churchman of the sixth century, born near Penally in Pembrokeshire. According to tradition he studied under Dubricius and Paulinus and became a close companion of David. He is said to have founded the monastery at Llandeilo Fawr and to have led the church at Llandaff. When a deadly plague struck Wales, he is said to have taken refuge in Brittany for some years before returning. Dozens of churches in Wales, Cornwall and Brittany bear his name. Legend adds that after his death three places claimed his body, and each received a miraculous copy.

UO-SIN-000853.name: Miguel Febres Cordero
UO-SIN-000853.life: Francisco Febres Cordero was born in 1854 in Cuenca, Ecuador, into a prominent family and was lame from birth. Against his family's wishes, he joined the Brothers of the Christian Schools at fourteen and took the name Miguel, the first Ecuadorian to do so. A gifted teacher in Quito, he wrote textbooks, including a widely used Spanish grammar, and was admitted to academies in Ecuador and Spain. Called to Europe in 1907 to translate texts for exiled brothers, he cared for novices in Spain, and died of pneumonia at Premià de Mar in 1910. He was canonised in 1984.

UO-SIN-000854.name: William of Maleval
UO-SIN-000854.life: William was a Frenchman, said to have lived a rough and worldly early life, who went to Rome and was sent by Pope Eugenius III on a penitential pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Returning to Italy about 1153, he lived as a hermit in the Tuscan countryside, moving from place to place until in 1155 he settled in the lonely valley of Maleval near Siena. Disciples gathered around him, and he was known for prophecy and miracles. He died there in 1157. His followers became the Hermits of Saint William, later absorbed into the Augustinians, and he was recognised as a saint in 1202.

UO-SIN-000656.name: The Consecration of Barbara Clementine Harris
UO-SIN-000656.life: On 11 February 1989, in Boston, Barbara Harris was consecrated suffragan bishop of Massachusetts, the first woman bishop in the Anglican Communion. Born in Philadelphia in 1930, she had worked in public relations and marched for civil rights in Selma and Mississippi before being ordained in 1980. Her election in 1988 drew fierce opposition, partly because she was a woman, a divorcee and a Black priest without seminary training. Some conservatives left to form a new body. Thousands attended the service, and more than sixty bishops laid hands on her. She served until 2002 and died in 2020.

UO-SIN-000857.name: Cædmon
UO-SIN-000857.life: Cædmon was an unlettered herdsman attached to the abbey of Whitby in the days of the abbess Hilda. Bede tells that he once left a feast in shame because he could not sing, and slept among the animals. In a dream someone told him to sing of creation, and he woke able to compose verses praising God. Hilda received him as a monk and had him taught the scriptures, which he turned into Old English song. His nine-line Hymn survives, among the earliest poems in English. He died between about 670 and 680, and a cross at Whitby recalls him.

UO-SIN-000657.name: Theodora the Empress
UO-SIN-000657.life: Born in Paphlagonia about 815, Theodora married the Byzantine emperor Theophilos in 830. Although he opposed the veneration of icons, she is said to have kept them secretly in the palace. When he died in 842 she became regent for their young son Michael III. In 843 she brought the long iconoclast controversy to an end, restoring the icons in a council and a procession on the first Sunday of Lent, still kept as the Triumph of Orthodoxy. After Michael came of age she withdrew from government, and she died about 867.

UO-SIN-000859.name: Meletius of Antioch
UO-SIN-000859.life: Meletius was born in Melitene in Armenia and became bishop of Sebaste before being chosen bishop of Antioch about 360, when the church hoped a moderate man might calm the quarrels over Arianism. Instead the emperors exiled him three times, and the Antiochene church split into rival Nicene groups. He was nevertheless admired for his gentleness and orthodoxy, and he ordained Basil as a deacon and baptised John Chrysostom. Restored to Antioch under a new emperor in 378 or 379, he presided at the Council of Constantinople in 381 and died during it.

UO-SIN-000860.name: Benedict of Aniane
UO-SIN-000860.life: Born Witiza about 750, the son of a Visigothic count in southern Gaul, he served at the Frankish court and in Charlemagne's army. After nearly drowning, he left that life for the cloister, and about 779 he founded a monastery on his own land at Aniane. There he first tried a severe ascetic life, then turned to the Rule of Saint Benedict. As chief adviser to Louis the Pious, he guided the Aachen synods of 816 and 817, which sought to bring the monasteries of the empire under one Rule. He died in 821 and is called the second Benedict.

UO-SIN-000861.name: Jordan of Saxony
UO-SIN-000861.life: Jordan was born about 1190 in Saxony and studied in Paris, where he met the Dominican friars and joined them in 1220. After Dominic died in 1221, the brothers chose Jordan to lead the order, and he held that office until 1237. A warm and persuasive preacher, he drew many university students into the order, among them the future scholar Albert the Great, and he saw it spread across Europe. He wrote the earliest life of Dominic and many affectionate letters to Dominican nuns. Returning from the Holy Land in 1237, he died in a shipwreck off the Syrian coast.

UO-SIN-000862.name: Valentine of Rome / Valentine traditions
UO-SIN-000862.life: The early martyrologies name more than one Valentine on 14 February. One was a priest at Rome and another a bishop of Interamna, now Terni, and both were said to be buried along the Flaminian Way. The surviving accounts of them are late and unreliable, and scholars suspect one man may stand behind both. According to tradition, a Valentine was beheaded outside Rome in the third century under Emperor Claudius for refusing to deny Christ. The link with romantic love came much later, in medieval England. The saint himself is remembered as a martyr of the early Roman church.

UO-SIN-000863.name: Sigfrid of Sweden
UO-SIN-000863.life: Sigfrid was an English missionary bishop of the early eleventh century, said by tradition to have come from Glastonbury or York. He worked in Norway and then in Sweden, where he is credited with baptising King Olof Skötkonung at Husaby, and with founding the church around Växjö, which became his resting place. According to legend, pagans murdered his three nephews while he was away, and when the king offered vengeance or payment, Sigfrid refused both. Details of his life are uncertain, but he is honoured as the apostle of Sweden, and he is said to have died in the 1040s.

UO-SIN-000864.name: Claude de la Colombière
UO-SIN-000864.life: Born in 1641 near Lyon, Claude entered the Jesuits in 1659 and became a noted preacher. In 1675 he was made superior of the Jesuit house at Paray-le-Monial, where he became confessor to the Visitation nun Margaret Mary Alacoque, and he took her visions of the Sacred Heart seriously and spread the devotion. Sent to London in 1676 as preacher to the Duchess of York, he was arrested in 1678 during the Popish Plot panic and imprisoned, and then banished. His health broken, he returned to Paray, where he died in 1682. He was canonised in 1992.

UO-SIN-000865.name: Onesimus
UO-SIN-000865.life: Onesimus was a slave of Philemon, a Christian of Colossae, who ran away and met Paul in prison, where he became a believer. Paul sent him back with the short letter to Philemon, asking that he be received no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother. He is also named in Colossians as a faithful companion who travelled with Tychicus. Later tradition, which cannot be verified, says that he became bishop of Ephesus, an office Ignatius of Antioch also attributes to an Onesimus, and that he was martyred under Trajan. His story shows the gospel's power to change relationships between master and servant.

UO-SIN-000866.name: Elias and Companions
UO-SIN-000866.life: Elias, Jeremiah, Isaiah, Samuel and Daniel were five Egyptian Christians who took the names of Old Testament prophets. During the persecution under Maximinus, they travelled to Cilicia to comfort fellow Christians condemned to work in the mines. On their return they were seized at the gates of Caesarea in Palestine and brought before the governor Firmilian. Asked where they came from, they answered that they were from Jerusalem, meaning the heavenly city. They were tortured and beheaded about 309. The historian Eusebius, who lived at Caesarea, recorded their witness, along with that of Porphyry, a servant who was burned for asking to bury them.

UO-SIN-000867.name: Finan of Lindisfarne
UO-SIN-000867.life: Finan was an Irish monk trained at Iona who succeeded Aidan as bishop of Lindisfarne in 651. Bede describes him as a stern and vigorous leader. He built a church on the island in the Irish manner, of hewn oak thatched with reeds. Under him the mission to the English spread: he baptised Peada, the son of the Mercian king, and Sigebert, king of the East Saxons, and sent priests and bishops, including Cedd, to those lands. He held the see for about ten years and died in 661, shortly before the Synod of Whitby settled the dispute over Easter.

UO-SIN-000868.name: The Seven Founders of the Servite Order
UO-SIN-000868.life: In 1233 seven prosperous merchants of Florence, Bonfilius, Alexis Falconieri, John Bonagiunta, Benedict dell'Antella, Bartholomew Amidei, Gerard Sostegni and Ricoverus Uguccione, withdrew together from the city to live in prayer and penance. Tradition says that the Virgin Mary appeared to them and called them into solitude. They settled first near Florence and then on Monte Senario, where they lived as hermits, and in time they became mendicant friars who served the poor and honoured Mary. Their community grew into the Order of the Servants of Mary, or Servites, and they were canonised together in 1888.

UO-SIN-000869.name: Tarasius of Constantinople
UO-SIN-000869.life: Tarasius was born about 730 into a distinguished family of Constantinople and served at court as imperial secretary. In 784 he was chosen patriarch while still a layman, and he accepted reluctantly, on condition that a general council be called to settle the quarrel over icons. He presided at the Second Council of Nicaea in 787, which restored the veneration of icons. He lived simply, gave generously to the poor, and boldly refused to approve Emperor Constantine VI's divorce and remarriage. He led the church for twenty-two years and died in 806, and was buried in a monastery he had founded on the Bosphorus.

UO-SIN-000870.name: Quodvultdeus of Carthage
UO-SIN-000870.life: Quodvultdeus was a deacon of Carthage and a friend of Augustine, who wrote to him and dedicated a work to him. He became bishop of Carthage by about 437. When the Arian Vandal king Gaiseric captured the city in 439, he seized the Catholic churches and exiled many clergy, and Quodvultdeus with them. They were put aboard poorly equipped ships, but reached Naples safely. There he lived out his years, preaching and writing against heresy. Several of his sermons were long mistaken for Augustine's. He died around 450, and the people of Naples honoured him as a saint.

UO-SIN-000871.name: Thomas Burgess
UO-SIN-000871.life: Thomas Burgess was born in 1756 in Odiham, Hampshire, the son of a grocer, and educated at Winchester and Oxford. A scholar and writer, he became bishop of St Davids in 1803 and set about reform. He insisted that Welsh-speaking parishes receive clergy who knew Welsh, supported Welsh literary gatherings, and in 1822 laid the foundation stone of St David's College, Lampeter, to train clergy. Moved to Salisbury in 1825, he served there until his death in 1837. He was also the first president of the Royal Society of Literature, and his influence on the church in Wales was lasting.

UO-SIN-000872.name: Eucherius of Orléans
UO-SIN-000872.life: Born about 687, Eucherius became a monk at Jumièges around 714 and was made bishop of Orléans in 721. He protested when the powerful Frankish ruler Charles Martel seized church property to pay for his armies. After the ruler's return from the campaign against the Saracens, Eucherius was sent into exile, first to Cologne and then to the region of Liège. He was allowed to retire to the abbey of Sint-Truiden, where he spent his last years in prayer and died in 743. A later legend claimed he saw Charles suffering in hell for his plundering of the church.

UO-SIN-000873.name: Wulfric of Haselbury
UO-SIN-000873.life: Wulfric was born about 1080 near Bristol and became a priest in Wiltshire, where he was fond of hunting until a conversation with a beggar changed him. In 1125 he enclosed himself in a cell beside the church at Haselbury Plucknett in Somerset, and he remained there for nearly thirty years. He fasted, prayed the psalms, wore chain mail, and bathed in cold water, yet found time to copy books. Many came to him for healing and counsel. He told Henry I of his coming death and rebuked King Stephen for bad government. He died on 20 February 1154.

UO-SIN-000874.name: Peter Damian
UO-SIN-000874.life: Born in Ravenna about 1007 to a poor family, Peter Damian studied with such success that he became a teacher before entering the hermitage of Fonte Avellana, which he later led. A severe ascetic and fiery writer, he attacked simony and clerical immorality and worked with the reforming popes of his day. Against his wishes he was made cardinal-bishop of Ostia in 1057, and he served as papal legate in several tense missions. He longed to return to his hermitage, and he finally did. He died at Faenza in 1072, on the way home from a mission, and was named a Doctor of the Church in 1828.

UO-SIN-000875.name: Robert Southwell
UO-SIN-000875.life: Robert Southwell was born about 1561 in Norfolk into a Catholic family and educated at Douai and Paris. He joined the Jesuits and was ordained in Rome in 1584. In 1586 he returned secretly to England, where it was a crime to be a Catholic priest, serving Catholic families and as chaplain to the Countess of Arundel. He wrote devotional prose and poetry, including The Burning Babe, which Ben Jonson admired. Arrested in 1592, he was tortured and held in the Tower of London for three years. He was hanged at Tyburn on 21 February 1595, and was canonised in 1970 among the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales.

UO-SIN-000876.name: Eric Liddell
UO-SIN-000876.life: Eric Liddell was born in 1902 in Tianjin, China, to Scottish missionary parents and was raised in Scotland. A gifted sprinter, he refused to run his best event, the 100 metres, at the 1924 Paris Olympics because the heats fell on a Sunday. He ran the 400 metres instead and won gold in a world record time. The next year he returned to China as a missionary teacher. After Japan invaded, he was interned at Weihsien in 1943, where he organised games and lessons and helped the old and the young. He died there of a brain tumour on 21 February 1945.

UO-SIN-000878.name: Papias of Hierapolis
UO-SIN-000878.life: Papias was bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia in the early second century and is counted among the Apostolic Fathers. According to Irenaeus he had known the apostle John, and he gathered what he could from those who had known the apostles, including the daughters of Philip, who lived at Hierapolis. He wrote a five-volume work, Exposition of the Sayings of the Lord, which survives only in quotations. These preserve early traditions about how the Gospels of Mark and Matthew came to be written. Eusebius thought Papias a man of limited understanding, but his fragments remain valuable evidence of the early church.

UO-SIN-000879.name: Mildburga
UO-SIN-000879.life: Mildburga was a daughter of Merewalh, a ruler in the Mercian west, and a niece of King Wulfhere. She became abbess of the nunnery of Wenlock in Shropshire, founded by her family, and received the veil, tradition says, from Archbishop Theodore. Stories tell of her healing the blind, protecting crops from birds and bringing forth a spring. After her death, her abbey fell to the Danes, but in the early twelfth century monks rediscovered what they believed was her body, and Wenlock became a pilgrimage place. Sources differ about the year of her death, but it was early in the eighth century.

UO-SIN-000880.name: Philip Lindel Tsen and Paul Shinji Sasaki
UO-SIN-000880.life: Philip Tsen, born in 1885 at Wuhu, became the first Chinese presiding bishop of the Chinese Anglican church after serving as bishop of Honan, and in 1930 was the first Chinese bishop at the Lambeth Conference. Paul Sasaki, born in 1885 in Japan, became Bishop of Mid-Japan and later of Tokyo. During the Second World War the two stood together as a sign of Christian unity: in 1937 they travelled to Canada to bear witness that Chinese and Japanese Christians were still one. Sasaki resisted government pressure to merge the churches, was imprisoned and tortured in 1944-45, and died in 1946. Tsen died in 1954.

UO-SIN-000881.name: Æthelberht of Kent
UO-SIN-000881.life: Æthelberht ruled Kent from about 589 until his death in 616 and was the first English king to become a Christian. He had married Bertha, a Christian Frankish princess, who was free to keep her faith at his court. When Augustine and his companions, sent by Pope Gregory the Great, landed in 597, the king received them, gave them a home in Canterbury, and was himself baptized. He did not force his people to follow him. He also issued the earliest surviving written law code in English, setting out fines for injuries and protecting the Church's property.

UO-SIN-000882.name: John Roberts
UO-SIN-000882.life: John Roberts was born in 1853 on a farm at Dyserth in north Wales and studied at Lampeter before ordination in 1878. After a short time as a chaplain in the Bahamas, he went in 1883 to the Wind River Reservation in Wyoming, where he spent the rest of his long life among the Shoshone and Arapaho peoples. He learned their languages, founded schools and congregations, and baptized the Shoshone chief Washakie. Unlike many missionaries of his day, he respected native customs. He was known as Elder Brother, and he died on the reservation in 1949, aged ninety-five.

UO-SIN-000883.name: Walburga
UO-SIN-000883.life: Walburga was born in Wessex around 710 and spent many years as a nun at Wimborne. When her uncle Boniface sought helpers for his mission to the Germans, she travelled to Francia with other English women. She joined her brother Wynnebald at Heidenheim, where he governed a monastery for both men and women, and after his death she ruled the whole community as abbess. She died there around 779, and her relics were later taken to Eichstätt. Pilgrims have long sought help at her shrine, and the festival of Walpurgis Night in Germany is named after her.

UO-SIN-000884.name: Porphyry of Gaza
UO-SIN-000884.life: Porphyry was born about 347 in Thessalonica, gave away his wealth, and lived as a monk in the Egyptian desert and then near Jerusalem. He was ordained priest in 392 and became bishop of Gaza in 395, where the pagan temples still dominated and Christians were few. He pleaded with the imperial court until, in 402, the great temples, including the Marneion, were pulled down; a church rose on the site of the chief shrine. Most of what we know comes from the life by his friend Mark the Deacon. Porphyry died in 420, having turned Gaza into a Christian city.

UO-SIN-000885.name: Julian and Companions of Alexandria
UO-SIN-000885.life: During the persecution under the emperor Decius, around 250, Julian of Alexandria was a man so crippled by gout that he could neither stand nor walk. Slaves carried him before the magistrate, and one of them, Cronion, stayed faithful with him while the other denied Christ. The two were set on camels, whipped through the city, and then burned. A soldier named Besas tried to protect them from the jeering crowd and was beheaded for it. Their story comes from Dionysius, the bishop of Alexandria, who lived through those days and wrote of many others who suffered.

UO-SIN-000886.name: Anna Julia Haywood Cooper and Elizabeth Evelyn Wright
UO-SIN-000886.life: Anna Julia Cooper was born in Raleigh, North Carolina, in 1858 and became a teacher, scholar and writer. She graduated from Oberlin, led the M Street High School in Washington, and wrote A Voice from the South, a landmark of Black feminist thought. At sixty-six she earned a doctorate in Paris, and she lived to 105. Elizabeth Evelyn Wright, born in Georgia in 1872, studied at Tuskegee and in 1897 opened a school in Denmark, South Carolina, that grew into Voorhees College. She died in 1906, aged thirty-four, but both women opened doors of education to African Americans.

UO-SIN-000888.name: Romanus of Condat
UO-SIN-000888.life: Romanus was born around 400 in the region of Gaul near the Jura mountains. At about thirty-five he withdrew to the wild country of Condat to live as a hermit. His younger brother Lupicinus soon joined him, and scholars and seekers gathered around them until the brothers had founded several monasteries, including Condat itself, which later became Saint-Claude, and Romainmôtier in what is now Switzerland. Hilary of Arles ordained Romanus a priest in 444. He and Lupicinus ruled these communities together, and Romanus died around 463. The Jura monasteries became an important centre of early Western monastic life.

UO-SIN-000889.name: Swithbert
UO-SIN-000889.life: Swithbert was an English monk who studied in Ireland and then joined Willibrord's mission to the pagan Frisians around 690, preaching in lands along the lower Rhine under the protection of the Frankish ruler Pepin. In 693 he was consecrated a missionary bishop by Wilfrid of York. When pagan Saxons overran his mission field, he withdrew to a small island in the Rhine, now Kaiserswerth near Düsseldorf, where he founded a monastery. Bede remembered his gentle and modest character. He died there on 1 March 713, and his relics were rediscovered at Kaiserswerth in 1626.

UO-SIN-000890.name: Albinus of Angers
UO-SIN-000890.life: Albinus, known in France as Aubin, was born around 470 to a noble family at Vannes in Brittany. He became a monk and, from 504, abbot of Tintillac, where he was admired for twenty-five years. In 529 he was chosen bishop of Angers, against his own wishes. He spoke out against marriages between close relatives among the nobility, took part in the Council of Orléans in 538, and used church funds to ransom captives seized by pirates. He died on 1 March 550. A church and abbey bearing his name rose over his tomb, and his fame spread across Europe.

UO-SIN-000891.name: Chad (Ceadda) of Lichfield
UO-SIN-000891.life: Chad was an Englishman trained at Lindisfarne under Aidan and perhaps in Ireland. With his brother Cedd he helped found Lastingham in Yorkshire, which he ruled after Cedd's death. King Oswiu made him bishop of the Northumbrians, but when Archbishop Theodore arrived in 669 he asked Chad to step down, and Chad accepted humbly. Theodore then sent him to Mercia, where he made Lichfield his see and founded monasteries, often travelling on foot. Bede recalls his holy life. He died of plague on 2 March 672, only about two and a half years after going to Mercia, and pilgrims soon came to his tomb.

UO-SIN-000892.name: Agnes of Bohemia
UO-SIN-000892.life: Agnes was born in 1211, the daughter of the king of Bohemia. Offered in marriage to several rulers, including the emperor Frederick II, she refused them all, and the pope helped her cause. Moved by the Franciscans who came to Prague, she built a hospital for the poor and then founded a convent of Poor Clares, which she entered in 1234. She served as abbess and nursed the sick and the lepers with her own hands. She died on 2 March 1282. Venerated in Bohemia from her death, she was canonized in 1989 and is honoured as a patron of the Czech lands.

UO-SIN-000893.name: Katharine Drexel
UO-SIN-000893.life: Katharine Drexel was born in 1858 into a wealthy banking family in Philadelphia. After her father's death she inherited a fortune and used it to help Native Americans and African Americans. When she asked Pope Leo XIII to send missionaries, he suggested she go herself. In 1891 she founded the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament, who opened dozens of schools across the country, and she helped found Xavier University in New Orleans. She gave away millions of dollars . She died in 1955 at ninety-six and was canonized in 2000.

UO-SIN-000894.name: Paul Cuffee
UO-SIN-000894.life: Paul Cuffe was born in 1759 on Cuttyhunk Island, Massachusetts, the son of a freed African father and a Wampanoag mother. Beginning as a whaler, he built ships and a trading business and became one of the wealthiest Black men in America. As a young man he protested paying taxes without the vote, which helped lead Massachusetts to extend rights to free people of colour. He joined the Quakers in 1808 and paid for a school. He made voyages to Sierra Leone, and in 1815 he carried thirty-eight free Black settlers there at his own expense. He died in Westport, Massachusetts, in 1817.

UO-SIN-000895.name: Casimir of Poland
UO-SIN-000895.life: Casimir was born in Kraków in 1458, a son of King Casimir IV of Poland. At thirteen he was sent at the head of an army to claim the Hungarian crown, but the campaign collapsed and he returned home. Afterwards he lived a life of prayer, fasting and justice, and when his father was away in Lithuania he governed Poland wisely. He refused a royal marriage to remain single. Weakened by tuberculosis, he died at Grodno on 4 March 1484, aged only twenty-five. Miracles were reported at his tomb in Vilnius, and he became a patron of Poland and Lithuania.

UO-SIN-000677.name: Gerasimus of the Jordan
UO-SIN-000677.life: Gerasimus came from Lycia in Asia Minor. After living as a monk in the Egyptian desert, he settled by the Jordan around 450 and founded a monastery near Jericho. His community lived in solitude through the week, eating only dry bread, roots and water, and gathered on Sundays for worship. For a time he was drawn toward the teaching of Eutyches until Euthymius the Great brought him back to the faith. Tradition tells that he healed a lion by removing a thorn from its paw, and the grateful beast served him until it died at his grave. Gerasimus died around 475.

UO-SIN-000897.name: Ciaran of Seirkeiran
UO-SIN-000897.life: Ciaran, also called Kieran of Saighir, is remembered as one of the earliest Irish saints. According to tradition he was born on Cape Clear Island, travelled to Rome to study and receive baptism, and was ordained a bishop. Back in Ireland he built a small cell in the woods of Ossory, living as a hermit until disciples gathered and a monastery grew up around him at Saighir, near Slieve Bloom. Stories say wild animals were his first companions. He died around 530. He is honoured as the patron of the diocese of Ossory, and St Kieran's College in Kilkenny bears his name.

UO-SIN-000898.name: William W. Mayo, Charles Menninger and Their Sons
UO-SIN-000898.life: William Worrall Mayo, born in England in 1819, settled in Rochester, Minnesota, as a physician. After a tornado in 1883 he worked with the Sisters of St Francis to open St Mary's Hospital, and his sons William and Charles joined him in building the practice that became the Mayo Clinic, a model of group medicine. In Topeka, Kansas, Charles Menninger and his sons Karl and William founded a psychiatric clinic in 1919 that grew into a major centre of treatment and training. Both families made care of the sick, in body and mind, a shared work of cooperation across generations.

UO-SIN-000899.name: Colette of Corbie
UO-SIN-000899.life: Colette was born Nicolette Boellet in 1381, the daughter of a carpenter at Corbie in Picardy. Orphaned at seventeen, she lived as an anchoress and joined the Third Order of St Francis. She came to believe she was called to restore the Poor Clares to the strict poverty of St Clare. With permission from Benedict XIII she founded her first reformed convent at Besançon in 1410, and the reform spread across France, Savoy and Flanders, with some eighteen convents founded in her lifetime. She worked with a friar to reform the men's branch too. She died in 1447 and was canonized in 1807.

UO-SIN-000900.name: Paul the Simple
UO-SIN-000900.life: Paul was an Egyptian farmer who, at about sixty, discovered his wife's unfaithfulness and left home to become a monk. He went to the great Anthony in the desert, who at first turned him away as too old, but Paul waited at the door and was taken in. Anthony tested him with fasting, rope-weaving, vigils and psalms, and Paul obeyed every word with childlike trust. Eventually Anthony gave him a cell of his own. Tradition says he gained power over demons, which Anthony himself said he lacked. His simplicity of heart gave him his name, and he died in the fourth century.

UO-SIN-000901.name: Geoffrey Anketell Studdert Kennedy
UO-SIN-000901.life: Studdert Kennedy was born in Leeds in 1883, studied at Trinity College, Dublin, and was ordained, serving in Rugby and Worcester. In the First World War he went to the Western Front as a chaplain and became known as Woodbine Willie for handing out cigarettes along with comfort to frightened soldiers. He won the Military Cross at Messines Ridge for tending the wounded under fire. His rough, honest poems spoke for the trenches. After the war he travelled the country as a preacher for the Industrial Christian Fellowship, speaking for workers and for peace. He died in 1929 at forty-five and was buried at Worcester.
UO-SIN-000901.place: Leeds, Worcester and the Western Front

UO-SIN-000902.name: Duthac of Tain
UO-SIN-000902.life: Duthac is remembered as a Scottish holy man of the eleventh century. Tradition holds that he was born at Tain in Ross and educated in Ireland, and that he became a renowned preacher and confessor, later regarded as bishop of Ross. Irish annals record his death at Armagh in 1065, calling him the chief confessor of Ireland and Scotland. His relics were brought back to Tain, where a chapel and later a collegiate church became a famous place of pilgrimage. Robert the Bruce and King James IV were among those who journeyed to his shrine, and Tain still honours him as its patron.

UO-SIN-000903.name: Frances of Rome
UO-SIN-000903.life: Frances was born in Rome in 1384 to a noble family. She longed to be a nun, but at twelve she was married to Lorenzo Ponziani, and the marriage proved a happy one. With her sister-in-law she visited the poor and the sick, and in times of hardship she turned her household's resources to relief and even made part of their estate into a hospital. In 1433 she gathered pious women into a community of oblates at Tor de' Specchi, living a religious life without strict cloister. After her husband died in 1436 she joined them. She died in 1440 and was canonized in 1608.

UO-SIN-000904.name: Catherine of Bologna
UO-SIN-000904.life: Catherine Vigri was born in Bologna in 1413 and grew up at the court of the Este family in Ferrara, where she received a fine education. At about thirteen she joined a group of devout women who became the Poor Clare convent of Corpus Domini, and she served for years as mistress of novices. She wrote a treatise on spiritual struggle, The Seven Spiritual Weapons, and painted and illuminated her own breviary, a rare surviving work by a nun-artist. In 1456 she went to found a new convent in Bologna and was its abbess until her death in 1463. She was canonized in 1712.

UO-SIN-000905.name: Macarius of Jerusalem
UO-SIN-000905.life: Macarius was bishop of Jerusalem from about 312 until shortly before 335, in the years when Christianity gained imperial favour. He was present at the Council of Nicaea in 325, where he opposed the teaching of Arius. Afterward he worked with Helena, the mother of Constantine, when excavations in the city uncovered the tomb of Christ. According to tradition, he identified the true cross by having the three crosses found touch a sick woman, who was healed by one of them. Constantine entrusted him with building the great church of the Holy Sepulchre. Macarius died around 335.

UO-SIN-000906.name: John Ogilvie
UO-SIN-000906.life: John Ogilvie was born around 1579 in Banffshire, Scotland, into a Calvinist family. While studying on the Continent as a teenager, he became a Catholic, and in 1599 he entered the Jesuits. Ordained in Paris, he asked repeatedly to be sent home and returned in 1613, disguised as a horse dealer called John Watson, saying Mass in private houses in Edinburgh and Glasgow. Betrayed in Glasgow in 1614, he was tortured and kept from sleep, yet would not name other Catholics. Refusing to accept the king's authority in spiritual matters, he was hanged at Glasgow Cross on 10 March 1615. He was canonized in 1976.

UO-SIN-000907.name: Eulogius of Cordoba
UO-SIN-000907.life: Eulogius was born into a noble family in Córdoba and became a priest and head of the city's main church school, studying with his close friend Alvarus. In 848 he travelled to northern monasteries and brought back precious books. When Christians in Muslim-ruled Córdoba were put to death from about 850, Eulogius was imprisoned and wrote an exhortation to martyrdom for two young women, Flora and Mary, and an account of the martyrs. Chosen archbishop of Toledo, he was never consecrated. In 859 he was beheaded after sheltering Leocritia, a young woman who had left Islam. He died on 11 March 859.

UO-SIN-000908.name: Theophanes the Confessor
UO-SIN-000908.life: Theophanes was born in Constantinople around 759 into a wealthy family and was raised at court. Married young, he persuaded his wife to live with him as a sister, and after her father's death they both entered religious life. He founded a monastery on an island in the Sea of Marmara, where he copied books, and he took part in the Second Council of Nicaea in 787, which upheld icons. When Emperor Leo V revived iconoclasm, he refused to yield, was imprisoned and banished to Samothrace, and died there around 817. He also continued the world chronicle of George the Synkellos, which preserves much of Byzantine history.

UO-SIN-000909.name: Roderick (Ruderic) of Cordoba
UO-SIN-000909.life: Roderick was a priest from Cabra, near Córdoba, in the ninth century, when Christians lived under Muslim rule. According to the traditional account, he tried to stop a quarrel between his two brothers, one a Muslim and the other careless of religion, and they beat him. His Muslim brother then told the authorities that Roderick had converted to Islam, which made his remaining Christian a capital offence. Roderick denied it and held to his faith. In prison he met another Christian, Salomon, and the two were beheaded together at Córdoba on 13 March 857.

UO-SIN-000910.name: Chiara Lubich
UO-SIN-000910.life: Chiara Lubich was born Silvia Lubich in Trent, Italy, in 1920, and worked as a schoolteacher. During the Second World War, as bombs fell, she and a few companions gathered to read the Gospel and resolved to live it by loving one another. Their little community was called Focolare, meaning hearth, and grew into a movement for unity, approved by the Church in 1962, with members in over a hundred and eighty countries. She reached out to Christians of other churches and to people of other faiths, and received the Templeton Prize in 1977. She died near Rome on 14 March 2008, aged eighty-eight.

UO-SIN-000970.name: Innocent of Tortona
UO-SIN-000970.life: Innocent was born into a noble family of Tortona in northern Italy and, as a young man, was imprisoned and stripped of his family property during Diocletian's persecution. After peace came to the Church he travelled to Rome, where Pope Sylvester ordained him deacon and then consecrated him bishop of his native city. He reorganised the scattered Christian community and worked against lingering paganism. Giving his inherited estates to the church, he paid for several new churches, among them a basilica on the hill above Tortona. He died around the middle of the fourth century and was buried in that basilica. Dates in the older accounts are uncertain.

UO-SIN-000971.name: Apollonius the Apologist
UO-SIN-000971.life: Apollonius was a learned Christian of Rome in the reign of the emperor Commodus. A slave denounced him as a Christian, and he was brought before the prefect Perennis and the Senate. Rather than deny Christ, he composed and delivered a thoughtful defence of his faith, speaking of the hope of eternal life and of living well. The Senate nonetheless condemned him, and he was put to death around the year 185. Accounts differ on the manner of his death, one recalling crushed legs, another beheading. Later writers remembered him as a philosopher-martyr who answered the empire with reasoned witness.

UO-SIN-000972.name: Laserian of Leighlin
UO-SIN-000972.life: Laserian, also called Molaise, was an Irish churchman of the late sixth and early seventh centuries who is said to have spent part of his youth in Scotland. According to tradition he studied in Rome and was ordained by Pope Gregory the Great. Returning to Ireland, he became abbot of the monastery at Old Leighlin in County Carlow, which grew into a famous community. He was a leading voice for the Roman reckoning of Easter in Ireland's debates on the question, and he is said to have been consecrated bishop by Pope Honorius I. He died around 639 and is honoured as Leighlin's patron.

UO-SIN-000974.name: Emma of Saxony
UO-SIN-000974.life: Emma was born around 975 into the Saxon nobility and married Count Liudger, a son of Duke Hermann Billung. After the emperor gave the couple an estate at Stiepel, she had a church dedicated to the Virgin Mary built there in 1008. When Liudger died in 1011 she withdrew to her property at Lesum near Bremen, where she gave generously to Bremen Cathedral and founded churches. Her chief concern was always the poor. She died in 1038 and was buried in Bremen. The people venerated her as a saint, though she was never formally canonised, and a relic of her hand is kept at Werden Abbey.

UO-SIN-000975.name: Agnes of Montepulciano
UO-SIN-000975.life: Agnes was born around 1268 into a noble family near Montepulciano in Tuscany. At nine she entered a convent of sisters living in great simplicity, and as a teenager she was sent with others to found a new community at Proceno, where she soon became prioress. She was known for prayer, austerity and reputed healings. In 1306 she was recalled to Montepulciano to lead the convent there, which came to follow the Dominican Rule, and she governed it until her death in 1317. Her body was said to remain incorrupt, and pilgrims gathered at her tomb. She was canonised in 1726.

UO-SIN-000976.name: Marcellinus of Embrun
UO-SIN-000976.life: Marcellinus was born in North Africa and came to Rome in the early fourth century with two companions, Vincent and Domninus. Sent to preach in Gaul, he made his way into the Alps and evangelised the region around Embrun. Tradition says that Eusebius of Vercelli ordained him as the town's first bishop, although he is said to have been reluctant. His preaching brought many pagans to baptism. Under the Arian emperor Constantius he suffered for the Catholic faith and, in old age, is said to have lived hidden in mountain caves. He died around 374.

UO-SIN-000977.name: Beuno
UO-SIN-000977.life: Beuno was a Welsh abbot of the seventh century, born in Powys and trained in the monastery at Bangor. He became a missionary with the support of King Cadfan of Gwynedd. After a dispute over land with Cadfan's son Cadwallon, a kinsman named Gwyddaint gave him the township of Clynnog Fawr on the Llyn peninsula, where he founded his chief monastery. According to tradition he restored seven people to life, including his niece Winefride, and was stern with hardened sinners but gentle with the suffering. He died in 640. His grave chapel survives at Clynnog.

UO-SIN-000978.name: Conrad of Parzham
UO-SIN-000978.life: Johann Birndorfer was born in 1818 into a poor farming family at Parzham in Bavaria, the ninth child, and grew up devoted to Our Lady and to the rosary. After his parents died he gave away his inheritance and at thirty-one joined the Capuchins as a lay brother, taking the name Conrad. He spent more than forty years as porter at the friary at Altötting, a great pilgrimage centre. There he welcomed every visitor, gave to the poor, spoke little and prayed through much of the night. He died in 1894 and was canonised in 1934.

UO-SIN-000979.name: Soter and Caius
UO-SIN-000979.life: Soter and Caius were bishops of Rome a century apart. Soter led the Roman church in the later second century and was remembered for generosity: Bishop Dionysius of Corinth praised him for sending aid to poorer churches and for welcoming Christians who came to Rome. Caius governed from 283 until his death in 296; tradition makes him a native of Dalmatia and says he laid down the clerical steps to be taken before a man could become bishop. Later legend called him a martyr, but modern scholars think he died in peace. Both are honoured as faithful shepherds of the early Roman church.

UO-SIN-000980.name: Opportuna of Montreuil
UO-SIN-000980.life: Opportuna lived in eighth-century Normandy. She became a Benedictine nun at a convent near Almenêches, taking the veil from her brother Chrodegang, bishop of Sées, and in time succeeded her cousin Lantildis as abbess. She was remembered as a true mother to her sisters, correcting faults with words rather than blows. Her grief was great when Chrodegang was murdered in 769 by a relative to whom he had entrusted his diocese; she buried him in her convent. She died the following year after a short illness made worse by sorrow. Her relics were later carried to several places in France.

UO-SIN-000722.name: Toyohiko Kagawa
UO-SIN-000722.life: Born in Kobe in 1888, Kagawa lost his parents early and was converted to Christianity as a youth through missionary teachers, which cost him his family's support. He studied in Japan and at Princeton, then in 1909 moved into a Kobe slum to live among the poor. He campaigned for labour unions, cooperatives and universal suffrage, was jailed for his activism, and as a pacifist founded an anti-war league and was arrested in 1940 for apologising to China. He wrote over 150 books, including best-selling novels. He died in Tokyo in 1960, asking for prayer for peace and for the church in Japan.

UO-SIN-000981.name: Adalbert of Prague
UO-SIN-000981.life: Born around 956 into a powerful Bohemian family, Adalbert (Vojtech) studied at Magdeburg and became bishop of Prague while still young. His reforms, including his stand against slave trading and pagan customs, aroused such opposition that he went to Rome more than once. He founded the monastery at Brevnov and became a travelling missionary, working in Hungary and Poland. In 997 he set out to preach to the pagan Prussians and was killed near the Baltic coast with his companions. The Polish duke Boleslaw is said to have ransomed his body for its weight in gold. He was canonised within two years and is a patron of Poland and Bohemia.

UO-SIN-000982.name: Genocide Remembrance
UO-SIN-000982.life: On the night of 24 April 1915, Ottoman authorities in Constantinople arrested hundreds of Armenian leaders, writers and thinkers, and began the destruction of the Armenian people of the empire. Over the next two years, huge numbers of Armenians were driven from their homes in deportation marches toward the Syrian desert; between six hundred thousand and a million and a half died by massacre, starvation and disease.  A civilisation of two thousand years in Anatolia was largely uprooted. Armenians and many others now keep 24 April as a day of mourning, and it is remembered as one of the first great atrocities of the modern age.

UO-SIN-000983.name: Fidelis of Sigmaringen
UO-SIN-000983.life: Mark Roy was born in 1577 at Sigmaringen in Germany, studied law and philosophy at Freiburg, and became a lawyer in Alsace known for defending the poor. Disillusioned by dishonesty in his profession, he joined the Capuchins in 1612 and took the name Fidelis, meaning faithful. He became an effective preacher, ministered to plague victims and won converts. In 1621 he was sent to preach in the largely Calvinist Swiss canton of Graubunden. On 24 April 1622, after preaching at Seewis, he was attacked and killed. He was canonised in 1746 and is remembered as the first martyr of the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith.

UO-SIN-000984.name: Anianus of Alexandria
UO-SIN-000984.life: According to tradition, Anianus was a cobbler in Alexandria. When the evangelist Mark came to the city and brought him a broken sandal to mend, an awl pierced Anianus's hand and he cried out that God is one. Mark healed him, taught him the faith and baptised him and his household. Before leaving for a time, Mark ordained Anianus bishop to care for the growing church. After Mark's martyrdom, Anianus led the Christians of Alexandria for some years, ordaining clergy and drawing in converts. He died in peace and was buried near Mark. The details come from tradition and cannot be firmly dated.

UO-SIN-000985.name: Ermin of Lobbes
UO-SIN-000985.life: Ermin came from the region of Laon in what is now northern France, studied at its cathedral school and was ordained priest. He entered the Benedictine abbey of Lobbes in present-day Belgium, a community founded by Landelin, and became a disciple of Ursmar, its abbot and a preacher among the still-pagan people of the region. Ursmar named him his successor, and Ermin became the second abbot. His biographer, a later abbot of Lobbes, wrote that he had the gift of prophecy. He died in 737 and was buried in the crypt of the abbey church, where he is still honoured locally.

UO-SIN-000725.name: Robert Hunt
UO-SIN-000725.life: Robert Hunt was an English parish priest, vicar of Reculver and then Heathfield, who was chosen as chaplain to the Virginia Company's first expedition. He sailed in 1606 and landed at Cape Henry on 26 April 1607, where a cross was planted and prayers were said. At Jamestown he led daily worship, at first under an old sail, and celebrated Holy Communion on 21 June 1607. John Smith praised him as an honest and courageous minister who calmed the colonists' quarrels. A fire in 1608 destroyed his library, yet he bore the loss gracefully. He died that spring, in about his fortieth year.

UO-SIN-000987.name: Cletus / Anacletus
UO-SIN-000987.life: Cletus, also called Anacletus, was the second successor of Saint Peter as bishop of Rome, coming after Linus and before Clement. Very little is certain about him. Ancient writers disagree on whether Cletus and Anacletus were one man or two, and the exact years of his ministry are unknown, though they are usually placed in the later first century. It is recorded that he ordained a number of priests, and tradition holds that he died as a martyr. His name is spoken in the Roman Canon of the Mass, a sign of the early church's reverence for him.

UO-SIN-000563.name: Christina Rossetti
UO-SIN-000563.life: Christina Rossetti was born in London in 1830, the youngest child of the Italian exile Gabriele Rossetti and sister of the painter Dante Gabriel. She was educated at home and began writing verse as a child. Devout in the Anglo-Catholic tradition, she broke off an engagement when her fiance became a Roman Catholic. Her collection Goblin Market (1862) made her name, and she also wrote children's rhymes in Sing-Song and many devotional poems; her Christmas carol lyrics are still sung. Though plagued by illness in later years, she kept writing. She died in London in 1894, leaving verse that joins passion with deep faith.

UO-SIN-000989.name: Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort
UO-SIN-000989.life: Born in 1673 at Montfort-sur-Meu in Brittany, Louis was educated by the Jesuits and walked to Paris to study for the priesthood, which he entered in 1700. Wishing for the mission field, he was instead sent by Pope Clement XI to preach in France. For about sixteen years he travelled through Brittany and the Vendee, drawing crowds to missions marked by the rosary, hymns and love of the poor, though he met opposition and even a poisoning attempt. He wrote True Devotion to Mary and, with Marie Louise Trichet, founded the Daughters of Wisdom and the Company of Mary. He died in 1716 aged forty-three.

UO-SIN-000990.name: Gianna Beretta Molla
UO-SIN-000990.life: Gianna Beretta was born in 1922 at Magenta near Milan, one of thirteen children in a devout family.
