She trained as a doctor at Pavia, specialised in children's medicine and opened a practice at Mesero, where she cared especially for mothers, babies and the elderly poor. In 1955 she married Pietro Molla, and they had three children. In 1961, expecting a fourth, she was found to have a growth in her womb and begged the surgeon to save the child above all. Her daughter was born on 21 April 1962, and Gianna died a week later, aged thirty-nine. She was canonised in 2004.

UO-SIN-000991.name: Hugh of Cluny
UO-SIN-000991.life: Hugh was born in 1024 into a noble Burgundian family, and although his father hoped to make him a knight, he entered Cluny at fourteen. At twenty-five he was elected abbot and ruled the great abbey for sixty years, until 1109. Under him Cluny's network of monasteries spread across France, Spain, Italy and England, and the monks began the immense third abbey church, long the largest in Europe. Hugh advised popes and kings, worked to end simony and clerical corruption, and sought peace between Emperor Henry IV and the papacy. He died in 1109 and was canonised in 1120.

UO-SIN-000992.name: Robert of Molesme
UO-SIN-000992.life: Born in Champagne around 1028, Robert became a Benedictine monk as a youth and served as prior and then abbot at several houses. Around 1075 he led a band of hermits to found Molesme in Burgundy, which became famous for its austerity. As wealth and recruits poured in, observance relaxed, and in 1098 Robert left with about twenty companions for a wild, marshy place called Citeaux, where they set out to follow the Rule of Saint Benedict strictly. The monks of Molesme soon begged for his return, and he went back, ruling there until his death in 1111. Citeaux grew into the Cistercian Order.

UO-SIN-000993.name: Pius V
UO-SIN-000993.life: Antonio Ghislieri was born in 1504 in northern Italy and entered the Dominicans at fourteen. A strict, austere friar and teacher, he rose to be bishop, cardinal and head of the Roman Inquisition before being elected pope in 1566. As Pius V he put the reforms of the Council of Trent into effect, issued a standard Roman Missal, and lived simply and prayerfully. He excommunicated Elizabeth I of England in 1570 and organised the Holy League whose fleet defeated the Ottomans at Lepanto in 1571. He died in 1572, refusing relief from a painful illness, and was canonised in 1712.

UO-SIN-000994.name: Erkenwald of London
UO-SIN-000994.life: Erkenwald was an Anglo-Saxon nobleman, born around 630, who founded two monasteries around 666: Chertsey in Surrey for men, where he became abbot, and Barking in Essex for women, where his sister Ethelburga was abbess. In 675 Archbishop Theodore appointed him bishop of London. He helped counsel King Ine of Wessex on his law code and worked to reconcile Roman and Celtic customs among his people. He died at Barking in 693 and was buried in Old Saint Paul's, where his shrine drew pilgrims until the Reformation. Londoners called him the Light of London.

UO-SIN-000996.name: Sigismund of Burgundy
UO-SIN-000996.life: Sigismund was born around 475, a son of the Burgundian king Gundobad, and was won from Arian belief to the Catholic faith by Bishop Avitus of Vienne. In 515 he founded or refounded the monastery of Saint Maurice at Agaune. Succeeding his father in 516, he fell into grievous sin when he allowed his son Sigeric to be put to death on a false charge, and he afterwards repented bitterly and withdrew to Agaune to do penance. In 523 the Franks invaded; he was captured and killed with his wife and children in 524, their bodies thrown into a well. He was venerated as a martyr.

UO-SIN-000997.name: Antoninus of Florence
UO-SIN-000997.life: Antonio Pierozzi was born in Florence in 1389 and joined the Dominicans at sixteen, becoming a leader in the movement for stricter observance and helping found the priory of San Marco. Against his wishes, Pope Eugene IV made him archbishop of Florence in 1446. He lived in his diocese, visited every parish, cared for the poor, and worked tirelessly during the plague of 1448 and the earthquake of 1453. A gifted scholar, he wrote a large work on moral theology and is often counted among the founders of Christian social ethics. He died in 1459 and was canonised in 1523.

UO-SIN-001000.name: Philip and James
UO-SIN-001000.life: Philip and James were two of the twelve apostles. Philip came from Bethsaida, was called by Jesus directly, and brought Nathanael to him; it was to Philip that some Greeks came wishing to see Jesus. Early tradition says he preached in Asia Minor and was buried at Hierapolis. James, son of Alphaeus, appears only in the lists of the Twelve, and little else is known with certainty; some traditions identify him with James the Less, and others with James the Just, leader of the Jerusalem church. They are honoured together as foundation witnesses of the gospel.

UO-SIN-001001.name: Florian
UO-SIN-001001.life: According to the traditional account, Florian was a Roman army officer in the province of Noricum, in present-day Austria, who is also said to have organised firefighting. During Diocletian's persecution, around 304, he was reported as not enforcing the laws against Christians. When the governor Aquilinus ordered him to sacrifice to the gods, he refused, declaring himself a Christian and was scourged. He was then thrown into the river Enns at Lorch with a stone tied round his neck. A pious woman recovered his body, and the great abbey of Saint Florian near Linz rose over his burial place. He is patron of firefighters.

UO-SIN-001002.name: English Martyrs
UO-SIN-001002.life: Between 1535 and 1679, many English and Welsh Catholics were put to death for treason or related offences under the laws of the Reformation. They included Carthusian monks who would not accept Henry VIII as head of the Church, and later seminary priests, Jesuits and lay people who sheltered them. Most were hanged, drawn and quartered, many at Tyburn. Among them were John Houghton, Richard Reynolds, Cuthbert Mayne, Edmund Campion and Margaret Clitherow, the York wife and mother. In 1970 Pope Paul VI canonised forty of them to stand for all who died for their faith in those hard years.

UO-SIN-000733.name: Martyrs of the Reformation Era
UO-SIN-000733.life: The religious upheavals of sixteenth-century England cost many lives on both sides. Under Mary I, several hundred Protestants were burned at the stake for refusing to return to Roman obedience, among them bishops Nicholas Ridley and Hugh Latimer and Archbishop Thomas Cranmer, who died at Oxford in 1555 and 1556. Catholics, for their part, were hanged as traitors under Henry VIII, Elizabeth I and later rulers, for refusing the royal supremacy or for serving as priests. Each group went to death convinced that it was being faithful to Christ, and together they remind the Church of the cost of division.

UO-SIN-001005.name: Dominic Savio
UO-SIN-001005.life: Dominic Savio was born in 1842 in the Piedmont village of Riva, near Chieri, the son of a blacksmith and a seamstress. He was devout from early childhood, served at Mass at five and begged to make his first communion at seven. At twelve he entered the Oratory in Turin run by John Bosco, who guided his schooling and prayer. Dominic was known for cheerfulness, kindness to schoolmates and a strict conscience. His health failed and he died on 9 March 1857, aged fourteen. Bosco wrote his life, and in 1954 he was canonised as a model of holiness for the young.

UO-SIN-001006.name: Flavia Domitilla
UO-SIN-001006.life: Flavia Domitilla was a Roman noblewoman of the late first century, a granddaughter of the emperor Vespasian and wife of the consul Titus Flavius Clemens. Their sons were named by Domitian as his heirs. Around 95, however, Domitian had Clemens put to death on a charge of godlessness, which writers have often taken to mean Christianity or attraction to Jewish practice, and Domitilla was banished to the island of Pandateria. Christian tradition honours her as a martyr, though historians disagree whether the Christian Domitilla and the empress's granddaughter were the same woman, or whether she was killed or only exiled.

UO-SIN-001008.name: Victor the Moor
UO-SIN-001008.life: Victor was born in Mauretania, in North Africa, to a Christian family, and served as a soldier in the Praetorian Guard of the emperor Maximian in Milan. When persecution came he refused to give up his faith or to continue in the army. He was whipped, imprisoned and tortured, and according to the old account of his martyrdom he was beheaded in a grove of elms around the year 303. Christians in Milan soon honoured his grave, and the church of San Vittore al Corpo stands there still. He is remembered as a friend of prisoners and exiles.

UO-SIN-001009.name: Wiro, Plechelm, and Otger
UO-SIN-001009.life: These three companions came, by most accounts, from Anglo-Saxon England, though one source calls Wiro Irish. They travelled to Rome together, where Plechelm was made a bishop and Otger served as deacon. They then crossed to the Continent as missionaries, and Pepin of Herstal gave them the hill of Sint Odiliënberg, near Roermond, where they built a monastery. From there they preached between the Rhine and the Meuse and helped bring Christianity to the Low Countries. After Viking raids their relics were carried to Utrecht, and Plechelm's later rested at Oldenzaal. Plechelm is traditionally said to have died about 730.

UO-SIN-000738.name: Comgall of Bangor
UO-SIN-000738.life: Comgall was born about 510-520 in Ulster, and was a soldier before he turned to the religious life. He studied under Finnian of Movilla and other great teachers, was ordained priest, and for a time lived in strict austerity with companions on an island in Lough Erne. Persuaded to stay in Ireland, he founded the monastery of Bangor on Belfast Lough about 552-555. It grew to thousands of monks and became famous for learning and discipline, and trained Columbanus, who later carried its spirit to the Continent. Comgall was a friend of Columba and Brendan. After a long illness he died at Bangor, about 602.

UO-SIN-001012.name: John of Avila
UO-SIN-001012.life: John was born in 1499 at Almodóvar del Campo in Spain. After studying law at Salamanca and theology at Alcalá, he was ordained in 1526, gave away his inheritance, and planned to go as a missionary to Mexico. The archbishop of Seville persuaded him to preach in Andalusia instead. His sermons drew great crowds, and his calls for reform brought him a spell in the Inquisition's prison. He founded schools and the University of Baeza, guided many disciples, and wrote the spiritual classic Audi, filia. He died in 1569 and was named a Doctor of the Church in 2012.

UO-SIN-001013.name: Solangia
UO-SIN-001013.life: Solangia, or Solange, was a young shepherdess from a poor, devout family in Villemont, near Bourges in central France, who lived in the ninth century. According to tradition she had vowed her virginity to Christ in childhood. A nobleman's son, said to be the son of the count of Poitiers, tried to win her and, when she refused, seized her and carried her off on his horse. She struggled free and he killed her with his sword, about 880. Legend says she carried her head to the village church. She became patron of the Berry region and was invoked in time of drought.

UO-SIN-001014.name: Mamertus of Vienne
UO-SIN-001014.life: Mamertus became bishop of Vienne in Gaul shortly before 462. He came from a learned family, and his brother Claudianus Mamertus, a writer and theologian, served as his priest. Mamertus was known for his scholarship and for pastoral energy, and he brought the relics of the martyr Ferreolus to a new church in Vienne. He is chiefly remembered because, when his city was struck by earthquakes and other disasters, he ordered days of fasting and litanies before Ascension Day. This practice spread through the Church as the Rogation Days. He also quarrelled with Pope Hilary over episcopal rights. He died about 475.

UO-SIN-001015.name: Francis di Girolamo
UO-SIN-001015.life: Francesco de Geronimo was born in 1642 at Grottaglie in southern Italy, the eldest of eleven children. He studied with the Jesuits, was ordained in Naples in 1666, and joined the Society of Jesus in 1670. He longed to be a missionary in Japan or India, but his superiors kept him in Naples. There he spent forty years preaching in plain words in streets, prisons and country villages, training lay helpers, and caring for the poor, for prisoners and for fallen women. His gift for simple preaching reached people of every rank. He died on 11 May 1716.

UO-SIN-001016.name: Nereus and Achilleus
UO-SIN-001016.life: Nereus and Achilleus were Roman martyrs of the early centuries, buried in the catacomb of Domitilla on the Via Ardeatina. A poem set up by Pope Damasus in the fourth century says that they were soldiers who served a cruel ruler, then were converted, threw down their arms and were put to death by the sword. A great basilica was built over their tomb, and a carved pillar showing their beheading survives. Later legends call them servants of Flavia Domitilla and tell of an exile on an island, but these tales are unreliable and little else is known for certain.

UO-SIN-001017.name: Epiphanius of Salamis
UO-SIN-001017.life: Epiphanius was born near Eleutheropolis in Judea about 310-320. As a young man he lived among monks in Egypt, then founded a monastery in Palestine, where he was famed for learning and languages. About 367 he became bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, and he held the office for nearly forty years. A zealous defender of orthodoxy, he travelled to Antioch and Rome and wrote the Panarion, a long refutation of eighty heresies. His campaign against the followers of Origen led him into conflict with the bishop of Jerusalem and with John Chrysostom. He died at sea in 403, returning from Constantinople.

UO-SIN-001018.name: Robert Bellarmine
UO-SIN-001018.life: Robert Bellarmine was born in 1542 at Montepulciano in Tuscany. He entered the Jesuits in 1560, studied at Padua and Louvain, and taught at the Roman College, where his lectures became the great work Disputations on the Controversies of the Christian Faith, a clear defence of Catholic teaching against the Reformers. He was made cardinal in 1599 and archbishop of Capua in 1602, and he took part in the cases of Giordano Bruno and Galileo. Admired for his learning and humility, he died in Rome in 1621. He was canonised in 1930 and declared a Doctor of the Church.

UO-SIN-001019.name: Boniface of Tarsus
UO-SIN-001019.life: According to tradition, Boniface was a household slave and steward in Rome, who lived with his mistress Aglaida in a sinful way, yet was generous to the poor and kind to strangers. Aglaida sent him east to bring back the relics of martyrs. At Tarsus in Cilicia he found Christians being tortured, declared himself a Christian, and was himself beheaded about 307. His body was carried back to Rome, and Aglaida, moved by his death, became a Christian, gave her wealth to the poor and spent years in repentance. The story is legendary, but it has long been told as a tale of conversion.

UO-SIN-001020.name: Dymphna
UO-SIN-001020.life: According to tradition, Dymphna was the daughter of a pagan petty king in Ireland, perhaps in the seventh century, raised as a Christian by her mother. After her mother's death her grieving father wished to marry her. Dymphna fled with her confessor, the priest Gerebernus, and settled near Geel in what is now Belgium. Her father tracked them down; his men killed Gerebernus, and when Dymphna still refused him, he cut off her head. She was about fifteen. Her story was written down only in the thirteenth century, and Geel became a place of pilgrimage and later of care for those who suffer mental illness.

UO-SIN-001021.name: Isidore the Farmer
UO-SIN-001021.life: Isidore was a poor farm worker born about 1070 in Madrid. He worked for the landowner Juan de Vargas, who in time made him his steward, and he shared his food with the poor and cared for animals. He heard Mass each morning before work, and a legend says that angels ploughed for him while he prayed. He married Maria Torribia, also honoured as a saint in Spain; their only son died young. Isidore died in 1130 and became the patron of farmers and of Madrid. He is a reminder that holiness can be found in ordinary daily labour.

UO-SIN-000744.name: Alexander of Jerusalem
UO-SIN-000744.life: Alexander was a pupil of Clement of Alexandria and a friend of Origen. He became bishop in Cappadocia, was imprisoned for his faith under the emperor Severus, and on release came to Jerusalem. There the aged bishop Narcissus asked him to stay as his helper, and Alexander eventually became bishop himself. He welcomed the scholar Origen to preach and teach, and built a great library in Jerusalem. During the persecution of Decius he was arrested again, in old age, and taken to Caesarea, where he died in prison about 251 after many tortures. Christians honour him as a martyr.

UO-SIN-001022.name: Possidius of Calama
UO-SIN-001022.life: Possidius was a close friend of Augustine for some forty years. He lived in Augustine's monastery at Hippo and about 397 became bishop of Calama in Numidia, where he started a monastery of his own. He stood firm against the Donatists, was once beaten and nearly killed, and joined Augustine in councils and in the great conference at Carthage in 411. He was present at Augustine's deathbed in 430. When the Arian Vandals overran North Africa he was driven from his see in 437. His Life of Augustine is the main source for the great bishop's story. He died in Italy not long afterwards.

UO-SIN-000745.name: Thurgood Marshall
UO-SIN-000745.life: Thurgood Marshall was born in Baltimore in 1908 and trained at Howard University School of Law. As chief lawyer of the NAACP Legal Defense Fund he argued case after case against racial segregation, winning twenty-nine of the thirty-two he took to the Supreme Court. His greatest victory was Brown v. Board of Education in 1954, which struck down segregated public schools. He served as a federal appeals judge, then as Solicitor General, and in 1967 became the first African American on the Supreme Court, where he served until 1991. He often dissented in defence of the poor and powerless. He died in 1993.

UO-SIN-001025.name: Paschal Baylon
UO-SIN-001025.life: Paschal Baylon was born in 1540 at Torrehermosa in Aragon to poor farming parents. He worked as a shepherd from the age of seven, sharing his food with the needy and teaching himself to read from his mother's prayer book. In 1564 he became a lay brother among the reformed Franciscans, and was known for strict poverty, courtesy and care for the sick. His chief devotion was to the Eucharist. On a journey through France he defended belief in the real presence and narrowly escaped a Huguenot mob. He died in 1592 and was later named patron of Eucharistic congresses.

UO-SIN-001026.name: Eric of Sweden
UO-SIN-001026.life: Eric Jedvardsson became king of Sweden about 1156 and ruled for a few years. Few facts are certain, but later tradition remembers him as a just king, defender of the poor and of women's rights, and a supporter of the Church. According to legend he led an expedition against pagan Finland, and brought the English bishop Henry of Uppsala to preach there. On 18 May 1160, it is said, enemies fell on him as he left Mass at Uppsala and killed him. His shrine at Uppsala became a centre of pilgrimage,.

UO-SIN-001027.name: Felix of Cantalice
UO-SIN-001027.life: Felix was born in 1515 to a peasant family at Cantalice in the Abruzzi, and worked as a shepherd and farm labourer until he was nearly thirty. He prayed as he worked, and after a narrow escape from a plough accident he asked to join the Capuchins. From 1547 he was sent to Rome to beg alms for his friary, and for forty years he walked the streets barefoot with his sack, answering every gift with Deo gratias. He aided the poor and sick and taught children simple hymns, and was a friend of Philip Neri. He died in 1587, the first Capuchin to be canonised.

UO-SIN-001028.name: Ivo of Kermartin
UO-SIN-001028.life: Ivo was born in 1253 into a Breton noble family at Kermartin, near Tréguier. He studied civil law at Paris and canon law at Orléans, and became a church judge, first at Rennes and then for the bishop of Tréguier. He was known for incorruptible fairness, for refusing bribes, and for defending widows, orphans and the poor, often at his own cost. Ordained priest, he served as parish priest at Tredrez and then Louannec, where he built a hospice and gave away his goods. He died in 1303 and was canonised in 1347. He is the patron of Brittany and of lawyers.

UO-SIN-001030.name: Bernardine of Siena
UO-SIN-001030.life: Bernardino degli Albizzeschi was born in 1380 near Siena and was orphaned at six. In 1400 he and companions ran a hospital through a plague, and in 1403 he joined the strict Franciscans. Ordained in 1404, he became one of the great preachers of his age, travelling on foot all over Italy and urging peace, honest dealing and a stronger faith. He spread devotion to the Holy Name of Jesus, and his preaching also had harsh moments. He helped reform the Franciscans in Italy. He died at Aquila in the Abruzzi on 20 May 1444 and was canonised in 1450.

UO-SIN-001031.name: Austregisilus of Bourges
UO-SIN-001031.life: Austregisilus, also known as Outrille, came from Bourges and was brought up for life at the royal court of King Guntram at Chalon-sur-Saône. Drawn instead to the religious life, he entered the monastery of Saint-Nizier at Lyon, was ordained priest, and became its abbot. In 612 he was chosen bishop of Bourges, and he served that church until his death in 624. He ordained Sulpicius the Pious, who later succeeded him, and the future missionary Amand studied under him. Several French villages still bear his name, and his flock mourned him and soon honoured him as a saint.

UO-SIN-001032.name: Lydia, Dorcas, and Phoebe
UO-SIN-001032.life: These three women appear in the New Testament as examples of faith and service. Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira, heard Paul preach at Philippi, was baptised with her household, and opened her home to the apostles. Tabitha, called Dorcas in Greek, was a disciple at Joppa who was full of good works and charity to widows; Peter raised her to life. Phoebe, a deacon of the church at Cenchreae near Corinth, helped many and was trusted by Paul, who commended her to the Romans, probably as the bearer of his letter. Together they show women at work in the early Church.

UO-SIN-001033.name: Godric of Finchale
UO-SIN-001033.life: Godric was born about 1065 at Walpole in Norfolk to poor parents, and became a pedlar, then a merchant and shipmaster who sailed to Scotland, Denmark, Flanders and beyond, and made pilgrimages to Rome and Jerusalem. Turning to the solitary life, he lived for a time with an old hermit, and then settled at Finchale on the River Wear near Durham. There he stayed for some sixty years in prayer and great austerity, welcoming visitors who sought his counsel. Songs that he is said to have learned in a vision are among the oldest English songs with surviving music. He died there in 1170.

UO-SIN-000280.name: Helena of Constantinople
UO-SIN-000280.life: Helena was born of humble origins, perhaps at Drepanum in Bithynia, about 250. She became the partner of Constantius Chlorus and bore him a son, Constantine. When Constantius took a different wife she lived in obscurity until her son became emperor, and then received the title Augusta. In her last years she made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem and the Holy Land, and was generous to the poor and to churches. Tradition holds that she found the True Cross and that she built churches at Bethlehem and on the Mount of Olives. She died about 330, and her son renamed her birthplace Helenopolis.

UO-SIN-001034.name: Rita of Cascia
UO-SIN-001034.life: Rita was born about 1381 at Roccaporena near Cascia in Umbria. Though she wished to be a nun, her parents married her to a violent man, and for some eighteen years she patiently strove to win him to gentleness. When he was murdered, she forgave his killers and sought to keep her two sons from revenge; both died young. After being refused several times because she was a widow, she was admitted to the Augustinian convent at Cascia. There she lived by prayer and penance, bearing, tradition says, a thorn-like wound on her forehead. She died about 1457 and is called the patron of hopeless causes.

UO-SIN-001036.name: Montanus, Lucius and Companions
UO-SIN-001036.life: Montanus, Lucius, Flavian, Julian and Victoricus were among a band of disciples of Cyprian who were arrested in Carthage during Emperor Valerian's persecution. They spent many months in a dark prison, short of food and water, yet wrote letters that kept up the courage of the church outside. In 259 they were sentenced to death and walked cheerfully to the place of execution, where they were beheaded. Montanus had prayed that Flavian, who was at first spared, would follow them on the third day, and so it happened. Their own letters and an eyewitness account preserved their story.

UO-SIN-001037.name: Desiderius of Langres
UO-SIN-001037.life: Desiderius was an early bishop of Langres in eastern Gaul, remembered as a good shepherd who gave his life for his people. When pagan invaders swept through the region, he went out with his clergy to meet them, hoping to protect his flock, and was killed with his followers. The date is uncertain: older writers placed it in the third century, while the Catholic Encyclopedia gives about 407, when Vandals and their allies ravaged Gaul. His people have always honoured him as their patron, and Langres still counts him among its founding saints.

UO-SIN-000750.name: Jackson Kemper
UO-SIN-000750.life: Jackson Kemper was born in 1789 in Pleasant Valley, New York, graduated first in his class at Columbia College, and was ordained priest in 1814. In 1835 the Episcopal Church consecrated him its first missionary bishop, sending him to Indiana and Missouri, and his care later stretched across the old Northwest. He travelled enormously, founding churches, ordaining clergy, and starting work among the Oneida and other Native peoples. With others he helped found Nashotah House and Racine College in Wisconsin. From 1859 he served as the first Bishop of Wisconsin and died near Nashotah in 1870.

UO-SIN-001039.name: Donatian and Rogatian
UO-SIN-001039.life: Donatian and Rogatian were brothers from a leading family of Nantes in Gaul. Donatian, the younger, became a Christian first and brought his older brother to the faith, though Rogatian had not yet been baptized. Around the turn of the fourth century, in the reign of Maximian, they were arrested and refused to sacrifice to the gods. They were racked, bound in prison, and spent their last night in prayer. Rogatian grieved at dying unbaptized, but Donatian assured him that martyrdom in his own blood would take baptism's place. Both were then beheaded outside the city, and pilgrims later honoured their tomb.

UO-SIN-001040.name: Aldhelm of Sherborne
UO-SIN-001040.life: Aldhelm was born around 639 into the royal house of Wessex and was schooled at Malmesbury by an Irish teacher, then at Canterbury under Hadrian, learning Latin, Greek and law. He became abbot of Malmesbury about 675, made it a famous school, and helped found monasteries at Frome and Bradford-on-Avon. A gifted poet, he was among the first Anglo-Saxons to write serious Latin verse, including a hundred riddles. Around 705 he became the first Bishop of Sherborne, still caring for his monastery. He died at Doulting in 709, and his body was carried to Malmesbury, with crosses marking the route.

UO-SIN-001041.name: Mary Magdalene de Pazzi
UO-SIN-001041.life: Born Caterina de' Pazzi in Florence in 1566, she came from one of the city's great families and was taught to meditate on Christ's Passion as a child. As a teenager she entered the Carmelite convent of Santa Maria degli Angeli, where she fell gravely ill but recovered enough to take her vows. She experienced long ecstasies, and her sisters wrote down what she said in them. She served as sacristan and mistress of novices, and endured years of sickness and spiritual darkness with patience. She died in 1607 at forty-one and was canonized in 1669.

UO-SIN-001042.name: Philip Neri
UO-SIN-001042.life: Born in Florence in 1515, Philip moved to Rome as a young man and spent years caring for the poor, pilgrims and the sick, helping found a confraternity for them. Ordained in 1551, he drew crowds to evening gatherings of prayer, readings, music and cheerful conversation, which grew into the Congregation of the Oratory, a society of secular priests. He began the pilgrim walk to Rome's seven churches and was famous for humour and humility. He also helped persuade the pope to reconcile Henry IV of France with the Church. Philip died in 1595 and was canonized in 1622.

UO-SIN-001043.name: Eleutherius of Rome
UO-SIN-001043.life: Eleutherius was a Greek from Nicopolis in Epirus who served the Roman church as a deacon under several bishops before becoming its bishop around 174. His time in office, lasting until about 189, saw relative peace under Emperor Commodus, and the church faced the stirrings of Montanism and Gnostic teachings. Later legend claimed that a British king named Lucius wrote to him asking for instruction in the faith, but scholars now reject the story, perhaps a confusion with a king of Edessa. Little else is certain about him, though his name was long remembered among Rome's early bishops.

UO-SIN-001044.name: Julius of Silistria
UO-SIN-001044.life: Julius was a Roman soldier born to pagan parents who, according to the story of his martyrdom, served for twenty-seven years in the army and fought in several campaigns. He became a Christian and was denounced by fellow soldiers during Diocletian's persecution. At Durostorum, now Silistra in Bulgaria, the prefect Maximus tried to win him over with bribes and promises, but Julius refused to sacrifice to the gods. He was beheaded, probably in 304, together with a number of companions. Though the account of his trial is not fully reliable, he has long been honoured as a martyr and as a patron of soldiers.

UO-SIN-001045.name: Lanfranc of Canterbury
UO-SIN-001045.life: Born in Pavia around 1005, Lanfranc trained in law before turning to teaching and then to the monastery of Bec in Normandy, where he became prior and a renowned master. He defended the church's teaching on the Eucharist against challenge and won William the Conqueror's trust. William made him abbot of Saint-Etienne at Caen and, after the Conquest, Archbishop of Canterbury in 1070. Lanfranc reorganized the English church, enforced discipline among clergy and separated church courts from secular ones. He helped William Rufus gain the throne and remained archbishop until his death in 1089.

UO-SIN-001046.name: Germanus of Paris
UO-SIN-001046.life: Germain was born near Autun around 496 and became abbot of the monastery of Saint-Symphorien before King Charibert had him made Bishop of Paris in 555. He was known as the father of the poor for his generous gifts, and he worked to soften the violence of the Frankish kings. He dared to excommunicate King Charibert for immoral conduct in 568. He consecrated the church Childebert built for the relics of Saint Vincent of Saragossa, and he was buried there when he died in 576. It later became the famous abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Pres.

UO-SIN-001047.name: Joan of Arc
UO-SIN-001047.life: Joan was a peasant girl born in Domremy around 1412, during the Hundred Years' War. From about the age of thirteen she heard voices which she believed to be those of saints urging her to help the French cause. In 1429 she persuaded Charles VII to give her troops, helped lift the siege of Orleans, and stood beside him at his coronation in Reims. Captured by the Burgundians in 1430 and handed to the English, she was tried for heresy and burned at Rouen on 30 May 1431. A later inquiry cleared her name, and she was canonized in 1920.

UO-SIN-001048.name: Bona of Pisa
UO-SIN-001048.life: Bona was born in Pisa around 1156, the daughter of a Corsican mother and a merchant father who left for the East. She felt drawn to God from childhood and joined the Augustinian third order as a girl. At about fourteen she travelled toward Jerusalem to find her father, but pirates captured and imprisoned her until she was ransomed. Later she became a pilgrim on the long road to Santiago de Compostela, helping weary travellers with encouragement, nursing and prayer, and the Knights of Saint James made her an official guide. She made the journey many times and died in Pisa in 1207, where pilgrims still honour her.

UO-SIN-001049.name: Ferdinand III of Castile
UO-SIN-001049.life: Ferdinand was born near Salamanca in 1198 and became King of Castile in 1217. He inherited Leon in 1230, joining the two kingdoms for good. A determined soldier, he led the Reconquest into the south of Spain, taking Cordoba in 1236 and Seville in 1248. At home he ruled justly, avoided heavy taxes, supported the University of Salamanca and founded churches and hospitals. Those who knew him spoke of his prayer, fasting and humility, and he is said to have feared one poor woman's curse more than an army. He died in Seville in 1252 wearing a Franciscan habit and was canonized in 1671.

UO-SIN-001050.name: Petronilla
UO-SIN-001050.life: Petronilla was an early Christian woman of Rome, honoured as a martyr since at least the fourth century. Her tomb lies in the Catacomb of Domitilla, where an early painting shows her welcoming a departed soul into heaven. She seems to have belonged to the Roman family of the Aurelii. According to later tradition, she was the daughter of the apostle Peter, who healed her of paralysis. Stories added that she was so beautiful that a pagan king, Flaccus, sought her hand, and that she fasted until she died rather than marry him. These tales are legend, and little that is certain is known of her.

UO-SIN-001051.name: Camilla Battista Varano
UO-SIN-001051.life: Camilla was born in 1458 in Camerino, the illegitimate daughter of its duke, and grew up in the splendour of his court. After hearing a Franciscan sermon on Christ's Passion as a child, she resolved to weep for him each Friday. She took a private vow of chastity in 1479 and, after her father's resistance, entered the Poor Clare monastery at Urbino in 1481. She moved to Camerino in 1484 and was later abbess. When her father and brothers were killed in 1502, she fled but later returned. She wrote mystical works on the Passion and died during a plague in 1524.

UO-SIN-001052.name: Pamphilus of Caesarea
UO-SIN-001052.life: Pamphilus was born into a wealthy family in Beirut, sold his property to help the poor, and studied at Alexandria before settling in Caesarea in Palestine, where he became a priest. There he founded a theological school and gathered a great library, copying Scripture and the works of Origen with his own hand. With the historian Eusebius he wrote a defence of Origen. Arrested in Diocletian's persecution in 307, Pamphilus spent two years in prison, still working on manuscripts, and was beheaded in 309 with several companions.

UO-SIN-001053.name: Erasmus / Elmo
UO-SIN-001053.life: Erasmus, also called Elmo, was according to tradition a bishop who fled the persecution of Diocletian, lived as a hermit on Mount Lebanon, and later suffered torture and martyrdom, finally coming to Formia in Italy, where he died. Scholars find no solid history behind these stories, and the accounts appear to blend him with another bishop of Antioch. His relics were kept at Formia until raiders destroyed it in 842, then moved to Gaeta. Sailors made him their patron, and the glow sometimes seen on ships' masts in storms is called Saint Elmo's fire. He is counted among the Fourteen Holy Helpers.

UO-SIN-001054.name: Pothinus of Lyons
UO-SIN-001054.life: Pothinus was the first bishop of Lyons, a Greek-speaking Christian from Asia Minor who is said to have been a follower of Polycarp of Smyrna and who was sent to bring the gospel to Gaul. For some twenty years he led the church there, made up largely of Greeks from the East. In 177, during the reign of Marcus Aurelius, a savage persecution broke out in Lyons and Vienne. Pothinus, then about ninety, was dragged before the governor and beaten by the mob. He died in prison soon after. Irenaeus succeeded him as bishop.

UO-SIN-001055.name: Charles Lwanga and Companions
UO-SIN-001055.life: In the 1880s King Mwanga II of Buganda grew alarmed at the influence of Christianity among the young pages of his court. Charles Lwanga, chief of the pages, taught and baptized the younger boys and protected them from the king's demands. Joseph Mukasa, a Christian court official, was beheaded earlier. On 3 June 1886 Lwanga and others were burned alive at Namugongo. Among those killed on the way were Pontian Ngondwe, Athanasius Bazzekuketta and Gonzaga Gonza. Catholic and Anglican converts alike died, and their courage helped Christianity take root in Uganda.

UO-SIN-001056.name: Kevin of Glendalough
UO-SIN-001056.life: Kevin was born into a noble Leinster family, traditionally in the later fifth century, and was educated by holy teachers before choosing the monastic life. Seeking solitude, he settled in the wooded valley of Glendalough in Wicklow, living as a hermit in a small cave. Disciples gathered around him, and the place grew into a famous monastery and pilgrimage site. Stories tell of wild animals drinking from his hands and of a blackbird nesting in his outstretched palm, which he held still until the eggs hatched. These tales are legend, and little reliable history survives. Tradition says he died on 3 June 618.

UO-SIN-001057.name: Clotilde
UO-SIN-001057.life: Clotilde was a Burgundian princess, born around 474, whose parents were killed in a family feud. A Catholic in a court where many held the Arian faith, she married the pagan Frankish king Clovis about 493 and pressed him to give up his idols. According to tradition he vowed to turn Christian if he won a battle against the Alemanni, and he was baptized at Reims with thousands of his people. After Clovis died in 511, she withdrew to Tours, living near the tomb of Saint Martin, giving to the poor and founding churches. She died in the mid-sixth century.

UO-SIN-001058.name: Dorotheus of Tyre
UO-SIN-001058.life: Dorotheus was a learned priest of Antioch who became bishop of Tyre. According to tradition he withdrew from the city during Diocletian's persecution, returned when peace came, and led his flock for many years, attending the Council of Nicaea in 325. A history of the prophets and apostles has long been credited to him, though scholars doubt it. When the emperor Julian opposed Christianity, the aged bishop was exiled to Odessos, now Varna on the Black Sea, where he is said to have died a martyr around 362 at more than a hundred years old. Much of this account rests on late tradition.

UO-SIN-001059.name: Sancho of Cordoba
UO-SIN-001059.life: Sancho was a young nobleman of Albi in southern Gaul who was taken prisoner in the wars of the 840s and carried to Cordoba, in Muslim Spain. He was raised at the emir's court and enrolled among the emir's guards. There he fell under the influence of the priest Eulogius and the Christians who were speaking out against the rules of the Muslim authorities. Accused and brought before the judge, he refused to renounce Christ and was put to death on 5 June 851. His body was impaled and displayed, then burned and the ashes thrown into the Guadalquivir.

UO-SIN-001060.name: Norbert of Xanten
UO-SIN-001060.life: Born about 1080 into a noble family at Xanten on the Rhine, Norbert lived comfortably at court until a violent thunderstorm that struck near him while he rode led him to change course. He was ordained, gave away his wealth and wandered as a preacher. About 1120 he settled at Premontre in France and founded the Premonstratensian canons, who joined the common life with preaching. He opposed the heresy of Tanchelm at Antwerp. Appointed Archbishop of Magdeburg in 1126, he worked to reform the clergy and recover church property. He died there in 1134 and was canonized in 1582.

UO-SIN-001061.name: Philip the Deacon
UO-SIN-001061.life: Philip was one of the seven men chosen in Jerusalem to oversee the daily care of the church's widows. After Stephen's martyrdom scattered believers, he preached in Samaria, where many came to faith. Directed by an angel, he met an Ethiopian official on the road to Gaza, explained the passage from Isaiah he was reading, and baptized him. Philip later settled in Caesarea, where Paul stayed in his house and where his four daughters prophesied. The New Testament calls him the evangelist, and he is not to be confused with the apostle Philip.

UO-SIN-001062.name: Robert of Newminster
UO-SIN-001062.life: Robert was born around 1100 at Gargrave in Yorkshire, studied at Paris, and served as a parish priest before becoming a monk. In 1132 he joined the monks who left York to found Fountains Abbey in a wild valley, where they lived in great poverty under the Cistercian rule. About 1138 he led a group to found Newminster, near Morpeth in Northumberland, and governed it as abbot for some twenty years. Newminster itself founded Pipewell, Roche and Sawley. Known as gentle, prayerful and merciful, he was a friend of Bernard of Clairvaux. He died on 7 June 1159.

UO-SIN-001063.name: Paul I of Constantinople
UO-SIN-001063.life: Paul was born in Thessalonica and served as secretary to Bishop Alexander of Constantinople, whom he succeeded in 337. He held firmly to the Nicene faith in the years when the Arian controversy divided the church, and the emperor Constantius, who favoured the Arians, drove him from his see three times. Western bishops and the emperor Constans supported him, and restored him more than once. After Constans died, Paul was banished to Cucusus in Armenia, where, about 350, he was strangled by his enemies while celebrating the liturgy. He is honoured as a confessor and martyr, and his remains were moved to Constantinople in 381.

UO-SIN-001064.name: William of York
UO-SIN-001064.life: William FitzHerbert, perhaps a relative of King Stephen, served as treasurer of York Minster before being elected archbishop in 1141. The Cistercians, led by Bernard of Clairvaux, opposed his election, and Pope Eugene III, himself a Cistercian, deposed him in 1147. William accepted his fate patiently and lived in retirement until his opponents died. He was restored in 1153 and returned to York to great rejoicing, famously crossing the Ouse bridge when it collapsed, though no one died. He died a few weeks later in 1154, perhaps poisoned. Miracles were reported at his tomb, and he was canonized in the thirteenth century.

UO-SIN-001065.name: Medard of Noyon
UO-SIN-001065.life: Medard was born around 456 in Picardy, the son of a Frankish father and a Gallo-Roman mother. Ordained as a mature man, he became bishop of Vermand about 530 and moved the see to Noyon. He later also took charge of Tournai, and the two dioceses stayed united for centuries. He is said to have given the veil to the Frankish queen Radegund. According to legend, an eagle once sheltered him from rain as a child, and so he came to be linked with weather and harvests. He died about 545, and King Clotaire buried him at Soissons, where an abbey rose over his tomb.

UO-SIN-000783.name: Alexander Jolly
UO-SIN-000783.life: Alexander Jolly was born in Stonehaven in 1756 and studied at Marischal College, Aberdeen. Ordained in the Scottish Episcopal Church, he served congregations at Turriff and Fraserburgh, and in 1798 became sole Bishop of Moray, while remaining a parish priest in Fraserburgh until his death. He lived simply, without servants, giving much of his small income to the poor and to books, and read the Hebrew Bible, the Greek New Testament and the Fathers daily. His writings on the Church and the Prayer Book services earned him wide respect. He died in 1838.

UO-SIN-001100.name: Emma of Gurk
UO-SIN-001100.life: Emma, also called Hemma, was a noblewoman of Carinthia, born around 980 and related to the imperial family. She married Count William of Friesach and bore two sons. After her husband and sons were killed, she inherited great wealth and turned it to the Church and the poor. She founded or endowed a number of churches and, in 1043, established a Benedictine convent at Gurk, where she spent her last years in prayer. She died in 1045. Her tomb in Gurk became a place of pilgrimage, and she is honoured as patron of Carinthia.

UO-SIN-001101.name: Irenaeus of Lyon
UO-SIN-001101.life: Irenaeus was born in Asia Minor, probably at Smyrna, and as a young man listened to the bishop Polycarp, who had known the apostle John's circle. He became a priest at Lyon in Gaul, and after the persecution there around 177 he succeeded the martyred Pothinus as bishop. His great work, Against Heresies, answered the Gnostic teachers by appealing to Scripture, the tradition handed down from the apostles, and the unbroken succession of bishops. He also worked to keep peace among quarrelling churches. He died about the year 200; later tradition counts him a martyr, though this is uncertain.

UO-SIN-001102.name: Leo II
UO-SIN-001102.life: Leo was born in Sicily and became known as a learned man and an accomplished singer. Elected Bishop of Rome in 681, he waited more than a year for his consecration in August 682. His short pontificate is remembered chiefly for confirming the Sixth General Council of Constantinople, which rejected the teaching that Christ had only one will, and for translating its decisions for the West. He also strengthened Rome's authority over the see of Ravenna and encouraged sacred music. He died in 683.

UO-SIN-001103.name: Peter the Apostle
UO-SIN-001103.life: Simon, a fisherman from Bethsaida who worked at Capernaum on the Sea of Galilee, was called by Jesus with his brother Andrew and given the name Peter, the Rock. He is named first among the Twelve and often speaks for them, confessing Jesus as the Christ yet also denying him three times on the night of his arrest. After the resurrection he led the first Christians in Jerusalem and opened the way for non-Jewish believers. Early tradition says he came to Rome and was crucified under Nero, about 64, and the Vatican hill marks his traditional burial.

UO-SIN-001104.name: Paul the Apostle
UO-SIN-001104.life: Born Saul at Tarsus in Cilicia, Paul was a Jewish tentmaker trained as a Pharisee who at first persecuted the followers of Jesus. On the road to Damascus he met the risen Christ, was baptized, and became the great apostle to the Gentiles. He travelled through Asia Minor and Greece, founding churches and writing letters, several of which fill the New Testament and have shaped Christian thought ever since. He was arrested in Jerusalem and taken to Rome. According to tradition he was beheaded there under Nero, around the year 64.
UO-SIN-001104.place: Tarsus; Damascus; Asia Minor, Greece; Rome

UO-SIN-001105.name: Raymond Lull
UO-SIN-001105.life: Ramon Llull was born about 1232 in Palma, Majorca, and grew up in the royal court as a poet and troubadour. Around the age of thirty, visions of Christ crucified turned him to a new life. He resolved to win Muslims to the faith by reason and love, not by arms. He founded a school of languages at Miramar to train missionaries, wrote many books in Catalan, Latin and Arabic, and devised his Art, a system of logic for presenting Christian truth. He made journeys to North Africa, and died in 1316, traditionally after being stoned at Bougie.

UO-SIN-000001.name: Pauli Murray
UO-SIN-000001.life: Pauli Murray was born in Baltimore in 1910 and raised by relatives in Durham, North Carolina. Denied entry to graduate study because of her race and later her sex, she graduated first in her class at Howard University Law School. Her book States' Laws on Race and Color became a handbook for civil rights lawyers, and she named and fought what she called Jane Crow, the discrimination faced by women. She helped found the National Organization for Women. In 1977 she became the first African American woman ordained a priest in the Episcopal Church. She died in Pittsburgh in 1985.
UO-SIN-000001.place: Durham, North Carolina; New York; Pittsburgh

UO-SIN-000182.name: Serf of Culross
UO-SIN-000182.life: Serf, or Servanus, is a Scottish saint of the sixth century whose life is wrapped in legend. According to tradition he founded a community at Culross on the Firth of Forth, where he is said to have lived and worked. When the princess Theneva came ashore there, carrying her child, Serf is said to have sheltered the boy, who became Saint Kentigern, or Mungo. Tradition also places him on an island in Loch Leven and tells how he killed a dragon at Dunning. Little can be known for certain, but his name lives on in many Fife churches.

UO-SIN-000185.name: Swithun
UO-SIN-000185.life: Swithun became Bishop of Winchester in 852 and died in 863, serving under King Æthelwulf of Wessex, whom he may have helped to teach. Very little was recorded of him in his own lifetime. Tradition says he asked to be buried outside the cathedral, where passers-by would walk over his grave and rain fall on it. In 971 his body was moved into a splendid new shrine, accompanied by reports of miracles. The English proverb of forty days of rain is attached to his name.

UO-SIN-000186.name: Walter Rauschenbusch, Washington Gladden, and Jacob Riis
UO-SIN-000186.life: These three men, working in the United States around the turn of the twentieth century, called Christians to care for the poor and to reform unjust conditions. Walter Rauschenbusch, a Baptist pastor in New York's Hell's Kitchen and later a professor at Rochester, wrote Christianity and the Social Crisis and became the leading voice of the Social Gospel. Washington Gladden, a Congregational pastor in Columbus, Ohio, defended labor and wrote the hymn O Master, Let Me Walk with Thee. Jacob Riis, a Danish-born journalist and photographer, exposed tenement misery in How the Other Half Lives.
UO-SIN-000186.place: Rochester and New York; Columbus, Ohio

UO-SIN-000004.name: Independence Day
UO-SIN-000004.life: On July 2, 1776, the Continental Congress meeting in Philadelphia voted that the thirteen American colonies were free of British rule. Two days later, on July 4, it approved the final wording of the Declaration of Independence, largely drafted by Thomas Jefferson, which declared that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights. The parchment copy was signed mostly in August. Americans soon kept July 4 with speeches, prayers, bells and fireworks, beginning within a year. The day is a time to give thanks for liberty and to pray for the nation's justice and peace.

UO-SIN-000191.name: Moninne of Killeavy
UO-SIN-000191.life: Moninne, also called Darerca or Bline, was among the earliest women saints of Ireland, born in County Down around 435. Tradition holds that Saint Patrick gave her the veil. She gathered a small community near Faughart in Louth, and later settled at Killeavy beneath Slieve Gullion in County Armagh, where she founded her convent. She also sought counsel from Saint Ibar and visited Saint Brigid at Kildare. She died about 517, and pilgrims still visit her holy well at Killeavy.

UO-SIN-000192.name: John Hus
UO-SIN-000192.life: Jan Hus was born about 1369 in Husinec, Bohemia, and became a priest, teacher and rector at Charles University in Prague. From 1402 he preached in Czech at the Bethlehem Chapel, criticizing the greed and immorality of clergy, and he was influenced by the writings of John Wycliffe. Excommunicated in 1410, he left Prague in 1412 and in 1414 travelled to the Council of Constance under a promise of safe conduct. There he was imprisoned and, refusing to retract what he said he had never taught, was burned at the stake on 6 July 1415.

UO-SIN-000193.name: Thomas More
UO-SIN-000193.life: Thomas More was born in London in 1478, trained as a lawyer, and became one of the leading scholars of Renaissance England, author of Utopia. He served Henry VIII and in 1529 became Lord Chancellor. He resigned in 1532 rather than support the king's break with Rome. Refusing in 1534 to swear the oaths of succession and supremacy, he was imprisoned in the Tower for over a year, convicted of treason, and beheaded on 6 July 1535, declaring himself the king's good servant, but God's first.

UO-SIN-000194.name: Pantaenus of Alexandria
UO-SIN-000194.life: Pantaenus was a Christian teacher in Alexandria in the later second century, said to have been a Stoic philosopher before his conversion. He led the catechetical school there, and his most famous pupil and successor was Clement of Alexandria, who spoke of him as the Sicilian bee for the way he gathered wisdom. Eusebius reports that he travelled to India to preach, where he found Christians using a Gospel of Matthew; the details are uncertain. None of his writings survive. He died about the year 200.

UO-SIN-000196.name: Disibod
UO-SIN-000196.life: Disibod was an Irish monk and bishop, born around 619, whose story comes chiefly from a life written centuries later by Hildegard of Bingen. According to that account, he grew discouraged with his work in Ireland and crossed to the continent as a missionary with a few disciples. Guided by a vision, he settled where the Glan meets the Nahe in what is now Germany, living as a hermit. Followers gathered around him, building small cells in the Irish manner, and the place became the monastery of Disibodenberg. He is traditionally said to have died about 700.

UO-SIN-000197.name: Kilian
UO-SIN-000197.life: Kilian was an Irish missionary bishop, born about 640, who left Ireland with a band of companions to preach in Franconia and Thuringia. He settled at Würzburg, where, according to tradition, he baptized the local duke, Gozbert. He and two companions, Colman and Totnan, were beheaded about 689 on the duke's orders. Their relics were honoured in Würzburg, where Kilian became the city's patron saint, and his name remains common in Germany and Ireland.

UO-SIN-000012.name: Drostan of Deer
UO-SIN-000012.life: Drostan was a Scottish abbot who lived about 600. Tradition says he was of noble Gaelic family and was trained as a monk by Columba, whom he accompanied from Iona to Buchan in north-east Scotland. There they founded a monastery at Deer, and Columba left him as its first abbot. Later he governed another house at Holywood, then withdrew to live as a hermit at Glenesk. People came to him for healing and counsel, and after his death his relics were kept at Aberdour.

UO-SIN-000201.name: Nathan Söderblom
UO-SIN-000201.life: Nathan Söderblom was born in 1866 in rural Sweden, in Trönö. He studied the history of religions, served as chaplain in Paris, and taught at Uppsala and Leipzig before becoming Archbishop of Uppsala in 1914. During and after the First World War he urged the churches to work together for peace and justice. He organized the 1925 Stockholm conference on Life and Work, a founding moment of the modern ecumenical movement, and strengthened ties between the Church of Sweden and the Church of England. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1930 and died the next year.

UO-SIN-000202.name: John Gualbert
UO-SIN-000202.life: John Gualbert was born about 985 into a noble family of Florence. According to tradition, when he met his brother's murderer on a narrow road one Good Friday and was about to take revenge, the man begged for mercy in Christ's name, and John spared him. He became a Benedictine at San Miniato, then withdrew to seek a stricter life and founded the monastery of Vallombrosa in the Tuscan hills around 1038. He preached against simony, the buying of church offices. He died in 1073, and was canonized in 1193.

UO-SIN-000204.name: Conrad Weiser
UO-SIN-000204.life: Conrad Weiser was born in 1696 in Württemberg and came as a boy with German settlers to New York. Living for a time among the Mohawk, he learned their language and ways. After moving to Pennsylvania in 1729 he became the colony's trusted interpreter and messenger to the Iroquois, helping to arrange treaties at Philadelphia, Lancaster and Logstown. His fairness and friendships helped keep peace on the frontier for many years. He also served as magistrate and soldier, and was a deeply religious man. He died in 1760, and Native friends were said to visit his grave.

UO-SIN-000205.name: Silas
UO-SIN-000205.life: Silas, also called Silvanus, was an early Christian leader in Jerusalem and a prophet. The church sent him to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas to carry word of its decision about Gentile believers. He then became Paul's companion on his second journey through Asia Minor and into Greece. At Philippi he was beaten and jailed with Paul, and an earthquake opened the prison doors. He later helped Paul in Thessalonica, Berea and Corinth, and his name appears in the letters to the Thessalonians. A Silvanus is also linked with Peter's first letter, probably the same man.

UO-SIN-000207.name: Samson Occom
UO-SIN-000207.life: Samson Occom was born in 1723 among the Mohegan people of Connecticut and became a Christian in his teens during the Great Awakening. He studied with Eleazar Wheelock, then taught and preached for years among the Montauk of Long Island, and in 1759 was ordained a Presbyterian minister. He toured England and Scotland preaching to raise funds for Wheelock's school, which eventually led to Dartmouth College, and he grew bitter at how the money was used. He wrote hymns and a short autobiography, and helped found Brothertown in New York, where he died in 1792.

UO-SIN-000209.name: Oxford Movement and Keble's Assize Sermon
UO-SIN-000209.life: On 14 July 1833 John Keble preached at Oxford before the assize judges on what he called national apostasy, protesting government interference in the Church of Ireland. Friends later counted it the start of the Oxford Movement. Keble, John Henry Newman, Edward Pusey and others published the Tracts for the Times, calling Anglicans to recover the Church's apostolic heritage, its sacraments and its life of prayer. Though Newman later became a Roman Catholic, the movement renewed Anglican worship, brought new religious communities, and inspired priests to serve the poor.

UO-SIN-000015.name: Bonaventure
UO-SIN-000015.life: Giovanni di Fidanza, known as Bonaventure, was born in 1221 at Bagnoregio in Italy. He joined the Franciscans, studied at Paris, and became a renowned teacher. Elected minister general of the Friars Minor in 1257, he guided the order through bitter disputes over poverty, and wrote the authorized life of Saint Francis. His books on theology and prayer joined learning to devotion. Pope Gregory X made him Cardinal Bishop of Albano in 1273. He died at Lyon in 1274 during the Council there, and is called the Seraphic Doctor.

UO-SIN-000212.name: The Righteous Gentiles
UO-SIN-000212.life: Righteous Among the Nations is the title given to non-Jews who, during the Holocaust, risked their lives to save Jews from the Nazis. Israel's Yad Vashem has recognized tens of thousands from dozens of countries, among them Poland, the Netherlands, France and Hungary. They hid people in homes, convents, farms and cellars, forged papers, and smuggled children to safety, often at terrible risk to themselves and their families. Oskar Schindler, Irena Sendler, Raoul Wallenberg and Jane Haining are among them. They remind us that ordinary people can choose courage and compassion when evil seems overwhelming.

UO-SIN-000214.name: Jane Haining
UO-SIN-000214.life: Jane Haining was born in 1897 on a farm at Dunscore in Dumfriesshire, and worked for ten years as a secretary in Paisley before volunteering for the Church of Scotland's mission in Budapest. From 1932 she was matron of the boarding house for girls at the mission school, most of them Jewish. When war came she was urged to return home but refused, asking how children who needed her in sunshine could need her less in darkness. Arrested by the Gestapo in April 1944, she was sent to Auschwitz and died there on 17 July 1944.

UO-SIN-000215.name: Marcellina
UO-SIN-000215.life: Marcellina was born around 330, probably at Trier, the elder sister of Ambrose, later Bishop of Milan. Her family was Roman and Christian. At Rome, probably on Christmas Day around 353, Pope Liberius gave her the veil of consecrated virginity, and she lived a life of prayer, fasting and austerity at home. After Ambrose became bishop in 374 she joined him in Milan, encouraging women to live the ascetic life. He dedicated to her his treatise on virginity. She outlived him by about a year, died around 398, and was buried near his tomb.

UO-SIN-000018.name: Bartolomé de las Casas
UO-SIN-000018.life: Bartolomé de las Casas was born in Seville in 1484 and sailed to Hispaniola as a young man, where he held Native people in forced labor. In 1514, reflecting on Scripture before a sermon, he renounced his holdings and spent the rest of his life defending the Indigenous peoples of the Americas. He became a Dominican friar, and served briefly as Bishop of Chiapas, where he refused absolution to those who would not free their slaves. His Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies shocked Spain, and he argued at Valladolid that Native peoples were fully human. He died at Madrid in 1566.

UO-SIN-000254.name: Hiroshima atomic bombing
UO-SIN-000254.life: On the morning of 6 August 1945, near the end of the Second World War, an American B-29 bomber, the Enola Gay, dropped a single atomic bomb on the Japanese city of Hiroshima. It exploded over the city at about 8:15, destroying most of its buildings and killing perhaps eighty thousand people at once; tens of thousands more died of burns and radiation before the year ended. Nagasaki suffered the same fate three days later, and Japan surrendered soon after. The event opened the nuclear age, and Hiroshima has since become a place where the world remembers the cost of war and prays for peace.

UO-SIN-000255.name: Catherine Winkworth
UO-SIN-000255.life: Catherine Winkworth was born in London in 1827 and grew up in Manchester and later Clifton, near Bristol. After a time in Dresden she became fascinated by German hymns, and from 1855 she published a series of collections, including Lyra Germanica and The Chorale Book for England, that put several hundred of them into graceful English verse. Her translations, such as the rendering of "Now thank we all our God", are still sung in many churches. She also worked tirelessly for the higher education of girls in Bristol and Clifton. She died suddenly in 1878 at Monnetier, in Savoy.

UO-SIN-000256.name: Sixtus II and Companions
UO-SIN-000256.life: Sixtus II became bishop of Rome in August 257, during a lull in persecution, and worked to mend relations with the churches of Africa and the East, which had been strained over the baptism of heretics. In 258 Emperor Valerian ordered bishops, priests and deacons put to death. Sixtus was seized while teaching his people and beheaded on 6 August, together with several of his deacons, including Januarius, Vincentius, Magnus, Stephanus, Felicissimus and Agapitus. His best-known deacon, Lawrence, followed him in death four days later. Sixtus is remembered as a faithful shepherd and is named in the Roman Canon of the Mass.

UO-SIN-000257.name: Mary MacKillop
UO-SIN-000257.life: Mary MacKillop was born in Melbourne in 1842, the eldest child of Scottish immigrants. As a young governess in South Australia she met Father Julian Tenison-Woods, and in 1866 they began a school for poor children at Penola. She took the name Mary of the Cross and founded the Sisters of St Joseph of the Sacred Heart, who taught in remote bush communities and cared for orphans and the destitute. Conflict with some bishops led to her brief excommunication, later lifted. She led her sisters until she died in Sydney in 1909. In 2010 she became Australia's first canonised saint.

UO-SIN-000258.name: Altman of Passau
UO-SIN-000258.life: Altmann, born in Westphalia around 1015, taught at the cathedral school of Paderborn and served as chaplain to Emperor Henry III before becoming bishop of Passau in 1065. A friend of Pope Gregory VII, he pressed for clerical reform and for the independence of the church from imperial control, and he founded the abbeys of St Nicholas in Passau and Göttweig. He was known for his care of the poor. His stand brought conflict with Emperor Henry IV, who drove him from his city, and he spent his last years in Austria, restoring monasteries there. He died in 1091.

UO-SIN-000050.name: Mary Sumner
UO-SIN-000050.life: Mary Heywood was born in 1828 and grew up in Herefordshire. In 1848 she married George Sumner, a clergyman who later became Bishop of Guildford, and in 1851 they settled at Old Alresford in Hampshire. In 1876, when her eldest daughter had a child, she remembered how lonely and anxious young motherhood could be. She invited the women of the parish, rich and poor alike, to meet for prayer and mutual support. From that gathering grew the Mothers' Union, which spread across the British Empire and beyond. Queen Victoria became its patron in 1897. Mary Sumner died in 1921.

UO-SIN-000260.name: Blane
UO-SIN-000260.life: Blane was a Scottish saint of the sixth century, said to have been born on the island of Bute. According to tradition his mother was Irish, and he was educated in Ireland under Comgall and Cainnech before becoming a monk. He returned to Scotland, where he served as a bishop among the Picts, with his church at Kingarth on Bute, where the ruins can still be seen. Later legend credits him with miracles, including raising a dead boy to life, but little is certain. His monastery at Dunblane later became the site of its cathedral, and several places in Scotland carry his name. He died about 590.

UO-SIN-000263.name: Consecration of Charles Inglis
UO-SIN-000263.life: Charles Inglis, born in County Donegal in 1734, went to America as a young man and became rector of Trinity Church, New York. A staunch Loyalist, he left after the Revolution. On 12 August 1787 he was consecrated at Lambeth as the first bishop of Nova Scotia, the first colonial bishop of the Church of England. His vast diocese stretched from Newfoundland and Bermuda to Quebec. He visited scattered congregations, confirmed thousands, encouraged the building of churches, and founded King's College at Windsor, the first university in British North America. He died in Halifax in 1816, remembered as the father of Anglicanism in Canada.

UO-SIN-000264.name: Ann Griffiths
UO-SIN-000264.life: Ann Griffiths was born in 1776 at Dolwar Fach, a farm in Montgomeryshire, Wales, and was raised in the parish church. Lively and fond of dancing in her youth, she was deeply changed by the preaching of Welsh Methodists and joined their society in 1797. After her mother died she ran the farm. She composed hymns of remarkable depth and beauty, which she recited to her maid, Ruth Evans, and which were later written down by Ruth's husband, John Hughes. She married in 1804 and died the following year, soon after the birth of her child, aged twenty-nine. Her hymns are among the finest in Welsh.

UO-SIN-000044.name: Jeremy Taylor
UO-SIN-000044.life: Jeremy Taylor, born in Cambridge in 1613 and the son of a barber, rose through the patronage of Archbishop Laud to become chaplain to Charles I. When the king's cause was lost he was imprisoned briefly, then found shelter in Wales as chaplain to the Earl of Carbery. There he wrote his best-loved works, Holy Living and Holy Dying, which shaped Anglican devotion for generations. After the Restoration he became bishop of Down and Connor in Ireland, where he struggled with Presbyterian opposition. Admired for the beauty of his prose, he was called the "Shakespeare of Divines". He died in Lisburn in 1667.

UO-SIN-000266.name: Radegund
UO-SIN-000266.life: Radegund was born about 520, a princess of Thuringia. After her father was killed she was carried off as a child by the Frankish king Clotaire and later forced to marry him. She gave herself to prayer and to the care of the poor, the sick and captives. When Clotaire murdered her brother she left the court, was consecrated a deaconess, and founded the convent of the Holy Cross at Poitiers, which became a centre of learning. She obtained a relic of the True Cross, for which her friend, the poet Venantius Fortunatus, wrote hymns including Vexilla Regis. She died at Poitiers in 587.

UO-SIN-000267.name: Pontian and Hippolytus
UO-SIN-000267.life: Pontian was bishop of Rome from 230 and Hippolytus a learned Roman priest and writer who had set himself up as a rival bishop, dividing the Roman church. In 235 the emperor Maximinus Thrax began persecuting church leaders, and both men were sent to the unhealthy island of Sardinia, to labour in the mines. There they were reconciled. Pontian resigned on 28 September so that Rome could elect a successor, and soon died from the hardships of exile. Hippolytus also perished there. Pope Fabian later brought their bodies back to Rome for honourable burial, and both are remembered as martyrs.

UO-SIN-000045.name: Jonathan Myrick Daniels
UO-SIN-000045.life: Jonathan Daniels was born in Keene, New Hampshire, in 1939, and graduated at the head of his class from the Virginia Military Institute. After a deep spiritual experience he entered Episcopal Theological School in Cambridge, Massachusetts. In March 1965 he answered Martin Luther King's call to join the Selma marchers, and stayed in Alabama to help Black residents register to vote. On 20 August 1965 in Hayneville, he pushed seventeen-year-old Ruby Sales aside and was killed by a shotgun blast meant for her. The man who shot him was acquitted by an all-white jury. Daniels was twenty-six.

UO-SIN-000270.name: Meinhard of Latvia
UO-SIN-000270.life: Meinhard was a German Augustinian canon from Segeberg in Holstein who travelled with merchants to the Daugava river in the 1180s to preach to the pagan Livonians in what is now Latvia. At Ikšķile he built a stone church and, with masons from Gotland, a fortress to shelter his converts from raiders. In 1186 he was consecrated bishop of Livonia, the first in the region. Some of his converts later turned against him, and the mission remained fragile. He died at Ikšķile in 1196, and his remains now lie in Riga Cathedral. He is honoured as the apostle of Latvia.

UO-SIN-000046.name: Saint Mary the Virgin
UO-SIN-000046.life: Mary was a young Jewish woman of Nazareth in Galilee who, according to the Gospels, was told by the angel Gabriel that she would bear the Son of God, and answered, "Let it be to me according to your word." She gave birth to Jesus at Bethlehem, raised him at Nazareth, and stood near the cross at his death. She was among the believers who prayed together after his ascension. Christian tradition honours her as the Mother of God. An ancient tradition holds that at the end of her life she was taken up into heaven.

UO-SIN-000047.name: Holy Women of the Old Testament
UO-SIN-000047.life: The Old Testament tells of many women through whom God worked. Sarah, Rebekah, Leah and Rachel, the matriarchs, are the ancestral mothers of Israel, and each is remembered for faith in God's promises to her family. Miriam sang at the Red Sea, and Deborah judged Israel and led it in prophecy. Hannah prayed for a child and gave her son Samuel to God's service. Ruth, a Moabite widow, chose loyalty to Naomi and became an ancestor of King David. Esther risked her life to save her people, and in the Apocrypha Judith is celebrated for her courage.

UO-SIN-000274.name: Roger Schütz
UO-SIN-000274.life: Roger Schütz was born in Switzerland in 1915, the youngest child of a Reformed pastor. In 1940, at twenty-five, he settled in the French village of Taizé, near the line dividing France, where he sheltered refugees, especially Jews. After the war other men joined him, and at Easter 1949 seven brothers made lifelong vows; he wrote their Rule. Known as Brother Roger, he made Taizé a community of Protestants and Catholics, devoted to reconciliation among Christians and peace among peoples. Thousands of young pilgrims came each week to pray. On 16 August 2005, during evening prayer, he was stabbed to death by a mentally ill woman, aged ninety.

UO-SIN-000275.name: Stephen of Hungary
UO-SIN-000275.life: Stephen, born about 975 as Vajk, was the son of the Hungarian chief Géza and was baptised as a boy. He married Gisela of Bavaria and, around the year 1000, was crowned the first king of Hungary with a crown sent by the pope. He worked to make his people Christian, founding bishoprics and monasteries, and issued laws protecting the church and the poor. His reign also gave Hungary firm borders and a settled government. He grieved deeply when his son Emeric died in a hunting accident. Stephen died on 15 August 1038 and was canonised in 1083.

UO-SIN-000276.name: John Stuart
UO-SIN-000276.life: John Stuart was born in Pennsylvania in 1740 and raised a Presbyterian, but became an Anglican. Ordained in England in 1770, he was sent as a missionary to the Mohawks at Fort Hunter, New York, where he served as pastor and teacher. He worked with the Mohawk leader Joseph Brant on a translation of St Mark's Gospel into Mohawk. A loyal subject of the Crown, he left New York during the Revolution, and in 1785 settled at Kingston, becoming the first resident Anglican clergyman in what is now Ontario. He built its first church and taught school. He died in Kingston in 1811.

UO-SIN-000277.name: Clare of Montefalco
UO-SIN-000277.life: Clare was born about 1268 at Montefalco in Umbria. At six she joined her sister Joan and other women who lived as devout tertiaries in a hermitage, and when they sought a stricter life in 1290 the bishop gave them the Rule of St Augustine. After Joan's death Clare became abbess of the convent of the Holy Cross, where she was a wise teacher and spiritual guide. She spoke often of carrying the cross of Christ in her heart, and she endured long illness with patience. She died on 18 August 1308 and was canonised in 1881.

UO-SIN-000278.name: Joan of the Cross
UO-SIN-000278.life: Jeanne Delanoue was born in 1666 at Saumur in France, the youngest of twelve children. She ran the family shop selling religious goods to pilgrims, and had a reputation for sharp business. A poor widow's prophecy that she would devote herself to the poor slowly came true. She closed the shop and opened her home, with its cellars along the Loire, to orphans, the sick and the elderly. In 1704 other women joined her, and they became the Sisters of St Anne of Providence. Taking the name Joan of the Cross, she died in 1736, and by then her sisters ran twelve houses.

UO-SIN-000279.name: Artemisia Bowden
UO-SIN-000279.life: Artemisia Bowden was born in Albany, Georgia, in 1879, the daughter of former slaves. After attending St Augustine's school in Raleigh, North Carolina, she taught there for several years. In 1902 she moved to San Antonio, Texas, to lead St Philip's, a small Episcopal school for Black girls. Over fifty-two years she built it into an accredited junior college, of which she became president in 1927, and in 1942 it joined the city's public school system. She retired in 1954. Honoured nationally as one of the outstanding women educators of her day, she died in San Antonio in 1969.

UO-SIN-000281.name: Jane Frances de Chantal
UO-SIN-000281.life: Jane Frances was born at Dijon in 1572, the daughter of a leading magistrate. She married Baron de Chantal and ran his estate well, but he was killed in a hunting accident in 1601, leaving her a widow with four young children. She sought a spiritual guide and found one in Francis de Sales, bishop of Geneva. With him she founded the Order of the Visitation at Annecy in 1610, a community for women who could not enter more austere orders. She guided its growth for thirty years, and when she died in 1641 there were eighty-six houses. She was canonised in 1767.

UO-SIN-000283.name: Blaise Pascal
UO-SIN-000283.life: Blaise Pascal was born at Clermont in France in 1623 and educated at home by his father. A brilliant boy, he wrote on geometry at sixteen and later built a mechanical calculator and did pioneering work on probability and the pressure of fluids. After a profound religious experience in 1654 he gave himself to faith, siding with the Jansenists of Port-Royal. His Provincial Letters satirised the moral laxity of some theologians, and his unfinished Pensées, a set of notes for a defence of Christianity, remains widely read. Always in poor health, he died in Paris in 1662, aged thirty-nine.

UO-SIN-000284.name: Louis of Anjou
UO-SIN-000284.life: Louis was born in 1274, the second son of Charles II of Anjou, king of Naples. As a boy he was held hostage in Aragon for seven years, and there Franciscan friars taught him and shaped his devotion. After his release he refused the crown of Naples, which he might have inherited, and chose to become a priest. Pope Boniface VIII named him bishop of Toulouse, but he first joined the Franciscans, and was consecrated in December 1296. In Toulouse he gave himself to the poor. He fell ill on a journey and died at Brignoles in August 1297, aged twenty-three.

UO-SIN-000285.name: William and Catherine Booth
UO-SIN-000285.life: William Booth, a Nottingham pawnbroker's apprentice, and Catherine Mumford, who grew up devout in Derbyshire, were both born in 1829 and married in 1855. Both were evangelists, and Catherine insisted that women should preach. In 1865 they began a mission to the poor of London's East End, which in 1878 became the Salvation Army, with its brass bands, uniforms and ranks. They fed the hungry, sheltered the homeless and rescued the lost. Catherine died of cancer in 1890, and William, as the first General, continued to lead the Army until his death in 1912.

UO-SIN-000286.name: Bernard Tolomei
UO-SIN-000286.life: Bernardo Tolomei was born at Siena in 1272 and baptised Giovanni. A gifted lawyer who taught at the university and held civic office, he turned to religion after a loss of sight from which he was healed. In 1313, with two companions, he withdrew to a wild place called Accona, south-east of Siena, and took the name Bernard. Their hermitage grew into the Benedictine congregation of Monte Oliveto, whose monks wore white. In 1348, when plague struck Siena, Bernard went to nurse the sick at the monastery in the city, where he and many of his monks died.

UO-SIN-000287.name: Pius X
UO-SIN-000287.life: Giuseppe Sarto was born in 1835 at Riese in the Veneto, the son of a postman. He served as a village priest, bishop of Mantua and patriarch of Venice before his election as pope in 1903. He took the name Pius X and gave himself to pastoral renewal: he encouraged frequent communion, allowed children to receive it at a young age, promoted congregational chant and catechism, and ordered the church's law to be codified. He also strongly opposed what he saw as modernist errors. He lived simply and cared for the poor. He died in August 1914, as war began, and was canonised in 1954.

UO-SIN-000288.name: Sidonius Apollinaris
UO-SIN-000288.life: Sidonius was born about 430 at Lyon into a wealthy Gallo-Roman family.
