He married the daughter of Avitus, who became western emperor, and wrote poems in praise of emperors, and in 468 served as prefect of Rome. Soon after, about 470, he reluctantly became bishop of Clermont, and he led its defence against the Visigoth king Euric, though the city finally fell and he was exiled for a time. He later returned to his see. His letters give a vivid picture of the last years of Roman Gaul. He died in the 480s.

UO-SIN-000291.name: Rose of Lima
UO-SIN-000291.life: Born Isabel Flores de Oliva in Lima, Peru, in 1586, she was nicknamed Rose after a servant said her face had seemed to turn into a rose. Inspired by Catherine of Siena, she fasted, practised severe penance and refused marriage, despite her parents' protests. She became a Dominican tertiary at about twenty, living in a small hut in the family garden. There she prayed for hours, while selling lace, embroidery and flowers to support her family and care for the sick and hungry she brought home. She died in 1617 and was the first person born in the Americas to be canonized.

UO-SIN-000292.name: Tydfil
UO-SIN-000292.life: Tydfil is the Welsh saint who gave her name to Merthyr Tydfil, the town whose name means 'Tydfil's martyrdom'. According to tradition she was a daughter of Brychan, the king of Brycheiniog, and made her home in the valley of the River Taff, caring for the sick and leading a small Christian community. She is said to have been killed there around 480 by raiders, perhaps pagans from outside Wales, as she knelt in prayer. Little can be known with certainty, but her memory has been honoured in the town and its old parish church for centuries.

UO-SIN-000293.name: Simone Weil
UO-SIN-000293.life: Born in Paris in 1909 to a secular Jewish family, Simone Weil became a brilliant philosopher and teacher. She was also a restless seeker of justice: she took a year of factory work to share the lot of workers and briefly joined an anarchist unit in the Spanish Civil War. Mystical experiences in the late 1930s drew her toward Christ, though she never sought baptism. Her writings on suffering, attention and obligation were published after her death. In 1943, working for the Free French in England, she fell ill and died in Kent, having eaten little in solidarity with occupied France.

UO-SIN-000295.name: Ebba of Coldingham
UO-SIN-000295.life: Ebba was a Northumbrian princess, daughter of King Aethelfrith and sister of the kings Oswald and Oswiu. After her father's death she fled north with her family into exile, where the children met Christianity among the Scots. Returning when her brothers ruled, she became a nun and founded monasteries at Ebchester and at Coldingham on the Berwickshire coast, a house for both monks and nuns that she governed for some thirty years. Bede called her a very wise and devout woman. She also used her influence to win the release of Bishop Wilfrid from prison. She died in 683.

UO-SIN-000296.name: Genesius of Arles
UO-SIN-000296.life: Genesius was a young man of Arles in Roman Gaul who worked as a notary, or court secretary, and had been preparing for baptism. According to the old account of his death, he was recording a magistrate's proceedings when an edict of persecution against Christians was read out. Appalled by its injustice, he threw down his writing tablets at the magistrate's feet and fled. He was caught and beheaded, around 303 under Diocletian and Maximian, and so was said to have been baptized in his own blood. A church at Arles was dedicated to him by the fourth century, and he became patron of notaries and secretaries.

UO-SIN-000297.name: Joseph Calasanz
UO-SIN-000297.life: Born in Aragon in the 1550s, Joseph Calasanz studied law and theology and was ordained a priest in 1583. In 1592 he moved to Rome, where he was shocked by the many poor children who had no schooling. In 1597 he and a few helpers opened what is regarded as the first free public school in Europe, and soon taught hundreds of boys. His companions grew into a religious order, the Piarists, who still run schools. Calasanz endured opposition and trouble late in life, but he held to his work for children until he died in Rome in 1648. He was canonized in 1767.

UO-SIN-000298.name: Tarsicius
UO-SIN-000298.life: Tarsicius was a young Roman Christian, perhaps an acolyte, who lived in the age of persecution, probably in the third century. According to the tradition, he was entrusted with carrying the consecrated bread to Christians imprisoned for their faith. On the way, a gang of pagan youths demanded to see what he carried. He refused to surrender it and was beaten to death, and his body was buried in the catacomb of Callixtus. In the fourth century Pope Damasus wrote verses praising him as a martyr who preferred to die rather than give up the Lord's Body, and he is remembered as a patron of altar servers.

UO-SIN-000299.name: Maximilian of Numidia
UO-SIN-000299.life: Maximilian was the son of a Roman army veteran in Numidia, in North Africa. When he was brought before the proconsul at Tebessa in 295 to be enlisted as a soldier, aged about twenty-one, he refused. 'I cannot serve,' he said. 'I cannot do evil. I am a Christian.' The proconsul urged him to relent, pointing out that other Christians served in the army, but Maximilian would not be moved, saying he was a soldier of Christ. He was condemned and beheaded. The surviving record of his trial is among the earliest accounts of a Christian refusing military service.

UO-SIN-000302.name: Poemen
UO-SIN-000302.life: Poemen, whose name means 'shepherd', was an Egyptian monk of the fifth century and one of the most quoted of the Desert Fathers. He lived at Scetis with his brothers, and when raiders overran the monasteries there around 407, he and his companions withdrew to Terenuthis beside the Nile. Monks sought him out for his wisdom, and nearly a quarter of the Sayings of the Desert Fathers are attributed to him or tell of him. He was known for gentleness toward the weak, for humility and for practical counsel about the inner struggle. He is thought to have died in the middle of the fifth century.

UO-SIN-000303.name: Caesarius of Arles
UO-SIN-000303.life: Born near Chalon in Burgundy about 470, Caesarius entered the monastery of Lérins as a young man, then was sent to Arles to recover his health. There he was ordained, and around 502 he was chosen bishop, serving until his death in 543. He presided over the Council of Agde in 506, and he was a tireless preacher whose simple sermons were copied and used across Gaul. He also wrote the first western rule for nuns, for the convent at Arles which his sister Caesaria led. The rule stressed equality, reading and the care of the sick, and it influenced convents for centuries.

UO-SIN-000304.name: John Bunyan
UO-SIN-000304.life: Born in 1628 at Elstow in Bedfordshire, John Bunyan was a tinker's son who served as a soldier and then underwent a long spiritual struggle, described in his autobiography, Grace Abounding. He became a Baptist preacher in Bedford, and after the Restoration he was jailed for twelve years for preaching without the Church of England's licence. In prison he wrote and supported his family by making laces. He later published The Pilgrim's Progress, an allegory of the Christian life as a journey, which became one of the most widely read books in English. He died in London in 1688.

UO-SIN-000305.name: Ignatius Rice
UO-SIN-000305.life: Edmund Rice was born in 1762 at Callan in Ireland and became a prosperous merchant in Waterford. After his young wife died, he grew more devoted to prayer and charity. Seeing the poor Catholic boys of the city with no schooling, at a time when penal laws still restricted Catholic education, he sold his business and in 1802 opened a school for them. Other men joined him, and they became the Christian Brothers, approved by Pope Pius VII in 1820, with schools spreading throughout Ireland and beyond. In religion he took the name Ignatius. Rice died at Waterford in 1844.

UO-SIN-000306.name: Charles Chapman Grafton
UO-SIN-000306.life: Born in Boston in 1830, Grafton trained as a lawyer before being ordained in the Episcopal Church. In England he helped found the Society of St. John the Evangelist, and later served as rector of the Church of the Advent in Boston. In 1889 he became Bishop of Fond du Lac, Wisconsin, where he gave much of his own wealth to build up the diocese and held to the Catholic tradition of the Church. He welcomed contact with other churches: at a consecration in 1900 he stood alongside the Russian Orthodox bishop Tikhon. His motto was 'Press on the Kingdom.' He died in 1912, having given away his fortune.

UO-SIN-000307.name: Robert McDonald
UO-SIN-000307.life: Born in 1829 at the Red River settlement, now Winnipeg, the son of a Hudson's Bay Company man, Robert McDonald trained at St. John's College and was ordained in 1852 and 1853. After nine years among the Ojibwe at White Dog, he went north in 1862 as the first Protestant missionary on the Yukon River. For some forty years he lived among the Gwich'in people, mostly at Fort McPherson, travelling the Arctic winter to nurse the sick during an epidemic. He learned their language, devised a written form of it, and translated the Bible, the Prayer Book and hymns. He became Archdeacon of Mackenzie River and died in 1913.

UO-SIN-000308.name: Fiacre
UO-SIN-000308.life: Fiacre was an Irish monk who, according to the traditional account, lived as a hermit by the River Nore in County Kilkenny before seeking greater solitude abroad. He reached Meaux in France in about 628, where Bishop Faro gave him land in the forest at Breuil. There he built a small chapel, a guesthouse for travellers and a cell, and he grew vegetables and prayed. Disciples gathered, and visitors came for healing. He died around 670 and his tomb became a place of pilgrimage. He is honoured as the patron of gardeners, and Paris cabs later took his name from the inn bearing his image.

UO-SIN-000309.name: Aidan and Cuthbert
UO-SIN-000309.life: Aidan, an Irish monk of Iona, came to Northumbria in 635 at King Oswald's request. He founded the monastery of Lindisfarne, walked the countryside speaking to ordinary people, and gave away gifts of the rich to the poor; he died in 651. Cuthbert, a shepherd boy from the Borders, entered the monastery of Melrose, nursed plague victims, and became prior of Lindisfarne. He sought solitude on the island of Farne, but was drawn out to be bishop of Lindisfarne in the 680s, and returned to Farne to die in 687. Together they are remembered as the great shepherds of the Northumbrian church.

UO-SIN-000310.name: Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus
UO-SIN-000310.life: Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus were two members of the Jewish council who, according to the Gospels, came to honour Jesus after his death. Joseph, a wealthy man who had been a disciple in secret, asked Pilate for the body of Jesus. Nicodemus, the Pharisee who had once visited Jesus by night to ask questions, brought about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes. Together they wrapped the body in linen and laid it in Joseph's new tomb in a garden. Once cautious, both showed courage at the moment when the closest followers had fled.

UO-SIN-000311.name: Paulinus of Trier
UO-SIN-000311.life: Paulinus came from Gaul and was educated at Poitiers before going to Trier, where he succeeded Maximinus as bishop around 349. At that time the emperor Constantius supported the Arian party, and bishops were pressed to condemn Athanasius of Alexandria, the great defender of the Nicene faith. At councils in Arles in 353 and Milan in 355, Paulinus refused to do so. For this he was banished to Phrygia in Asia Minor, where he died in exile in about 358. His body was brought back to Trier in 395 and laid in the church that bears his name.

UO-SIN-000312.name: Simeon Stylites the Elder
UO-SIN-000312.life: Born about 388 on the Syrian border, Simeon was a shepherd boy who entered a monastery, where his severe fasting and discipline puzzled the monks. Seeking solitude, he moved to a small enclosure, but crowds followed him to ask for prayer and advice. He then took up life on a pillar, first low and later some fifty feet high, near Aleppo, where he lived for decades. Visitors climbed a ladder to speak with him, and he wrote letters and preached to the people below. Theodoret of Cyrrhus, who knew him, wrote his life. Simeon died in 459 and inspired many imitators.

UO-SIN-000313.name: Giles
UO-SIN-000313.life: According to tradition, Giles was a Greek of noble birth who left home to live as a hermit in Gaul, in the forests near Nîmes and the Rhone, in the seventh century. The story says he shared his retreat with a hind, and that a hunter's arrow meant for the animal wounded him instead. The king, moved by the hermit's holiness, supported him in founding a monastery in the valley, under the Rule of Benedict, where Giles was abbot until his death in the early eighth century. The abbey of Saint-Gilles became a famous stop for pilgrims, and he was honoured widely across Europe.

UO-SIN-000314.name: Joshua and Gideon
UO-SIN-000314.life: Joshua and Gideon were two leaders of Israel in the early days after the Exodus. Joshua, Moses' assistant and chosen successor, led the tribes across the Jordan into Canaan, took Jericho and began the settlement of the land, ending his life urging Israel to serve the Lord. Some generations later, Gideon, a farmer's son from Manasseh, was called by an angel to save Israel from Midianite raiders. With three hundred men he routed a huge army, trusting God's strength rather than numbers, and Israel had peace for forty years. The Books of Joshua and Judges tell their stories.

UO-SIN-000315.name: Nikolai Grundtvig
UO-SIN-000315.life: Born in 1783 in Udby, Denmark, Grundtvig was a pastor's son who became one of the most influential figures in Danish life. As a pastor, poet and historian, he renewed the Danish church with a vision rooted in baptism, the creed and the living word. He wrote about a thousand hymns, many of which are still sung in Denmark and in translation worldwide. He urged an education that would awaken ordinary people, which inspired the folk high school movement after 1844. He served as preacher at Vartov Hospital in Copenhagen and received the title of bishop in 1861. He died in 1872.

UO-SIN-000316.name: September Martyrs of Paris
UO-SIN-000316.life: In early September 1792, in the fear and violence of the French Revolution, mobs entered the Paris prisons and killed hundreds of prisoners. Among the dead were many priests and religious who had refused to swear an oath to the new civil constitution of the clergy. About 190 of them, including bishops, priests and laymen, were held at the Carmelite convent, and on 2 September were killed in its church and garden. Principal among them were the Franciscan John Francis Burté, the Capuchin Apollinaris of Posat and the Franciscan tertiary Severin Girault. They were beatified in 1926 as witnesses who died for their faith.

UO-SIN-000319.name: Prudence Crandall
UO-SIN-000319.life: Born in Rhode Island in 1803 to a Quaker family, Prudence Crandall opened a girls' school in Canterbury, Connecticut, in 1831. When she admitted Sarah Harris, a young Black woman who hoped to teach, white families withdrew their daughters. Crandall refused to expel her and reopened the school in 1833 for Black girls. Townspeople boycotted and harassed it, and Connecticut passed a law forbidding the schooling of out-of-state Black students. Crandall was arrested and tried; her conviction was overturned, but in 1834 a mob attacked the building and she closed the school. She later taught in Illinois and Kansas and died in 1890. Connecticut named her its state heroine.

UO-SIN-000320.name: Aigulf of Lérins
UO-SIN-000320.life: Aigulf, also called Ayoul, was a monk from the Loire region who became abbot of the island monastery of Lérins off the south coast of France in the 660s. He tried to reform the community and bring it under a stricter rule, and the strictness stirred resentment. According to the tradition, he and a few companions were attacked and cruelly mutilated, exiled to the island of Capraia, and there killed, about 676. Some accounts blame pagans or pirates, others say the attackers were monks who disliked his reforms. His relics were returned to Lérins, and some were taken to Provins.

UO-SIN-000321.name: Moses
UO-SIN-000321.life: Moses is the central figure of the Old Testament and the lawgiver of Israel. According to the book of Exodus, he was born a Hebrew in Egypt, placed in a basket on the Nile and raised in Pharaoh's household. After fleeing to Midian, he met God in the burning bush and was sent to free his people from slavery. He led them through the sea and across the wilderness, and on Mount Sinai received the Ten Commandments and the covenant. He guided Israel for forty years and died within sight of the Promised Land. Jews, Christians and Muslims all revere him.

UO-SIN-000322.name: Birinus of Dorchester
UO-SIN-000322.life: Birinus was a missionary bishop sent from Italy to England by Pope Honorius I, arriving in Wessex in 634 or 635. According to Bede, he chose to preach to the West Saxons because they were still pagan. He won the support of King Cynegils, who was baptized in 635 with Oswald of Northumbria as his sponsor, and the king gave Birinus the old Roman town of Dorchester-on-Thames as his see. From there he founded churches across the region. He died around 650. His relics were later moved to Winchester, and he is remembered as the apostle of Wessex.

UO-SIN-000323.name: Albert Schweitzer
UO-SIN-000323.life: Born in Alsace in 1875, Albert Schweitzer became a pastor, theologian and organist. His study of Jesus, The Quest of the Historical Jesus, and his writing on Bach made him famous, but at thirty he began to study medicine so that he could serve in Africa. In 1913 he and his wife Helene opened a hospital at Lambaréné in Gabon. He worked there for most of his remaining years, rebuilding it after the First World War, and called his guiding idea 'reverence for life'. He received the Nobel Peace Prize, and died at Lambaréné on 4 September 1965.

UO-SIN-000067.name: Katharina Zell
UO-SIN-000067.life: Born in Strasbourg about 1498, Katharina Schütz was a devout young woman who found assurance of God's grace through the teaching of the early Reformers. In 1523 she married Matthew Zell, a leading reforming priest, and defended clerical marriage in print. The Zells opened their home to refugees, and she cared for the afflicted and wrote letters of consolation. She edited a hymnbook and, with her pen and voice, became the leading woman author of the early Reformation. She sought reconciliation among Protestants who quarrelled and showed kindness to those of other views. She died in Strasbourg in 1562.

UO-SIN-000324.name: Teresa of Calcutta
UO-SIN-000324.life: Born Agnes Bojaxhiu in 1910 in Skopje, she joined the Sisters of Loreto in Ireland and was sent to India, where she taught in Calcutta. In 1946 she felt a second call to serve the poorest of the poor, and in 1948 she began working in the city's slums. She founded the Missionaries of Charity, whose sisters opened homes for orphans, the dying and people with leprosy, and the order spread to many countries. She received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979. She died in Calcutta in 1997 and was canonized by Pope Francis in 2016.

UO-SIN-000325.name: Gregorio Aglipay
UO-SIN-000325.life: Gregorio Aglipay was born in 1860 at Batac in the Philippines and became a Roman Catholic priest. During the Philippine Revolution he rallied nationalist clergy and fought as a military leader, and he was excommunicated in 1899. After the war a group of Filipino labour leaders, led by Isabelo de los Reyes, proclaimed an independent national church to end Spanish clerical domination. Aglipay accepted leadership of it and became its first Supreme Bishop in 1903. He guided the Philippine Independent Church for almost four decades, and died in Manila on 1 September 1940.

UO-SIN-000327.name: Allen Gardiner
UO-SIN-000327.life: Allen Gardiner was born in 1794 and served as an officer in the Royal Navy before giving himself to missionary work. After the death of his wife he went to Zululand in 1834, then laboured in Chile and Tierra del Fuego, hoping to bring the gospel to peoples few had visited. When established societies declined to support him, he helped found a society for South America. In 1850 he led a small party to Tierra del Fuego, but supplies failed. He and his companions died of hunger and exposure, Gardiner apparently the last, in September 1851. His journals inspired later work in Patagonia.

UO-SIN-000328.name: Zechariah
UO-SIN-000328.life: Zechariah was a prophet of Judah in the years after the Babylonian exile. His book names him as son of Berechiah and grandson of Iddo, and he is thought to have come from a priestly family. He began to prophesy in 520 BC, in the second year of King Darius of Persia, alongside Haggai, urging the returned exiles to rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem. His book records a series of night visions of angels, a lampstand, and horsemen, and promises that God will dwell again with his people. Christians have long read his picture of a humble king riding on a donkey as pointing to Christ.

UO-SIN-000329.name: Allen Crite
UO-SIN-000329.life: Allan Rohan Crite was born in New Jersey in 1910 but lived almost all his life in Boston, where he trained at the Museum of Fine Arts school. His early paintings and drawings showed ordinary Black families of the South End and Roxbury at work, play and worship, as dignified and ordinary neighbours. A lifelong Episcopalian, he also made liturgical art, setting biblical scenes and spirituals in modern city streets and drawing on the church's vestments and ceremonial. He worked as a naval shipyard draftsman for decades, mentored younger artists, and died in 2007 aged ninety-seven.

UO-SIN-000330.name: Élie Naud
UO-SIN-000330.life: Élie Neau, sometimes spelled Naud, was born in 1662 in western France to a Protestant family. After Protestants lost their rights in France he fled across the Atlantic and became a merchant, first in the Caribbean and then in New York. On a voyage in 1692 he was captured by a French privateer and, refusing to deny his faith, was condemned to the galleys and held in prison at Marseille for years. Released in 1697, he returned to New York, became an Anglican, and served as catechist to enslaved Africans, teaching them to read and preparing many for baptism until his death in 1722.

UO-SIN-000331.name: Cloud
UO-SIN-000331.life: Cloud, or Clodoald, was born in 522, a grandson of the Frankish king Clovis. When his father died, his uncles murdered his two brothers to seize the kingdom, and Cloud escaped. He later gave up any claim to the throne, cut his royal hair, and became a monk and hermit. He studied under the recluse Severinus near Paris, spent years in Provence, and was ordained priest at Paris in 551. He then settled on the Seine at Nogent, now called Saint-Cloud, where he founded a monastery, taught the local people, and gave away his inheritance. He died there about 560.

UO-SIN-000332.name: John of Lodi
UO-SIN-000332.life: John was born about 1025 at Lodi Vecchio in Lombardy and in the 1060s joined the hermits of Fonte Avellana in the Apennines. There he became the disciple and secretary of Peter Damian, the prior and reformer, and after Damian's death in 1072 wrote his biography. John twice served as prior of the hermitage. In 1104 he was made bishop of Gubbio, an office he held until he died in 1106. He is remembered for his charity, especially a long journey on foot to Apulia during the famine of 1085 to obtain grain for the poor of Gubbio.

UO-SIN-000333.name: Isaac the Great
UO-SIN-000333.life: Isaac, called Sahak in Armenian, was born about 350, the son of the patriarch Nerses and a descendant of Gregory the Illuminator. He studied in Greek cities, lost his wife, and became leader of the Armenian Church about 387. He rebuilt churches destroyed in wars, founded schools, and encouraged monastic life. With the monk Mesrop Mashtots he developed the Armenian alphabet, then led scholars in translating the Bible and Christian writings from Greek and Syriac into Armenian, giving the nation a written language and liturgy. The Persians deposed him for a time, but he returned and died about 438, the last of Gregory's line to lead the church.

UO-SIN-000334.name: Søren Kierkegaard
UO-SIN-000334.life: Søren Kierkegaard was born in Copenhagen in 1813, the youngest child of a wealthy merchant, and studied theology at the university there. Living on his inheritance, he wrote a remarkable series of books, many under invented names, on faith, anxiety, choice and love. He insisted that Christianity is not a set of ideas to be admired but a way of life demanding commitment from each single individual before God. He grew sharply critical of the comfortable state church of Denmark. Often mocked in his lifetime, he died in Copenhagen in November 1855, and is now regarded as a father of existentialist thought.

UO-SIN-000335.name: Frederick Ozanam
UO-SIN-000335.life: Frédéric Ozanam was born in Milan in 1813 and raised in Lyons and Paris. As a young law student at the Sorbonne he defended the Christian faith against sceptical classmates, who challenged him to show what his faith did for the poor. In 1833, with friends, he began visiting poor families in Paris, a work that grew into the Society of St Vincent de Paul. He became a respected professor of literature, a husband and father, and wrote on medieval Christian culture. Worn out by illness, he died in Marseille in September 1853, aged forty, and was beatified in 1997.

UO-SIN-000336.name: Ciaran of Clonmacnoise
UO-SIN-000336.life: Ciaran was born in Ireland early in the sixth century, the son of a craftsman, and studied at Finnian's monastic school at Clonard, where he knew other great Irish saints of his age. He lived for a time on the Aran Islands, then travelled inland and, in 544, founded a monastery at Clonmacnoise on the Shannon, with the help of King Diarmait. It grew into one of the great centres of Irish learning and art. Ciaran lived there only a short while before dying young, probably of plague, a few years after its founding, and pilgrims have gathered at the site on his day ever since.

UO-SIN-000337.name: Peter Claver
UO-SIN-000337.life: Peter Claver was born in Catalonia in 1580 and became a Jesuit. Sent to Cartagena in Colombia, the chief slave port of the Spanish Americas, he was ordained there in 1616. Whenever a slave ship arrived he went aboard with food, medicine and interpreters, tending the sick and frightened captives, teaching the faith and baptizing. He called himself the slave of the Africans forever, and kept up this work for decades despite criticism from the colonial elite. Illness left him largely helpless in his final years. He died in Cartagena in September 1654, and was canonized in 1888.

UO-SIN-000338.name: Charles Fuge Lowder
UO-SIN-000338.life: Charles Lowder was born in Bath in 1820 and, influenced by the Oxford Movement at Oxford, was ordained in the Church of England. In 1855 he and five other priests founded the Society of the Holy Cross to support a disciplined priestly life. The next year he began a mission among the poor dockworkers of Wapping and St George in the East in London's East End. With the help of a sisterhood he ran schools, relief and care for the vulnerable, despite riots against his Catholic ceremonial. Lowder gave his strength to this work and built St Peter's, London Docks. He died worn out in 1880.

UO-SIN-000339.name: Edmund James Peck
UO-SIN-000339.life: Edmund Peck was born in England in 1850 and served in the Royal Navy as a teenager before training with the Church Missionary Society. In 1876 he sailed for Hudson Bay, learning Inuktitut on the voyage. He lived among the Inuit of northern Quebec for years and, in 1894, founded the first Anglican mission on Baffin Island, where the first church was built of sealskin. Peck translated Scripture, prayers and hymns into Inuktitut, using syllabic writing so that people could read for themselves, and compiled a dictionary. The Inuit called him Uqammaq, the one who speaks well. He died in 1924.
UO-SIN-000339.place: Hudson Bay and Baffin Island, Canada

UO-SIN-000340.name: William Salesbury and William Morgan
UO-SIN-000340.life: William Salesbury, a Welsh scholar who studied at Oxford, believed his countrymen should hear the Scriptures in their own tongue. With Bishops Richard Davies and Thomas Huet he produced the first Welsh New Testament in 1567. He died about 1584. A younger Cambridge-educated priest, William Morgan, then completed the task: his Welsh Bible of 1588 was the first to contain the whole of Scripture in Welsh, drawing on Salesbury's New Testament. Morgan became bishop of Llandaff and then St Asaph, and died in 1604. Their work helped secure the survival of the Welsh language.

UO-SIN-000341.name: Ambrose Barlow
UO-SIN-000341.life: Edward Barlow was born in 1585 near Manchester into a gentry family that had suffered for refusing the new religion. Raised in the Church of England, he became a Catholic in 1607, studied in Douai and Spain, and joined the Benedictines, taking the name Ambrose. Ordained in 1617, he returned secretly to Lancashire, where he ministered to Catholics for about twenty-four years, often walking between homes. Arrested for the last time on Easter Sunday 1641 while preaching, he was held at Lancaster Castle, and hanged and quartered there on 10 September 1641. He was canonized in 1970.

UO-SIN-000342.name: Mordecai Johnson
UO-SIN-000342.life: Mordecai Wyatt Johnson was born in Tennessee in 1890, the son of a mill worker and preacher. He studied at Morehouse College, the University of Chicago and Harvard, and became a Baptist minister. In 1926, aged thirty-six, he was chosen as the first African American president of Howard University in Washington. He led it for thirty-four years, strengthening its faculty and schools, winning federal funding, and building it into a major national university, while his preaching and speeches urged justice for Black Americans. He retired in 1960 and died in September 1976.

UO-SIN-000343.name: Harry Thacker Burleigh
UO-SIN-000343.life: Harry Burleigh was born in Erie, Pennsylvania, in 1866, the grandson of a man who had bought his freedom from slavery. A gifted baritone, he studied in New York and introduced the composer Dvorak to the spirituals he had grown up hearing. In 1894 he became soloist at St George's Episcopal Church in New York, despite some objections to his race, and sang there for over fifty years. Burleigh wrote and arranged art songs and spirituals for concert singers, helping bring the music of enslaved African Americans into the concert hall. He died in 1949.

UO-SIN-000344.name: Paphnutius
UO-SIN-000344.life: Paphnutius was an Egyptian monk, a disciple of Anthony the Great, who became a bishop in the Upper Thebaid in the early fourth century. During the persecution under the emperor Maximinus he was maimed, losing an eye and being lamed, and was sentenced to the mines. According to the historians, he later attended the Council of Nicaea in 325, where the emperor Constantine honoured the scarred confessor. Tradition says he persuaded the bishops not to force married clergy to part from their wives. He was also present at the Council of Tyre in 335 and defended orthodox teaching.

UO-SIN-000346.name: Ailbhe
UO-SIN-000346.life: Ailbhe, also known as Ailbe, is honoured as the first bishop of Emly in Munster and one of the early apostles of southern Ireland, who may have lived before or alongside Patrick. Little reliable is known of him; the old accounts of his life are mostly legend. According to tradition, he was abandoned as a baby and suckled by a she-wolf, and later as bishop he sheltered an old wolf from hunters. An early poem praises him as generous in hospitality. He died in the early sixth century, and is patron of the archdiocese of Cashel and Emly.

UO-SIN-000347.name: Japanese Martyrs of Omura
UO-SIN-000347.life: In the early seventeenth century Christianity was banned in Japan, and missionaries and Japanese Christians were hunted down. The prison of Omura held foreign friars and Japanese believers, some for years. On 12 September 1622, in the same season as the great Nagasaki martyrdom, a group from Omura were burned alive for refusing to renounce their faith. Among them was the Spanish Dominican Thomas of Zumárraga, captured in 1617, with Japanese companions such as Francis of Saint Bonaventure and Paul of Saint Clare. The Church of Japan later survived underground for generations, and these martyrs were beatified in 1867.

UO-SIN-000352.name: James Chisholm
UO-SIN-000352.life: James Chisholm was born in Massachusetts in 1815, moved to Virginia to teach, and became an Episcopal priest. He was the first rector of St John's Church in Portsmouth. When yellow fever struck the city in 1855, killing thousands, most prominent citizens, including doctors and clergy, fled. Chisholm, a quiet and shy man whose wife had died that year, stayed. He nursed and prayed with the sick and dying of every faith, brought food, and helped bury the dead, working beside the local Catholic priest. Exhausted and grieving the death of a son, he himself died of the fever on 15 September 1855.

UO-SIN-000355.name: Cornelius
UO-SIN-000355.life: Cornelius became bishop of Rome in 251, after the persecution under the emperor Decius had left the see vacant for over a year. His election was challenged by Novatian, a Roman priest who refused to readmit Christians who had lapsed under persecution. Cornelius, supported by Cyprian of Carthage and most bishops, held that the repentant could be restored after penance, and a synod in Rome condemned Novatian. When persecution returned he was exiled to Centumcellae, now Civitavecchia, where he died in June 253, and the church honours him as a martyr and confessor.

UO-SIN-000356.name: Ludmila of Bohemia
UO-SIN-000356.life: Ludmila was born about 860 and married Bořivoj, the first Christian duke of Bohemia; according to tradition, they were baptized together about 871. After his death she lived at Tetín and took charge of the upbringing of her grandson Wenceslas, teaching him the faith. When Wenceslas's father died, his mother Drahomíra, who favoured the old religion, grew jealous of Ludmila's influence. Two nobles, sent by her, strangled Ludmila at Tetín on 15 September 921, tradition says with her own veil. She is honoured as Bohemia's first martyr, and her grandson Wenceslas became patron saint of the country.

UO-SIN-000357.name: Lambert of Maastricht
UO-SIN-000357.life: Lambert was born about 636 into a noble Frankish family and became bishop of Maastricht about 670. Exiled for some years during a political upheaval, he returned and spread the faith among the pagan peoples of the Low Countries. He was known for fearless speech, and criticized Pepin of Herstal for his relationship with Alpais. Around 705 Alpais's brother had him murdered at Liège while he was at prayer. The place became a centre of pilgrimage, and his successor Hubert moved the bishop's seat there; the city of Liège grew around his shrine. He is honoured as a martyr.

UO-SIN-000358.name: Robert Bellarmine
UO-SIN-000358.life: Robert Bellarmine was born in 1542 at Montepulciano in Tuscany and joined the Jesuits at eighteen. He taught in Louvain and Rome, and wrote the Controversies, the first thorough defence of Catholic teaching against Protestant arguments, which was admired for its fairness. Made a cardinal in 1599, he became archbishop of Capua before returning to Rome, where he served popes as adviser and wrote a catechism widely used for centuries. He was also known for personal simplicity and for charity to the poor. He died in Rome on 17 September 1621, and was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church in 1931.

UO-SIN-000359.name: Dag Hammarskjöld
UO-SIN-000359.life: Dag Hammarskjöld was born in Sweden in 1905 and became an economist and civil servant before serving as second Secretary-General of the United Nations from 1953. He worked tirelessly to ease international crises and to strengthen the UN as a servant of peace. In September 1961 he was flying to negotiate a ceasefire in the Congo when his plane crashed near Ndola in what is now Zambia, killing all aboard. His private journal, published after his death as Markings, reveals a deep life of prayer and a sense of public service as obedience to God. He was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize posthumously.

UO-SIN-000360.name: Founders, Benefactors, and Missionaries of the Anglican Church of Canada
UO-SIN-000360.life: Anglican worship came to Canada with early explorers and chaplains, and continuous services began in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia in the early eighteenth century. Charles Inglis became bishop of Nova Scotia in 1787, the first Anglican bishop outside the British Isles. Missionary societies and many clergy, teachers, and lay supporters carried the church across the country, from settlements in the east to the Arctic, among Indigenous peoples and newcomers alike. Out of this work grew separate dioceses and, in 1893, the first General Synod, joining them as one national church. This day remembers those whose labour and gifts built it.

UO-SIN-000361.name: Joseph of Cupertino
UO-SIN-000361.life: Joseph Desa was born in 1603 in the village of Cupertino in southern Italy to a poor family. A slow, awkward boy given to ecstasies, he failed at several trades and was turned away by two religious orders before the Conventual Franciscans took him in. Ordained a priest in 1628, he became known for prayer and austerity, and many witnesses reported that he was lifted into the air during Mass. His superiors, wary of the attention, moved him from house to house, and he was even examined by the Inquisition. He died at Osimo on 18 September 1663 and was canonized in 1767.

UO-SIN-000400.name: Gerard of Brogne
UO-SIN-000400.life: Gerard was born about 895 at Staves, near Namur, into a noble family, and began life as a soldier. While on business in Paris around 917 he stayed at the abbey of Saint-Denis and was so moved by the monks' life that he became one himself. Ordained about 928, he returned to Brogne, where he had rebuilt a family chapel, and replaced its lax clerics with monks. Called on to reform other houses in Flanders and Hainaut, he eventually governed eighteen abbeys under the Rule of Benedict. He died at Brogne on 3 October 959.

UO-SIN-000401.name: Columba Marmion
UO-SIN-000401.life: Joseph Marmion was born in Dublin in 1858 to an Irish father and a French mother. Ordained a priest in Rome in 1881, he served as a curate and seminary professor before entering the Benedictine abbey of Maredsous in Belgium in 1886, taking the name Columba. He helped found Mont Cesar at Louvain, where he taught theology and became a trusted spiritual director, and in 1909 he was elected abbot of Maredsous. His retreat talks, gathered in books such as Christ, the Life of the Soul, taught countless readers to live by the grace of baptism. He died on 30 January 1923.

UO-SIN-000402.name: Ammon of Nitria
UO-SIN-000402.life: Ammon, also called Amoun, was an Egyptian ascetic of the fourth century and a contemporary of Anthony the Great. Orphaned young, he was pressed into marriage by his uncle, but on the wedding night persuaded his bride to live with him as brother and sister. After some eighteen years, with her agreement, he withdrew to the desert of Nitria, west of the Nile delta. Disciples gathered around him, and within a generation thousands of monks lived there, some alone and some in community. Because he drew so many into this common life he is often called a father of Egyptian monasticism. He died before Anthony, around 350.

UO-SIN-000403.name: Maurus and Placid
UO-SIN-000403.life: Maurus and Placid were boys given by their Roman noble families to Benedict at Subiaco in the early sixth century, and so were among the first pupils of the monastic life he taught. Gregory the Great tells how Placid fell into the lake and Maurus, obeying Benedict, ran out over the water and drew him to safety. According to tradition, Maurus later brought the Benedictine Rule to Gaul and founded the abbey of Glanfeuil on the Loire. Placid was sent to Sicily as abbot at Messina, and is said to have been killed there with his companions by raiders around the 540s.

UO-SIN-000404.name: Raymund of Capua
UO-SIN-000404.life: Raymund della Vigna was born at Capua about 1330 and became a Dominican while studying law at Bologna. Sent to Siena as confessor to Catherine, he spent years guiding her, and she once nursed him through the plague. He travelled with her, helped her work to bring the pope back from Avignon to Rome, and later wrote her life. After Catherine's death in 1380 he was elected Master General of the Dominicans. Through the troubled years of the Great Schism he laboured to restore strict observance in the Order, so that he is called its second founder. He died at Nuremberg on 5 October 1399.

UO-SIN-000405.name: Flora of Beaulieu
UO-SIN-000405.life: Flora, or Fleur, was a nun of the Hospitaller Order of Saint John at Beaulieu, near Issendolus in Quercy, in southern France. Her medieval life says she was born at Maurs to a noble family, refused the marriage her relatives planned, and entered the convent as a girl. Her early years there were hard, marked by temptations and by the suspicion of sisters who thought her ecstasies a kind of madness. In later life she was known for visions of Christ's Passion and devotion to the Eucharist. She died in 1347, and many miracles were reported at her tomb.

UO-SIN-000408.name: Faith of Agen
UO-SIN-000408.life: Faith, known in France as Sainte Foy, is said to have been a young girl of Agen in southern Gaul. According to tradition she was arrested in a Roman persecution, probably around the year 300, refused to sacrifice to the gods, and was put to death, in the best-known story by being roasted on a brazier. Her original account is lost and the details are legendary. Her cult grew strong, and in the ninth century her relics were taken to the abbey of Conques, which became a great pilgrimage stop on the roads to Compostela. She is honoured as a virgin martyr.

UO-SIN-000409.name: Henry Melchior Muhlenberg
UO-SIN-000409.life: Born in Einbeck, Germany, in 1711, Muhlenberg studied at Gottingen and Halle, where he absorbed the Pietist concern for the poor. In 1742 he answered a call from German Lutheran congregations in Pennsylvania and sailed to Philadelphia. Settling at Trappe, he travelled constantly on horseback, gathering scattered congregations, writing a church order and preaching in English as well as German. In 1748 he helped found the first Lutheran synod in North America. He and his sons supported the colonies in the War of Independence. Often called the patriarch of American Lutheranism, he died at Trappe on 7 October 1787.

UO-SIN-000411.name: Justina of Padua
UO-SIN-000411.life: Justina was a young woman of Padua in northern Italy who, by tradition, was of noble family and vowed herself to Christ. The old story tells that she was put to death with a sword during the persecution under Diocletian, around the year 304, after refusing to deny her faith before the local prefect. The details come from late legend, but her cult is ancient. A church was built in her honour in Padua by the fifth century, and the poet Venantius Fortunatus urged pilgrims to visit her tomb. She remains a patron of Padua, and a great abbey bears her name.

UO-SIN-000412.name: William Dwight Porter Bliss and Richard Theodore Ely
UO-SIN-000412.life: Bliss and Ely were American Episcopalians who argued that the gospel speaks to the way society is ordered. Bliss, born in Constantinople to missionary parents, left the Congregationalists for the Episcopal Church, served in Boston and founded the Church of the Carpenter and the Society of Christian Socialists; he died in 1926. Ely, a Progressive economist who taught at Johns Hopkins and Wisconsin, helped found the American Economic Association and the Christian Social Union, and wrote widely on labour and reform; he died in 1943. Together they called the Church to address poverty and unjust working conditions.

UO-SIN-000413.name: Simeon the God-Receiver
UO-SIN-000413.life: Simeon appears only in the second chapter of Luke's Gospel. He was a righteous and devout man of Jerusalem, who had been promised by the Holy Spirit that he would not die before he had seen the Lord's Messiah. When Mary and Joseph brought the infant Jesus to the Temple to present him, Simeon took the child in his arms and blessed God, saying that his eyes had seen salvation, a light for the Gentiles and glory for Israel. His song, the Nunc dimittis, is sung daily in evening prayer. He also warned Mary that a sword would pierce her own soul.

UO-SIN-000414.name: Pelagia of Antioch
UO-SIN-000414.life: According to tradition, Pelagia was a celebrated and wealthy entertainer of Antioch, known for her glittering display. One day she heard the bishop Nonnus preach, wept over her life, and asked for baptism. She gave away her riches to the poor and went to Jerusalem, where she lived in a cell on the Mount of Olives, disguised as a monk named Pelagius. Her severe fasting and prayer brought her great respect, and only after her death did the brethren discover that the holy hermit was a woman. The story comes from a legend written in the fifth century, and some details may be literary.

UO-SIN-000415.name: Demetrius of Sirmium
UO-SIN-000415.life: Demetrius was a deacon of the church at Sirmium, in what is now Serbia, serving under Bishop Irenaeus in the early fourth century. He is said to have guarded the Church's sacred books when the Emperor Diocletian ordered Christian scriptures surrendered. For this he was condemned by the governor and put to death in 304, a short way outside the city on the road to Bassianae. Other deacons and several consecrated virgins are recorded as dying the same day. A basilica was later built over the place of his martyrdom. His memory is often mixed up with that of the better known Demetrius of Thessaloniki.

UO-SIN-000416.name: Wilfred Thomason Grenfell
UO-SIN-000416.life: Wilfred Grenfell was born in 1865 at Parkgate, Cheshire, the son of a clergyman-schoolmaster, and trained as a physician at the London Hospital. Moved by a sermon, he joined the mission to deep-sea fishermen, and in 1892 sailed to Labrador. For four decades he served the scattered fishing communities of Labrador and northern Newfoundland, building hospitals, nursing stations, schools, orphanages and cooperative industries, often travelling by dog team and boat. He was knighted in 1927 and wrote many books to raise support. He held that Christian faith meant practical service of others. He died at Charlotte, Vermont, on 9 October 1940.

UO-SIN-000417.name: Dionysius the Areopagite
UO-SIN-000417.life: Dionysius was a member of the Areopagus, the court of Athens, who heard Paul preach there and became a believer, as the Acts of the Apostles records. Later tradition made him the first bishop of Athens and a martyr in Gaul, though this identification is unreliable. In the early sixth century a body of mystical writings, including The Divine Names and The Celestial Hierarchy, began to circulate under his name. Scholars now think they were written about 500 by an unknown Syrian author, called Pseudo-Dionysius. Even so, they shaped Eastern and Western teaching on God, the angels and the soul's ascent to God.

UO-SIN-000418.name: Abraham
UO-SIN-000418.life: Abraham is the first of the patriarchs in the book of Genesis, honoured by Jews, Christians and Muslims as a father of faith. Originally Abram, he lived in Ur and Haran before God called him to leave his country for a land he would be shown. He went, trusting the promise that his descendants would be numerous and would bless all nations. Genesis tells of his long wait for a son, the birth of Isaac, and the testing of his faith on Mount Moriah. He is buried at Machpelah near Hebron. The New Testament holds him up as the model of trusting God.

UO-SIN-000419.name: John Leonardi
UO-SIN-000419.life: John Leonardi was born in 1541 at Diecimo, near Lucca, and worked as an apothecary's assistant before being ordained in 1572. He gathered lay helpers to serve in hospitals and prisons, then, inspired by the Council of Trent, founded a community of priests, the Clerks Regular of the Mother of God, approved in 1583 though bitterly opposed for years. He advised Pope Clement VIII on reform of the monasteries of Vallombrosa and Monte Vergine, and helped plan the college that became Propaganda Fide in Rome. He died in Rome on 9 October 1609 after catching a fever while caring for the sick.

UO-SIN-000420.name: Paulinus of York
UO-SIN-000420.life: Paulinus was a Roman monk sent to Kent in 601 by Pope Gregory the Great to help convert the English. Consecrated bishop in 625, he travelled north with Ethelburga of Kent, who was to marry King Edwin of Northumbria. He preached tirelessly, and Edwin was baptised at York in 627, followed by many of his people. Paulinus built churches and baptised in rivers across the north. When Edwin was killed in 633 and the kingdom collapsed, Paulinus fled with the queen to Kent, where he became Bishop of Rochester. He died on 10 October 644.

UO-SIN-000421.name: Francis Borgia
UO-SIN-000421.life: Born in 1510, Francis Borgia was a Spanish nobleman, great-grandson of Pope Alexander VI, who served the Emperor Charles V and became Duke of Gandia. Devoted to his wife Eleanor and their eight children, he was shaken by her death in 1546, and after settling his family's affairs he gave up his title and joined the newly founded Jesuits. Ordained, he preached widely and helped the order grow in Spain and Portugal. In 1565 he was elected third Superior General, and he sent missionaries to the Americas and Asia and encouraged Jesuit schools. He died in Rome on 1 October 1572, and is remembered for his humility.

UO-SIN-000422.name: Daniel Comboni
UO-SIN-000422.life: Daniel Comboni was born in 1831 near Lake Garda in northern Italy, the child of poor farmers, and was ordained in 1854. He went to Sudan in 1857, but illness drove him back. He then proposed a plan to save Africa with Africans, and in 1867 founded an institute for missionary priests and brothers, later adding sisters. Appointed bishop for Central Africa in 1877, he travelled between Europe and Africa raising support, opposed the slave trade, and shared the sufferings of his people through famine and fever. He died in Khartoum on 10 October 1881, and was canonised in 2003.

UO-SIN-000423.name: Kenneth / Canice
UO-SIN-000423.life: Cainnech, known as Canice in Ireland and Kenneth in Scotland, was born about 515 in Ulster and became one of the leading Irish monastic saints of the sixth century. According to tradition he studied in Wales, was ordained priest, and was a close friend of Columba and Comgall. He founded the monastery of Aghaboe and is said to have preached among the Picts in Scotland. Kilkenny, the Church of Canice, is named after him, and its cathedral bears his name. Most of what is told of him comes from later legend, but Adomnan mentions him in his life of Columba. He died about 600.

UO-SIN-000424.name: James the Deacon
UO-SIN-000424.life: James was a deacon from Rome who came to northern England with Paulinus, when Ethelburga of Kent travelled north to marry King Edwin of Northumbria. When Edwin was killed in 633 and Paulinus fled, James stayed behind in the north, preaching and baptising in the face of renewed paganism. He lived near Catterick, in a village that Bede says was named after him, and worked around Lincoln. He taught his people church music, and in the following decades helped keep the Roman customs alive. Bede says he lived to a great age and was still active after 671.

UO-SIN-000425.name: Ethelburga of Barking
UO-SIN-000425.life: Ethelburga, or Aethelburh, was the first abbess of Barking Abbey, east of London, which her brother Erconwald, later Bishop of London, founded for her in the 660s. Bede describes her as upright in life and constantly planning for the needs of her community, and records miracles and visions among her nuns, including their faithful endurance of plague. Barking became a notable double house in which women and men lived under her rule. She is thought to have lived into the mid-680s, and Bede says no one who knew her should doubt that heaven was opened to her.

UO-SIN-000426.name: Bruno of Cologne
UO-SIN-000426.life: Bruno the Great, born in 925, was the youngest son of King Henry the Fowler and brother of Emperor Otto I. Educated for the Church, he became his brother's chaplain and, in 953, Archbishop of Cologne, soon also Duke of Lorraine. He used his power to bring order to the realm, and acted as regent in the west and in Germany when Otto was away. A learned man, he fostered schools and the study of classics, and founded and endowed monasteries, including St Pantaleon at Cologne. He died at Reims on 11 October 965 and was buried at St Pantaleon.

UO-SIN-000427.name: Elizabeth Fry
UO-SIN-000427.life: Born Elizabeth Gurney in 1780 into a wealthy Quaker family in Norwich, she married the banker Joseph Fry and raised eleven children. In 1813 she visited Newgate prison in London and was horrified by the overcrowded women's quarters, where prisoners and their children lived in squalor. She returned to provide clothing, schooling, work and Bible reading, and helped found a society for the reform of female prisoners. She also visited convict ships and prisons across Britain and Europe, and spoke before Parliament on prison conditions and the death penalty. She died at Ramsgate on 12 October 1845.

UO-SIN-000428.name: Wilfrid of Ripon
UO-SIN-000428.life: Wilfrid was born about 634 in Northumbria, studied at Lindisfarne, Canterbury and Rome, and became abbot of Ripon. At the Synod of Whitby in 664 he led those who argued for the Roman date of Easter, and the king decided in their favour. He became Bishop of York, but a long dispute with kings and archbishops led to exile and appeals to Rome. He preached to the South Saxons in Sussex, baptising many during a famine and teaching them to fish, and he built fine churches at Ripon and Hexham. He died in 709 at Oundle, and was buried at Ripon.

UO-SIN-000429.name: Edwin of Northumbria
UO-SIN-000429.life: Edwin, born about 586, was a prince of Deira who spent years in exile before becoming king of Deira and Bernicia about 616, and the most powerful ruler in Britain of his day. He married Ethelburga, a Christian princess of Kent, and under the preaching of Paulinus was baptised at York at Easter 627, with many of his nobles. He promoted the Church in the north. In 633 he was defeated and killed at Hatfield Chase by the Welsh king Cadwallon and the pagan Penda of Mercia. Later generations honoured him as a martyr, and his head was long preserved at York.

UO-SIN-000430.name: Gerald of Aurillac
UO-SIN-000430.life: Gerald was born about 855 into the nobility of the Auvergne in France and inherited large estates. He wanted to become a monk, but a bishop persuaded him that he could do more good as a layman. He remained in the world, ruling as count with unusual justice, aiding the poor, refusing to profit from the weak, and living in chastity. He is said to have fought only reluctantly, ordering his men to fight with the blunt ends of their weapons. He founded the abbey at Aurillac, and went blind in his later years. He died about 909, and Odo of Cluny wrote his life.

UO-SIN-000431.name: Comgan
UO-SIN-000431.life: Comgan was an Irish prince of Leinster who lost his throne through the schemes of neighbouring rulers. Rather than fight on, he left Ireland with his sister Kentigerna, her son Fillan and several companions, and sailed to the Scottish Highlands. He settled at Lochalsh, facing the Isle of Skye, where he founded a monastery and ruled it as abbot, known for a severe and ascetic way of life. After his death, Fillan is said to have buried him on Iona and built a church in his memory. Place names such as Kilchoan still recall him across the western Highlands.

UO-SIN-000432.name: Esther John
UO-SIN-000432.life: Born Qamar Zia in 1929 into a Muslim family in British India, she attended a Christian school and was moved by the fifty-third chapter of Isaiah. Her family moved to Pakistan after Partition, and she eventually fled home to escape an arranged marriage, taking the name Esther John. She worked in an orphanage in Karachi and a mission hospital at Sahiwal, then trained as a Bible teacher at Gujranwala. Afterwards she travelled by bicycle among the villages near Chichawatni, teaching women to read and speaking of Christ. She was murdered in her bed on 2 February 1960, and a statue of her stands at Westminster Abbey.

UO-SIN-000433.name: Callistus I
UO-SIN-000433.life: Callistus began as a slave in Rome, where he was entrusted with Christian funds and later sent to the mines of Sardinia for his faith. After his release, Pope Zephyrinus made him a deacon and put him in charge of the Christian cemetery on the Appian Way, which still bears his name. Elected bishop of Rome around 217, he eased the harsh penitential rules and held that serious sins, including adultery, could be forgiven. This drew fierce criticism from the theologian Hippolytus, who set himself up as a rival bishop. Callistus died about 222, and tradition honours him as a martyr.

UO-SIN-000434.name: Justus of Lyon
UO-SIN-000434.life: Justus became bishop of Lyon around the middle of the fourth century and was respected for his learning. He attended the councils of Valence and Aquileia, which dealt with church discipline and the Arian controversy, and corresponded with Ambrose of Milan. According to the old account of his life, a man pursued by a mob took refuge in his church, and Justus handed him to the magistrates, who promised fair treatment; the crowd killed the man anyway. Burdened with guilt, Justus resigned and slipped away to Egypt with his lector Viator. He lived as a monk at Scetis and died about 389. His body was later brought home to Lyon.

UO-SIN-000435.name: Richard Gwyn
UO-SIN-000435.life: Richard Gwyn was born about 1537 at Llanidloes in Montgomeryshire and studied at Oxford and Cambridge. He taught school at Overton and Wrexham, and having at first conformed to the Elizabethan church, he returned to the Catholic faith when missionary priests reached Wales. For refusing to attend Protestant services he was repeatedly arrested, imprisoned and even carried into church in chains. He also wrote Welsh poems and carols, some of which survive. Tried for treason in October 1584, he was offered his life if he would acknowledge the queen as head of the Church. He refused and was hanged, drawn and quartered at Wrexham on 15 October 1584.

UO-SIN-000436.name: Hugh Latimer and Nicholas Ridley
UO-SIN-000436.life: Latimer and Ridley were English bishops of the Reformation. Latimer, a farmer's son from Leicestershire, became a Cambridge preacher of reforming views and was Bishop of Worcester under Henry VIII. Ridley served as Bishop of Rochester and then of London, and helped shape the first Book of Common Prayer. When the Catholic Mary I came to the throne, both were arrested and tried for heresy at Oxford. They were burned together on 16 October 1555. Latimer is said to have encouraged his companion with the words that they would light such a candle in England as would never be put out.

UO-SIN-000437.name: Gall
UO-SIN-000437.life: Gall was an Irish monk who trained at Bangor and went with Columbanus to the continent around 590. When Columbanus was driven out of Burgundy and made his way to Lake Constance, Gall went with him. In 612, when fever stopped Gall from following Columbanus into Italy, he stayed behind and lived as a hermit in the forests near the lake, preaching to the Alemanni. Disciples gathered around him, and after his death about 645 their hermitage grew into the great abbey of Saint Gall, long a centre of learning and manuscript copying. Tradition tells of a bear that brought him firewood.

UO-SIN-000438.name: Hedwig of Silesia
UO-SIN-000438.life: Hedwig was born at Andechs in Bavaria and married Duke Henry the Bearded of Silesia at the age of twelve. As duchess she persuaded her husband to found a large Cistercian convent at Trzebnica, which also educated girls from poor noble families, and she supported hospitals and the poor. After Henry died in 1238 she lived with great austerity, often walking barefoot and wearing coarse clothing. Her son Henry the Pious was killed fighting the Mongols at Legnica in 1241, and she bore the loss with remarkable calm. She died at Trzebnica in 1243 and was canonized in 1267; she is patron of Silesia.

UO-SIN-000439.name: Margaret Mary Alacoque
UO-SIN-000439.life: Born in 1647 at L'Hautecour in Burgundy, Margaret Mary suffered poor health and a hard youth before entering the Visitation convent at Paray-le-Monial. Between 1673 and 1675 she reported a series of visions in which Christ showed her his heart as a sign of his love for humanity. Her community doubted her at first, but her confessor, the Jesuit Claude de la Colombiere, believed her and supported her. She urged a feast of the Sacred Heart, devotions of reparation and the practice of receiving communion on the first Friday of the month. She died in 1690 and was canonized in 1920.

UO-SIN-000440.name: Daniel Rowland
UO-SIN-000440.life: Born about 1713 in Cardiganshire, Daniel Rowland was ordained in the Church of England and became curate of Llangeitho and Nantcwnlle. Around 1735 he was awakened to a deep faith under the preaching of Griffith Jones, and his own sermons soon drew crowds from across Wales. Llangeitho became a place of pilgrimage, especially on communion Sundays, when thousands gathered. He worked with Howel Harris to spread the Welsh Methodist revival and wrote hymns as well. The bishop deprived him of his curacy about 1763, but he continued to preach to the people of Llangeitho until his death on 16 October 1790.

UO-SIN-000441.name: John the Dwarf
UO-SIN-000441.life: John was born in Egypt around 339 and went at eighteen with his brother into the desert of Scetis, where he became a disciple of Abba Pambo. A well-known story tells how Pambo gave him a dry stick to water daily; after three years it put out leaves and fruit, and Pambo shared it with the other monks as the fruit of obedience. John was renowned for humility and taught the great Arsenius. When raiders overran Scetis in 395, he moved to Mount Colzim near Suez, where he died around 405. His sayings are preserved among the desert fathers.

UO-SIN-000442.name: Etheldreda
UO-SIN-000442.life: Etheldreda, also called Audrey, was a daughter of King Anna of East Anglia, born in the early 630s. Married for political reasons first to Tondberht and then to King Ecgfrith of Northumbria, she is said, following Bede, to have remained a virgin in both marriages. With the help of Bishop Wilfrid she was finally allowed to become a nun, and in 673 she founded a double monastery at Ely, living there as abbess in great simplicity. She died of plague in 679. Sixteen years later her body was found uncorrupted, and her shrine at Ely became one of the greatest in medieval England.

UO-SIN-000443.name: Ursuline Martyrs of Valenciennes and the Laval Martyrs
UO-SIN-000443.life: During the French Revolution, two groups of Catholics died for their faith in 1794. At Valenciennes, after French troops retook the town, eleven Ursuline nuns, led by Mother Clotilde Angela Paillot, were condemned for having returned to France under Austrian occupation. Five were guillotined on 17 October and six on 23 October, as were Brigittine and Poor Clare sisters nearby. At Laval, nineteen people were executed that January, including the Franciscan priest Jean-Baptiste Triquerie, a number of diocesan priests and a laywoman. Most had refused to take the oath required by the Civil Constitution of the Clergy. Both groups were beatified in the twentieth century.

UO-SIN-000446.name: Jean de Brebeuf, Isaac Jogues and Companions
UO-SIN-000446.life: These eight French Jesuits and lay helpers brought the gospel to the Huron (Wendat) people and the Mohawk in what is now Ontario and New York. Jean de Brebeuf lived among the Hurons from 1625, mastered their language and compiled their grammar. Isaac Jogues was captured by the Mohawk in 1642, tortured and mutilated, then ransomed by the Dutch; he returned to seek peace and was killed in 1646. Brebeuf and Gabriel Lalemant died under torture in 1649 when the Iroquois destroyed a mission village. Others, including Rene Goupil, Antoine Daniel, Charles Garnier and Noel Chabanel, were killed between 1642 and 1649. They were canonized in 1930.

UO-SIN-000447.name: Frideswide
UO-SIN-000447.life: Frideswide is the patron saint of Oxford. According to tradition, she was a Mercian princess, daughter of a sub-king, who founded a community of women at Oxford, on the site that later became Christ Church. A king named Algar wished to marry her against her vow, and when she fled, the people of Oxford would not betray her and he was struck blind. She withdrew to Binsey, where a well of healing water is said to have sprung up at her prayer. She died around 727, and her shrine drew pilgrims through the Middle Ages, among them Catherine of Aragon.

UO-SIN-000448.name: William Carey
UO-SIN-000448.life: Born in 1761 in Paulerspury, Northamptonshire, William Carey worked as a shoemaker and teacher before becoming a Baptist pastor. His 1792 essay on the duty of Christians to take the gospel to the world led to the founding of the Baptist Missionary Society, and in 1793 he sailed for India. Settling at Serampore with Joshua Marshman and William Ward, he translated the Bible into several Indian languages and parts of it into many more, wrote grammars and dictionaries, taught at Fort William College and founded Serampore College. He also campaigned against infanticide and widow-burning. He died in India in 1834 and is called the father of modern missions.

UO-SIN-000449.name: Paul of the Cross
UO-SIN-000449.life: Paolo Danei was born in 1694 at Ovada in northern Italy. After a deep spiritual experience, he gave himself in 1720 to a life of prayer and began drawing up a rule for a community devoted to the memory of Christ's Passion. He and his companions lived in simple mountain retreats, combining solitude and prayer with preaching missions among ordinary people. Paul became one of the most sought-after preachers in Italy. Papal approval came in 1741 and again in 1769, and he also helped found a community of Passionist nuns. He died in Rome in 1775 and was canonized in 1867.

UO-SIN-000450.name: Acca of Hexham
UO-SIN-000450.life: Acca was a Northumbrian who served in the household of Bishop Bosa before attaching himself to Wilfrid, whom he accompanied on journeys that included Rome. Wilfrid made him abbot of Hexham, and he succeeded Wilfrid as bishop in 709. He adorned the church, gathered relics, built a fine library and brought the cantor Maban from Kent to teach Roman chant. Bede, who praised his learning, dedicated commentaries to him, and Acca encouraged the life of Wilfrid. Driven from his see in 732 for reasons unknown, he is thought to have lived for a time in Galloway. He died about 740 and was honoured as a saint.

UO-SIN-000451.name: Andrew of Crete
UO-SIN-000451.life: Andrew was born in Damascus about 660 and became a monk at the monastery of Saint Sabbas near Jerusalem. He was sent to Constantinople, where he served as a deacon at the great church of Hagia Sophia, and later became archbishop of Gortyna in Crete. He is best remembered as a hymn writer, credited with introducing the canon, a form of hymn made up of nine odes, into the Greek liturgy. His Great Canon of Repentance, with some 250 verses, is still sung during Lent in the Orthodox Church. He died around 740, on the island of Lesbos.

UO-SIN-000452.name: Bertilla Boscardin
UO-SIN-000452.life: Anna Francesca Boscardin was born in 1888 into a poor farming family at Brendola in northern Italy. Her childhood was marked by hardship, her father was violent; she was mocked as slow. At sixteen she entered the Dorothean Sisters at Vicenza, taking the name Bertilla, and was sent to nurse at the hospital in Treviso, working first in the children's diphtheria ward. During the First World War she cared for wounded soldiers, staying with patients through air raids. A painful tumour ended her life in 1922 at the age of thirty-four. She was canonized in 1961 and is a patron of the rejected and abused.

UO-SIN-000453.name: Mary Teresa de Soubiran
UO-SIN-000453.life: Sophie-Therese de Soubiran was born in 1834 at Castelnaudary in southern France. She gave up thoughts of becoming a Carmelite to serve the needs of girls and working women, and in 1864, with the help of the Jesuit Paul Ginhac, she founded the Society of Mary Auxiliatrice at Toulouse. Her community cared for young women and orphans and kept Eucharistic adoration. After a sister falsified accounts and made accusations against her, she was forced out of the community she had founded. She lived quietly in a Paris convent until her death in 1889, and was later cleared of all blame. She was beatified in 1946.

UO-SIN-000454.name: Fintan Munnu
UO-SIN-000454.life: Fintan, called Munnu, was born into the northern Ui Neill and trained in the monastic life under Comgall at Bangor and Sinell at Cluain-inis on Lough Erne. Around 597 he set out for Iona to join Columba, but Columba had just died, and Baithene, his successor, sent him back to Ireland to found a community of his own. He established the monastery of Taghmon in County Wexford, where about a hundred and fifty monks lived under his rule. He was a strict ascetic and a gifted teacher, said to have healed the sick. He died about 635, and churches in Ireland and Scotland bear his name.

UO-SIN-000455.name: Ursula and Companions
UO-SIN-000455.life: According to medieval tradition, Ursula was a British princess who, before her marriage, sailed to Rome on pilgrimage with a great company of virgins. On the way back they were massacred at Cologne by the Huns after she refused to marry their chief. The historical basis is slight: an inscription from around 400 mentions holy virgins who died at Cologne, and the story grew over the centuries, with the number of companions swelling to eleven thousand. Whatever the truth of the details, Ursula became one of the most loved saints of the Middle Ages, patron of Cologne, of schools and of the Ursuline sisters.

UO-SIN-000456.name: Malchus
UO-SIN-000456.life: Malchus is known from the life written by Jerome, who interviewed him in Syria. Born near Nisibis, he left home to become a monk in the desert of Chalcis, but later set out to claim his father's inheritance. Captured by Saracen raiders, he was made a shepherd slave and compelled to marry a fellow captive. The two agreed to live together as brother and sister, and eventually escaped on inflated goatskins. According to Jerome, a lioness killed their pursuers as they hid in a cave. They reached a Roman fort and later lived in chastity as monastics in the Syrian village of Maronia, where Malchus died around 390.

UO-SIN-000114.name: Ignatius of Jesus OSB (Joseph Leycester Lyne)
UO-SIN-000114.life: Joseph Leycester Lyne was born in London in 1837 and, as a young deacon of strong High Church views, set himself to revive Benedictine monastic life in the Church of England. Calling himself Father Ignatius, he founded communities at Claydon and Norwich, and in 1869 bought land at Capel-y-ffin in the Black Mountains of Wales, where he built Llanthony Abbey. A gifted and fiery preacher, he travelled widely, even to America, to raise funds, and often met hostility. His methods and impatience of authority brought trouble, yet he held to his vision to the end. He died on 16 October 1908, and his abbey later became home to Eric Gill.

UO-SIN-000457.name: Albercius of Hieropolis
UO-SIN-000457.life: Albercius was bishop of Hieropolis in Phrygia in the second century. According to his later life, he travelled widely, even to Rome, preaching and healing, and died about 167. He is best known through the epitaph he composed for his own tomb, carved on a stone now kept in the Vatican Museums. It tells of his journey to Rome and across the Euphrates, speaks of a people bearing a shining seal, which is taken to mean baptism, and of the bread and wine of the Eucharist. It is one of the earliest Christian inscriptions to survive.

UO-SIN-000458.name: John Paul II
UO-SIN-000458.life: Karol Wojtyla was born in 1920 at Wadowice in Poland. During the Second World War he worked in a quarry and chemical plant while secretly preparing for the priesthood, and was ordained in 1946. He became archbishop of Krakow in 1964 and took part in the Second Vatican Council. Elected pope on 16 October 1978, he was the first non-Italian pope in over four hundred years. He travelled to well over a hundred countries, spoke out against communism and dictatorship, and reached out to Jews, Muslims and the Orthodox. He died on 2 April 2005 and was canonized in 2014.

UO-SIN-000461.name: Boethius
UO-SIN-000461.life: Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius was born in Rome about 480 into a distinguished senatorial family. He rose swiftly in the service of the Ostrogothic king Theodoric, becoming consul and later head of the royal administration. He set out to translate Aristotle and Plato into Latin and wrote on logic, music, mathematics and theology. Accused of treason around 523, he was imprisoned at Pavia and executed in 524. In prison he wrote The Consolation of Philosophy, a dialogue on fortune, suffering and providence that became one of the most widely read books of the Middle Ages.

UO-SIN-000462.name: John of Capistrano
UO-SIN-000462.life: Giovanni da Capestrano was born in 1386 in the Abruzzo. A lawyer and governor of Perugia, he was imprisoned there in 1412 during a war, and the experience led him in 1416 to join the Franciscans. Ordained in 1426, he became one of the most famous preachers of his age, travelling through Italy, Germany, Bohemia and Hungary, and with Bernardine of Siena he promoted the strict Observant reform of his order. In 1456, when he was seventy, he helped rally the army that lifted the Turkish siege of Belgrade. He died soon afterwards, probably of plague, on 23 October 1456, and was canonized in 1690.

UO-SIN-000463.name: Ethelfleda of Romsey
UO-SIN-000463.life: Ethelfleda was a late tenth-century abbess of Romsey Abbey in Hampshire, thought to have been a daughter of King Edgar. After his death she was raised at the abbey under Abbess Merewenna and, around 1003, succeeded her as head of the community. Tradition says she gave away the convent's money to the poor, and she was remembered for severe devotion, including reciting the psalms at night while standing in the cold River Test. She died around 1016 and was buried as she had asked. Her tomb is still honoured in the abbey church, which bears her name.

UO-SIN-000464.name: Antony Mary Claret
UO-SIN-000464.life: Born in 1807 at Sallent near Barcelona, Antony Claret began life as a weaver before being ordained in 1835. He became a tireless preacher of parish missions and in 1849 founded the Claretians, a congregation of missionary priests. Named Archbishop of Santiago de Cuba in 1851, he reformed the seminary, built schools and a hospital, and survived many attempts on his life. Recalled to Spain, he served as confessor to Queen Isabella II. A prolific writer who spread inexpensive Christian books, he died in exile at Fontfroide in France in 1870 and was canonised in 1950.

UO-SIN-000465.name: Maglorius
UO-SIN-000465.life: Maglorius, also called Magloire, was a sixth-century Briton who, according to tradition, studied under Illtud in Wales and then crossed to Brittany with his cousin Samson. There the two founded monasteries, and Maglorius became abbot of one near Dol. When Samson died he is said to have succeeded him as bishop, but he soon resigned the office and withdrew to the island of Sark. He founded a small monastic community there and died around 575. Stories of miracles, including one of driving off a dragon on Jersey, were written down long after his death.

UO-SIN-000466.name: Felix of Thibiuca
UO-SIN-000466.life: Felix was bishop of Thibiuca in Roman North Africa when the emperor Diocletian ordered Christian scriptures to be surrendered and burned. Summoned by the magistrate Magnillian, he refused to hand over the sacred books and endured imprisonment and questioning for his stand. He was put to death in 303, together with a few companions, among them Audactus, Fortunatus, Januarius and Septimus. Accounts differ on the place of his death: some say he was beheaded at Carthage, others that he was sent to Italy and died at Venosa, where he was long honoured as a patron.

UO-SIN-000467.name: The Forty Martyrs of England and Wales
UO-SIN-000467.life: These forty men and women were put to death between 1535 and 1679 for refusing to accept the monarch's authority over the church or for exercising their priesthood in England. They include Carthusian monk John Houghton, Jesuits Edmund Campion and Robert Southwell, Philip Howard, Earl of Arundel, and Margaret Clitherow of York, who was pressed to death rather than stand trial. Most were hanged, drawn and quartered. The group consists of priests, monks, friars and seven lay people, three of them mothers. Selected from a far larger number of victims, they were canonised together in 1970.

UO-SIN-000468.name: Crispin and Crispinian
UO-SIN-000468.life: Crispin and Crispinian were, according to tradition, twin brothers from a noble Roman family who fled persecution and settled at Soissons in Gaul. There they preached the gospel by day and made shoes by night, refusing payment from their converts. The governor Rictiovarus had them tortured, and legend says they survived being thrown into a river with millstones round their necks. They were finally beheaded around 286 under Maximian. Their bodies were later divided between Soissons, Osnabruck and Rome. They became patrons of shoemakers and leatherworkers, and their day is famous in England through Shakespeare's Agincourt speech.

UO-SIN-000470.name: Cedd and Eata
UO-SIN-000470.life: Cedd and Eata were Northumbrian monks trained at Lindisfarne under Aidan. Cedd led a mission to the Middle Angles, became bishop of the East Saxons, founded monasteries at Bradwell-on-Sea and Lastingham, and served as interpreter at the Synod of Whitby; he died of plague at Lastingham in 664. Eata became abbot of Melrose, then founded a house at Ripon, where he welcomed the young Cuthbert. Made a bishop in 678, he governed Lindisfarne and then Hexham. Bede praised him as gentle and holy. He died in 686 and was buried at Hexham.

UO-SIN-000471.name: Bean
UO-SIN-000471.life: Bean, in Gaelic Beoan, is remembered as the first bishop of Mortlach in Banffshire, a see later transferred to Aberdeen. Medieval Scottish writers say King Malcolm II founded the bishopric around 1012 in thanks for victory over the Danes, and that Bean was its first bishop, appointed at the king's wish.
