Tradition places his dwelling at Balvenie, near Mortlach. Almost nothing else is securely known: the date of his death is uncertain, and he has often been confused with another Bean named in the life of Saint Cathroe. He is nevertheless honoured as an early father of the northeastern Scottish church.

UO-SIN-000472.name: Frumentius
UO-SIN-000472.life: Frumentius was born at Tyre in Phoenicia. As a boy he and his brother Edesius were captured when their ship was attacked and brought to the court of the king of Axum. Raised to positions of trust, they helped the widowed queen govern and educate her young son Ezana, and Frumentius encouraged Christian merchants to worship openly. He travelled to Alexandria, where Athanasius consecrated him as the first bishop of Axum. He baptised Ezana, and churches rose across the kingdom. Called Abba Salama, the Father of Peace, he is honoured as the apostle of Ethiopia and is thought to have died around 383.

UO-SIN-000473.name: Nestor of Thessalonica
UO-SIN-000473.life: Nestor was a young Christian of Thessalonica, perhaps about twenty, who lived during the persecution under Maximian in the early fourth century. According to tradition, a huge gladiator named Lyaeus delighted in mocking and killing Christians in the arena. Nestor visited his friend Demetrius in prison and asked his blessing, then entered the arena and struck Lyaeus down. The furious emperor ordered Nestor put to the sword. Sources give his death year variously as 290, 296 or 306. He is remembered as a companion of Saint Demetrius and as a patron of wrestlers and athletes.

UO-SIN-000475.name: Colman of Kilmacduagh
UO-SIN-000475.life: Born about 560 at Kiltartan in County Galway, Colman was educated on Inishmore and lived there for years as a hermit, building two small churches. Around 590 he sought deeper solitude in the Burren, where he lived in a cave at Keelhilla. His kinsman King Guaire of Connacht urged him to found a community, and in 610 Colman established the monastery of Kilmacduagh, which became the centre of the surrounding diocese. Reluctantly accepting ordination as bishop, he governed as abbot-bishop until his death in 632. Pilgrims still visit his hermitage, and stories tell of his gentle friendship with animals.

UO-SIN-000477.name: John Wyclif
UO-SIN-000477.life: John Wyclif was an English theologian born in Yorkshire around 1330. A leading teacher at Oxford, he served the crown in negotiations with the papacy and later became rector of Lutterworth. He argued that Scripture, not the pope, held final authority, that the church should give up worldly wealth, and he rejected the doctrine of transubstantiation. He inspired the first complete English Bible and his followers, the Lollards, spread his ideas. He suffered a stroke while at Mass and died on the last day of 1384. Later called the morning star of the Reformation, he was condemned at Constance in 1415.

UO-SIN-000478.name: Alphonsus Rodriguez
UO-SIN-000478.life: Born in 1533 at Segovia, Alphonsus took over his family's cloth business after his father's death. Then came sorrow: his wife, children and mother died and the business failed. Turned away at first because of his age and little schooling, he entered the Jesuits in 1571 at thirty-seven as a lay brother and was sent to the college at Palma on Majorca. From 1579 he was its doorkeeper, receiving visitors, running errands, helping the poor and counselling troubled people, among them the young Peter Claver. His quiet prayer and humble service made him a model of holiness in ordinary work. He died in 1617.

UO-SIN-000479.name: Wolfgang of Regensburg
UO-SIN-000479.life: Wolfgang was born around 934 into a Swabian noble family and studied at Reichenau and Wurzburg. After becoming a Benedictine monk and priest, he preached to the Magyars settled near Hungary, and in 972 he was made bishop of Regensburg. He tutored the future emperor Henry II, reformed monasteries and convents, and gave St Emmeram's Abbey its own abbots again. For a time he lived as a hermit in the Austrian mountains, near the lake that bears his name. He fell ill while travelling and died at Pupping in 994. Canonised in 1052, he became patron of woodcutters and carpenters.

UO-SIN-000480.name: Saints of the Reformation Era
UO-SIN-000480.life: This group recalls the men and women of the sixteenth century who sought to renew the church and make Scripture available to ordinary people, many at the cost of their lives. William Tyndale translated the New Testament into English from Greek and was strangled and burned near Brussels in 1536. Thomas Cranmer, Hugh Latimer and Nicholas Ridley, bishops and leaders of the English reformation, were burned at Oxford under Mary I, Latimer and Ridley in 1555 and Cranmer in 1556. Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer still shapes Anglican worship.

UO-SIN-000482.name: Foillan
UO-SIN-000482.life: Foillan was an Irish monk of the seventh century, brother of Saints Fursey and Ultan. Around 633 he followed Fursey to East Anglia, where the king gave them an old Roman fort for a monastery, probably at Burgh Castle, and Foillan later became its abbot. When Mercian raiders ravaged the community around 651 he led the survivors to the Frankish lands. Helped by Itta, mother of Saint Gertrude, he founded a monastery at Fosses. While travelling around 655 he and his companions were attacked and killed by robbers in the Sonian Forest. He is honoured as a martyr.

UO-SIN-000485.name: Odilo of Cluny
UO-SIN-000485.life: Born about 962 into a noble family of Auvergne, Odilo became a monk at Cluny when he was about twenty-nine and in 994 was chosen as its fifth abbot. He led it for fifty-four years, a period when it became the greatest monastery in western Europe and many houses came under its care. Known for gentleness and generosity, he supported the Truce of God, which limited warfare. He ordered that the day after All Saints be set aside to pray for all the faithful departed, a custom that spread through the western church as All Souls' Day. He died on New Year's Day, 1049.

UO-SIN-000486.name: Margaret of Lorraine
UO-SIN-000486.life: Margaret was born in 1463 in the castle of Vaudemont in Lorraine and, orphaned young, was raised by her grandfather King Rene of Anjou. In 1488 she married Rene, Duke of Alencon, and bore three children. Widowed in 1492, she governed the duchy, saw to her children's education, and became known as a protector of the poor, widows and orphans. Later she founded a Poor Clare convent at Argentan. She took the habit there and made her vows in October 1520. After one year of simple, austere life she died on 2 November 1521. She was beatified in 1921.

UO-SIN-000487.name: Martin de Porres
UO-SIN-000487.life: Martin was born in Lima in 1579, the son of a Spanish nobleman and a freed woman of African descent. Barred by his mixed ancestry from full membership in a religious order, he first served the Dominican convent of the Rosary as a helper and was admitted as a lay brother in 1603. He spent years caring for the sick in the infirmary and became known for healing and humility. He fed the poor from alms, aided enslaved Africans, and founded an orphanage and school for abandoned children. Many wonders were reported of him. He died in 1639 and was canonised in 1962.

UO-SIN-000488.name: Winefride / Gwenfrewi
UO-SIN-000488.life: Winefride was a Welsh woman of the seventh century, said to have been the daughter of a nobleman in Flintshire and niece of Saint Beuno. According to tradition, when she refused the advances of a prince named Caradog, he struck off her head in anger. A spring of water rose where it fell, and Beuno prayed and restored her to life. She later withdrew inland to Gwytherin, where she became abbess of a community of nuns and died, around 660. The well at Holywell has drawn pilgrims for centuries, and her relics were taken to Shrewsbury in 1138.

UO-SIN-000489.name: Malachy of Armagh
UO-SIN-000489.life: Born in Armagh in 1094, Malachy was ordained in 1119 and became abbot of Bangor and bishop of Connor, then in 1132 reluctantly archbishop of Armagh. He restored church discipline, brought Irish worship into closer agreement with Rome, and gave up Armagh in 1138 so that others could continue the work. In 1139 he travelled to Rome and obtained papal recognition for the Irish sees. On the way he befriended Bernard of Clairvaux, and in 1142 he founded Mellifont, the first Irish Cistercian abbey. He died at Clairvaux in Bernard's arms on 2 November 1148 and was the first Irish-born saint formally canonised.

UO-SIN-000490.name: Saints of the Old Testament
UO-SIN-000490.life: This group honours the faithful men and women of Israel's story who looked toward God's promise before Christ came. The letter to the Hebrews names many: Abel, Enoch and Noah, then Abraham and Sarah, who left home at God's call, and their descendants Isaac, Jacob and Joseph. It recalls Moses, who led the people out of slavery, and later figures such as Samuel, David, Gideon and Samson, as well as prophets and unnamed sufferers. Christians see them as spiritual ancestors, people who trusted in what they could not yet see.

UO-SIN-000491.name: Charles Borromeo
UO-SIN-000491.life: Born in 1538 at Arona in a noble Lombard family, Charles studied law at Pavia. When his uncle became Pope Pius IV he was made a cardinal at twenty-one and helped bring the Council of Trent to its close. Ordained a priest and named archbishop of Milan, he arrived in 1565 to find disorder and set about reform, founding seminaries to train clergy and schools for religious teaching. During the plague of 1576 he stayed in the city, spending his own money to feed and tend the sick. Worn out by his labours, he died in 1584 at forty-six and was canonised in 1610.

UO-SIN-000492.name: John Zedazneli and Companions
UO-SIN-000492.life: According to Georgian tradition, in the sixth century a band of thirteen monks came from Syria or Mesopotamia to strengthen the faith in Georgia. Their leader was John of Zedazeni, who founded a monastery on Mount Zedazeni near Mtskheta. Among his companions were David of Gareja, who began the desert monasteries of Gareja, Abibos of Nekresi, Shio of Mgvime and Joseph of Alaverdi. They founded monasteries and hermitages and spread the monastic life across the land. Scholars think the number thirteen is symbolic, and tradition names as many as nineteen monks. Their foundations shaped Georgian Christian life.

UO-SIN-000493.name: Cybi
UO-SIN-000493.life: Cybi was a sixth-century Welsh saint, said by medieval lives to have been of Cornish noble birth. Tradition holds that he travelled as a pilgrim to the Holy Land and, on returning, turned down a kingdom to serve God, founding churches in Cornwall. He later moved to Wales and received from King Maelgwn of Gwynedd an old Roman fort at Holyhead on Anglesey, where he founded a monastery. The place is still called Caer Gybi, the fort of Cybi. His community continued as a church for centuries. Later stories tell of his friendship with Seiriol of Penmon, but the early lives of Cybi are of doubtful reliability.

UO-SIN-000494.name: Bernard Lichtenberg
UO-SIN-000494.life: Born in 1875 in Silesia, Bernhard Lichtenberg was ordained in 1899 and served in Berlin parishes before becoming provost of St Hedwig's Cathedral. After the Kristallnacht attacks of November 1938 he declared that the burning synagogue was also a house of God, and he prayed publicly each day for Jews and other persecuted people. He also helped Catholics of Jewish descent to emigrate and protested the murder of the disabled. Arrested in 1941, he served two years in prison and was then sent toward Dachau. Gravely ill, he died on the journey in November 1943. He was beatified in 1996.

UO-SIN-000495.name: Gomidas Keumurgian
UO-SIN-000495.life: Gomidas was born in Constantinople around 1656, married at twenty, and became a priest of the Armenian Church, serving in the Galata district. A gifted preacher, he was also a leader of those who sought union with Rome, and he and his family entered Catholic communion in the 1690s. Arrested in 1707 amid hostility toward Catholics, he was accused of treason and of baptising Muslims. The judge offered him freedom if he would become a Muslim. He refused, and on 5 November 1707 he was beheaded before a large crowd, reciting the Creed. He was beatified in 1929.

UO-SIN-000496.name: Illtud
UO-SIN-000496.life: Illtud was a Welsh monastic teacher of the late fifth and early sixth centuries. Later tradition says he was a soldier before turning to the religious life, and some say he came from Brittany. He founded a famous monastery school at Llanilltud Fawr, now Llantwit Major in Glamorgan, where learning in Scripture and the classics was preserved after Roman rule ended. An early life of Samson of Dol called him the most learned of the Britons. His pupils included David, Samson, Gildas and Paul Aurelian. Churches in south-east Wales and Brittany bear his name.

UO-SIN-000497.name: Leonard of Noblac
UO-SIN-000497.life: Leonard is said by tradition to have been a noble at the court of the Frankish king Clovis, who was converted around 496 and then became a disciple of Remigius. He refused a bishopric, became a monk near Orleans, and then withdrew as a hermit into the forests of Limousin. Followers gathered about him, and his hermitage grew into the monastery of Noblac, now Saint-Leonard-de-Noblat. He was remembered for his care of prisoners and captives, and many were said to have been freed by his prayers. He died around 559. Devotion to him spread widely in the twelfth century, and he became patron of prisoners.

UO-SIN-000498.name: Richard Davies
UO-SIN-000498.life: Born in Wales around 1501, Richard Davies studied at Oxford and became a Protestant clergyman in Buckinghamshire. When Mary I came to the throne he lost his posts and lived in exile on the Continent. Returning under Elizabeth I, he became bishop of St Asaph in 1560 and of St Davids in 1561. A scholar of Greek and Welsh, he worked with William Salesbury and Thomas Huet on the Welsh New Testament and Prayer Book, published in 1567, translating 1 Timothy, Hebrews and the letters of James and Peter. He also contributed to the Bishops' Bible. He died in 1581 and was buried at Abergwili.

UO-SIN-000499.name: Elizabeth of the Trinity
UO-SIN-000499.life: Élisabeth Catez was born in 1880 at a French army camp and grew up in Dijon, a gifted pianist with a fierce temper that she learned to master. After her father's early death she kept her heart set on the Carmelite monastery near her home, and entered it in 1901. There she found God in laundry and prayer alike, and came to call herself Laudem Gloriae, Praise of Glory. Her letters and short retreat writings on the indwelling Trinity are loved by many. Addison's disease took her life in 1906, at twenty-six. She was canonized in 2016.

UO-SIN-000500.name: John Duns Scotus
UO-SIN-000500.life: Born around 1266 at Duns in Berwickshire, John joined the Franciscans as a young man and was ordained priest at Northampton in 1291. He studied and lectured at Oxford and Paris, where he was briefly expelled for siding with the pope in a quarrel with the French king. His subtle, rigorous thinking earned him the title Doctor Subtilis, and he argued strongly for the Immaculate Conception of Mary and for the primacy of love and will in the life with God. Sent to the Franciscan house at Cologne, he died there in 1308.

UO-SIN-000501.name: All Saints and Martyrs of England / All Saints of Wales
UO-SIN-000501.life: This day gathers the countless holy men and women of the island of Britain, known and unknown. It remembers Alban, the first recorded British martyr, who gave his life for a fugitive priest; the Welsh founders such as David, Dyfrig and Teilo; and the Anglo-Saxon missionaries, bishops, abbesses and scholars, among them Aidan, Cuthbert, Hilda and Bede. It also recalls the martyrs of later centuries, who died for their faith in the troubled years of the Reformation. Their churches, wells and place-names still mark the land, and the day gives thanks for their witness across fifteen hundred years.

UO-SIN-000503.name: Margery Kempe
UO-SIN-000503.life: Born about 1373 in Bishop's Lynn, now King's Lynn, Margery was the daughter of a mayor and married a town official, John Kempe, bearing at least fourteen children. After a severe crisis following her first childbirth she believed Christ had visited her, and she turned to a life of devotion marked by weeping and visions. She travelled to Jerusalem, Rome and elsewhere, and sought counsel from Julian of Norwich. Unable to write, she dictated the Book of Margery Kempe, often called the first autobiography in English. She was tried for heresy but never convicted, and was still living in 1438.

UO-SIN-000504.name: George Hay Forbes
UO-SIN-000504.life: George Hay Forbes was born in 1821, brother of Alexander Penrose Forbes, bishop of Brechin. Frail in body, he became a priest of the Scottish Episcopal Church and served the town of Burntisland in Fife, where he opened a mission and built up the congregation's life. He set up the Pitsligo Press there and printed liturgical and scholarly works, including studies of the Scottish Communion Office, old missals, and editions of Gregory of Nyssa. Learned, patient and devout, he laboured at Burntisland to the end of his life. He died in 1875, not long after the sudden death of his brother.

UO-SIN-000506.name: Radboud of Utrecht
UO-SIN-000506.life: Radboud was born around 850 into a noble Frankish family, with a Frisian mother said to descend from the Frisian king of the same name. He was educated under his uncle, the archbishop of Cologne, and at the court of Charles the Bald, whose chaplain he became. Chosen bishop of Utrecht in 899, he lived at Deventer because Viking raiders had wrecked his cathedral city. He listed the diocese's lost possessions, travelled to Rome to settle a dispute, and is credited with lives of Boniface and other missionary saints. He died in 917 on a journey through Drenthe.

UO-SIN-000507.name: Justus of Canterbury
UO-SIN-000507.life: Justus was sent from Rome by Pope Gregory the Great to help convert the English, arriving about 601 with the second band of missionaries. In 604 Augustine consecrated him the first bishop of Rochester. When King Aethelberht of Kent died in 616 and pagan reaction followed, Justus fled to Gaul, but he returned the next year when the new king relented. In 624 he became the fourth archbishop of Canterbury and sent missionaries north to Northumbria, where Paulinus carried the gospel. He died on 10 November, sometime between 627 and 631, and was buried at Canterbury.

UO-SIN-000508.name: Kristallnacht remembrance
UO-SIN-000508.life: On the night of 9 to 10 November 1938, Nazi leaders unleashed a pogrom against Jews across Germany, Austria and the Sudetenland, using the shooting of a German diplomat in Paris as pretext. Mobs and storm troopers burned about a thousand synagogues, smashed the windows of Jewish shops, homes and schools, and killed dozens of people. Some thirty thousand Jewish men were arrested and sent to concentration camps. The name Night of Broken Glass recalls the shattered shards that covered the streets. The event marked a turning point in the persecution that led to the Holocaust, and Christians remember it with repentance for their failure to resist.

UO-SIN-000509.name: Theodore the Studite
UO-SIN-000509.life: Born in Constantinople in 759 to a family of palace officials, Theodore became a monk and in 799 abbot of the Stoudios monastery. There he drew up a rule that shaped Byzantine monastic life, with disciplined worship, manual work and study, and he encouraged copying of manuscripts and writing of hymns. A fearless defender of the veneration of icons, he opposed the emperors, was beaten and repeatedly exiled, yet kept encouraging his monks by letters and sermons. He did not live to see icons restored for good. He died in exile in 826 and is honoured as a confessor of the faith.

UO-SIN-000510.name: Armistice Day
UO-SIN-000510.life: At five in the morning on 11 November 1918, in a railway carriage in the forest of Compiegne, German delegates signed an armistice with the Allied commanders. The guns fell silent at eleven o'clock that morning, ending more than four years of war that had killed some ten million soldiers and left whole villages in ruins. Crowds in London, Paris and elsewhere poured into the streets in relief and grief. Each year the day is kept as a time to remember the fallen, to pray for the bereaved and wounded, and to ask God for a peace that is more than the absence of fighting.

UO-SIN-000511.name: Machar
UO-SIN-000511.life: According to tradition, Machar was an Irish nobleman baptized by Colman, who joined Columba on Iona and went with him to preach among the Picts. Late legend says God told him to build a church where a river bends like a bishop's crook, and the Don curves in just that way at Old Aberdeen, where his church was said to be founded about 580. Later stories, written down many centuries afterward, call him the first bishop of Aberdeen and even archbishop of Tours, which cannot be trusted. Little is certain, but his name endures in St Machar's Cathedral and the north-east of Scotland.

UO-SIN-000512.name: Tysilio
UO-SIN-000512.life: Tysilio was a Welsh prince, scholar and holy man of the seventh century, said to be a son of Brochwel Ysgithrog, king of Powys. He studied at Meifod under the abbot Gwyddfarch and later succeeded him there. Around 630 he withdrew to an island in the Menai Strait, now called Church Island, where he lived as a hermit and preached across Anglesey for seven years before returning to Meifod. There he founded a church that bore his name. Many churches and places in Wales, including the long village name Llanfairpwll, honour him. Later tradition credited him with a chronicle of the Welsh kings, though that is a much later compilation.

UO-SIN-000513.name: Josaphat Kuntsevych
UO-SIN-000513.life: Born Ivan Kuntsevych around 1580 at Volodymyr in Volhynia, he entered the Basilian monastery of the Holy Trinity in Vilnius in 1604 and became a priest and later its abbot. In 1617 he was consecrated bishop of Polotsk, and the next year archbishop. He worked tirelessly to reform clergy and monks and to promote the Union of Brest, which joined much of the Ruthenian Church to Rome, and his zeal brought bitter opposition. On 12 November 1623, during a visit to Vitebsk, a mob killed him with an axe and threw his body into the river. He was canonized in 1867.

UO-SIN-000514.name: Abbo of Fleury
UO-SIN-000514.life: Abbo was born near Orleans about 945 and raised at the Benedictine abbey of Fleury, then studied in Paris and Reims, learning philosophy, mathematics and astronomy. He spent two years at Ramsey in England, teaching and helping reform monastic life, and wrote an account of the martyrdom of King Edmund of East Anglia. Elected abbot of Fleury in 988, he mediated between kings, bishops and popes and helped calm the fears that the world would end in the year 1000. In 1004 he went to reform the monastery of La Reole, where a brawl broke out and he was fatally wounded by a lance while trying to make peace.

UO-SIN-000515.name: Nicholas I
UO-SIN-000515.life: Born in Rome about 800 into a noble family, Nicholas served several popes before being elected pope himself in 858. He worked to uphold the authority of the Roman see and the moral law, even against kings. When Lothair II of Lotharingia sought to put away his wife Teutberga, Nicholas refused to approve it and overruled a council that had. He also defended the rights of bishops against powerful archbishops and supported Ignatios in his conflict with Photios at Constantinople, which worsened relations with the East. He sent missionaries to the Bulgarians. Nicholas died in Rome in 867 and is called Nicholas the Great.

UO-SIN-000516.name: Samuel Seabury
UO-SIN-000516.life: Born in 1729 in Connecticut, Samuel Seabury was ordained in the Church of England and served parishes in New Jersey and New York. A loyalist during the Revolution, he was chosen in 1783 by the clergy of Connecticut to be their bishop. English bishops could not consecrate him without an oath to the Crown, so he turned to the Scottish Episcopal Church, and on 14 November 1784 bishops in Aberdeen consecrated him, making him the first American Episcopal bishop. He agreed to seek a eucharistic rite drawn from the Scottish liturgy, and so shaped American worship. He served as bishop of Connecticut and Rhode Island until his death in 1796.

UO-SIN-000517.name: Dyfrig / Dubricius
UO-SIN-000517.life: Dyfrig, also called Dubricius, lived in the late fifth and sixth centuries and is honoured as the evangelist of Ergyng, now Herefordshire, and of much of south-east Wales. According to tradition he was born at Madley, the child of a princess, and became a renowned teacher whose pupils included Teilo and Samson. He founded monasteries at Hentland and Moccas and served as bishop, with a district later associated with Llandaff. Legend says he resigned his see in favour of David and retired to Bardsey Island, where he died around 550, and that he crowned King Arthur. His relics were moved to Llandaff in 1120.

UO-SIN-000518.name: Lawrence O'Toole
UO-SIN-000518.life: Lorcan Ua Tuathail was born in 1128 in County Kildare, a king's son who was given as a hostage as a boy. Entering the monastery of Glendalough, he became its abbot at twenty-six, caring for the poor in time of famine. In 1162 he was chosen archbishop of Dublin and brought the reform of the Irish Church into the city. When the Normans invaded, he mediated between the Irish kings and the invaders, and he travelled to England to plead for his people. He died at Eu in Normandy in 1180 on such a journey, and was canonized in 1225.

UO-SIN-000519.name: Nicholas of Sibenik and Companions
UO-SIN-000519.life: Nicholas Tavelic, born at Sibenik in Croatia, became a Franciscan friar and spent about twelve years preaching in Bosnia. In 1383 he went to the Holy Land, where he joined three other friars, Deodat of Rodez, Peter of Narbonne and Stephen of Cuneo, at the Franciscan house on Mount Zion in Jerusalem. After years of quiet service at the holy places and learning Arabic, they decided to preach Christ openly before the local judge. Arrested, they refused to renounce their faith and were put to death near the Jaffa Gate on 14 November 1391. Nicholas is the first canonized Croatian saint.

UO-SIN-000520.name: Albert the Great
UO-SIN-000520.life: Born around 1200 at Lauingen in Swabia, Albert became a Dominican friar and studied and taught at Paris and Cologne, where one of his students was Thomas Aquinas. He wrote on theology, philosophy and nature, studying plants, animals and minerals with careful observation, and helped bring Aristotle's thought into Christian learning. Reluctantly made bishop of Regensburg in 1260, he resigned after two years to return to teaching and preaching. He also worked to settle disputes between neighbours and cities. He died at Cologne in 1280, was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1931, and is patron of natural scientists.

UO-SIN-000521.name: Francis Asbury and George Whitefield
UO-SIN-000521.life: George Whitefield, an Anglican priest born in Gloucester in 1714, was a spellbinding open-air preacher who stirred great revivals in Britain and the American colonies, and who died at Newburyport, Massachusetts, in 1770. Francis Asbury, born in 1745 near Birmingham, England, crossed the Atlantic in 1771 as one of John Wesley's preachers. He stayed through the Revolution, travelled thousands of miles on horseback, and became the first Methodist bishop in America, shaping a church that spread across the frontier. He died in Virginia in 1816. Both men sought to bring ordinary people to living faith.

UO-SIN-000522.name: Roque Gonzalez and Companions
UO-SIN-000522.life: Roque Gonzalez was born in 1576 at Asuncion, the son of a Spanish settler and a mother of partly Guarani descent, and spoke Guarani from childhood. Ordained a priest, he joined the Jesuits in 1609 and became the first missionary among the Guarani, founding reductions such as San Ignacio Mini and others in what is now Paraguay, Argentina and Brazil. He earned the trust of local people, though some chiefs and shamans opposed him. On 15 November 1628, as a new bell was being hung at Caaro, he and Juan del Castillo were killed, and Alonso Rodriguez soon after. They were canonized in 1988.

UO-SIN-000523.name: Malo
UO-SIN-000523.life: Malo, also known as Maclou or Machutus, was according to tradition born in Wales about 520 and trained at Llancarfan, becoming a follower of Brendan the Navigator and joining in legendary voyages. He later crossed to Brittany, where he served under the hermit Aaron at Aleth and, after Aaron's death, became its first bishop. Stories tell of many miracles. When disorder forced him away he was begged to return, and he restored peace. He ended his days seeking solitude and died on a journey to Saintonge, around the early seventh century. He is one of the seven founding saints of Brittany, and the city of Saint-Malo bears his name.

UO-SIN-000524.name: Edmund Rich of Canterbury
UO-SIN-000524.life: Born at Abingdon around 1175, Edmund studied at Oxford and Paris and became a respected teacher of theology and mathematics at Oxford. Later he served as treasurer of Salisbury cathedral and preached a crusade. In 1233 the pope named him archbishop of Canterbury. He soon came into conflict with King Henry III over the king's foreign favourites and with the pope over Roman demands for money and appointments. Worn out by the struggle, he left England in 1240 and died at Soisy in France on 16 November, and was buried at the abbey of Pontigny. He was canonized in 1246.

UO-SIN-000525.name: Otmar of Saint Gall
UO-SIN-000525.life: Otmar was of Alemannic descent, educated at Chur and ordained priest. In 720 he was appointed to oversee the cell of Saint Gall in what is now Switzerland, and gathered the monks there into a regular monastery as its first abbot. He founded a school and a hospital, and is said to have built the first leper house in the region, caring for the poor and sick. About 747 he introduced the Benedictine Rule. When two local counts tried to seize the abbey's lands he resisted and was imprisoned on an island in the Rhine, where he died in 759. A barrel that never ran dry is his emblem.

UO-SIN-000526.name: Hugh of Lincoln and Robert Grosseteste
UO-SIN-000526.life: Two great bishops served the see of Lincoln. Hugh, born in Burgundy about 1140, became a Carthusian monk, was called to England by Henry II to head the charterhouse at Witham, and in 1186 became bishop of Lincoln. He began rebuilding the cathedral, stood up to kings, and protected Jews from mobs. He died in 1200. Robert Grosseteste, born in Suffolk about 1175, was a scholar of Oxford, a first teacher of the Franciscans there, and a pioneer of natural science who translated Greek works. As bishop from 1235 he pressed for strict pastoral care, and he died in 1253.

UO-SIN-000527.name: Fergus
UO-SIN-000527.life: Fergus was a bishop of Pictish origin who, according to the Aberdeen Breviary, had served for years in Ireland before coming as a missionary to Scotland with companions. He is said to have settled near Strageath in Strathearn and built churches there, then preached in Caithness, founding churches at Wick and Halkirk, and in Buchan, and finally settled at Glamis, where his well still flows. He may have been the Fergus who attended a synod at Rome in 721. He died around 730 and was buried at Glamis. His head was later enshrined at Scone. He is patron of Glamis and Wick.

UO-SIN-000529.name: Nerses I of Armenia
UO-SIN-000529.life: Nerses was a great-grandson of Gregory the Illuminator, educated in Caesarea in Cappadocia, who served at the Armenian court before becoming catholicos around 353. About 356 he called the council of Ashtishat, which set laws on marriage, fasting and worship. He built schools, hospitals and homes for lepers and the poor, and sent monks to preach in the countryside. He challenged the kings who supported Arianism and ruled harshly, was exiled for years, and fell out with the young King Pap. Early historians say Pap had him poisoned at a banquet in 373. He is revered as Nerses the Great.

UO-SIN-000530.name: Mechthild of Magdeburg
UO-SIN-000530.life: Born around 1207 into a noble Saxon family, Mechthild said she first saw a vision of the Holy Spirit at twelve. About 1230 she left home to live as a Beguine in Magdeburg, a woman devoted to prayer and service without formal vows, and came under the guidance of the Dominicans. Urged by her confessor, she wrote The Flowing Light of the Godhead, the first major mystical work in German, full of visions, poems and dialogues with God. Her sharp criticism of church leaders drew enemies. Old and blind, she found shelter about 1272 in the Cistercian convent of Helfta, where she died around 1282.

UO-SIN-000531.name: Obadiah
UO-SIN-000531.life: Obadiah is one of the twelve Minor Prophets, and almost nothing is known of him beyond his name, which means servant of the Lord. His book, a single chapter of twenty-one verses, is the shortest in the Hebrew Bible. It condemns Edom, the neighbouring nation descended from Esau, for pride and for standing aloof, even gloating, when Jerusalem was ravaged, most likely at the Babylonian conquest of 587 BC. The prophet declares that the Lord will humble the proud and that deliverance will come to Mount Zion. Tradition has sometimes identified him with the servant of Ahab who sheltered the prophets, but that is uncertain.

UO-SIN-000532.name: Priscilla Lydia Sellon
UO-SIN-000532.life: Lydia Sellon, born in 1821 and raised partly in Monmouthshire, answered a call from the Bishop of Exeter in 1848 to help the poor of Plymouth and Devonport. She gathered women around her and founded the Devonport Sisters of Mercy, later the Society of the Most Holy Trinity, the first Anglican sisterhood of the modern era. They ran schools, an orphanage and a night school, and nursed the sick through the cholera of 1849. Some of her sisters later served with Florence Nightingale. Despite fierce suspicion of nuns in England, she persevered, though paralysed in her last years. She died in 1876.

UO-SIN-000533.name: Bernward of Hildesheim
UO-SIN-000533.life: Bernward, born into a noble Saxon family around 960, was tutor to the young emperor Otto III before becoming Bishop of Hildesheim in 993. A gifted craftsman, he is said to have worked metal with his own hands, and he turned his cathedral city into a centre of art. He commissioned the church of St Michael and the great bronze doors with scenes from Scripture, and raised walls to defend Hildesheim against raiders. Near the end of his life he took the monastic habit. He died on 20 November 1022 and was declared a saint in 1193.

UO-SIN-000535.name: William Byrd, John Merbecke, and Thomas Tallis
UO-SIN-000535.life: Three musicians shaped English church music in the sixteenth century. John Merbecke, organist at Windsor, narrowly escaped burning for heresy in the 1540s, then set the first English Prayer Book liturgy to simple chant in 1550. Thomas Tallis served four monarchs at the Chapel Royal, from Henry VIII to Elizabeth I, and wrote anthems, motets and the forty-voice Spem in alium. His pupil William Byrd, a lifelong Catholic who endured fines for refusing the state church, composed superb music for both Anglican and Catholic worship. Tallis died in 1585, Byrd in 1623.
UO-SIN-000535.period: Merbecke and Tallis died 1585; Byrd died 1623

UO-SIN-000536.name: Paulinus of Wales
UO-SIN-000536.life: Paulinus was a Welsh holy man of the late fifth or sixth century, remembered chiefly as a teacher. According to the Life of Saint David, he was a scribe and a disciple of Germanus, and he taught the young David the Scriptures for years at Whitland in Carmarthenshire. Tradition says that when Paulinus went blind, David restored his sight, and that an angel then told him to send David out to preach. A stone near Llandovery reading HIC PAULINUS IACIT may mark his grave, and several Welsh churches honoured him. His son Peulan became a saint on Anglesey.

UO-SIN-000537.name: Columbanus
UO-SIN-000537.life: Columbanus, born in Leinster about 543, trained at the monastery of Bangor and around 590 crossed to Gaul with twelve companions. In the Vosges he founded Annegray and Luxeuil, which became great centres of prayer and learning under his strict rule. His outspoken rebukes of the Burgundian court and his Irish way of dating Easter brought conflict, and he was expelled in 610. He preached among the Alemanni, then crossed the Alps and founded Bobbio in northern Italy. He died there on 23 November 615, leaving sermons, letters, poems and a monastic rule.

UO-SIN-000538.name: Cecilia of Rome
UO-SIN-000538.life: Cecilia is one of the best-loved martyrs of Rome. According to tradition, she was a young noblewoman married against her wishes to a pagan, Valerian; she won him and his brother Tiburtius to the faith, and all three were put to death. Her story says that at her wedding she sang in her heart to the Lord, and in later centuries this made her patron of church musicians. She was buried in the catacomb of Callistus, and a church in Trastevere bore her name by the fifth century. The details of her death are legendary, and its date is uncertain, probably the second or third century.

UO-SIN-000539.name: Philemon
UO-SIN-000539.life: Philemon was a Christian of Colossae in Asia Minor whose home served as a meeting place for the church. Paul wrote him a short, warm letter, now in the New Testament, asking him to welcome back Onesimus, a man who may have been his runaway slave, as a beloved brother rather than as property. The letter stands as an early lesson in forgiveness and reconciliation. Later tradition names Philemon a bishop, perhaps of Gaza, and says that he and his wife Apphia were stoned to death under Nero, together with their friend Archippus.

UO-SIN-000540.name: Amphilochius of Iconium
UO-SIN-000540.life: Amphilochius was born about 340 in Cappadocia, a cousin of Gregory of Nazianzus. He trained as a lawyer and practised in Constantinople, but left for a life of prayer. Around 374 he became Bishop of Iconium, probably with the help of Basil the Great, who dedicated his treatise On the Holy Spirit to him. Amphilochius defended the full divinity of the Spirit against the Macedonians, took part in the Council of Constantinople in 381, and opposed the Messalian movement. A letter against the Macedonians survives. He died some time between 394 and 403.

UO-SIN-000541.name: Lucy Menzies
UO-SIN-000541.life: Lucy Menzies, born in 1882, was a Scottish spiritual writer and member of the Episcopal Church. She wrote lives of Saint Columba and Saint Margaret of Scotland, and translated mystical works by Malaval, de Tourville and Mechthild of Magdeburg for English readers. For ten years she was warden of the retreat house at Pleshey in Essex, where she worked closely with her friend Evelyn Underhill. After Underhill died in 1941, Menzies became her literary executor and saw her later writings into print. The University of St Andrews gave her an honorary doctorate in divinity in 1954, the year of her death.

UO-SIN-000542.name: Andrew Dung-Lac and the Martyrs of Vietnam
UO-SIN-000542.life: Between 1745 and 1862 many thousands of Vietnamese Christians were killed for their faith under successive rulers, most severely after Emperor Minh Mang banned Christianity in 1831. Believers were told to trample on the crucifix, and those who refused were tortured and put to death. Andrew Dung-Lac, born to a poor non-Christian family near Hanoi, became a priest in 1823, was arrested more than once, and was beheaded in Hanoi in 1839 with Father Peter Thi. In 1988 one hundred and seventeen of them, Vietnamese, Spanish and French, were canonized together, standing for a far larger company.

UO-SIN-000543.name: Colman of Cloyne
UO-SIN-000543.life: Colman, born around 530 in Munster, was trained as a poet and became a royal bard before turning to the religious life. He is said to have been moved by an encounter with Saint Brendan. The king of Munster gave him land, and he founded the monastery of Cloyne in County Cork, which became a centre of learning, perhaps with a school of poetry. Some of his verses survive, among the earliest Irish writing, including a poem in praise of Brendan. He is remembered as a bishop and patron of the diocese of Cloyne. He died about 600, traditionally on 24 November.

UO-SIN-000544.name: Catherine of Alexandria
UO-SIN-000544.life: According to tradition, Catherine was a learned young noblewoman of Alexandria who, around 305, confronted the emperor over his cruelty to Christians. Summoned philosophers were sent to argue her out of her faith, but she is said to have won them over instead. She was condemned to die on a spiked wheel, which shattered, and was then beheaded. Angels were said to carry her body to Mount Sinai, where a famous monastery bears her name. Scholars doubt that her story is historical, yet in the Middle Ages she was among the most honoured saints, patron of students, teachers and philosophers.

UO-SIN-000149.name: Isaac Watts
UO-SIN-000149.life: Isaac Watts, born at Southampton in 1674, was a Congregational minister in London and is called the father of English hymnody. Dissenting from the established church, he found the singing of metrical psalms alone too limiting, and wrote hymns that voiced Christian experience directly. His collections, from 1707 onward, gave the church When I Survey the Wondrous Cross, Joy to the World and Our God, Our Help in Ages Past. He also wrote verses for children and widely used books on logic, astronomy and other subjects. In poor health, he lived his last decades in the home of friends, and died in 1748.

UO-SIN-000545.name: Moses of Rome
UO-SIN-000545.life: Moses was a priest of Rome in the middle of the third century, possibly of Jewish background, and a respected leader among the confessors, Christians imprisoned for the faith. When Novatian set himself up as a rival bishop to Cornelius, demanding that those who had lapsed under persecution be refused forgiveness, Moses refused to share communion with him. Arrested in the Decian persecution, he spent about eleven months in prison, encouraged by letters from Cyprian of Carthage. He died there around the beginning of 251. Pope Cornelius wrote that he had suffered a glorious and admirable martyrdom.

UO-SIN-000547.name: Peter of Alexandria
UO-SIN-000547.life: Peter became Bishop of Alexandria in 300, after teaching at the city's famous catechetical school. When Diocletian's persecution began in 303, he went into hiding and wrote to guide his people. Meletius of Lycopolis, claiming Peter was too lenient toward Christians who had lapsed, set up his own rival clergy, and Peter excommunicated him; the Meletian schism lasted long after. Peter also wrote canons for restoring those who had fallen, and opposed some extreme ideas drawn from Origen. In 311 he was arrested and beheaded, and the church has honoured him as a martyr ever since.

UO-SIN-000548.name: Silvester Gozzolini
UO-SIN-000548.life: Silvester Gozzolini was born about 1177 at Osimo in Italy and studied law at Bologna and Padua before turning to theology. As a canon at Osimo he rebuked his bishop for a scandalous life and was shunned for it. Around 1227, shaken by the sight of a decaying corpse, he withdrew to live as a hermit, eating herbs and sleeping on bare ground. Disciples gathered, and at Monte Fano near Fabriano he founded a community under the Rule of Saint Benedict, the Silvestrines, confirmed in 1247 by Pope Innocent IV. He died in 1267 at about ninety.

UO-SIN-000549.name: Leonard of Port Maurice
UO-SIN-000549.life: Leonard was born in 1676 at Porto Maurizio on the Ligurian coast and joined the Franciscans after studying with the Jesuits in Rome. For over forty years he preached missions and retreats across Italy, drawing crowds so large that churches could not hold them. He worked especially to spread the devotion of the Stations of the Cross, setting up more than five hundred, including those in the Roman Colosseum. He also founded retreat houses, promoted devotion to the Sacred Heart and the Blessed Sacrament, and wrote many sermons. Alphonsus Liguori called him the great missionary of the eighteenth century. He died in Rome in 1751.

UO-SIN-000550.name: Humilis of Bisignano
UO-SIN-000550.life: Born Luca Antonio in 1582 at Bisignano in Calabria, Humilis joined the Franciscans as a lay brother, taking the name that means humble. He could neither read nor write, yet he explained deep points of doctrine so clearly that learned churchmen were amazed. Those who knew him spoke of ecstasies in prayer, wise counsel and tender care for the poor. He lived for many years in Rome, where Popes Gregory XV and Urban VIII sought his advice, and he also served in Naples. He died at Bisignano on 26 November 1637 and was declared a saint in 2002.

UO-SIN-000551.name: Stephen the Younger
UO-SIN-000551.life: Stephen was born in Constantinople around 715 and became a monk at Mount Auxentius in Bithynia, where he later served as abbot. When Emperor Constantine V forbade the veneration of icons, Stephen refused to accept the council of 754 that condemned them. He was exiled, then imprisoned in Constantinople with hundreds of other monks. Accused on false charges, he was killed in 764 by soldiers, and his body was dragged through the streets. He became the best-known martyr of the struggle over icons, and later generations honoured him as a defender of holy images.

UO-SIN-000552.name: Catherine Labouré
UO-SIN-000552.life: Catherine Labouré, born in 1806 in Burgundy, was the ninth of eleven children and lost her mother at nine. She joined the Daughters of Charity in Paris in 1830. That year, as a young novice, she reported three visions of the Virgin Mary, who asked her to have a medal struck; it became the Miraculous Medal, spread quickly during a cholera epidemic, and is worn by millions. For some forty years she cared for elderly and poor residents at a hospice in Paris. She died on 31 December 1876 and was canonized in 1947.

UO-SIN-000553.name: Saturninus of Toulouse
UO-SIN-000553.life: Saturninus, also called Sernin, was the first bishop of Toulouse, said to have arrived around the year 250. According to the old account of his death, the pagan priests blamed him for the silence of their oracles, since he passed their temple often. When he would not sacrifice to the gods, he was tied to a bull that dragged him through the city until the rope broke. Two Christian women gathered his remains and buried them. A church later rose at the place where the bull stopped, and his relics now rest in the great basilica of Saint-Sernin. Later legends linking him to other churches are doubtful.

UO-SIN-000554.name: Francis of Lucera
UO-SIN-000554.life: Francesco Antonio Fasani, born in 1681 at Lucera in southern Italy, joined the Conventual Franciscans as a boy and became a friar. After earning a doctorate in theology in 1709, he was known as Father Master. He trained novices, served as guardian of his friary and parish priest, and led his province as minister provincial. For nearly forty years he was famous in Apulia for fervent preaching, devoted hearing of confessions and generous care for the poor, orphans and prisoners. He encouraged devotion to Our Lady Immaculate. He died in Lucera in 1742, and was canonized in 1986.

UO-SIN-000555.name: Cuthbert Mayne
UO-SIN-000555.life: Cuthbert Mayne, born in Devon about 1543, was ordained a Church of England minister while still a teenager and studied at Oxford, where friends drew him toward the Catholic faith. Fleeing to Douai, he was reconciled to Rome and ordained a priest in 1575. The next year he returned to England in secret and served Catholics in Cornwall. Arrested in June 1577 at the house of Francis Tregian, he was convicted of high treason for his priesthood and for refusing to acknowledge the queen's headship of the church. He was hanged, drawn and quartered at Launceston on 29 November 1577, the first seminary priest to die in this way.

UO-SIN-000556.name: Eligius of Noyon
UO-SIN-000556.life: Eligius, born near Limoges around 590, trained as a goldsmith and impressed the Frankish king Clotaire II with his skill and honesty. Under King Dagobert he became a trusted counsellor, while giving much of his wealth to the poor and ransoming captives. He founded the monastery of Solignac and other houses, was ordained, and in about 640 became Bishop of Noyon and Tournai. From there he preached to the pagans of Flanders and the North Sea coast. Strict with himself and generous to others, he died on 1 December 660 and became patron of goldsmiths and metalworkers.

UO-SIN-000557.name: Edmund Campion and Companions
UO-SIN-000557.life: Edmund Campion, born in London in 1540, was a brilliant Oxford scholar favoured by Queen Elizabeth's court. Troubled in conscience, he left England, became a Catholic priest and joined the Jesuits in Rome. He returned in secret in 1580 to strengthen persecuted Catholics, writing a bold defence of his faith, Decem Rationes. Betrayed by a spy and arrested at Lyford Grange in July 1581, he was racked in the Tower of London, yet held his own in public debates. Condemned for treason, he was hanged, drawn and quartered at Tyburn on 1 December 1581 with the priests Ralph Sherwin and Alexander Briant.

UO-SIN-000558.name: Bibiana
UO-SIN-000558.life: Bibiana was a young Roman woman who, according to tradition, suffered for her faith in the fourth century under Julian the Apostate. The story says her father Flavian was exiled, her mother Dafrosa beheaded and her sister Demetria died after confessing Christ. Bibiana herself was handed to a woman who tried to corrupt her, and when she stood firm she was tied to a pillar and beaten with lead-weighted whips until she died. The details are legendary, but a church holding her body was consecrated in Rome in the fifth century, and the basilica of Santa Bibiana still stands there.

UO-SIN-000560.name: Sophonius / Zephaniah
UO-SIN-000560.life: Zephaniah was a prophet of Judah in the seventh century before Christ, active in the early reign of King Josiah. His book gives his ancestry back four generations to a Hezekiah, possibly the king. He denounced the worship of Baal and other gods in Jerusalem and warned of the Day of the Lord, a day of searching judgment that would sweep away corruption. Yet he also promised that a humble remnant who sought the Lord would be sheltered, and he ended with a joyful vision of God rejoicing over a restored people. His short book is the ninth of the Minor Prophets.

UO-SIN-000561.name: Barbara of Nicomedia
UO-SIN-000561.life: According to the old legend, Barbara was the beautiful daughter of a wealthy pagan named Dioscorus, who shut her in a tower to guard her from the world. She secretly became a Christian and refused the husband he chose. Handed over to a magistrate, she was tortured and then beheaded, and her father, who carried out the sentence, was struck by lightning. Some tales place her in Nicomedia, others in Egypt. Scholars find no historical record of her before the seventh century, yet she became a very popular saint, called on against lightning and sudden death, and patron of miners and gunners.

UO-SIN-000562.name: Sabas the Sanctified
UO-SIN-000562.life: Sabas was born in Cappadocia in 439 and entered a monastery as a boy. At about eighteen he went to Palestine and, after years of training under other monks, settled in the Judaean desert near Jerusalem. As disciples gathered he founded the Great Lavra, Mar Saba, around 483, and later more monasteries and hospices across the region. Ordained priest in 491, he was made leader of the desert monks. He defended the Council of Chalcedon against opponents, even travelling to Constantinople to plead with the emperor. He died near Jerusalem on 5 December 532, and his monastery, home to John of Damascus, still stands.

UO-SIN-000564.name: Emilian of Cogolla
UO-SIN-000564.life: Emilian, said to have been born about 472 at Berceo in La Rioja, Spain, was a shepherd until he felt called to the hermit life. He learned from an older hermit named Felix, then lived alone in the mountains. The bishop of Tarazona ordained him priest for his home parish, but when his giving of church funds to the poor drew criticism, he returned to his hermitage. Followers gathered around him, and from his cell grew the monastery of San Millan de la Cogolla, long a pilgrimage centre and cradle of early written Spanish. Tradition says he lived to a great age, dying around 574.

UO-SIN-000565.name: Major Roger Williams
UO-SIN-000565.life: Roger Williams was born in London around 1603 and trained at Cambridge before being ordained in the Church of England. Seeking freedom of conscience, he sailed to Massachusetts in 1631, but his conviction that civil rulers had no power over the soul brought a sentence of banishment in 1635. He fled through winter snow and, in 1636, founded Providence on land bought from the Narragansett. There he built a settlement open to people of every belief, helped found the first Baptist church in America, and won a charter for Rhode Island. He worked for peace with Native neighbours and died in Providence in early 1683.

UO-SIN-000566.name: Maria Joseph Rossello
UO-SIN-000566.life: Benedetta Rossello was born in 1811 at Albissola on the Ligurian coast, the fourth of ten children in a devout, hard-working family. She joined the Franciscan Third Order at sixteen and, after family bereavements, supported her household by service in others' homes. When Bishop Agostino De Mari sought women to teach and help the poor of Savona, she answered, and in 1837 the Daughters of Our Lady of Mercy began. Taking the name Maria Giuseppa, she served as superior for forty years, caring for the poor, the sick and girls without dowries. She died in Savona on 7 December 1880 and was canonized in 1949.

UO-SIN-000567.name: Charles Garnier
UO-SIN-000567.life: Charles Garnier was born in Paris in 1606 into a well-connected family and joined the Jesuits at eighteen. Ordained in 1635, he won his father's reluctant consent and sailed for New France the next year. Among the Huron, who called him Ouracha, he learned their language and worked beside Jean de Brébeuf. He spent years ministering to the Petun people, gradually overcoming their suspicion that the missionaries had brought disease. In December 1649, when Iroquois warriors attacked the Petun village where he served, he was shot while helping his flock and was killed as he tried to reach a dying man. He was canonized in 1930 among the Canadian Martyrs.

UO-SIN-000568.name: Richard Baxter
UO-SIN-000568.life: Richard Baxter was born in 1615 in Rowton, Shropshire, and was ordained in 1638. From 1641 he served the weaving town of Kidderminster, where his preaching and patient visiting of every household changed the life of the parish. He was a chaplain to Parliament's army during the Civil War, yet always pleaded for moderation and unity among Christians. After the Restoration he refused a bishopric because he could not accept the Act of Uniformity, and he lived as a Nonconformist, often harassed. In 1685 he was jailed for eighteen months. His writings, including The Reformed Pastor, still shape ministry. He died in London on 8 December 1691.

UO-SIN-000570.name: Romaric
UO-SIN-000570.life: Romaric was a Frankish nobleman at the Merovingian court in Austrasia in the late sixth and early seventh centuries. His family had been ruined by Queen Brunhilda, and he lived as a wanderer until her fall restored his lands. Stirred by the preaching of the monk Amatus of Luxeuil, he gave up courtly ambition, freed the serfs on his estate and became a monk at Luxeuil. Around 625 he and Amatus founded a double monastery for men and women on his former property in the Vosges, which became Remiremont. Romaric succeeded Amatus as abbot, led the community for some thirty years, and died there in 653.

UO-SIN-000571.name: Leocadia of Toledo
UO-SIN-000571.life: Leocadia was a young Christian woman of Toledo in Spain who died during the persecution under Emperor Diocletian, around the year 304. According to the later account of her sufferings, the governor Decianus had her arrested and tortured to make her renounce Christ. She refused, and was returned to prison, where she died of her injuries. Her grave became a place of prayer, and a church built over it was the meeting place of several Councils of Toledo in the seventh century. Her relics were later carried away and eventually brought back. She is honoured as patron of Toledo, and artists often show her with a tower, recalling her imprisonment.

UO-SIN-000572.name: Peter Fourier
UO-SIN-000572.life: Peter Fourier was born in 1565 at Mirecourt in Lorraine and studied with the Jesuits at Pont-à-Mousson before joining the canons regular and being ordained in 1589. In 1597 he became parish priest of Mattaincourt, where he renewed the faith of a troubled village, set up a bank to lend to the poor without interest, and taught through lively dialogue. With Alix Le Clerc he founded the Congregation of Notre Dame to give girls free schooling. He also reformed the canons regular of Lorraine. Driven into exile at Gray during the wars, he died there on 9 December 1640 while caring for plague victims, and was canonized in 1897.

UO-SIN-000573.name: Karl Barth
UO-SIN-000573.life: Karl Barth was born in Basel in 1886 and served as a Reformed pastor in the Swiss village of Safenwil from 1911 to 1921. Shaken when his liberal teachers backed the war in 1914, he turned back to the Bible and wrote his powerful commentary on Romans, which made his name. He then taught in Göttingen, Münster and Bonn. In 1934 he was the chief author of the Barmen Declaration, which declared that Christ alone is the church's Lord against Nazi pressure. Dismissed in 1935 for refusing an oath to Hitler, he returned to Basel and wrote the vast Church Dogmatics. He died there on 10 December 1968.

UO-SIN-000574.name: Eulalia of Mérida
UO-SIN-000574.life: Eulalia was a girl of about twelve who lived in Mérida in Spain and died for her faith around the year 304, in the persecution under Diocletian. According to tradition, her mother kept her in the countryside for safety, but she slipped away to the court of the governor, declared herself a Christian and denounced the worship of idols. She was tortured with hooks and torches and died when flames caught her hair. Tradition says a dove flew from her mouth and snow covered her body. A great shrine rose over her grave at Mérida, and the poet Prudentius sang her praise. Her fame spread widely across Spain.

UO-SIN-000575.name: John Roberts
UO-SIN-000575.life: John Roberts was born about 1577 at Trawsfynydd in north Wales and studied at Oxford and then law in London. On the Continent he became a Catholic in Paris in 1598, then joined the Benedictines at Valladolid and was ordained. He returned to England in 1603 as a missionary priest and tended plague victims in London. Banished several times, he always came back. During one exile he helped found the monastery of St Gregory at Douai, from which Downside Abbey descends. Seized in December 1610 after celebrating Mass, he was condemned as a priest and hanged, drawn and quartered at Tyburn on 10 December. He was canonized in 1970.

UO-SIN-000576.name: Daniel the Stylite
UO-SIN-000576.life: Daniel was born around 409 in Mesopotamia and entered a monastery at twelve. On a journey he met Simeon the Stylite, whom he came to revere. Around 451 he settled near Constantinople and took up life on a pillar, where he lived for some thirty-three years exposed to cold and storm. He was ordained priest and became a trusted counsellor, visited by emperors including Leo I and Zeno, and he cared for the sick and troubled who gathered below. In 475 he left his pillar to urge the emperor Basiliscus to uphold the true faith. He died there in 493, aged about eighty-four.

UO-SIN-000577.name: Damasus I
UO-SIN-000577.life: Damasus was bishop of Rome from 366 until his death in 384. Probably born around 305, he served as a deacon in the church of Saint Lawrence before a bitterly disputed election in which a rival, Ursinus, was set up against him. As pope he restored the tombs of Rome's martyrs and set up verse inscriptions in their honour, and he insisted on the authority of Peter's see. He brought the scholar Jerome to Rome as his secretary and urged him to revise the Latin Bible, work that led to the Vulgate. He opposed the Arian and other teachings of his day, and died on 11 December 384.

UO-SIN-000579.name: Spyridon of Trimythous
UO-SIN-000579.life: Spyridon was born about 270 on the island of Cyprus and began as a shepherd and farmer. After his wife's death he gave himself to the Church and became bishop of Trimythous. Tradition holds that at the Council of Nicaea in 325 his plain words refuted a learned opponent of the Trinity, and that he worked many wonders, healing the sick, raising the dead and bringing rain in drought. He was remembered as a man of simple, generous faith. He died around 348. His body was carried to Constantinople and, in 1453, to Corfu, where it is still honoured and where he is patron of the island.

UO-SIN-000580.name: Samuel Johnson
UO-SIN-000580.life: Samuel Johnson was born in Guilford, Connecticut, in 1696 and graduated from Yale in 1714. After serving as a tutor, he became a Congregational minister at West Haven in 1720, but in 1722 he and other colleagues announced they were drawn to the Church of England. He was ordained in England and returned as a missionary of the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel, serving as rector at Stratford for over thirty years. A learned friend of Bishop Berkeley, he wrote on philosophy and argued for an American bishop. He became first president of King's College in New York in 1754 and died at Stratford in 1772.

UO-SIN-000581.name: Odile of Alsace
UO-SIN-000581.life: Odile was born around 660 in Alsace, the daughter of the nobleman Adalrich. According to tradition she was born blind, and her father rejected her, so she was raised away from home. Legend says that when she was baptized, around the age of twelve, she received her sight. Reconciled with her father, she became abbess of the convent he founded for her on the Hohenburg, now Mont Sainte-Odile, and she later founded a second house at Niedermünster with a hospital for the needy. She died around 720. She is honoured as patroness of Alsace, and is often shown holding a book on which lie two eyes.

UO-SIN-000582.name: Venantius Fortunatus
UO-SIN-000582.life: Venantius Fortunatus was born near Treviso in northern Italy around 530 and educated in Ravenna. In 566 he crossed the Alps to Gaul, partly to venerate Saint Martin at Tours, and found patrons among Frankish kings and bishops. At Poitiers he became close friend and adviser to Queen Radegund, who had founded a convent there, and he befriended Gregory of Tours. Ordained priest, he later became bishop of Poitiers around 600. He wrote graceful poems, a life of Martin and lives of saints, and two great hymns to the Cross, Vexilla Regis and Pange lingua, still sung today. He died early in the seventh century.

UO-SIN-000583.name: Nimatullah Kassab Al-Hardini
UO-SIN-000583.life: Youssef Kassab was born in 1808 in the Lebanese mountain village of Hardine and was taught by Maronite monks. He entered the Lebanese Maronite Order in 1828, took the name Nimatullah, meaning grace of God, and was ordained in 1833. He taught in the order's seminary at Kfifan, where one of his pupils was the future Saint Charbel. He was known for hours of prayer before the Blessed Sacrament, for gentleness toward his brothers and for his love of Mary. He declined election as superior general, choosing humbler service. He died of illness on 14 December 1858 and was canonized in 2004. He is remembered as the Saint of Kfifan.

UO-SIN-000585.name: Maria Crocifissa di Rosa
UO-SIN-000585.life: Paola di Rosa was born in 1813 into a wealthy family in Brescia, Italy, and was educated by the Visitation sisters. As a young woman she helped run her father's mill and cared for the girls who worked there. During the cholera epidemic of 1836 she nursed the sick in the city's hospital, and she also supported a home for deaf women. In 1840 she took the name Maria Crocifissa and began the Handmaids of Charity, devoted to the poor and the sick, which received papal approval in 1850. She died in Brescia on 15 December 1855 and was canonized in 1954.

UO-SIN-000586.name: Ado of Vienne
UO-SIN-000586.life: Ado was born around 800 in the Frankish lands and educated at the abbeys of Ferrières and Prüm. He spent some years in Rome and Ravenna, where he found an old martyrology that inspired his own. Given the parish of Saint-Romain near Vienne, he was chosen archbishop of Vienne in 860 against some local opposition. He governed his diocese for some fifteen years and wrote lives of saints. He is best remembered for his Martyrology, which gave fuller accounts of the saints than earlier lists, and for a world chronicle from creation to his own day. He died in the 870s and was buried in Vienne.

UO-SIN-000587.name: Adelaide of Italy
UO-SIN-000587.life: Adelaide was born in 931 into the royal house of Burgundy and at fifteen married Lothair, king of Italy. When he died in 950, Berengar II, who seized the crown, imprisoned her for refusing to marry his son. She escaped and found refuge with Otto I of Germany, who married her in 951. In 962 she was crowned empress alongside him in Rome. Her bond with her son Otto II was strained but mended, and after his death she governed as regent for her grandson Otto III until 994. Generous to the poor and a founder of monasteries, she retired to the abbey of Selz and died there in 999.

UO-SIN-000588.name: Isaac of Nineveh
UO-SIN-000588.life: Isaac was born in the region of Qatar on the Arabian shore of the Persian Gulf and became a monk before being made bishop of Nineveh around 676. Within a few months he gave up the office, and retired first to the mountains and then to the monastery of Rabban Shabur in southwestern Persia. There he gave himself to prayer and study and wrote homilies on the spiritual life, stressing humility, silence and the boundless mercy of God. Tradition says he lost his sight through his studies. He died around 700. His writings, translated into Greek, Arabic and many other languages, have nourished Eastern and Western Christians ever since.

UO-SIN-000589.name: William Lloyd Garrison and Maria Stewart
UO-SIN-000589.life: William Lloyd Garrison and Maria Stewart were two Americans who spoke out against slavery in the early 1830s. Garrison, born in Newburyport, Massachusetts, in 1805, founded The Liberator in 1831 and called for immediate emancipation, and in 1835 he was nearly lynched by a Boston mob. Maria Stewart, born free in Hartford in 1803 and widowed young, became the first known American woman to lecture publicly on abolition, speaking in Boston in 1832 and 1833. Her essays appeared in the Liberator. She later taught in New York, Baltimore and Washington and worked at Freedmen's Hospital. Both died in 1879, Garrison in May and Stewart on 17 December.

UO-SIN-000590.name: Sturmi of Fulda
UO-SIN-000590.life: Sturmi was born around 705 in Bavaria and was entrusted as a boy to Saint Boniface, who had him trained at Fritzlar. After ordination he worked as a missionary in Hesse. In 744 Boniface sent him to found a monastery on the Fulda river, and he became its first abbot. He travelled to Monte Cassino to learn the Benedictine way of life, and Fulda grew into a great centre of prayer and learning, where Boniface was later buried. Quarrels with a bishop led to his exile in Normandy around 763, but the monks asked for him back. He joined Charlemagne's Saxon mission and died at Fulda on 17 December 779.

UO-SIN-000591.name: Daniel and the Three Holy Youths
UO-SIN-000591.life: These four young Jews were carried off to Babylon from Jerusalem in the days of King Nebuchadnezzar and trained for the royal court. The three, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, known as Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, refused to bow to a great golden image and were thrown into a furnace heated seven times hotter. The king saw a fourth figure walking with them, and they came out unharmed. Daniel, who interpreted the king's dreams, was later cast into a den of lions for praying to his God and was kept safe. Together they are remembered for faithfulness under pressure and trust that God rules over every earthly kingdom.

UO-SIN-000171.name: Expectation of the Blessed Virgin Mary / O Antiphons context
UO-SIN-000171.life: This observance, kept in the last days of Advent, invites us to share the waiting of Mary as she carried Jesus before his birth. It began in Spain, where the Tenth Council of Toledo in 656 established a feast of the Expectation on 18 December, and it spread to other lands. Its keeping heightens the anticipation of Christmas. At the same season, from 17 to 23 December, the church sings the O Antiphons at evening prayer, each calling on Christ by an ancient title such as Wisdom, Root of Jesse or Emmanuel. Together they form the longing that lies behind the hymn O Come, O Come, Emmanuel.
UO-SIN-000171.place: Spain and the wider Western church

UO-SIN-000592.name: Flannan
UO-SIN-000592.life: Flannan was an Irish churchman of the seventh century, said to be the son of a chieftain of Munster. He entered the monastery of Mo Lua at Killaloe, became known as a fine preacher and, according to tradition, went to Rome, where Pope John IV consecrated him bishop. He returned as the first bishop of Killaloe and is honoured as its patron. Tradition links him with work in the Hebrides, and the remote Flannan Isles take their name from a saint of that name, though which one is uncertain. He died at Killaloe, and his memory lives on in the diocese and its college.

UO-SIN-000593.name: Wunibald
UO-SIN-000593.life: Wunibald was born in Wessex around 702, brother of the saints Willibald and Walburga and son of Richard the Pilgrim. About 721 he travelled with his father and brother to Rome, and when his father died on the way, he stayed to study in Rome while Willibald went on to the Holy Land. In 737 Saint Boniface summoned him to Germany. He reached Thuringia in 740 and was ordained priest. Later he founded a monastery, which he moved to Heidenheim, where he and Willibald built a double house for men and women as a school for priests. He served as its first abbot until his death on 18 December 761.

UO-SIN-000596.name: Nemesius of Alexandria
UO-SIN-000596.life: Nemesius was an Egyptian Christian who died at Alexandria around 250 during the persecution under the emperor Decius. He was first denounced as an associate of robbers, but he cleared himself of that charge before the centurion. Then he was accused of being a Christian and brought in chains to the governor, who had him tortured and scourged twice as severely as the robbers. He was then burned between two thieves, an end that recalled the death of Christ. His story is known from the bishop Dionysius of Alexandria, who lived through those days and wrote of him in a letter preserved by the historian Eusebius.

UO-SIN-000173.name: Katharina von Bora
UO-SIN-000173.life: Katharina von Bora was born in 1499 in Saxony and entered a convent as a child, later taking vows at the Cistercian house of Nimbschen. Moved by the reforming message, she wrote to Martin Luther for help, and at Easter 1523 she escaped with other nuns hidden in a herring merchant's wagon. She came to Wittenberg and in 1525 married Luther. In the former Augustinian monastery they raised six children, and she ran the household, farm, orchard and brewery and welcomed guests. After Luther died in 1546 she knew poverty and twice fled war. She died at Torgau on 20 December 1552 after an accident while fleeing plague.

UO-SIN-000597.name: Dominic of Silos
UO-SIN-000597.life: Dominic was born around 1000 at Cañas in La Rioja and worked as a shepherd before becoming a priest and, for a time, a hermit. He joined the Benedictines at San Millan de la Cogolla and became prior. About 1041 he clashed with King Garcia of Navarre, who wanted the monastery's lands, and Dominic left for Castile under the protection of King Ferdinand I. He was given the ruined abbey of San Sebastian de Silos, which he restored, adding a scriptorium and cloister. He gave generously to the poor and raised funds to ransom Christians held captive by the Moors. He died at Silos on 20 December 1073.

UO-SIN-000599.name: Peter Canisius
UO-SIN-000599.life: Born in Nijmegen in 1521, Peter Canisius became the first Dutchman to join the Jesuits, entering the Society in 1543 and being ordained three years later. In the turmoil of the Reformation he laboured across Germany, Austria, Bohemia and beyond, preaching, teaching and founding colleges, among them the school at Innsbruck and, in his last years, Fribourg. His clear catechisms, first published in the 1550s, went through hundreds of editions and shaped the instruction of generations. Known as the second apostle of Germany, he died at Fribourg on 21 December 1597 and was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1925.

UO-SIN-000600.name: Forefathers of Christ / Genealogy witnesses
UO-SIN-000600.life: Before Christmas the Church remembers the long line of ancestors through whom, in the Gospels, Jesus is traced to Israel's beginnings. Matthew follows the line forward from Abraham, through Isaac, Jacob, Judah, David and Solomon, in three sets of fourteen generations down to Joseph; he also names four women, Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Bathsheba, a striking mark of God's surprising ways. Luke runs backward from Jesus through David's son Nathan all the way to Adam, linking Christ with all humanity. Both genealogies proclaim that Jesus comes in fulfilment of the promises made to Abraham and David.

UO-SIN-000174.name: Charlotte Digges Moon
UO-SIN-000174.life: Known as Lottie, Charlotte Moon was born in 1840 on a Virginia plantation to a devout Baptist family. Unusually well educated for a woman of her day, she earned a master's degree in 1861 and later taught in schools in Kentucky and Georgia. Appointed a missionary in 1873, she joined her sister in Shandong, China, and after some years of teaching turned to evangelism in the villages, living much as her neighbours did. She urged greater roles for women in mission and helped inspire a Christmas offering for missions. Sharing her food through famine, she grew gravely weak and died aboard ship at Kobe, Japan, on 24 December 1912.

UO-SIN-000602.name: Victoria and Anatolia
UO-SIN-000602.life: According to tradition, Victoria and Anatolia were Roman sisters of the third century who refused marriages arranged with pagan nobles because they wished to remain faithful to Christ. Their suitors confined them on country estates, hoping to wear down their resolve, but they would not yield. Victoria is said to have been stabbed through the heart at Trebula Mutuesca, north-east of Rome, during the persecution under Decius around 250. Anatolia, the story goes, was shut in with a poisonous snake that would not harm her, and she was finally put to the sword at a place in the Abruzzo hills that now bears her name.

UO-SIN-000604.name: Adam and Eve
UO-SIN-000604.life: In the book of Genesis, Adam and Eve are the first man and woman, created by God and set in the garden of Eden. Tempted by the serpent, they ate the forbidden fruit and were sent out of the garden, to toil, to bear children in pain, and to know death. Their sons included Cain, Abel and Seth. Christian tradition sees in Adam's disobedience the beginning of humanity's brokenness, and in Christ the new Adam who undoes it, with Mary as the new Eve. Eastern Christians honour the pair as righteous ancestors, rescued from death when Christ descended among the dead.

UO-SIN-000608.name: Fabiola of Rome
UO-SIN-000608.life: Fabiola was a wealthy Roman noblewoman of the late fourth century. Her first husband was a dissolute man, and she divorced him and married again while he still lived, a breach of church teaching. After her second husband died she did public penance at the Lateran basilica at Easter,. She then gave up her fortune, founded a hospital in Rome and tended the sick herself, even those with the most repulsive sores. About 395 she visited Jerome at Bethlehem to study Scripture, returned to Rome, and with the senator Pammachius built a hospice for pilgrims at Porto. She died in 399 or 400.

UO-SIN-000611.name: Trophimus of Arles
UO-SIN-000611.life: Trophimus is remembered as the first bishop of Arles, in southern Gaul. Gregory of Tours reports that he was one of seven bishops sent from Rome to Gaul around the year 250, though the see of Arles probably dates from earlier. Nothing certain is known of his life; the earliest mention is a letter of Pope Zosimus in 417, which treats him as the source of Christianity in Gaul. Later tradition confused him with the Trophimus who accompanied Saint Paul, an identification scholars reject. His relics rest in Arles, and the great Romanesque church there, built from the twelfth century, bears his name.

UO-SIN-000613.name: Sabinus and Companions
UO-SIN-000613.life: Sabinus was bishop of Assisi when Diocletian's persecution broke out in 303. Arrested with members of his clergy, he refused to sacrifice, and according to the old account he smashed the idol put before him, whereupon his hands were cut off. His deacons Marcellus and Exuperantius were tortured and died. Tradition adds that Sabinus restored the sight of a blind boy and cured the eyes of the governor Venustianus, who was converted and himself later put to death. Sabinus was finally beaten to death at Spoleto. The details come from a later narrative, but the bishop and his deacons were honoured early in central Italy.

UO-SIN-000614.name: Samuel Ajayi Crowther
UO-SIN-000614.life: Born about 1809 in Yoruba country, Ajayi was seized as a boy of twelve by slave raiders and sold to Portuguese traders. The Royal Navy freed him at sea and landed him in Sierra Leone, where he took the name Samuel Crowther, became a Christian and studied at the new Fourah Bay College. A gifted linguist, he joined the Niger expeditions, helped open the Abeokuta mission, and produced grammars and translations, including the Yoruba Bible. In 1864 he was consecrated at Canterbury as the first African Anglican bishop. Late in life he saw his African-led Niger mission dismantled by European missionaries; he died in Lagos on 31 December 1891.
UO-SIN-000614.place: Yoruba country, Sierra Leone, Lagos, Niger

UO-SIN-000615.name: Sylvester I
UO-SIN-000615.life: Sylvester was bishop of Rome from 314 until his death on 31 December 335, the first decades after Constantine ended the persecution of Christians. Little is certain about him beyond his father's name, Rufinus, and his earlier service as a presbyter. In his time the emperor funded great Roman churches, among them the Lateran basilica and Old Saint Peter's. He sent legates to the Council of Nicaea in 325, which condemned Arianism.
