A medieval legend says he baptized Constantine and cured him of leprosy, and a forged Donation of Constantine was later attributed to him. He was buried in the Catacomb of Priscilla.

UO-SIN-000912.name: Louise de Marillac
UO-SIN-000912.life: Louise de Marillac was born in 1591, the unacknowledged daughter of a Paris nobleman, and raised without a settled home. Denied entry to a convent, she married Antoine Le Gras, bore a son, and nursed her husband through a long illness until his death in 1625. Guided by Vincent de Paul, she turned her grief and gifts to the sick poor of Paris. In 1633 she gathered young women into her home and trained them as the first Daughters of Charity, a company of sisters who served in streets and hospitals rather than behind cloister walls. She died in Paris in 1660.

UO-SIN-000913.name: Clement Mary Hofbauer
UO-SIN-000913.life: Born in 1751 to a poor Moravian family, Clement Hofbauer worked as a baker and for a time lived as a hermit before he could pursue his longing for the priesthood. He joined the Redemptorists in Rome in 1785 and was sent north of the Alps. In Warsaw he ran a church for over twenty years, preaching, hearing confessions, and caring for orphans and the poor. Expelled when the political tide turned, he settled in Vienna, where his sermons and counsel drew students, artists and the unchurched. He died there in 1820, remembered as the Apostle of Vienna.

UO-SIN-000914.name: Jean de Brébeuf and Gabriel Lalemant
UO-SIN-000914.life: Jean de Brébeuf, a Norman Jesuit, reached Quebec in 1625 and spent most of his remaining years among the Wendat, or Huron, people near Georgian Bay, learning their language and writing a grammar and catechism for it. Gabriel Lalemant, a frailer Parisian priest, joined him in 1648. In March 1649 an Iroquois war party overran the mission village of Saint-Louis. Both priests refused to flee, were captured and tortured at Saint-Ignace, and died, Brébeuf on 16 March and Lalemant the following day. They were canonized in 1930 among the eight Canadian Martyrs.

UO-SIN-000915.name: Heribert of Cologne
UO-SIN-000915.life: Heribert was born about 970 at Worms and educated at the cathedral school there and at Gorze. Ordained in 994, he became chancellor to the young Emperor Otto III, first for Italy and then for Germany, and in 999 was chosen Archbishop of Cologne. After Otto's early death in 1002 he first hesitated to accept Henry II as king, but later served him and won his friendship. Heribert gave generously to the poor and founded the abbey of Deutz across the Rhine, where he was buried after dying on 16 March 1021. Many people honoured him as holy even in his lifetime.

UO-SIN-000916.name: Gertrude of Nivelles
UO-SIN-000916.life: Gertrude was the daughter of Pepin of Landen, a powerful steward at the Frankish court. Tradition says that at ten years old she refused a marriage arranged for political gain, declaring she would have no bridegroom but Christ. After her father died, her mother Itta founded a double monastery at Nivelles, in present-day Belgium, and Gertrude became its first abbess. She studied the Scriptures, and spent her inheritance on churches, monasteries and hospices. Worn down by fasting, she resigned in her early thirties and died on 17 March 659. Travellers later invoked her protection.

UO-SIN-000917.name: Edward the Martyr
UO-SIN-000917.life: Edward, eldest son of King Edgar, became king of the English as a boy in 975. His accession was disputed by supporters of his younger half-brother Æthelred, but Archbishop Dunstan backed him and he was crowned. His short reign was troubled by quarrels among the nobility over land. In March 978 he was killed at Corfe in Dorset, on the estate of his stepmother, and hurriedly buried at Wareham. Because a king's murder shocked the nation, he was soon revered as a martyr, and his body was moved with honour to Shaftesbury Abbey. Sources differ on the exact circumstances of his death.

UO-SIN-000918.name: Salvator of Horta
UO-SIN-000918.life: Salvator was born in 1520 in Catalonia to poor parents and was orphaned young. He worked as a shoemaker in Barcelona, then entered the Franciscans as a lay brother in 1541. Assigned as cook, porter and beggar for the friars, he became known for humility and for healing the sick with the sign of the cross. Crowds, sometimes thousands a week, came to him, and his anxious superiors moved him from house to house. He was denounced to the Inquisition but not condemned. He died at Cagliari in Sardinia on 18 March 1567, praying that he commended his spirit into God's hands.

UO-SIN-000919.name: Joseph of Nazareth
UO-SIN-000919.life: Joseph was a carpenter of Nazareth in Galilee, a descendant of David, betrothed to Mary. The Gospels tell that when he learned she was with child he planned to quietly end the engagement, but an angel told him in a dream to take her as his wife and to name the child Jesus. He protected the family, taking them to Egypt to escape Herod and later settling again in Nazareth. Scripture records no words of his, and he is last seen when Jesus was twelve. Christians honour him as the quiet guardian and earthly father of Christ.

UO-SIN-000920.name: Herbert of Derwentwater
UO-SIN-000920.life: Herbert was an Anglo-Saxon priest who became a hermit on a small island in Derwentwater, in the Lake District. He was a close friend and disciple of Cuthbert of Lindisfarne, and each year he travelled to Cuthbert to receive spiritual guidance. In 686, when they met at Carlisle, Cuthbert told him that they would not meet again in this world. Herbert wept and begged that they might die together, and Cuthbert promised that they would. Herbert fell ill soon afterward and died on 20 March 687, the very day of Cuthbert's death. Remains of his cell are still seen on the island.

UO-SIN-000921.name: Wulfram of Sens
UO-SIN-000921.life: Wulfram was born near Fontainebleau, the son of a knight at the Frankish court, and was educated there and ordained. Called to the court of King Theodoric III, he was elected Archbishop of Sens around 690, but resigned after a few years and retired to the abbey of Fontenelle on the lower Seine. Later accounts say he preached among the pagan Frisians and baptised the son of their king, Radbod. One story tells how he prayed over a man who had been hanged as a sacrifice, and the rope broke. Wulfram died at Fontenelle about 703, and is invoked for safety at sea.

UO-SIN-000922.name: Nicholas of Flüe
UO-SIN-000922.life: Nicholas was a prosperous Swiss farmer from the mountain village of Flüeli, who served as a soldier, a councillor and a judge, and raised ten children with his wife. In 1467, with her consent, he left home to live as a hermit in the nearby Ranft gorge. People reported that he took no food but the Eucharist, and pilgrims and rulers sought his counsel. In 1481, when the Swiss cantons stood on the brink of civil war, his advice carried to the assembly at Stans helped reconcile them. He died on 21 March 1487 and is honoured as Switzerland's patron saint.

UO-SIN-000923.name: Lea of Rome
UO-SIN-000923.life: Lea was a wealthy Roman widow of the fourth century. We know of her chiefly from a letter of Jerome to her friend Marcella, written after she died in 384. After her husband's death she gave up her fine clothes and her position, took up sackcloth, and joined the community of women gathered around Marcella. She became their superior, yet chose the humblest tasks, serving everyone in the household and spending her nights in prayer. Jerome praised her for teaching others by example rather than by speeches, and urged Marcella to remember that no one can possess both Christ and the world.

UO-SIN-000924.name: Turibius of Mogrovejo
UO-SIN-000924.life: Toribio de Mogrovejo was a Spanish lawyer and university professor, chosen by King Philip II to be Archbishop of Lima although he was not yet ordained. He was consecrated in 1580 and reached Peru the next year. For nearly twenty-five years he travelled his enormous diocese, mostly on foot, through mountains and jungle, learning native languages, baptising and confirming hundreds of thousands, among them Rose of Lima and Martin de Porres. He reformed the clergy, built schools, hospitals and roads, founded a seminary in 1591, and called councils. He died at Sañá, on one of his journeys, on 23 March 1606.

UO-SIN-000925.name: Óscar Romero
UO-SIN-000925.life: Óscar Romero was born in 1917 in a small town in El Salvador, was ordained in 1942, and became Archbishop of San Salvador in 1977, expected to be a cautious leader. Within weeks, his friend Fr Rutilio Grande, who worked with the poor, was murdered, and Romero became a fearless voice for the poor and persecuted. In radio sermons he named the killings and disappearances of the civil conflict and begged soldiers not to obey orders to kill. On 24 March 1980 he was shot dead while celebrating Mass in a hospital chapel. He was canonized in 2018.

UO-SIN-000926.name: Catherine of Sweden
UO-SIN-000926.life: Catherine was the daughter of Bridget of Sweden, born about 1331. Married young to a devout German nobleman, she persuaded him to share a vow of chastity, and she was widowed while visiting Rome with her mother in 1349. She stayed to share Bridget's labours, travelled with her to the Holy Land, and after her mother's death in 1373 carried her body home to Sweden for burial at Vadstena. There Catherine led the new community of the Bridgettine order and shaped its common life. She returned to Rome to press for her mother's canonization, and died on 24 March 1381.

UO-SIN-000927.name: Dismas, the Penitent Thief
UO-SIN-000927.life: In Luke's Gospel, two criminals were crucified beside Jesus. One mocked him; the other rebuked his companion, admitted that they were justly punished, and said, "Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom." Jesus answered, "Today you will be with me in Paradise." The Gospel never names him. Later tradition called him Dismas, and legends grew up about his earlier life. Christians have long seen in him the promise that God's mercy can reach a person at the very last moment, and he is honoured in both East and West as a saint.

UO-SIN-000928.name: Richard Allen
UO-SIN-000928.life: Richard Allen was born into slavery in 1760 and raised in Delaware. He became a Methodist as a teenager, taught himself to read, preached, and purchased his freedom. Settling in Philadelphia, he worked as a minister at St George's Methodist church until Black worshippers were pushed into segregated seating and he led a walkout. With Absalom Jones he helped found the Free African Society, and in 1794 opened Bethel Church. He gathered black Methodist congregations into the African Methodist Episcopal Church, whose first bishop he became in 1816. He also worked to found schools. He died in Philadelphia in 1831.

UO-SIN-000929.name: Ludger
UO-SIN-000929.life: Ludger was born about 742 into a noble Frisian family. As a boy he saw Boniface, whose martyrdom made a lasting impression on him, and he studied at Utrecht and in York under Alcuin. After his ordination in 777 he preached in Frisia until Saxon invasions forced him out. He then spent time at Monte Cassino before Charlemagne sent him back to the Frisians and then to the Saxons in Westphalia. He founded a monastery at Münster, which gave the town its name, and the abbey of Werden. About 805 he became Münster's first bishop, and he died on 26 March 809.

UO-SIN-000930.name: Rupert of Salzburg
UO-SIN-000930.life: Rupert was a Frankish nobleman, said by tradition to be of the Merovingian royal house, who became bishop of Worms. Driven out by the hostility of the townspeople, he accepted the invitation of Duke Theodo of Bavaria around the year 700 and preached along the Danube. He settled among the Roman ruins of Juvavum, which he renamed Salzburg, restored the monastery of St Peter, and began a church there. He also founded the convent of Nonnberg. He died in the early eighth century and is remembered as the apostle of Bavaria and Austria and patron of Salzburg.

UO-SIN-000931.name: John of Egypt
UO-SIN-000931.life: John was born about 305 in Lycopolis in Egypt and trained as a carpenter. At twenty-five he put himself under an old hermit's guidance, and after years of travel among monasteries he withdrew to a cliff-top near his home. There he walled himself into small cells with a single window, through which he spoke to the crowds who came for counsel and prayer. Visitors sought his advice, and he was said to have the gift of foresight, even foretelling victories to the emperor Theodosius. He lived for about fifty years in solitude, eating only after sunset, and died about 394.

UO-SIN-000932.name: Patrick Forbes and the Aberdeen Doctors
UO-SIN-000932.life: Patrick Forbes, born in 1564, was a Scottish landowner who was ordained only in middle age and became Bishop of Aberdeen in 1618. He reorganised the university, endowed chairs in divinity, and gathered about him a circle of scholars known as the Aberdeen Doctors, among them William Leslie, John Forbes of Corse, Robert Baron and Alexander Ross. After his death in 1635 they remained loyal to bishops and the Perth Articles. In 1638 they publicly questioned the National Covenant, pressing the Covenanters with written demands. They were known for learning, courtesy and a spirit of peace in a bitterly divided church.

UO-SIN-000934.name: Berthold of Mount Carmel
UO-SIN-000934.life: Berthold is remembered as a crusader from southern France who became a hermit on Mount Carmel. According to tradition he was in Antioch during a siege, where a vision of Christ led him to leave soldiering, and about 1185 he gathered hermits on the mountain, living in imitation of the prophet. Later Carmelite writers honoured him as the first leader of their order, though historians doubt that he can be linked with its origins, and few firm facts about him survive. He is said to have ruled the community for many years and to have died in 1195.

UO-SIN-000699.name: Mary of Egypt
UO-SIN-000699.life: Mary of Egypt is known from a life attributed to Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem, in the seventh century. According to that tradition she left home young for Alexandria and lived a dissolute life for seventeen years, then joined pilgrims sailing to Jerusalem. At the church of the Holy Sepulchre she felt unable to enter until she prayed before an icon of the Virgin and promised to change. She crossed the Jordan and lived as a hermit in the desert for decades. The monk Zosimas met her there, gave her communion, and later buried her. She became a model of repentance.

UO-SIN-000936.name: Innocent of Alaska
UO-SIN-000936.life: Ivan Popov was born in 1797 in Siberia, the son of a church sexton, and took the name Veniaminov at seminary. Ordained a priest, he volunteered in 1823 to serve in the Aleutian Islands, travelling with his family to Unalaska. There he built a church and school, learned the Aleut language, devised a written form for it, and translated the Gospel. Later a widower, he became a monk with the name Innocent and in 1840 the first bishop of Alaska. Walking and sailing through the north, he sought to teach and heal. Eventually he became Metropolitan of Moscow, and died in 1879.

UO-SIN-000939.name: Guido of Pomposa
UO-SIN-000939.life: Guido was born about 970 at Ravenna. After studying the liberal arts, he made a pilgrimage to Rome, visited the Holy Land, and then lived as a hermit under the monk Martin, abbot of Pomposa. About 1008 Guido became abbot himself. Under his leadership the Benedictine monastery of Pomposa near the Adriatic flourished, attracting many monks, new buildings and renown for learning, and the music teacher Guido of Arezzo worked there. He supported church reform and enjoyed the favour of popes and emperors. Summoned by Emperor Henry III to a council at Pavia, he fell ill on the road and died at Borgo San Donnino in 1046.

UO-SIN-000940.name: Hugh of Grenoble
UO-SIN-000940.life: Hugh was born in 1053 near Valence and was made a canon while still a layman. At the Council of Avignon in 1080 he was chosen Bishop of Grenoble, then ordained by Pope Gregory VII, and set about reforming a diocese troubled by simony and lax clergy. Discouraged, he tried to retire to a monastery, but the pope sent him back. In 1084 he welcomed Bruno of Cologne and six companions and gave them the wild valley of Chartreuse, where the Carthusian order began. Hugh visited them often and adopted much of their austere life. He died on 1 April 1132, having served as bishop for over fifty years.

UO-SIN-000941.name: Francis of Paola
UO-SIN-000941.life: Francis was born around 1416 in the Calabrian town of Paola, to poor and devout parents. At about fifteen he withdrew to a cave by the sea to live as a hermit, and disciples soon gathered around him. From them grew the Order of Minims, "the least" of the friars, who vowed a perpetual Lenten fast from meat and animal products. Francis was never ordained a priest. In 1482 the dying King Louis XI of France summoned him, and Francis spent his last years in France as an adviser to the court. He died on Good Friday, 2 April 1507, and was canonized in 1519.

UO-SIN-000942.name: Nicetas of Medikion
UO-SIN-000942.life: Nicetas was born in Bithynia, in what is now northwestern Turkey, and lost his mother within days of his birth. Raised by his grandmother, he entered the monastery of Medikion as a young man and was ordained priest in 790. He later succeeded his abbot, Nicephorus, as head of the community, and his holiness drew many monks to it. Because he refused to give way to the iconoclast emperors, who forbade the veneration of holy images, he was imprisoned and exiled more than once, especially under Leo V. He died in 824 near Constantinople, and his body was taken back to Medikion.

UO-SIN-000943.name: Sixtus I
UO-SIN-000943.life: Sixtus, sometimes called Xystus, was bishop of Rome in the early second century, probably from about 117 to about 126, between Alexander and Telesphorus. Early lists give his father's name as Pastor and call him a Roman by birth, though one modern account says he was of Greek descent. Very little is certain about his life. Later tradition credited him with rules about who may handle the sacred vessels and with the custom of the people joining the priest in singing the Sanctus at the Eucharist. Some ancient lists also honour him as a martyr, but nothing reliable is known about how he died.

UO-SIN-000944.name: Ambrose of Milan
UO-SIN-000944.life: Ambrose was a Roman governor trained in law and rhetoric who was sent to Milan to keep order when the city's bishop died in 374. As he addressed the quarrelling crowd, the people cried out for him as bishop, though he was not yet even baptized. Within a week he was baptized and consecrated. He became a courageous defender of the Nicene faith against the Arians, a gifted preacher, and the writer of hymns still sung today. He stood firm against the emperor Theodosius after a massacre. His preaching helped bring the young Augustine to faith. Ambrose died on 4 April 397.

UO-SIN-000945.name: Benedict the Black
UO-SIN-000945.life: Benedict was born around 1526 in San Fratello, Sicily, the son of enslaved Africans who had been freed for their faithful service. Unable to read, he worked as a shepherd and gave his earnings to the poor. After being mocked for his skin colour, he was invited to join a band of hermits following the Franciscan way, and later became their leader. When the group was merged into the Franciscan Order, he served in Palermo, first as cook, then as master of novices and guardian, though he remained a lay brother. People came to him for counsel and healing. He died in 1589.

UO-SIN-000946.name: Pandita Ramabai
UO-SIN-000946.life: Ramabai was born in 1858 into a Brahmin family in western India and taught Sanskrit by her father. Orphaned in a famine, she travelled the country reciting scripture and won the titles Pandita and Sarasvati from the University of Calcutta. Widowed young, she went to England in 1883, where she became a Christian. She then raised support in America and founded a home for child widows in Pune. At Kedgaon she established the Mukti Mission, which sheltered thousands of famine victims, orphans and outcast women. She also translated the Bible into her native Marathi from the original languages. She died on 5 April 1922.

UO-SIN-000947.name: Emily Ayckbowm
UO-SIN-000947.life: Emily Ayckbowm was born in 1836 in Heidelberg, the daughter of an English clergyman who later became rector of Holy Trinity, Chester. In 1864 she began the Church Extension Association for good works, and she was praised for her help during Chester's cholera outbreak in 1866. In 1870 she founded the Community of the Sisters of the Church, an Anglican order, and became its first novice and its first Mother Superior. Under her the sisters' work for the poor, for children and for schools grew, reaching South Africa before her death. She died on 5 June 1900, and Sisters she had trained soon founded Perth College in Australia.

UO-SIN-000706.name: Daniel G. C. Wu
UO-SIN-000706.life: Born in China in 1883, Daniel Wu came as a child to Honolulu, where a deaconess, Emma Drant, taught him English while he taught her Cantonese. Moved by her faith, he became a Christian. After the 1906 San Francisco earthquake he joined her work on the mainland, helping establish missions among Chinese immigrants in San Francisco and Oakland. He studied at the Church Divinity School of the Pacific and was ordained in 1912, serving both congregations until 1944. With his wife, King Yoak Won, he ran English classes and Chinese-language schools and helped newcomers settle while keeping their heritage. He died on 6 April 1956.

UO-SIN-000948.name: Prudentius of Troyes
UO-SIN-000948.life: Prudentius was born in Spain, probably in Aragon, and while still young came to the Frankish kingdom, taking the name Prudentius in place of Galindo. Educated at the royal palace school, he became a trusted scholar at the court of Louis the Pious and later bishop of Troyes, around 845. He took over the Annals of Saint-Bertin about 835 and kept them until his death, leaving a valuable record of his age. In the dispute over predestination he opposed Archbishop Hincmar of Reims and argued for a double predestination. He also wrote a life of Saint Maura and some verse. He died on 6 April 861.

UO-SIN-000950.name: Henry Walpole
UO-SIN-000950.life: Henry Walpole was born in 1558 at Docking, Norfolk, and trained as a lawyer at Gray's Inn. In 1581 he watched the execution of the Jesuit Edmund Campion, and was so moved that he left the law and wrote verses in Campion's honour. He fled abroad, studied for the priesthood, joined the Jesuits, and was ordained in Paris in 1588. He served English exiles as chaplain. Landing on the Yorkshire coast in 1593, he was arrested almost at once, held for sixteen months and tortured in the Tower. Tried at York, he refused the Oath of Supremacy and was executed there on 7 April 1595.

UO-SIN-000951.name: John Baptist de La Salle
UO-SIN-000951.life: John Baptist de La Salle was born in 1651 into a wealthy family in Reims and became a canon of the cathedral. Ordained priest in 1678, he came to help a schoolmaster who was opening a school for poor boys, and found himself drawn into teaching the teachers. He brought them to live with him, gave up his canonry, and distributed his inheritance to the poor during a famine. From this grew the Brothers of the Christian Schools, a community of lay teachers. He taught in French rather than Latin and started training colleges for teachers. He died at Saint-Yon, near Rouen, on Good Friday 1719.

UO-SIN-000708.name: William Augustus Muhlenberg
UO-SIN-000708.life: Muhlenberg was born in Philadelphia in 1796, a descendant of a famous Lutheran family, and was ordained in the Episcopal Church. A pioneer of church schools, he led the Flushing Institute on Long Island, whose methods were widely copied. In 1846 he became rector of the Church of the Holy Communion in New York, a free church where he started the first Episcopal sisterhood of deaconesses. Their work led him to found St. Luke's Hospital, and in 1866 he established St. Johnland, a Long Island community for the aged and for children. He also wrote hymns. He died on 8 April 1877 in the hospital he founded.

UO-SIN-000953.name: Julie Billiart
UO-SIN-000953.life: Julie Billiart was born in 1751 to a farming family in Cuvilly, a village in Picardy. Even as a child she taught the catechism to her friends. After the trauma of seeing her father shot, a mysterious illness left her paralyzed, and she lay bedridden for some twenty-two years, praying and teaching visitors. During the French Revolution she had to flee, and in Amiens she met Françoise Blin de Bourdon. Together in 1804 they founded the Sisters of Notre Dame to educate poor girls. Julie recovered her strength and travelled to found schools in France and Belgium. She died at Namur on 8 April 1816.

UO-SIN-000269.name: Dietrich Bonhoeffer and Maximilian Kolbe
UO-SIN-000269.life: Dietrich Bonhoeffer, a German Lutheran pastor and theologian, opposed the Nazi regime through the Confessing Church, trained pastors in an underground seminary, and wrote The Cost of Discipleship. Arrested in 1943 for helping Jews and for his links with the resistance, he was hanged at Flossenbürg on 9 April 1945. Maximilian Kolbe, a Polish Franciscan friar, built a large friary near Warsaw and published widely. Sent to Auschwitz, he volunteered in 1941 to take the place of a condemned man with a family. He was starved in a cell, comforting the others, and killed by injection on 14 August 1941.

UO-SIN-000954.name: Mary Cleophas
UO-SIN-000954.life: Mary of Clopas appears in only one verse of the New Testament, John 19:25, where she stands beside the cross of Jesus with his mother and Mary Magdalene. The Greek wording leaves unclear whether she was Clopas's wife or daughter; most have read it as wife. An early writer, Hegesippus, called Clopas a brother of Joseph. Many have identified her with the "other Mary" or Mary the mother of James and Joses who watched at the burial and went to the tomb on Easter morning. Later legend places her with the Marys said to have come to southern France. Beyond the Gospels, very little is known of her.

UO-SIN-000956.name: Ezekiel
UO-SIN-000956.life: Ezekiel was a priest, the son of Buzi, who was carried into exile in Babylon with the leaders of Judah. By the Kebar canal he received his call in an overwhelming vision of God's glory borne on a chariot of living creatures. Before and during the fall of Jerusalem in 587 BC he warned that the city and Temple would be destroyed, often through striking symbolic acts. After the disaster he turned to hope, promising that God would give his people a new heart and raise them like dry bones into new life. He is thought to have died about 570 BC.

UO-SIN-000955.name: Macarius of Antioch
UO-SIN-000955.life: Tradition says that Macarius, called Macharius in Dutch, came from Armenia and claimed to have been archbishop of Antioch. He travelled as a pilgrim, and according to the legend, pagans in Jerusalem nailed him down and laid a burning stone on his chest, only for the earth to shake and set him free. He journeyed west through several towns and reached Ghent in 1011, where he was welcomed at the abbey of Saint Bavo. When plague struck the city, tradition holds he prayed for its deliverance and offered his own life. He died there on 10 April 1012 and became a patron against contagious disease.

UO-SIN-000957.name: Stanislaus of Szczepanów
UO-SIN-000957.life: Stanislaus was born about 1030 at Szczepanów in southern Poland, studied for the priesthood, and became a well-known preacher in Kraków. He was chosen bishop in 1072, accepting only on the pope's command. He supported the restoration of the church's organization and encouraged the founding of monasteries. He then fell out with King Bolesław II, whom he rebuked and, by tradition, excommunicated for cruelty and immorality. Accounts differ on the exact cause. The king had him put to death in 1079, reportedly killing him himself at an altar outside Kraków. Stanislaus is honoured as a martyr and is the patron saint of Poland and of Kraków.

UO-SIN-000958.name: Guthlac of Crowland
UO-SIN-000958.life: Guthlac was born about 674 to a noble Mercian family and spent his youth as a warrior. At about twenty-four he became a monk at Repton, but two years later sought a hermit's life. In 699 he settled on a lonely island in the Lincolnshire fens at Crowland, living in a hollowed burial mound on a diet of barley bread and muddy water. According to his biographer Felix, demons tormented him, but angels consoled him. Many sought his advice, including the exiled prince Æthelbald, whom he said would become king. Guthlac died on 11 April 714, and Æthelbald later built an abbey there.

UO-SIN-000959.name: Julius I
UO-SIN-000959.life: Julius, a native of Rome, was elected bishop of Rome in 337 and served until his death on 12 April 352. His pontificate was dominated by the Arian controversy. When Athanasius of Alexandria was deposed by Arian bishops and fled to Rome, Julius received him, held a synod that cleared his name, and wrote firmly to the Eastern bishops that such a case should have been referred to Rome. He helped bring about the Council of Sardica, which affirmed these decisions. Julius also built several churches in Rome. Later tradition credited him with fixing 25 December for Christmas, but that claim rests on a spurious letter.

UO-SIN-000960.name: Teresa of Los Andes
UO-SIN-000960.life: Juana Fernández Solar was born in Santiago, Chile, in 1900, to a well-off family. A spirited child, she struggled with pride and temper, but reading Thérèse of Lisieux's autobiography turned her toward God alone. At fourteen she resolved to become a Carmelite, and after her father consented she entered the Discalced Carmel at Los Andes in May 1919, taking the name Teresa of Jesus. She wrote many letters sharing her faith. Within a year she caught typhus. She made her vows on her deathbed on 7 April 1920 and died on 12 April, aged nineteen. She is Chile's first saint, canonized in 1993.

UO-SIN-000961.name: Hermenegild
UO-SIN-000961.life: Hermenegild was the eldest son of Liuvigild, the Arian king of the Visigoths in Spain. Married in 579 to Ingund, a Catholic Frankish princess, he was sent to govern in the south, where Leander, bishop of Seville, brought him into the Catholic faith. He rebelled against his father in 580, and the revolt failed when Seville fell in 584. Imprisoned, he refused Communion from an Arian bishop at Easter and was executed on 13 April 585. Contemporary Spanish writers speak only of a rebellion. Pope Gregory the Great portrayed him as a martyr and linked his death with the later conversion of his brother Reccared.

UO-SIN-000962.name: Caradoc of Llancarfan
UO-SIN-000962.life: The Caradoc remembered on this day was a Welsh hermit who died in 1124. A native of Brecknockshire, he played the harp at the court of Rhys ap Tewdwr until he lost two of his lord's greyhounds and, rather than face punishment, chose to serve a higher Master. He was tonsured at Llandaff, lived as a hermit at Llangennech, and was ordained priest at St Davids. Bishop Bernard later settled him at Haroldston near Haverfordwest. Admired for his holiness, he died around Easter 1124 and was buried at St Davids. He is not to be confused with the twelfth-century writer Caradoc of Llancarfan, author of saints' lives.

UO-SIN-000963.name: Edward Thomas Demby and Henry Beard Delany
UO-SIN-000963.life: Demby and Delany were the first Black bishops of the Episcopal Church in the United States, both consecrated in 1918 as suffragans for work among African Americans. Delany, born into slavery in Georgia in 1858, trained at St. Augustine's College in Raleigh, where he taught, designed its chapel and became a priest in 1892. He served as bishop in North Carolina until his death in 1928. Demby, born free in Delaware in 1869, served parishes in the South and became bishop in Arkansas and the Southwest, working for schools, hospitals and racial equality in the church. He died in 1957. Both persevered despite segregation.
UO-SIN-000963.place: North Carolina; Arkansas and the Southwest

UO-SIN-000964.name: Tiburtius, Valerian, and Maximus
UO-SIN-000964.life: Tiburtius, Valerian and Maximus are three Roman martyrs buried in the catacomb of Praetextatus on the Appian Way, near Rome. That is almost all that can be said with certainty. A later legend tells that Valerian was the husband of Saint Cecilia and Tiburtius his brother, that Cecilia's faith led both to baptism, and that they were put to death with Maximus, an officer who was won over as he watched them suffer. Scholars regard the story as pious fiction, written in the fifth century, but the three have been honoured at Rome from early times as martyrs.

UO-SIN-000965.name: Damien of Molokai
UO-SIN-000965.life: Jozef De Veuster was born in 1840 in Tremelo, Belgium, and joined the Sacred Hearts Fathers, taking the name Damien. Sent to Hawaii in 1864, he was ordained there and served rural parishes. In 1873 he volunteered to go to Kalawao on Molokai, where people with leprosy were forcibly exiled with little care. He built a church, houses and a reservoir, dressed wounds, dug graves and lived among them as a friend. Eventually he contracted the disease himself and kept working until his death on 15 April 1889. His devotion drew world attention, and he is remembered as a patron of those with leprosy.

UO-SIN-000966.name: Paternus of Avranches
UO-SIN-000966.life: Paternus, called Pair in French, was born about 480 at Poitiers and became a monk at Ansion. Seeking solitude, he withdrew with a companion, Scubilio, to the forest of Scissy in Normandy, where Bishop Leontianus of Coutances ordained him and sent him to preach to the people. He founded several monasteries and, at about seventy, became bishop of Avranches around 552. He died about 565, and Saint Lô buried him in the oratory at Scissy, now the church of Saint-Pair-sur-Mer. Some writers have confused him with the Welsh-Breton abbot Padarn, and the two are sometimes held to be one man.

UO-SIN-000967.name: Bernadette Soubirous
UO-SIN-000967.life: Bernadette was born in 1844, the eldest child of a miller in Lourdes who fell into extreme poverty. Frail and asthmatic, she could scarcely read. In 1858, aged fourteen, she reported eighteen appearances of a lady in the grotto at Massabielle, who asked for prayer, penance and a chapel and who named herself the Immaculate Conception. After investigation her account was judged credible, and Lourdes became a great pilgrimage site. Bernadette shunned the attention and in 1866 entered the Sisters of Charity at Nevers, where she nursed the sick and bore long illness. She died of tuberculosis on 16 April 1879, aged thirty-five.

UO-SIN-000968.name: Magnus of Orkney
UO-SIN-000968.life: Magnus Erlendsson was born about 1080, a member of the ruling family of Orkney. The sagas describe a gentle, pious man. Forced to join a Norwegian raid on Anglesey, he refused to fight and sang psalms on the ship. He later returned to Orkney and shared the earldom with his cousin Haakon until their followers quarrelled. They agreed to meet on the island of Egilsay at Easter, but Haakon came with more ships than agreed. Magnus was condemned to death. After he prayed for those who killed him, he was struck down with an axe about 1117. Bishop William declared him a saint in 1136.

UO-SIN-000969.name: Stephen Harding
UO-SIN-000969.life: Stephen Harding was born in southwest England about 1060, spent his youth at Sherborne Abbey, and later travelled to Scotland, France and Rome. He joined the monastery at Molesme in Burgundy and in 1098 left with Robert and Alberic to found a stricter community at Cîteaux. He became its third abbot in 1109 or 1110, when it was small and poor. The arrival of Bernard of Clairvaux with thirty companions brought rapid growth. Stephen wrote the Charter of Charity, which bound the new houses together, and he valued simplicity in building, worship and music. Failing eyesight led him to resign in 1133, and he died in March 1134.

UO-SIN-001066.name: Columba of Iona
UO-SIN-001066.life: Columba, whose Irish name Colmcille means dove, was born in 521 in Donegal into a royal Ulster family. He studied under Finnian at Movilla and Clonard and founded monasteries including Derry, Durrow and Kells. About 563 he sailed with twelve companions to the island of Iona, where he established the abbey that became a great centre of learning and a base for mission among the northern Picts. He met King Bridei near Inverness and served as a respected counsellor in the politics of the region. According to his biographer Adomnán, he died on Iona in 597 after blessing his monks.

UO-SIN-001067.name: Ephrem the Syrian
UO-SIN-001067.life: Ephrem was born about 306 in Nisibis, a frontier city of the Roman Empire in Mesopotamia, and grew up under its bishop Jacob. A teacher and deacon, he wrote hymns, verse sermons and biblical commentaries in Syriac, the language of his own people. When Nisibis was handed to Persia in 363, he went west with fellow Christians and settled at Edessa, where he spent his last years in simple asceticism, teaching and defending the faith against rival sects. His hymns were sung by choirs of women. He died in 373, and in 1920 the Catholic Church named him a Doctor of the Church.

UO-SIN-001068.name: Margaret of Scotland
UO-SIN-001068.life: Margaret was born about 1045 in Hungary, daughter of the exiled English prince Edward. Her family returned to England in 1057, and after the Norman conquest she fled north and married King Malcolm III of Scotland about 1070. A devout queen, she gave generously to the poor and founded a ferry over the Firth of Forth for pilgrims travelling to St Andrews, which gave Queensferry its name. She bore Malcolm several sons, among them kings Edgar, Alexander and David, and a daughter who became queen of England. She died at Edinburgh Castle on 16 November 1093, days after her husband and a son were killed in battle.

UO-SIN-001070.name: Paula Frassinetti
UO-SIN-001070.life: Paula Frassinetti was born in Genoa in 1809, one of five children. Her mother died when she was nine, and by twelve she was running the household. At nineteen she went to stay with her brother Giuseppe, a priest at Quinto, where she gathered local girls to teach them. In 1834 she and six companions formed a small community, and in 1835 they took up the Pious Work of Saint Dorothy for poor children, becoming the Sisters of Saint Dorothy. She opened a house in Rome in 1841, and schools and orphanages followed across Italy and abroad. She died on 11 June 1882 and was canonized in 1984.

UO-SIN-001072.name: Onuphrius
UO-SIN-001072.life: Onuphrius was a hermit who lived in the desert of Upper Egypt, probably in the fourth or fifth century. Almost everything known of him comes from the account of Paphnutius, a monk who, according to tradition, wandered the desert for seventeen days before meeting a wild, long-haired figure clothed in leaves. Onuphrius explained that he had once lived in a great monastery in the Thebaid and had spent seventy years alone, fed by God. After a night of prayer together, he blessed Paphnutius and died, and Paphnutius buried him. He became one of the best-loved models of desert solitude in both East and West.

UO-SIN-001073.name: Eskil of Strängnäs
UO-SIN-001073.life: Eskil was an English-born missionary bishop who worked in Södermanland in Sweden in the late eleventh century. Tradition says he was sent to the Lake Mälaren region by Sigfrid of Växjö and made the village of Tuna, now Eskilstuna, his base. Around 1080 he went to the old holy place at Strängnäs, where, according to the legend, he interrupted a pagan sacrifice and was stoned and cut down with axes on the orders of the heathen king Blot-Sweyn. His body was taken to Tuna for burial. Strängnäs Cathedral later rose on the site, and Eskil is patron of Södermanland.

UO-SIN-000770.name: The First Book of Common Prayer
UO-SIN-000770.life: On Whitsunday, 9 June 1549, the Church of England began to use the first Book of Common Prayer, required by Parliament's Act of Uniformity under the young Edward VI. It was chiefly the work of Archbishop Thomas Cranmer, who drew on many older sources. For the first time the full services for daily and Sunday worship were gathered in English in one book: Morning and Evening Prayer, the Litany, Holy Communion, baptism, marriage and burial. It replaced the many Latin service books and local uses. Some found it too traditional and others resisted it, as in the Prayer Book Rebellion, but its language shaped Anglican worship ever after.

UO-SIN-001075.name: Aventinus of Larboust
UO-SIN-001075.life: Aventinus was a hermit of the Larboust valley in the French Pyrenees, remembered as a martyr of the eighth century. Little is certain about him, and his story is largely legend. According to tradition he was born near Bagnères to a pagan mother, raised as a Christian and became a monk or priest, then withdrew to a mountain solitude, where he once drew a thorn from a bear's paw. He preached to the valley people until Saracen raiders seized and beheaded him. The village of Saint-Aventin and its fine Romanesque church preserve his memory, and pilgrims long gathered there on his day.

UO-SIN-001076.name: Elisha
UO-SIN-001076.life: Elisha was a prophet of the northern kingdom of Israel in the ninth century before Christ. He was the son of Shaphat, a farmer, and was called to follow Elijah when Elijah threw his cloak over him as he ploughed with twelve yoke of oxen. After Elijah was taken up in a whirlwind, Elisha took up the fallen cloak and led the prophets. The Books of Kings tell that he purified the waters of Jericho, raised the Shunammite woman's son, and healed the Syrian commander Naaman of leprosy in the Jordan. He advised and rebuked kings through several reigns, and Jesus mentions him in Luke's Gospel.

UO-SIN-001077.name: Methodius I of Constantinople
UO-SIN-001077.life: Methodius was born to a wealthy family and became a monk and abbot in Bithynia. During the second period of iconoclasm he defended the veneration of icons, travelling to Rome in 815 and suffering exile and imprisonment under the iconoclast emperors. After Emperor Theophilos died in 842, the regent Theodora restored the icons, and in March 843 Methodius became Patriarch of Constantinople. On 11 March he led a procession to Hagia Sophia that marked the end of the controversy, still celebrated as the Triumph of Orthodoxy. He dealt gently with former iconoclasts, wrote sermons and hymns, and died on 14 June 847.

UO-SIN-001078.name: Vitus
UO-SIN-001078.life: Vitus was a young martyr of Sicily who died in the persecution under Diocletian, traditionally about 303. Little is known for certain. The legend says he was a boy from Mazara whose tutor Modestus and nurse Crescentia secretly raised him as a Christian against his father's wishes and carried him to Lucania in southern Italy. There he healed the sick and was arrested, tortured and put to death with his companions. He is a patron of Prague and of Serbia, and through the old disorder called Saint Vitus' dance, he became patron of dancers and sufferers from epilepsy, as well as of actors.

UO-SIN-001079.name: Lotharius of Séez
UO-SIN-001079.life: Lotharius, also called Lohier or Loyer, came from Lorraine and became a Benedictine monk. He was chosen sixteenth bishop of Séez in Normandy and served the diocese for more than thirty years. In the forest near Argentan he founded a monastery, and the parish that grew around it, Saint-Loyer-des-Champs, still carries his name. Late in life he gave up his bishopric to prepare himself for death in prayer. He died in 756. Few details of his ministry have survived, but the monastery and parish named for him kept his memory alive in the countryside around Séez, where he is still remembered as a holy bishop.

UO-SIN-001080.name: Lutgardis of Aywières
UO-SIN-001080.life: Lutgardis was born in 1182 at Tongeren in what is now Belgium. Her dowry having been lost, she was placed at twelve in the Benedictine convent of Saint-Trond, with little desire for religious life. A vision of Christ showing his wounds changed her, and she became devout and was chosen prioress in 1205. Seeking a stricter rule, she joined the Cistercian nuns at Aywières in 1208, where the community spoke French rather than her native Flemish. She was known for mystical experiences, long fasts offered for others, and devotion to Christ's passion. She was blind from 1235 and died on 16 June 1246.

UO-SIN-001081.name: Botolph of Iken
UO-SIN-001081.life: Botolph was a Saxon abbot who died about 680. His life was written four centuries later and is uncertain, but the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that in 654 he began to build a monastery at Icanho, probably Iken in Suffolk on the River Alde. According to that life, he was born to noble Christian parents, studied abroad with his brother Adulf, and on returning to England was allowed by a local king to choose a wild, watery place for his foundation. Monks gathered there, and he also travelled as a missionary. He became the patron of travellers, and Boston in Lincolnshire is said to be named for him.

UO-SIN-001082.name: Adulf of Utrecht
UO-SIN-001082.life: Adulf is remembered as the brother of Botolph, the Saxon abbot of Icanho, and died about 680. Very little is known about him. According to the life of Botolph written in the eleventh century, the two brothers studied on the Continent, where Adulf stayed and became a bishop, at Utrecht or Maastricht, though this is now widely thought to rest on confusion of names. Later report holds that when Botolph's bones were moved to Thorney Abbey, Adulf's remains were found with them and could not be separated, so the two saints were venerated together. For that reason Adulf is often honoured with Botolph as a bishop.
UO-SIN-001082.place: East Anglia and the Low Countries

UO-SIN-001083.name: Elisabeth of Schönau
UO-SIN-001083.life: Elisabeth was born about 1129 in the Rhineland and entered the Benedictine double monastery of Schönau, where she made her profession in 1147 and became abbess of the nuns in 1157. Severe fasting and illness marked her early years. From 1152 she began to experience visions during Mass and the Office, in which Christ, Mary or the saint of the day instructed her. She wrote them down, and her brother Eckebert, a monk of Schönau, edited and published them. Her fame spread widely, and Hildegard of Bingen wrote to counsel her toward moderation. She died on 18 June 1164 and was buried in the abbey church.

UO-SIN-001084.name: Romuald
UO-SIN-001084.life: Romuald was born in Ravenna about 951 into a noble family. After he saw his father kill a relative in a duel, he did forty days of penance at the abbey of Sant'Apollinare in Classe and became a monk there. Wanting a stricter life, he lived as a hermit near Venice and then at Cuxa in Catalonia. For about thirty years he travelled through Italy founding and reforming monasteries and hermitages. About 1012 he received land at Camaldoli, near Arezzo, where he built cells for hermits, the beginning of the Camaldolese order, which joins solitude with shared worship. He died about 1027.

UO-SIN-001085.name: Gervase and Protasius
UO-SIN-001085.life: Gervase and Protasius were twin brothers who died as martyrs at Milan, probably in the second century. According to their traditional acts, they were the sons of the martyrs Vitalis and Valeria, and were scourged and beheaded for their faith. Their burial place was forgotten until 386, when Bishop Ambrose, seeking relics for his new basilica, was guided by a dream to the cemetery church of Saints Nabor and Felix and found their remains. He carried them in solemn procession to the basilica. Their discovery greatly encouraged the Christians of Milan, and veneration of the two brothers spread widely across the Church.

UO-SIN-001086.name: Silverius
UO-SIN-001086.life: Silverius was the son of Pope Hormisdas, born at Frosinone before his father entered the clergy. He was a subdeacon when the Ostrogothic king Theodahad pressed the Romans to elect him bishop of Rome in 536. When Belisarius's Byzantine army entered Rome, Silverius was caught between Goths and Greeks, and the empress Theodora pressed him to restore a deposed patriarch. Accused of treason, he was deposed in March 537 and exiled, and Vigilius took his place. Silverius died that year of hunger on the barren island of Palmarola, and the Church has honoured him as a martyr for his sufferings.

UO-SIN-001087.name: Ralph of Bourges
UO-SIN-001087.life: Ralph, also called Rodulf or Raoul, was born into a noble family of Quercy and Limousin. His parents gave him to the monastery of Solignac in 823. Around 840 he became archbishop of Bourges, where he was known as a skilled mediator between King Charles the Bald and Pippin II of Aquitaine and as a supporter of church reform. In 860 he consecrated the new Benedictine monastery of Beaulieu, granting the monks the right to elect their own abbot, and he helped found a convent at Cahors, where his sister was first abbess. He died at Bourges on 21 June 866 and was buried in the basilica of Saint Ursinus.

UO-SIN-001088.name: Leutfridus of Évreux
UO-SIN-001088.life: Leutfridus, known in French as Leufroy, was born near Évreux in Normandy and studied at Évreux and Chartres. He then received the monastic habit from the holy abbot Sidonius near Rouen, and for a time lived as a hermit. Around 690 he founded a monastery in honour of the Cross by the River Eure, which later took his name as Saint-Leufroy, and he governed it as abbot for about forty years. He was remembered for fasting, vigils and prayer. After his death in 738 he was succeeded by his brother Agofroi, and during the Norman raids the monks carried his relics to safety in Paris.

UO-SIN-001089.name: Paulinus of Nola
UO-SIN-001089.life: Paulinus was born about 354 at Bordeaux into a wealthy senatorial family and was taught by the poet Ausonius. He became a consul and then governor of Campania. Influenced by his Spanish wife Therasia, by Martin of Tours and by the death of their infant son, he was baptized and gave away much of his fortune. He was ordained in Barcelona in 394 and moved the next year to Nola, near the tomb of Saint Felix, where he built a hospice and basilicas, wrote poems in Felix's honour, and later served as bishop. He corresponded with Augustine and Jerome. He died in 431.

UO-SIN-001090.name: John Fisher and Thomas More
UO-SIN-001090.life: John Fisher and Thomas More were English Catholics put to death by Henry VIII in 1535. Fisher, a scholar, was bishop of Rochester from 1504 and chancellor of Cambridge. More was a lawyer and humanist, author of Utopia, who served as Lord Chancellor from 1529 to 1532. Both refused to acknowledge the king as supreme head of the Church of England and were imprisoned in the Tower of London. Fisher was named a cardinal shortly before he was beheaded on 22 June, and More followed on 6 July, declaring he died the king's good servant, but God's first. Both were canonized in 1935.

UO-SIN-001091.name: Moluag of Lismore
UO-SIN-001091.life: Moluag was an Irish nobleman from Ulster who became a missionary to the Picts in the sixth century, a contemporary of Columba. According to tradition he left Ireland with twelve followers and in 562 founded a community on the island of Lismore in Loch Linnhe, once a sacred place of the western Picts. From there he is said to have established other centres, including Rosemarkie and Mortlach, and churches in Aberdeenshire. Bernard of Clairvaux later wrote that one of the monks of Bangor named Lua founded a hundred monasteries. Moluag lived to a great age and died in 592. He is remembered as patron saint of Argyll.
UO-SIN-001091.place: Lismore and the Pictish lands, Scotland

UO-SIN-001092.name: Joseph Cafasso
UO-SIN-001092.life: Joseph Cafasso was born in 1811 at Castelnuovo d'Asti in Piedmont, to peasant parents, with a deformed spine and frail health. Ordained in 1833, he taught moral theology at the priests' college in Turin, becoming its rector in 1848, and he steered his students away from harsh rigorism toward gentleness and devotion. A sought-after preacher and confessor, he encouraged his former pupil John Bosco in his work for the boys of Turin. He is best known for accompanying prisoners condemned to death, earning the name priest of the gallows. He lived very simply and died on 23 June 1860. He was canonized in 1947.

UO-SIN-001093.name: Bartholomew of Farne
UO-SIN-001093.life: Bartholomew was born at Whitby in Northumbria of Scandinavian parents and was first named Tostig, later calling himself William. He travelled on the Continent and was ordained a priest in Norway. Returning to England, he entered the Benedictine monastery at Durham, where he saw a vision of Saint Cuthbert. He then withdrew to the Farne Islands off the Northumbrian coast, to live as a hermit in Cuthbert's old cell. He remained there for forty-two years, and was known as a worker of miracles. A monk of Durham named Geoffrey wrote his life. Bartholomew died in 1193.

UO-SIN-001095.name: Prosper of Aquitaine
UO-SIN-001095.life: Prosper was a layman from Aquitaine, born about 390, who became the leading defender of Augustine's teaching on grace. By 428 he was living among the monks of Marseilles, who held that the first step toward faith was a person's own. He wrote to Augustine, who replied with his works on the predestination of the saints and the gift of perseverance. In 431 Prosper and his friend Hilary went to Rome to appeal to Pope Celestine, and he later wrote against the monk Cassian. He also composed theological poems and a world chronicle reaching to the Vandals' sack of Rome in 455. He died after that, perhaps about 455.

UO-SIN-001096.name: Adalbert of Egmond
UO-SIN-001096.life: Adalbert was an English-born deacon of the late seventh century, possibly of noble family, who became a missionary in the Low Countries. In 690 he left his monastery to join Willibrord in evangelizing Frisia. Though never ordained beyond deacon, he was valued for patience and kindness and became archdeacon of Utrecht. About 702 he went to preach in northern Holland and built a church at Egmond, where he died about 705 and was buried. His tomb became a place of pilgrimage, and in 923 the counts of Holland founded an abbey there in his honour. His first biography was written some two centuries later, so many details are uncertain.

UO-SIN-001097.name: Robert Leighton
UO-SIN-001097.life: Robert Leighton was born in London in 1611 to Scottish parents; his father was tortured for attacking bishops. After study at Edinburgh and time in France, he became minister of Newbattle in 1641 and later principal of Edinburgh University. In 1661 he accepted the bishopric of Dunblane, asking for the poorest see, and in 1670 became archbishop of Glasgow, hoping to reconcile Presbyterians and Episcopalians. Finding no support for his gentle policy, he resigned in 1674 and retired to Sussex. He died in London on 25 June 1684. Known for humility and piety, he left his books to Dunblane, and his commentary on First Peter is still read.

UO-SIN-001098.name: Josemaría Escrivá
UO-SIN-001098.life: Josemaría Escrivá was born on 9 January 1902 at Barbastro in Spain and was ordained a priest at Zaragoza in 1925. Moving to Madrid, he studied law, and on 2 October 1928 he believed he saw what became Opus Dei, a way for ordinary Christians to seek holiness through their daily work. He guided its growth through the Spanish Civil War, when he fled Madrid, and settled in Rome in 1946. His best-known book is The Way. He died on 26 June 1975 and was canonized in 2002, though he and Opus Dei have remained subjects of both devotion and criticism.

UO-SIN-000218.name: Elizabeth of Russia
UO-SIN-000218.life: Born Princess Elisabeth of Hesse, a granddaughter of Queen Victoria, she married Grand Duke Sergei of Russia in 1884 and became known for her beauty and charity. After revolutionaries murdered her husband in 1905, she visited his killer in prison to offer forgiveness, then sold her jewels and founded the Convent of Martha and Mary in Moscow, where she lived as a nun serving the poor and sick. Arrested by the Bolsheviks in 1918, she was taken to Alapayevsk and thrown alive into a mine shaft with other members of the imperial family, reportedly singing hymns and tending the wounded until the end.

UO-SIN-000219.name: Camillus de Lellis
UO-SIN-000219.life: Camillus was born in 1550 in the Abruzzo region of Italy and spent his youth as a soldier and a compulsive gambler. A leg wound that would not heal brought him to the hospital of San Giacomo in Rome, where he was converted and began to nurse the incurable. Appalled at the neglect of the sick, he gathered companions, was ordained priest under the guidance of Philip Neri, and founded the Ministers of the Sick, later called Camillians. Their red cross became a sign of mercy on battlefields and in plague wards. He died in 1614 and is a patron of the sick and of nurses.

UO-SIN-000221.name: Arsenius
UO-SIN-000221.life: Arsenius was a Roman of senatorial family who, according to tradition, was brought to Constantinople around 383 to tutor the sons of Emperor Theodosius. Though comfortable at court, he felt called to leave it, and about 400 he fled to the desert of Scetis in Egypt to live among the monks. He was famous for silence, humility and prayer, and for a short saying often attributed to him: flee, be silent, pray always. In old age he withdrew still further, to Troe near the Nile, where he died around 450. The sayings of the desert fathers preserve many stories of his austere gentleness.

UO-SIN-000222.name: Margaret / Marina of Antioch
UO-SIN-000222.life: Margaret, called Marina in the East, is among the best-loved virgin martyrs of the early church. According to tradition she was the daughter of a pagan priest at Antioch in Pisidia, who disowned her when she became a Christian. A Roman official desired her, and when she refused him he had her tortured and finally beheaded, probably in the age of Diocletian. Legends tell of her miraculous deliverance from fire and boiling water and her triumph over a dragon or demon. Historians cannot confirm the details, but her devotion spread widely across both East and West, and she became a patron of women in childbirth.

UO-SIN-000223.name: Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Amelia Bloomer, and Sojourner Truth
UO-SIN-000223.life: These three American reformers worked for freedom and equality in the nineteenth century. Elizabeth Cady Stanton (1815-1902) helped organise the 1848 Seneca Falls convention and drafted its Declaration of Sentiments, demanding rights and votes for women. Amelia Bloomer (1818-1894) edited The Lily, a newspaper for women, and promoted practical dress reform and the suffrage cause. Sojourner Truth (about 1797-1883), born into slavery in New York, walked to freedom, became a travelling preacher and gave stirring speeches against slavery and for women's rights. Each, in her own way, spoke up for the dignity of those whom society ignored.

UO-SIN-000224.name: Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Amelia Bloomer, Sojourner Truth, and Harriet Ross Tubman
UO-SIN-000224.life: These four American reformers worked for freedom and equality in the nineteenth century. Elizabeth Cady Stanton (1815-1902) drafted the Declaration of Sentiments at Seneca Falls in 1848, demanding rights and votes for women. Amelia Bloomer (1818-1894) edited a newspaper for women and promoted dress reform. Sojourner Truth (about 1797-1883), born into slavery in New York, became a travelling preacher who spoke for abolition and women's rights. Harriet Tubman (about 1822-1913) escaped slavery in Maryland, then returned many times to guide others to freedom along the Underground Railroad, and later served the Union army as nurse and scout.
UO-SIN-000224.place: New York and Maryland, United States

UO-SIN-000225.name: Albert Luthuli
UO-SIN-000225.life: Albert Luthuli was born around 1898 in Rhodesia to a Zulu family from Groutville, Natal, where he grew up and trained as a teacher. A devout Christian, he became chief of his people in 1935 and joined the African National Congress, which he led as President-General from 1952. Dismissed as chief for refusing to leave the movement, he led nonviolent resistance to apartheid, was repeatedly banned and arrested, and stood trial for treason. In 1960 he became the first African to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Confined to his village, he died in 1967 after being struck by a train near Groutville.

UO-SIN-000226.name: Laurence of Brindisi
UO-SIN-000226.life: Born Giulio Cesare Russo in Brindisi in 1559, Laurence joined the Capuchin Franciscans and became a gifted preacher and scholar who mastered Hebrew, Greek and several European languages. He rose to lead the order and founded Capuchin houses in Germany, Austria and Bohemia in a time of religious division. He served as chaplain to the imperial army against the Ottomans and is said to have ridden into battle at Székesfehérvár holding only a crucifix. Later he acted as a papal envoy and peacemaker in Bavaria, Spain and Naples. He died in Lisbon in 1619, on his sixtieth birthday, and was named a Doctor of the Church in 1959.
UO-SIN-000226.place: Brindisi; Germany and Central Europe; Lisbon

UO-SIN-000228.name: Bridget of Sweden
UO-SIN-000228.life: Bridget was born about 1304 to a noble Swedish family and married at thirteen, becoming the mother of eight children. Widowed in 1344, she gave herself to prayer and care for the poor and sick, and she recorded the visions she believed she received. She founded the Order of the Most Holy Saviour at Vadstena, known as the Bridgettines. In Rome from 1349, she pleaded for the pope to return from Avignon and rebuked church corruption. She died in Rome in 1373, soon after a pilgrimage to the Holy Land. She was canonized in 1391, and her daughter Catherine is also remembered as a saint.

UO-SIN-000229.name: Declan of Ardmore
UO-SIN-000229.life: Declan was an early Irish bishop who is remembered as the apostle of the Déisi, the people of what is now County Waterford. According to the tradition of his later Life, he was of royal Déisi stock, studied in Rome, was ordained bishop, and on his return met Saint Patrick, who encouraged him to found a monastery at Ardmore on the Waterford coast. From there he preached to the Déisi and won them to the faith. Later writers made him a forerunner of Patrick, but the details are legendary and dates uncertain. Probably he lived in the fifth century, and his monastery, with its round tower, stands as his memorial.

UO-SIN-000230.name: Boris and Gleb
UO-SIN-000230.life: Boris and Gleb were young sons of Prince Vladimir of Kiev, the ruler who brought Christianity to the Rus. When Vladimir died in 1015, their half-brother Sviatopolk seized power and, according to the early chronicles, resolved to kill rivals. Boris, warned and urged to resist, refused to raise his hand against his elder brother and was murdered in his tent. Gleb, summoned on a false pretext, was killed by his own cook. Both accepted death rather than violence and were honoured as passion-bearers, the first saints of the Russian church, venerated for meekness, non-resistance and brotherly love.

UO-SIN-000231.name: Sharbel Makhluf
UO-SIN-000231.life: Born in 1828 in the mountain village of Bekaa Kafra in Lebanon, Youssef Makhlouf was a shepherd boy drawn to prayer. At twenty-three he entered the Lebanese Maronite Order, taking the name Charbel, and was ordained priest in 1859. After many years of common life at the monastery of Annaya, he withdrew in 1875 to a hermitage nearby, where he lived in silence, fasting and prayer for twenty-three years. He died on Christmas Eve 1898. Many reported healings at his tomb, and people of all faiths in Lebanon came to him. Pope Paul VI canonized him in 1977.

UO-SIN-000233.name: John Comper
UO-SIN-000233.life: John Comper was born in 1823 in Sussex, and as a young man trained as a teacher before seeking ordination in the Scottish Episcopal Church. A follower of the Oxford Movement, he served in Nairn, Inverness, Stonehaven and finally Aberdeen, where he was rector of St John's. In 1867 he founded a mission among the slums of the Gallowgate, caring for poor children, street people and women in desperate need, and he brought sisters of the Society of Saint Margaret to the city. His warm liturgical life and practical charity made him widely loved. He died suddenly in 1903, and his son Ninian became a famous church architect.

UO-SIN-000234.name: Brooke Foss Westcott
UO-SIN-000234.life: Born in Birmingham in 1825 and educated at Cambridge, Westcott taught at Harrow before returning to Cambridge as Regius Professor of Divinity in 1870. With his friend Fenton Hort he spent nearly thirty years preparing a critical Greek text of the New Testament, published in 1881, which shaped modern Bible translation. He also wrote commentaries on John, Hebrews and the Epistles of John. As Bishop of Durham from 1890 he took a keen interest in the working people of his diocese, and in 1892 he helped to settle a bitter coal strike. He died in 1901, admired for scholarship joined to pastoral concern.

UO-SIN-000235.name: Pantaleon
UO-SIN-000235.life: Pantaleon was a physician of Nicomedia, in what is now Turkey, who lived around the beginning of the fourth century. Raised by a Christian mother and a pagan father, he came to the faith through the priest Hermolaus. He treated the poor without payment, which earned him the title of unmercenary healer, and he is also called Panteleimon, meaning all-merciful. When persecution came under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian he was denounced, refused to sacrifice to the gods and was put to death, about 305. Tradition adds many details of his tortures and miracles. He is a patron of physicians and is greatly loved in the East.

UO-SIN-000236.name: Johann Sebastian Bach, George Frideric Handel, and Henry Purcell
UO-SIN-000236.life: Three great composers gave their gifts to the praise of God. Henry Purcell (1659-1695), organist of Westminster Abbey, wrote anthems, odes and songs of unmatched beauty for the English church and court. Johann Sebastian Bach (1685-1750), a devout Lutheran who served in Leipzig for his last decades, wrote cantatas, Passions, the Mass in B minor and organ works, often dedicating them to the glory of God. George Frideric Handel (1685-1759), born in Germany and settled in London, wrote anthems and oratorios, most famously Messiah, which has drawn countless hearers into the story of redemption.

UO-SIN-000237.name: Samson of Dol
UO-SIN-000237.life: Samson was born in south Wales and educated by Illtud at Llantwit, then became a monk and abbot on Caldey Island. After a time in Ireland he was consecrated bishop, around 521, and travelled to Cornwall, where he founded a monastery. From there he crossed to Brittany and established the great monastery of Dol, from which he preached and organised the church. He also intervened in Breton politics, pleading with the Frankish king Childebert on behalf of a wronged prince. He died about the middle of the sixth century and is counted among the seven founding saints of Brittany.

UO-SIN-000239.name: Philadelphia Eleven
UO-SIN-000239.life: On 29 July 1974, at the Church of the Advocate in Philadelphia, three retired bishops ordained eleven women as priests of the Episcopal Church. They were Merrill Bittner, Alla Bozarth-Campbell, Alison Cheek, Emily Hewitt, Carter Heyward, Suzanne Hiatt, Marie Moorefield, Jeannette Piccard, Betty Bone Schiess, Katrina Swanson and Nancy Wittig. The church had not yet authorised such ordinations, so the service was irregular and caused great controversy, but General Convention approved the ordination of women in 1976, and the women's ministries were later recognised. The event opened priesthood to women in the Episcopal Church and encouraged similar changes across the Anglican Communion.

UO-SIN-000240.name: Lupus of Troyes
UO-SIN-000240.life: Lupus was born around 383 in Toul and trained as a lawyer. After six years of marriage he and his wife agreed to part, and he gave away his possessions and joined the monastery of Lérins. Around 426 he became bishop of Troyes, serving for about fifty years. In 429 he travelled with Germanus of Auxerre to Britain to oppose the Pelagian heresy. According to later tradition, when Attila and the Huns approached Troyes in 451, Lupus went out in his vestments to meet the king, and the city was spared. He died around 478 and was praised by his contemporary Sidonius Apollinaris as a father among bishops.

UO-SIN-000241.name: Peter Chrysologus
UO-SIN-000241.life: Peter was born about 380 in Imola in northern Italy and became bishop of Ravenna around 433, when that city was capital of the Western Roman Empire. He was known for short, vivid and practical sermons that explained Scripture and urged the faithful to prayer, charity and frequent communion. Because of his eloquence he was given the name Chrysologus, meaning golden-worded. He also encouraged the Eastern monk Eutyches to accept the Council of Ephesus. He is said to have returned to Imola to die about 450. Hundreds of his sermons survive, and in 1729 he was declared a Doctor of the Church.

UO-SIN-000242.name: Germanus of Auxerre
UO-SIN-000242.life: Germanus was a Gallic nobleman trained in law at Rome who served as a provincial governor before being chosen bishop of Auxerre around 418. He gave up his worldly career and lived simply, caring for the poor. In 429 he travelled to Britain with Lupus of Troyes to oppose Pelagian teaching, and according to his biographer he also helped the Britons win a bloodless victory over raiders with an Easter shout of Alleluia. He promoted devotion to Saint Alban and visited Britain again later. He travelled to Ravenna to plead for his people and died there about 448, and his body was carried home to Auxerre.

UO-SIN-000243.name: Æthelwold of Winchester
UO-SIN-000243.life: Æthelwold was born in Winchester early in the tenth century and served at the court of King Athelstan before he was ordained priest alongside Dunstan. He studied at Glastonbury and then became abbot of Abingdon, where he restored the Benedictine Rule. As bishop of Winchester from 963 he led the revival of English monastic life, expelling secular clergy from the Old and New Minsters and refounding abbeys such as Ely and Peterborough. He promoted learning and manuscript art and wrote guidance for monks, the Regularis Concordia being a product of this reform. In a famine he sold church treasures to feed the poor. He died in 984.

UO-SIN-000244.name: Alphonsus de Liguori
UO-SIN-000244.life: Alphonsus was born near Naples in 1696 and became a successful lawyer before he gave up the law at twenty-seven for the priesthood. He preached to the poor of the Neapolitan countryside and in 1732 founded the Redemptorists to work among the most neglected. Appointed bishop of Sant'Agata de' Goti in 1762, he reformed his diocese, and he later resigned because of ill health. He wrote widely, including a celebrated work of moral theology, and also hymns and devotional books. His last years were clouded by illness and by a dispute within his own congregation. He died in 1787 and was named a Doctor of the Church in 1871.

UO-SIN-000245.name: Peter Julian Eymard
UO-SIN-000245.life: Peter Julian Eymard was born in 1811 in La Mure, in the French Alps, and was ordained priest in 1834. He joined the Marist Fathers but became increasingly convinced that his calling was to promote devotion to Christ present in the Eucharist. In 1856 he founded the Congregation of the Blessed Sacrament, whose members spend time in adoration, and later helped to found a sister community. He encouraged frequent communion at a time when many received rarely, and promoted Eucharistic congresses. Worn out by his labours, he died in 1868 at La Mure. He was canonized in 1962.

UO-SIN-000246.name: Eusebius of Vercelli
UO-SIN-000246.life: Eusebius was born in Sardinia about 283 and became a reader in Rome before being chosen first bishop of Vercelli in northern Italy around 340. He gathered his clergy into a common life, a pattern that influenced later monasticism in the West. When the emperor Constantius pressed bishops at the Council of Milan in 355 to condemn Athanasius, Eusebius refused and was sent into exile in Palestine, Cappadocia and Egypt, where he suffered harsh treatment. Recalled under Julian, he worked with Athanasius to heal the church of the Arian division, and he died at Vercelli in 371, honoured as a confessor of the faith.

UO-SIN-000247.name: George Freeman Bragg, Jr.
UO-SIN-000247.life: George Freeman Bragg was born into slavery in North Carolina in 1863 and raised in Petersburg, Virginia. After editing a newspaper for Black readers, he was ordained priest in 1888 and became one of the early African American priests of the Episcopal Church. In 1891 he became rector of St James Church in Baltimore, serving for decades. He campaigned against discrimination in church and society, helped to found a home for Black orphans and joined other early civil rights efforts. He also wrote a history of Black Episcopalians, preserving a record that might otherwise have been lost. He died in 1940.

UO-SIN-000250.name: John Vianney
UO-SIN-000250.life: Jean-Marie Vianney was born in 1786 near Lyon, in the turmoil of the French Revolution. His schooling was interrupted and he struggled with study, but he was finally ordained in 1815 and in 1818 sent to the poor village of Ars. There he lived austerely, visited his people and spent many hours each day hearing confessions. Pilgrims came from all over France, sometimes thousands each year, drawn by his simple wisdom. He longed to retire to a life of prayer but remained at Ars until his death in 1859. He is honoured as the patron of parish priests.

UO-SIN-000036.name: Oswald of Northumbria
UO-SIN-000036.life: Oswald was born about 604, a son of King Æthelfrith of Northumbria, and spent his exile among the monks of Iona, where he became a Christian. In 634 he returned and defeated the Welsh king Cadwallon at Heavenfield, setting up a wooden cross before the battle. As king he asked Iona for a missionary, and Aidan came and established the monastery on Lindisfarne, with Oswald sometimes interpreting for him. He was known for generosity to the poor. In 642 he was killed in battle at Maserfield by the pagan king Penda of Mercia, reportedly praying for his soldiers as he fell. He was soon honoured as king and martyr.

UO-SIN-000252.name: Albrecht Dürer, Matthias Grünewald, and Lucas Cranach the Elder
UO-SIN-000252.life: These three German painters worked in the age of the Reformation. Albrecht Dürer (1471-1528) of Nuremberg, master of the woodcut and engraving, produced the Apocalypse series and portraits, and his work reflected a deep biblical faith. Matthias Grünewald (died 1528) painted the Isenheim Altarpiece for a hospital monastery, with a stark crucifixion intended to console the suffering. Lucas Cranach the Elder (1472-1553), court painter in Wittenberg and friend of Martin Luther, painted portraits and religious scenes that made the Reformation visible. Each used his art to bring the gospel before ordinary people.

UO-SIN-000362.name: Januarius
UO-SIN-000362.life: Januarius was bishop of Benevento in southern Italy and is remembered as a martyr of the Great Persecution under Diocletian. Little reliable detail survives. According to later accounts, he sheltered fellow Christians and was arrested when he visited imprisoned friends. He was condemned to the beasts, but the sentence was changed and he was beheaded near Pozzuoli, around the year 305. The earliest firm mention of him, from the early fifth century, calls him a bishop and an illustrious martyr of the church of Naples. He became the beloved patron of Naples, where his preserved blood is said to liquefy each year.

UO-SIN-000364.name: Andrew Kim Taegon, Paul Chong Hasang, and the Martyrs of Korea
UO-SIN-000364.life: The Christian faith reached Korea through books carried from China, and ordinary Koreans embraced it long before any priest arrived. Because the new faith recognized all people as equal, the Confucian rulers of the Joseon dynasty saw it as a threat, and persecutions in 1801, 1839, 1846 and 1866 killed thousands, most of them lay people. Among them was Andrew Kim Taegon, the first Korean priest, beheaded near Seoul in 1846 at about twenty-five. Paul Chong Hasang, a layman who made repeated journeys to Beijing pleading for priests to be sent, was put to death in 1839 after steadfastly refusing to renounce Christ.

UO-SIN-000365.name: Methodius of Olympus
UO-SIN-000365.life: Methodius was a bishop and theologian of the late third century, probably of Olympus in Lycia, though some manuscripts connect him with other sees. Learned in Greek philosophy, he wrote in the form of dialogues. His best-known work, the Symposium, is a banquet of ten virgins praising Christian purity, modelled on Plato. He defended human free will against Gnostic ideas, and argued against Origen that the body raised at the resurrection is truly the same body that lived and died. Tradition says he was martyred at the end of the persecutions, about 311, probably in Greece. Only fragments of most of his writings survive.

UO-SIN-000366.name: Saints, Martyrs, and Missionaries of Australasia and the Pacific
UO-SIN-000366.life: The Christian faith spread through the islands of the South Pacific through the work of missionaries and the faithfulness of island believers. Bishop George Selwyn began the Melanesian Mission from New Zealand in 1849, and John Coleridge Patteson, an English scholar who learned some twenty-three island languages, became its first bishop. He was killed on Nukapu in the Solomon Islands on 20 September 1871. Others died after him, including Charles Godden in 1906. In 2003, seven brothers of the Melanesian Brotherhood, among them Nathaniel Sado, were killed in the Solomon Islands while seeking peace between warring groups. Together they stand for all who carried the gospel across the Pacific.

UO-SIN-000369.name: Henri Nouwen
UO-SIN-000369.life: Henri Nouwen was a Dutch Catholic priest, born in 1932, who became one of the most widely read spiritual writers of his time. Trained in psychology as well as theology, he taught at Notre Dame, Yale and Harvard, drawing students and readers with honest writing about loneliness, prayer and the longing for God. In 1986 he left the university to become pastor of L'Arche Daybreak, a community near Toronto where people with and without disabilities live together. There he found a deeper sense of being beloved, and wrote movingly about his friend Adam. He died suddenly of a heart attack in the Netherlands on 21 September 1996.

UO-SIN-000370.name: Maurice and the Theban Legion
UO-SIN-000370.life: According to the earliest account, written by Bishop Eucherius of Lyon, Maurice commanded a legion of Christian soldiers raised in Thebes in Egypt and sent to Gaul under the emperor Maximian around 287. Ordered to take part in pagan sacrifice, or to attack local Christians, they refused.
