Maximian had every tenth man killed, and when the survivors held firm, he ordered the whole legion put to death at Agaunum in the Alps. The details are uncertain, and historians debate how many died. The place is now called Saint-Maurice in Switzerland. Maurice became a favourite patron of soldiers and of the medieval emperors.

UO-SIN-000371.name: Emmeram
UO-SIN-000371.life: Emmeram was a Frankish bishop, said to have been born at Poitiers, who travelled to Bavaria around the middle of the seventh century to preach to a people still partly pagan. Duke Theodo welcomed him at Regensburg, and he laboured there for about three years. Our chief account was written a century later by Arbeo of Freising. It says Emmeram set out on pilgrimage to Rome but was overtaken by the duke's son Lantpert, who had him tortured and killed near Munich around 652. Later legends about the reason for the attack are unreliable. He was buried at Regensburg, where a great abbey bears his name.

UO-SIN-000373.name: Adomnán of Iona
UO-SIN-000373.life: Adomnán was born about 624 in the north of Ireland and joined the monastic family founded by Columba. He became the ninth abbot of Iona in 679, and is best remembered for writing the Life of Columba, the most important surviving book from early Christian Scotland. He also wrote an account of the Holy Land, based on the reports of a pilgrim named Arculf. A friend of King Aldfrith of Northumbria, he travelled to secure the release of Irish captives. In 697 he promoted the Law of the Innocents, protecting women, children and clerics from violence in war. He died on Iona in 704.

UO-SIN-000374.name: Linus
UO-SIN-000374.life: Linus was an early leader of the church in Rome. Paul's second letter to Timothy sends his greetings, placing him with Paul in Rome near the end of the apostle's life. Irenaeus, writing around 180, says the apostles Peter and Paul entrusted the office of bishop to him after they had founded the church there. Later lists name him as the first or second bishop of Rome after Peter, and place his time in office somewhere between the 60s and the 70s. Nothing certain is known of his life or death, and the later tradition that he was martyred cannot be confirmed.

UO-SIN-000375.name: Pius of Pietrelcina (Padre Pio)
UO-SIN-000375.life: Francesco Forgione was born in 1887 to a peasant family at Pietrelcina in southern Italy. At fifteen he entered the Capuchin friars and took the name Pius. He spent most of his life at the friary of San Giovanni Rotondo, where he was ordained priest and became famous for hearing confessions for hours each day. Many reported that he bore the wounds of Christ on his hands, feet and side, and the Vatican investigated and for a time restricted his ministry. Crowds nevertheless sought him out. He founded a hospital, the Home for the Relief of Suffering, and died in 1968. He was canonized in 2002.
UO-SIN-000375.place: Pietrelcina and San Giovanni Rotondo, Italy

UO-SIN-000376.name: Gerard of Csanád
UO-SIN-000376.life: Gerard was born in Venice about the year 1000, and as a boy entered a Benedictine monastery. On pilgrimage to the Holy Land he was blown off course and ended up in Hungary, where King Stephen persuaded him to stay and preach. He tutored the king's son Emeric and lived for a time as a hermit in the Bakony Hills. Around 1030 Stephen made him the first bishop of Csanád,. Gerard worked patiently among its people. During the pagan uprising that followed Stephen's death, he was killed on 24 September 1046, according to tradition by being hurled from a hill beside the Danube.

UO-SIN-000377.name: Robert of Knaresborough
UO-SIN-000377.life: Robert Flower was born in York around 1160, the son of a wealthy citizen. After a brief time as a novice at a Cistercian abbey he sought solitude and settled in a cave beside the River Nidd at Knaresborough. His life was far from quiet. Bandits and the local constable each destroyed his hermitage, and he repeatedly returned to the cave. He lived on herbs, roots and water, and became known for his generosity to the poor, especially in paying to free prisoners. Followers and benefactors gathered around him. Robert died in 1218, and pilgrims long afterwards sought healing at his cave, which can still be visited.

UO-SIN-000378.name: Anton Martin Slomšek
UO-SIN-000378.life: Anton Martin Slomšek was born in 1800 to a peasant family in Slovenia and was ordained in 1824. As a priest, then as bishop of Lavant from 1846, he devoted himself to teaching the people in their own language. He wrote textbooks and sermons, opened schools, composed songs, and helped found the Hermagoras Society, the oldest Slovene publishing house. A gifted preacher and a modest pastor, he also encouraged friendly dialogue with the Orthodox and other Christians. He moved his see to Maribor in 1859 and died there on 24 September 1862. Slovenes honour him as a founder of their culture, and he was beatified in 1999.

UO-SIN-000380.name: Ceolfrith
UO-SIN-000380.life: Ceolfrith was born around 642 into a Northumbrian family devoted to the monastic life, and trained at Gilling and Ripon. Benedict Biscop brought him to help found Wearmouth and made him head of its twin house at Jarrow. After Biscop's death he governed both communities as abbot, and doubled their famous library. He cared for the young Bede, who entered the monastery at seven, and served with him through the plague. Three great Bibles were made under him, and one, the Codex Amiatinus, survives. In 716, aged about seventy-four, he set out for Rome with the Bible as a gift for the pope, but died on the way at Langres.

UO-SIN-000381.name: Nicholas von Flüe
UO-SIN-000381.life: Nicholas was born in 1417 into a farming family in central Switzerland. A farmer, a captain in the army, a councillor and a judge, he was respected for his integrity. Drawn to a life of prayer, in 1467 he left his wife and ten children and settled as a hermit in the Ranft gorge near his home. He lived there nearly twenty years, reportedly eating nothing but the Eucharist, and visitors came from far away for counsel. In 1481 the Swiss cantons were on the brink of civil war at Stans, and his wise advice restored peace. Called Brother Klaus, he died in 1487 and is Switzerland's patron saint.

UO-SIN-000382.name: Wilson Carlile
UO-SIN-000382.life: Wilson Carlile was born in London in 1847 and became a prosperous businessman, until the economic depression of the 1870s brought a breakdown and a deep spiritual change. He came to serve Christ and the poor, helped with the music at Dwight Moody's meetings, and was ordained in the Church of England in 1880. Working as a curate, he left parish duties to take the gospel into the slums. In 1882 he founded the Church Army, which trained ordinary working men and women as evangelists and sent them to parishes and the streets. Known as the Chief, he led the work until his death on 26 September 1942.

UO-SIN-000383.name: Cosmas and Damian
UO-SIN-000383.life: Cosmas and Damian were, according to tradition, twin brothers born in Arabia who practised medicine in the seaport of Aegeae in Cilicia. They accepted no payment and so were called the silverless ones, and many came to faith through their healing. When the Diocletian persecution began, the governor Lysias had them arrested, and they were put to death for refusing to renounce Christ, probably around 287. Later legends added many wonders. Churches rose over their tombs, and Emperor Justinian, believing himself healed through their prayers, rebuilt their church at Constantinople. Christians in East and West have long honoured them as patrons of physicians and surgeons.

UO-SIN-000384.name: Nilus of Rossano
UO-SIN-000384.life: Nilus was born around 910 into a Greek-speaking family of Rossano in Calabria, then under Byzantine rule. He married and had a daughter, but illness turned him to God and he became a monk, following the rule of Basil. He lived as a hermit and teacher, refusing to be made a bishop. Raiders drove him from place to place, and he spent years among the Benedictines of Monte Cassino. In 998 he went to Rome to plead for the mutilated antipope John Philagathos, boldly rebuking the pope and emperor. Near the end of his life he founded the Greek monastery of Grottaferrata, near Rome, and died about 1005.

UO-SIN-000385.name: Colmán Elo
UO-SIN-000385.life: Colmán was born around 555 in Glenelly in what is now County Tyrone, and was a kinsman of Columba, who helped him to found a monastery at Lynally in the midlands. He later founded the abbey of Muckamore in County Antrim and is remembered as an abbot and as bishop of Connor. He is traditionally credited with a collection of devotional sayings, the oldest surviving prose work in Old Irish. A story told of Columba says he sensed from afar that Colmán, crossing the sea near the whirlpool of Corryvreckan, was in danger and praying for safety. Colmán died at Lynally on 26 September 611.

UO-SIN-000386.name: Thomas Traherne
UO-SIN-000386.life: Thomas Traherne was born around 1636 at Hereford, the son of a shoemaker, and studied at Oxford. He served for ten years as rector of Credenhill, and then as chaplain to Sir Orlando Bridgeman at Teddington near London, where he died in 1674. Only a little of his writing was published in his lifetime. In 1896 and 1897 his manuscripts were found by chance among books headed for the rubbish, and were at first mistaken for the work of another poet. His poems and Centuries of Meditations show a childlike joy in creation, and celebrate the world as a gift in which God is seen everywhere.

UO-SIN-000387.name: Vincent de Paul
UO-SIN-000387.life: Vincent de Paul was born in 1581 to a peasant family in Gascony and became a priest in 1600. Captured by Barbary pirates on a sea voyage, he spent two years as a slave in Tunis. Back in France, he served as a chaplain and tutor in the Gondi household, and saw the neglect of poor country people and of clergy. In 1625 he founded the Congregation of the Mission to preach in villages, and in 1633, with Louise de Marillac, the Daughters of Charity to nurse and teach the poor. He organized relief for the sick, orphans, prisoners and war victims, and died in Paris in 1660.

UO-SIN-000388.name: Wenceslas of Bohemia
UO-SIN-000388.life: Wenceslas was born around 907, a prince of the Přemyslid family of Bohemia. His grandmother Ludmila raised him as a Christian, but after her murder his mother ruled as regent and turned against the church. About 922 Wenceslas took power himself, supported by the Christian nobles. He sought peace with the neighbouring German king, built churches and favoured the clergy, and was known for his piety and charity. Resentment grew among those who opposed his policies, and his younger brother Boleslav had him murdered at a church door in 929 or 935. Honoured as Bohemia's patron saint, he is the "good King Wenceslas" of the Christmas carol.

UO-SIN-000389.name: Lioba
UO-SIN-000389.life: Lioba was born in Wessex around 710 and was educated at the abbey of Wimborne, where she became a nun and a gifted scholar. Her relative Boniface, who was labouring to convert the Germans, asked for her help, and about 748 she travelled to Germany with other nuns. She was made abbess at Tauberbischofsheim and also helped found houses at Kitzingen and Ochsenfurt. Bishops and the Frankish court respected her wisdom. When Boniface left for Frisia he entrusted her with his monastic cowl. Her letter to him contains the earliest known poem by an Englishwoman. She died around 782, and was buried near Boniface.

UO-SIN-000390.name: Lorenzo Ruiz and Companions
UO-SIN-000390.life: Lorenzo Ruiz was born in Manila about 1594 to a Chinese father and a Tagalog mother. A skilled calligrapher and parish clerk, he was a married layman with two sons and a daughter. In 1636 he was falsely accused of a killing and fled on a ship carrying Dominican priests, bound for Japan. There he was arrested during the Tokugawa persecution, and after two years in prison he was tortured at Nagasaki with the Dominicans Antonio González, Guillermo Courtet and Miguel de Aozaraza, the Japanese priest Vicente Shiwozuka de la Cruz and the leper Lazaro of Kyoto. He died on 29 September 1637, and became the first Filipino saint.

UO-SIN-000394.name: George Whitefield
UO-SIN-000394.life: George Whitefield was born at Gloucester in 1714 and studied at Oxford, where he joined the Wesleys' Holy Club. After a profound spiritual awakening he was ordained in 1736 and quickly became famous for his voice and fervour. When churches closed their doors to him, he preached to crowds in fields, among them Kingswood miners. Unlike the Wesleys, he held Calvinist views. He crossed the Atlantic seven times and drew huge crowds in Britain and the American colonies, helping to ignite the Great Awakening. He founded the Bethesda orphanage in Georgia in 1740. Whitefield died at Newburyport, Massachusetts, on 30 September 1770, after preaching the day before.
UO-SIN-000394.place: Gloucester, England and the American colonies

UO-SIN-000395.name: Bavo
UO-SIN-000395.life: Bavo, born about 622 near Liège, was a nobleman who lived a wild and violent life as a young man. After the death of his wife he heard the preaching of Saint Amand, who spoke of the emptiness of worldly things, and was moved to change. He gave his wealth to the poor and received the tonsure from Amand. He then joined Amand's missionary journeys in France and Flanders. Remembering that he had once sold a man into slavery, he asked that same man to lead him in chains to prison, in penance. He ended his days as a monk and hermit near Ghent, where he is the patron saint.

UO-SIN-000397.name: Leodegar of Autun
UO-SIN-000397.life: Leodegar, born around 615 of a noble Burgundian family, was educated at Poitiers and became abbot of a monastery there. Queen Bathilde called him to court, and in 659 he was made bishop of Autun. He reformed clergy and monasteries, repaired the city walls and cared for the poor. He became a leader of the nobles who opposed the Neustrian mayor of the palace, Ebroin. Ebroin took revenge by having Leodegar's eyes put out and his tongue cut, and later had him exiled and condemned. Leodegar was beheaded in a forest in 679, and was honoured as a martyr, also known by the French name Léger.

UO-SIN-000398.name: Thomas Cantilupe of Hereford
UO-SIN-000398.life: Thomas Cantilupe was born around 1218 into a noble English family and studied at Oxford, Paris and Orléans. He became chancellor of Oxford University and, for a time, of England. In 1275 he was made bishop of Hereford, where he was an energetic reformer, careful of his diocese and its rights. His fierce quarrel with Archbishop John Peckham over church jurisdiction led to his excommunication, and he died in 1282 near Orvieto on his way to appeal to the pope. His tomb at Hereford soon attracted pilgrims who reported healings. Pope John XXII canonized him in 1320. His shrine is still a place of pilgrimage in Hereford Cathedral.

UO-SIN-000399.name: George Kennedy Allen Bell
UO-SIN-000399.life: George Bell was born in 1883, and served as dean of Canterbury from 1925, where he encouraged the arts and commissioned T. S. Eliot's Murder in the Cathedral. As bishop of Chichester from 1929 until his death, he became a pioneer of the ecumenical movement. After 1933 he was the leading ally abroad of the German Confessing Church, speaking out against Nazi persecution of Jews and befriending Dietrich Bonhoeffer. During the Second World War he courageously criticized the bombing of German cities and worked to help refugees. He died on 3 October 1958, remembered as a bishop of independent conscience and of lasting friendships across national and church divisions.

UO-SIN-000933.name: Gundelina of Niedermünster
UO-SIN-000933.life: Gundelina was born into the ducal family of Alsace in the later seventh century, a daughter of Duke Adalbert and a niece of Saint Odile, the blind abbess of Hohenburg. Raised among the nuns on the Odilienberg, she took the veil and joined her aunt's second foundation at Niedermünster, which sheltered pilgrims and the sick at the foot of the mountain. When Odile died around 720 she succeeded her as abbess and governed the house for about two decades. She was succeeded by Werentrude, and the nuns of Niedermünster long honoured her as a saint.
sources: The Book of Saints, entry Ottilia

UO-SIN-000935.name: Armogastes and Companions
UO-SIN-000935.life: Armogastes, Archinimus and Saturus were Catholic Christians of high rank at Carthage in the fifth century, when the Arian Vandal kings Gaiseric and Huneric pressed the African church to abandon the Nicene faith. Armogastes, a count at court, endured torture and was sent to work in the mines and then to herd cattle near Carthage; he bore it cheerfully and died around 463. Archinimus, standing under the executioner's axe, was reprieved and later put to death. Saturus, steward of Huneric's household, was stripped of property and family and beaten. Their story is told by the contemporary bishop Victor of Vita.
sources: The Book of Saints, entry Armogast, Archinimus and Saturninus

UO-SIN-000232.name: Charles Raymond Barnes
UO-SIN-000232.life: Charles Raymond Barnes, an American Episcopal priest trained at General Theological Seminary, was ordained in 1920 and served in Pennsylvania and in British Honduras before going to the Dominican Republic in 1936 as vicar of Epiphany Church in Santo Domingo. When the dictator Rafael Trujillo's forces massacred thousands of Haitian immigrants in 1937, Barnes wrote privately to contacts in Washington, hoping outside pressure might end the killing. After a friend was caught carrying his writings, he was shot dead at his rectory on 26 July 1938. He lies buried in the chancel of the church he served.
sources: A Great Cloud of Witnesses, entry Charles Raymond Barnes

UO-SIN-000354.name: Dora P. Chaplin
UO-SIN-000354.life: Dora Chaplin was born in 1906, educated in England, and came to the United States, where she worked for the National Council of the Episcopal Church on the religious education of children. Her book Children and Religion appeared in 1948, followed by The Privilege of Teaching in 1962. In 1953 she joined the faculty of General Theological Seminary in New York, teaching Christian education and pastoral theology to future priests until her retirement in 1971. Named a full professor in 1964, she was the first woman to hold that rank at the seminary. She died in 1990.
sources: A Great Cloud of Witnesses, appendix listing for Dora P. Chaplin

UO-SIN-000379.name: Finnbar of Caithness
UO-SIN-000379.life: The saint of Caithness called Finbarr is a shadowy figure. Local tradition says he came from Ulster to Dornoch around 540, founded a small Christian settlement there, and gave his name to places such as Templebar; Dornoch's medieval cathedral was first dedicated to him. Scholars suspect his cult is really a memory of Finnian of Movilla, the Ulster teacher of Columba, whose day is 10 September, the date of Dornoch's old Saint Barr's Fair. His calendar date, 25 September, belongs to Finbar of Cork, the sixth-century hermit of Gougane Barra who founded Cork's monastery and school. The traditions have been blended.
UO-SIN-000379.place: Dornoch, Caithness and Sutherland; Cork, Ireland
sources: The Oxford Dictionary of Saints, entry Finbar

UO-SIN-000988.name: Tertullian of Bologna
UO-SIN-000988.life: Tertullian was an early bishop of Bologna. According to local tradition, he helped establish or protect a monastic community at Sacerno. His memory is kept among the city's holy bishops.
UO-SIN-000988.period: Dates uncertain; traditionally late fifth century
UO-SIN-000988.sourceNote: Narrative limited to episcopal identity, locally preserved monastic tradition and local ecclesial veneration. The historical April 27 date was retained by the curator on 2026-10-05; Book of Saints PDF p.719 marks deletion from the revised Roman Martyrology. Former Bologna observance April 18; present collective September 28.
